gru.wylie: gzhi grub na rdzas su grub pa ma gtogs pa'i gzhan gsum du grub pas khyab, kun btags la dogs pa cung zad yod, dngos po yin na rdzas su grub par 'dod pas khyab pa'i phyir
gru.english: And this is true because they believe that--if something exists--it must necessarily exist as the three left over after you exclude a thing that existed as a substantial thing. There is some discussion about the status of constructs; but they believe that, if something is a functional thing, it must exist as a substantial thing.

gru.acip: THAL RANG GNYIS KA'I LUGS LA GNAS LUGS SU GRUB PA, DON DAM BDEN PAR GRUB PA, CHOS NYID DU GRUB PA RNAMS DON DAM LA DPYOD PA'I RTAGS KYI DGAG BYA MTHAR THUG TU MI BZHED DE,
gru.wylie: thal rang gnyis ka'i lugs la gnas lugs su grub pa, don dam bden par grub pa, chos nyid du grub pa rnams don dam la dpyod pa'i rtags kyi dgag bya mthar thug tu mi bzhed de
gru.english: Neither those who follow the Consequence system, nor those who follow the Independent system, accept that any of the following could be the final form of the idea denied by the reasoning which examines the ultimate: a thing that existed as the way things really are; a thing that existed as ultimate reality; and a thing that existed as the real nature of things.

gru.acip: DON DAM BDEN PA YIN NA DE GSUM DU GRUB PAS KHYAB PA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: don dam bden pa yin na de gsum du grub pas khyab pa'i phyir te
gru.english: And this is true because--if something is ultimate reality--it must always exist as these three as well.

gru.acip: RNAM BSHAD DGONGS PA RAB GSAL LAS, RIGS PA DRUG CU PA'I 'GREL PAR MYANG 'DAS KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR GSUNGS PA'I DON, MYANG 'DAS DON DAM PA'I BDEN PAR YOD PA BLO KUN RDZOB PA LA BLTOS NAS 'JOG DGOS PA'I DON DU GSUNGS PA DANG , DRANG NGES RNAM 'BYED LAS KYANG CHOS NYID CHOS NYID DU GRUB PAR GSUNGS PA DANG , BSKAL BZANG MIG 'BYED LAS KYANG GNAS LUGS SU GRUB PA TZAM GYIS DON DAM PAR GRUB MI DGOS PAR GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rnam bshad dgongs pa rab gsal las, rigs pa drug cu pa'i 'grel par myang 'das kun rdzob bden par gsungs pa'i don, myang 'das don dam pa'i bden par yod pa blo kun rdzob pa la bltos nas 'jog dgos pa'i don du gsungs pa dang , drang nges rnam 'byed las kyang chos nyid chos nyid du grub par gsungs pa dang , bskal bzang mig 'byed las kyang gnas lugs su grub pa tsam gyis don dam par grub mi dgos par gsungs pa'i phyir
gru.english: And this is true first of all because the Perfect Explanation, an Illumination of the True Thought, states that--when the commentary to the Sixty Verses of Reasoning describes nirvana as deceptive reality--what it means is that nirvana must be established as existing as ultimate reality with reference to a deceived state of mind. Distinguishing between the Figurative and the Literal also states that the real nature of things exists as the real nature of things; and Opening the Eyes of the Good and Fortune states that it doesn't automatically mean that something exists ultimately just because it exists as the real nature of things.

gru.acip: THAL RANG GNYIS LA DON DAM LA DPYOD PA'I RTAGS KYI DGAG BYA MTHAR THUG LA PHRA RAGS KYI KHYAD PAR DE LTAR YOD PAR 'THAD DE, RANG RGYUD PA RNAMS KYIS RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS BZHED PA, GZHAN SKYE BZHED PA, RDZAS SU GRUB PA BZHED PA RNAMS LAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA YOD PAR BZHED PA'I PHYIR DANG ,
gru.wylie: thal rang gnyis la don dam la dpyod pa'i rtags kyi dgag bya mthar thug la phra rags kyi khyad par de ltar yod par 'thad de, rang rgyud pa rnams kyis rang rgyud kyi gtan tshigs bzhed pa, gzhan skye bzhed pa, rdzas su grub pa bzhed pa rnams las rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa yod par bzhed pa'i phyir dang
gru.english: It would be correct to say then that there is a difference in subtlety between the Consequence and Independent versions of the final form of the idea denied by the reasoning which examines the ultimate. This is true first of all because the Independent group accepts the concept that things can exist by definition, through their accepting the concepts of an independent logical reason; of something that could grow from something other than itself; and of something that could exist as a substantial thing.

gru.acip: SLOB DPON LEGS LDAN 'BYED KYIS KUN BTAGS RANG GIS MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PA SEMS TZAM PAS 'KHOR LO BAR PA'I DGONGS PAR BSHAD PA LA DGAG PA RGYAS PAR BRJOD PA DANG , ZHI 'TSO YAB SRAS GNYIS KYIS 'KHOR LO THA MAS BAR PA'I DGONGS PA 'GREL BA'I TSE, KUN BTAGS DON DAM PAR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB CING , THA SNYAD DU RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR GSUNGS PA'I DRANG NGES 'GREL TSUL MDZAD PA LAS KYANG GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: slob dpon legs ldan 'byed kyis kun btags rang gis mtshan nyid kyis ma grub pa sems tsam pas 'khor lo bar pa'i dgongs par bshad pa la dgag pa rgyas par brjod pa dang , zhi 'tsho yab sras gnyis kyis 'khor lo tha mas bar pa'i dgongs pa 'grel ba'i tshe, kun btags don dam par rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub cing , tha snyad du rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par gsungs pa'i drang nges 'grel tshul mdzad pa las kyang grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: The idea is moreover supported by the manner in which the schools explain the concept of what is literal and what is figurative. Master Bhavaviveka denies extensively the idea that the Mind-Only School explains the true intent of the middle turning of the wheel to be the concept that constructs do not exist by definition. And when Shantarakshita and his spiritual son explain the way in which the final turning of the wheel comments upon the middle turning, they explain it as meaning that constructs do not exist by definition in an ultimate way, but do exist by definition in a nominal way. ************ The following selection is drawn from the same text, the Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom (Part Five, ff. 9a-10a). It gives an idea of how valid the Consequence group considers the division of selflessness into three differing degrees of subtlety:

gru.acip: YID KYI RNAM PAR SHES PA GANG ZAG NI YIN TE, LEGS LDAN 'BYED KYI LUNG RIGS GNYIS KAS BSGRUBS SHING , SLOB DPON 'DI YANG DE DANG MTHUN PAR BZHED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: yid kyi rnam par shes pa gang zag ni yin te, legs ldan 'byed kyi lung rigs gnyis kas bsgrubs shing , slob dpon 'di yang de dang mthun par bzhed pa'i phyir
gru.english: Consciousness of the thought is [considered to be] the person: Master Bhavaviveka proves this through both scriptural authority and reasoning, and the master we are dealing with here concurs with him.

gru.acip: 'O NA RANG LUGS LA SGRIB GNYIS KYI DRI MA SPONG TSUL JI LTAR BYED SNYAM NA, BDAG MED PHRA RAGS GSUM RIM PA BZHIN DU THOS BSAM GYIS GTAN LA PHAB NAS SGOM BYUNG GIS BSGOMS PAS MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA NA NYON MONGS PA'I SGRIB PA DANG , SHES SGRIB RAGS PA DANG , SHES SGRIB PHRA MO GSUM RTZA BA NAS ZAD PAR BYED NUS ZHES STON PA YIN PAS, DNGOS SMRA BA 'DOD PA LTAR DRI MA BDEN GRUB KHAS BLANGS NAS SPONG BA MIN GYI, DRI MA BDEN MED BSGOMS NAS DRI MA SPONG BA YIN NO ZHES RANG LUGS KYI SGRIB GNYIS SPONG TSUL GTZO BOR STON PA YIN,
gru.wylie: 'o na rang lugs la sgrib gnyis kyi dri ma spong tshul ji ltar byed snyam na, bdag med phra rags gsum rim pa bzhin du thos bsam gyis gtan la phab nas sgom byung gis bsgoms pas mngon sum du mthong ba na nyon mongs pa'i sgrib pa dang , shes sgrib rags pa dang , shes sgrib phra mo gsum rtsa ba nas zad par byed nus zhes ston pa yin pas, dngos smra ba 'dod pa ltar dri ma bden grub khas blangs nas spong ba min gyi, dri ma bden med bsgoms nas dri ma spong ba yin no zhes rang lugs kyi sgrib gnyis spong tshul gtso bor ston pa yin
gru.english: "Well then," you may think to yourself, "how do we in our own position describe the process by which one eliminates the various impurities?" It has been taught that: One can gain the ability to put a total end to the three--that is, to the obstacles of the mental afflictions, to the gross obstacles to omniscience, and to the subtle obstacles to omniscience--if one meditates with that wisdom which grows from meditation and which sees directly the three degrees of the lack of a self-nature; this itself grows from following the practices of study and meditation to come to an understanding of these three. Given this statement, it is not the case that in our own position we believe--as do those who assert the existence of functional things which exist truly--that one can eliminate impurities that one asserts exist in truth. The citation rather is demonstrating the principal tenet of how our own system describes the process of eliminating the two obstacles; that is, that we eliminate impurities by meditating upon how these same impurities lack any true existence. ************ We turn next to comments on whether the lower degrees of selflessness are true emptiness; these are taken from "The Cloud of Offerings, which Pleases the Wise, and Illuminates the True Thought of the Treatise known as the 'Ornament of Realizations,'" being a Combined Word Commentary and Dialectical Analysis of the Fifth Chapter of the Treatise. This work was composed by Choney Lama Drakpa Shedrup (1675-1748),

gru.acip: DE LA BSHAD BYA'I LUNG 'GOD PA DANG , LUNG GI DON BSHAD PA GNYIS, DANG PO LA, THEG BSDUS LAS, YI DVAGS DUD 'GRO MI RNAMS DANG , , LHA RNAMS JI LTAR RIGS RIGS SU, , DNGOS GCIG YID NI THA DAD PHYIR, , DON MA GRUB PAR 'DOD PA YIN, , ZHES DANG , DE'I BSHAD SBYAR DGE BSNYEN BTZUN PA NGO BO NYID MED PAS MDZAD PA LAS,
gru.wylie: de la bshad bya'i lung 'god pa dang , lung gi don bshad pa gnyis, dang po la, theg bsdus las, yi dvags dud 'gro mi rnams dang , , lha rnams ji ltar rigs rigs su, , dngos gcig yid ni tha dad phyir, , don ma grub par 'dod pa yin, , zhes dang , de'i bshad sbyar dge bsnyen btsun pa ngo bo nyid med pas mdzad pa las
gru.english: In reply we will first set forth a relevant passage, and then we will explain the passage. Here is the first. The text called The Abbreviation of the Greater Way says, Insofar as craving spirits, animals, Humans, and pleasure beings, each according To their class, have differing perceptions Of a single thing, we say it has no reality. Asvabhava, the holy layman with lifetime vows, has explained the passage. His words include the following: When they look at a single thing, a stream of water, each one sees what the ripening of his particular karma forces him to see. A craving spirit sees the river full of pus and blood and the like.

gru.acip: DE YANG DANG POR GRUB TZAM NAS CHA SHAS GSUM LDAN DU GRUB CING , MTHAR MA ZHIG GI BAR DU CHA SHAS GSUM LDAN DU GNAS PA MA YIN TE, BRLAN ZHING GSHER BA CHU PHOR PA GANG PO DE'I CHA SHAS GCIG GIS NYER LEN DANG , YI DVAGS KYI LAS KYIS LHAN CIG BYED RKYEN BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS DE'I CHA SHAS GCIG GI RIGS 'DRA PHYI MA RNAG KHRAG TU SKYE BA DANG ,
gru.wylie: de yang dang por grub tsam nas cha shas gsum ldan du grub cing , mthar ma zhig gi bar du cha shas gsum ldan du gnas pa ma yin te, brlan zhing gsher ba chu phor pa gang po de'i cha shas gcig gis nyer len dang , yi dvags kyi las kyis lhan cig byed rkyen byas pa la brten nas de'i cha shas gcig gi rigs 'dra phyi ma rnag khrag tu skye ba dang
gru.english: It is not though the case that, from the time it first started, the glass of water came with the three different parts, or that they stay with the glass of water until it eventually ends. What happens is that one of the parts of the glass filled with wet and flowing water provides a material cause, and the karma of the craving spirit provides a contributing factor; and then based on both of these the later continuation of one part of the glass of water starts being blood and pus.

gru.acip: DANG POR GANG DU GNAS PA DE YANG 'GRO BA GSUM PO DE'I RANG RANG GI THUN MONG MA YIN PA'I LAS LA BRTEN NAS GRUB PA'I SNOD KYI 'JIG RTEN GANG NAS BLANGS PA DE NYID DU GRUB PA YIN TE, MI'I THUN MONG MA YIN PA'I LAS LA BRTEN NAS GRUB PAS MI'I 'JIG RTEN GYI CHU DVANGS SHING BSIL BA NAS BLANGS NA DE NYID DU GNAS PA SOGS YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dang por gang du gnas pa de yang 'gro ba gsum po de'i rang rang gi thun mong ma yin pa'i las la brten nas grub pa'i snod kyi 'jig rten gang nas blangs pa de nyid du grub pa yin te, mi'i thun mong ma yin pa'i las la brten nas grub pas mi'i 'jig rten gyi chu dvangs shing bsil ba nas blangs na de nyid du gnas pa sogs yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: How the glass of liquid exists originally all depends on the particular outer world from where it has been taken, for each of the three different beings has a different outer world, depending on the specific karma he himself has collected. If the glass of liquid were sweet, cool water taken from the world of humans--a world created by the specific karma of the human in the group--then that would be its original condition, and so on.

gru.acip: BRLAN ZHING GSHER BA PHOR PA GANG LA LAS CAN GYI 'GRO BA GSUM GYIS CIG CAR DU BLTAS PA DE'I TSE NA DNGOS PO TSAD MAS GRUB PA GSUM SKYE BA'I DPE YANG YOD DE, LCAGS GONG DMAR 'BAR BA'I CHA SHAS GCIG GIS NYER LEN DANG LCAGS SNGAGS KYIS LHAN CIG BYED RKYEN BYAS PA LA BRTEN NAS, LCAGS SNGAGS BTAB PA'I LAG PAS REG PA DE'I TSE NA TSA BA'I REG BYA MI MYONG REG BYA GZHAN ZHIG MYONG BA DANG , LCAGS SNGAGS MA BTAB PA'I LAG PAS REG PA DE'I TSE NA, TSA BA'I REG BYA MYONG REG BYA GZHAN MI MYONG BA DANG ,
gru.wylie: brlan zhing gsher ba phor pa gang la las can gyi 'gro ba gsum gyis cig car du bltas pa de'i tshe na dngos po tshad mas grub pa gsum skye ba'i dpe yang yod de, lcags gong dmar 'bar ba'i cha shas gcig gis nyer len dang lcags sngags kyis lhan cig byed rkyen byas pa la brten nas, lcags sngags btab pa'i lag pas reg pa de'i tshe na tsha ba'i reg bya mi myong reg bya gzhan zhig myong ba dang , lcags sngags ma btab pa'i lag pas reg pa de'i tshe na, tsha ba'i reg bya myong reg bya gzhan mi myong ba dang
gru.english: There is, moreover, an example we can use for how, when the three different types of beings with their three karmas look all together at a glass full of something wet and flowing, there start to be three different objects, each confirmed by a valid perception. Suppose there is a ball of red-hot steel; one piece of this ball provides the material cause, and the "mantra of steel" provides a contributing factor. Due to these two, a person who has used the mantra of steel on his hand can touch the ball, but he doesn't undergo any sensation of heat; instead, he feels some other sensation. A person who has not used the mantra on his hand touches the ball and does feel a sensation of heat, and no other kind of sensation.

gru.acip: DE'I TSE NA, TSAD MTSUNGS NGES PAR MI DGOS KYANG , TSAD MTSUNGS GSUM YOD PA SRID PA YIN TE, LAS KYI DBANG GIS DNGOS PO TSAD GRUB PA GSUM BSKYED NUS PA SNGAR GYI RIGS PAS 'GRUB, DE BSKYED NUS NA, LAS KYI DBANG GIS SNOD TSAD MTSUNGS GSUM SKYE BA YOD PAR YANG MTSUNGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: de'i tshe na, tshad mtshungs nges par mi dgos kyang , tshad mtshungs gsum yod pa srid pa yin te, las kyi dbang gis dngos po tshad grub pa gsum bskyed nus pa sngar gyi rigs pas 'grub, de bskyed nus na, las kyi dbang gis snod tshad mtshungs gsum skye ba yod par yang mtshungs pa'i phyir
gru.english: Again consider this same situation. Even though it is not necessarily true that the valid perceptions are identical, it is possible for there to be three valid perceptions here which happen to be identical. This is because, as we have already established logically, there can be a case where by the force of karma three different objects, each one confirmed by a valid perception, start to exist. And since this is possible, then it is equally possible that, by the force of karma, three equivalent valid perceptions of a vessel could start to exist as well. ************ When the text of the Essence of Eloquence was taught by Geshe Tupten Rinchen, he took great pains to point out that it is not correct--as some Western scholars have stated--that Je Tsongkapa himself adhered to the tenets of the Mind-Only School. The following selection to show that he follows, of course, the beliefs of the Consequence group is taken the concluding pages of our root text [ACIP electronic text S5396, ff. 112a-112b].

gru.acip: ,ZLA BA LAS 'ONGS LEGS BSHAD 'OD DKAR GYIS, ,BLO MIG KUN TA'I TSAL RAB PHYE BA'I TSE, ,SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS KYIS BSTAN PA'I LAM MTHONG NAS, ,KLU SGRUB LUGS BZANG GTZO BOR MI 'DZIN SU, ,ZHES KHO BO CAG NI DE SKAD DU SMRA'O, ,
gru.wylie: zla ba las 'ongs legs bshad 'od dkar gyis, ,blo mig kun ta'i tshal rab phye ba'i tshe, ,sangs rgyas bskyangs kyis bstan pa'i lam mthong nas, ,klu sgrub lugs bzang gtso bor mi 'dzin su, ,zhes kho bo cag ni de skad du smra'o,
gru.english: And when this pure white light of the Moon,* this excellent explanation, Has opened wide the night-blooming lotus, the eyes of the intellect, And we finally see that path set before us by Buddhapalita, Who then would fail to hold as their core Nagarjuna's excellent way? [*Translator's note: The "Moon" here (chandra in Sanskrit) is an allusion to Master Chandrakirti.]

gru.acip: DE LTAR SNGAR BSHAD PA'I TSUL GYIS GSUNG RAB KYI DRANG NGES PHYE NAS DE KHO NA NYID GTAN LA 'BEBS PA'I SHING RTA'I SROL GNYIS PO 'DI NI PHA ROL TU PHYIN PA'I THEG PA'I SKABS SU RGYAS MOD KYANG , GSANG SNGAGS KYI GZHUNG 'GREL BA'I PAndI TA DANG , GRUB THOB RNAMS KYIS KYANG DE GNYIS GANG RUNG CIG DANG MTHUN PAR DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON GTAN LA 'BEBS PA LAS GZHAN PA'I PHUNG GSUM MED PAS TSUL 'DI NI GSUNG RAB MDO SNGAGS MTHA' DAG GI DE KHO NA NYID GTAN LA 'BEBS PA'I LAM DU SHES PAR BYA'O, ,
gru.wylie: de ltar sngar bshad pa'i tshul gyis gsung rab kyi drang nges phye nas de kho na nyid gtan la 'bebs pa'i shing rta'i srol gnyis po 'di ni pha rol tu phyin pa'i theg pa'i skabs su rgyas mod kyang , gsang sngags kyi gzhung 'grel ba'i paNDi ta dang , grub thob rnams kyis kyang de gnyis gang rung cig dang mthun par de kho na nyid kyi don gtan la 'bebs pa las gzhan pa'i phung gsum med pas tshul 'di ni gsung rab mdo sngags mtha' dag gi de kho na nyid gtan la 'bebs pa'i lam du shes par bya'o,
gru.english: And so--in the context of the way of the perfections--it is the systems of the two great innovators that have spread widely; systems by which, in the ways we have described above, the meaning of that highest of spoken words is divided into the literal and the figurative, to determine what thusness really is. But it is also the case that those wise men who have commented upon the great works of the way of the secret word, and the eminent practitioners of this way, have set forth the meaning of thusness in keeping with one or the other of these very two systems; there is no third system between the two. You should understand then that this method is the path for determining the meaning of thusness for each and every one of the works of the highest of speech, whether we are talking of the open or the secret teachings.

gru.acip: JI TZAM SHES PA DE TZAM DU SGRUB PA SNYING POR BYAS TE RGYAL BA'I BSTAN PA RING DU GNAS PAR 'DOD PA'I RNAM DPYOD CAN RNAMS LA KHO BOS LEGS PAR BSHAD PA'I SNYING PO 'DI GTAM DU BYAS SO, ,
gru.wylie: ji tsam shes pa de tsam du sgrub pa snying por byas te rgyal ba'i bstan pa ring du gnas par 'dod pa'i rnam dpyod can rnams la kho bos legs par bshad pa'i snying po 'di gtam du byas so,
gru.english: And suppose that a person did want to rely on one of these systems, but had not spent a good deal of time acquanting themselves with their great books. Suppose, in particular, that they were relying only on a few short descriptions to determine the difference between those teachings of the Buddha which were figurative, and those which were literal--without having a proper understanding of the subtle, crucial points of reasoning involved. People like this would be taking refuge in words only; and even if they were to attempt to talk about thusness, it would be only words, without any essence.

gru.acip: JI TZAM SHES PA DE TZAM DU SGRUB PA SNYING POR BYAS TE RGYAL BA'I BSTAN PA RING DU GNAS PAR 'DOD PA'I RNAM DPYOD CAN RNAMS LA KHO BOS LEGS PAR BSHAD PA'I SNYING PO 'DI GTAM DU BYAS SO, ,
gru.wylie: ji tsam shes pa de tsam du sgrub pa snying por byas te rgyal ba'i bstan pa ring du gnas par 'dod pa'i rnam dpyod can rnams la kho bos legs par bshad pa'i snying po 'di gtam du byas so,
gru.english: Take then lastly whatever you have understood and make it the very heart of your own personal spiritual practice: it is for the likes of you, for those of intelligence who hope to see the teachings of the Victorious Ones remain long in our world, that I have set down into words this Essence of Eloquence.

gru.acip: ,KHAMS GSUM SEMS CAN THAMS CAD DANG, ,KHYAD PAR RANG GI SEMS NYID NI, ,THOG MED GTAN MED DUS RANG NAS, ,MA RIG SEMS NI NAM GRUB DUS, ,SEMS KYI GNAS LUGS LHAN CIG GNAS, ,DE NI GZHI YI PHYAG CHEN YIN,
gru.wylie: khams gsum sems can thams cad dang, ,khyad par rang gi sems nyid ni, ,thog med gtan med dus rang nas, ,ma rig sems ni nam grub dus, ,sems kyi gnas lugs lhan cig gnas, ,de ni gzhi yi phyag chen yin
gru.english: What is Mahamudra In a person as they normally are? It is the true nature of their mind— The minds of every living creature In all three parts of the universe, And for each of us especially The reality of our own mind. It is the nature of the mind As it has existed For time beyond beginning at all, For as long as the mind Has misunderstood The way that all things are.

gru.acip: ,DES NA DON LA BDAG GRUB PA, ,'KHRUL BA LAS KYANG CHES 'KHRUL BAS, ,DA NAS BZUNG STE DUS KUN TU, ,BDAG 'DZIN 'KHRUL BA KHYOD SPONG BAS, ,KHYOD RANG MI DGA' MA BYED PAR, ,GAR 'GRO'I GNAS SU KHYOD RGYUG CIG ,
gru.wylie: des na don la bdag grub pa, ,'khrul ba las kyang ches 'khrul bas, ,da nas bzung ste dus kun tu, ,bdag 'dzin 'khrul ba khyod spong bas, ,khyod rang mi dga' ma byed par, ,gar 'gro'i gnas su khyod rgyug cig
gru.english: Thinking that things could exist As themselves in actuality Would be a mistake which was far beyond Every other mistake there is. From this moment on then, And for all of time, I will give you up, You great mistake, The idea that things could be themselves. And I ask you not to take offense; Leave now this place, And go where else you will. Here we are introduced to the Devil of our story: which is none other than our innate, mistaken tendency to believe that the pen, or anything else, could be coming from its own side: the feeling that it does not exist as a composite of pictures flying forth from seeds in our mind planted by how we behave towards other people. As long as we have the Devil of this misperception in our mind, then we will fail to treat others with the same love and care that we treat ourselves.  And then we will be denied a perfect life, since we are denying ourselves the seeds that create it. Second Canto Is Misunderstanding A Permanent Resident of the Mind? The entrance of an eternal false friend

gru.acip: ,SEMS NI GANG DU GRUB TZAM NAS, ,SEMS DANG DUS MNYAM 'ONGS NAS NI, ,KHA 'DZIN GSHAGS 'DEBS NGES BYAS SHING,
gru.wylie: sems ni gang du grub tsam nas, ,sems dang dus mnyam 'ongs nas ni, ,kha 'dzin gshags 'debs nges byas shing
gru.english: I have been your mind's companion For as long as the mind has existed; And so surely now you are arguing With someone who has always cared for you. And in fact the mind has existed since forever, since it takes a moment of mind to trigger any particular, later moment of mind.

gru.acip: ,SEMS NI THOG MAR GRUB TZAM NAS, ,YE NAS YOD NI MA MYONG NA, ,KHYOD NI SU DANG LHAN CIG GNAS,
gru.wylie: sems ni thog mar grub tsam nas, ,ye nas yod ni ma myong na, ,khyod ni su dang lhan cig gnas
gru.english: The mind itself, since the very moment That it ever began has never existed; Who then is it that you claim To have always accompanied? Again, our mind has existed since beginningless time; but in all of that time, it has never existed from its own side.  That is, not only outside objects but also our own mind is a composite of pictures coming out of karmic seeds within that mind, planted by how we have treated others in the past.

gru.acip: ,YANG DAG DON DU NGA BAS NI, ,KHYOD RANG YANG NI GTAN MED NA, ,KHYOD KYIS SU YI PHYOGS 'DZIN BYED, ,YOD CHOS RDUL TZAM MA GRUB NA, ,'ONG DANG MI 'ONG KHYOD 'DOD DAM,
gru.wylie: yang dag don du nga bas ni, ,khyod rang yang ni gtan med na, ,khyod kyis su yi phyogs 'dzin byed, ,yod chos rdul tsam ma grub na, ,'ong dang mi 'ong khyod 'dod dam
gru.english: In an absolute sense, As you've suggested yourself, It is you who ever much more than me Have never existed at all. Whose side then in this disagreement Are you qualified to take? You're the one who claims that there Is not a single atom of anything That could exist here in the universe; And so might I presume to ask you Whether you think that anything Could ever come, or not come? The Devil is misquoting us—one of his favorite things to do.  We didn't say that not a single atom of anything could exist; rather, we said that there wasn't a single atom of anything that could exist from its own side, and not through pictures flying out of karmic seeds in our mind.

gru.acip: ,RANG BZHIN GZHAN DU MI 'GYUR DANG, ,BDEN PAR GRUB DANG YANG DAG GRUB, ,DON DAM GRUB DANG RANG BZHIN GRUB,
gru.wylie: rang bzhin gzhan du mi 'gyur dang, ,bden par grub dang yang dag grub, ,don dam grub dang rang bzhin grub
gru.english: Their nature then would be such That they could never change to something else; They would exist in reality, And exist absolutely; They would exist in an ultimate way, And by their very nature. Here we see the Angel using an extremely popular style of argument known as a “necessary consequence” approach; it is so famous and so effective that the higher of the two subgroups within the highest of all Buddhist schools—the Middle Way—is named after it: the Consequence Group.  Here that consequence is to say that, if things did not exist in dependence on seed-pictures, then they could never change into something else; for example, they could never age. It's vital for us to reaffirm, at this point, that things produced by seed-pictures really do work: the bumper on a car speeding towards us as we cross the street may be resulting from a picture coming out of a mental seed, but it can still break our leg and send us to the hospital for a huge bill to come afterwards.  The steel bumper and the hospital and the invoice are all coming from seed-pictures, all in a flow, one after another. “Existing ultimately” and “existing by their own nature” and so on all just refer to things that could exist in some other way rather than through pictures flying forth from our mind, from karmic seeds planted there by how we have treated other people.

gru.acip: ,RGYAS PAR ZUNG DU BSGRUBS YOD AANG, ,CHA SHAS TSOGS PA'ANG KHYOD MIN ZHING, ,RE RE'ANG KHYOD MIN KHYOD KYANG MIN,
gru.wylie: rgyas par zung du bsgrubs yod aang, ,cha shas tshogs pa'ang khyod min zhing, ,re re'ang khyod min khyod kyang min
gru.english: You could go further and check Whether it goes both ways: The sum of all your parts is not you, Nor is it that any one part is you; And neither can we say That you are you! The grand, unifying picture of you is not you by itself either, without all the component pictures that it ties together.  Truly feeling that I am an individual—like everything else in the universe—depends on the appropriate picture for that feeling.  What would be the karmic cause—how would we have to treat others around us—to see this picture coming out of our mind, as the karmic seed opens? Mental parts & wholes

gru.acip: ,DE YANG SKRA RTZE 'BUM GSHAGS TSE, ,SEMS KYI NGO BO GANG DU YANG, ,RANG BZHIN GYIS NI MA GRUB NA, ,KHYOD KYI PHUNG MTSANG RDOL BA YIN,
gru.wylie: de yang skra rtse 'bum gshags tshe, ,sems kyi ngo bo gang du yang, ,rang bzhin gyis ni ma grub na, ,khyod kyi phung mtshang rdol ba yin
gru.english: You can go to a single hair on your head And split it into a million strands But you'll never come to some point Where you find some quality of the mind Which exists in and of itself— Now everyone can see The game that you've been playing! There is a feeling in certain schools of thought—such as modern science—that the further you break a thing down, the more likely you are to find something which is final and singular, at the very bottom of things: that smallest atom of all—the one which can no longer be split, and which therefore must be ultimate reality. We need to step back a level then and see if there's not something else creating the tiny pieces of everything. The tree without its roots

gru.acip: ,NYON MONGS LA SOGS CHOS KUN NI, ,GTAN NAS SKYE BA MED PA YIN, ,GNAS LUGS DON ZHIG MTHONG BA YIN, ,YE NAS YOD MA MYONG BA YIN, ,GSHIS SU GRUB PA MED PA YIN,
gru.wylie: nyon mongs la sogs chos kun ni, ,gtan nas skye ba med pa yin, ,gnas lugs don zhig mthong ba yin, ,ye nas yod ma myong ba yin, ,gshis su grub pa med pa yin
gru.english: None of our negative emotions— And nothing else, in fact— Has ever even begun. Now we see the way That all things really are: They were never there at all, They have been, forever, never. As an example here we can take the very first mark that a pen makes on some paper, when we sit down to write out a whole sentence.  As with the pen itself, we tend to believe—deep down inside of us—that this first mark exists from its own side, and that it is therefore appearing to us, from its side. But the truth is the same as with the pen: the writing itself is pouring out of seeds in our mind.  The content expressed by the writing gives us some clues about just how we planted those seeds originally.

gru.acip: ,RANG BZHIN GDOD NAS MA GRUB PA, ,SEMS KYI RANG NGO MTHONG BA YIN, ,GNAS LUGS ZANGS THAL CHEN PO YIN,
gru.wylie: rang bzhin gdod nas ma grub pa, ,sems kyi rang ngo mthong ba yin, ,gnas lugs zangs thal chen po yin
gru.english: We have seen now the real nature That the mind itself really has: For it has never possessed a single quality Of its own since time began. This is the mighty nature of things Which no thing can ever stop. With a bit of time and careful thought—just from the evidence of the fact that the dog and the human react so differently to the pen—we can begin to recognize that the pen is somehow coming from us, and not at us.  Our awareness of our own thoughts necessarily runs in a parallel manner to how our perception of a pen does; but it's almost always more difficult for a person to grasp how the mind might work the same as a pen, as far as being a production of seed-pictures too.

gru.acip: ,BYIS PA RGAS PA'I RGAN PO DE, ,SKYES TZAM NYID NAS RGAN PO RANG, ,GRUB GRUB 'DRA BA'I SNANG BA DANG, ,DE LA ZHEN PA NYID DANG MTSUNGS,
gru.wylie: byis pa rgas pa'i rgan po de, ,skyes tsam nyid nas rgan po rang, ,grub grub 'dra ba'i snang ba dang, ,de la zhen pa nyid dang mtshungs
gru.english: An old man is a boy grown old; But a boy who was old in actual fact From the moment he was born; And yet it seems to us That he grows old gradually. The way we believe now the world is real Is exactly the same as how we believe That the boy is how he appears to be. What really happens as we pass through a doorway?  A picture of a smaller doorway flies out; then a picture of a larger doorway as we pass through it; and then a final picture of another smaller doorway as we walk on to where the door leads. Aging is the same.  An avoidable tragedy.

gru.acip: ,DPYAD DON GRUB PA NGAS MA MTHONG, ,DE RNAMS BYUNG YANG SEMS LAS BYUNG, ,THIM YANG SEMS STONG RANG LA THIM,
gru.wylie: dpyad don grub pa ngas ma mthong, ,de rnams byung yang sems las byung, ,thim yang sems stong rang la thim
gru.english: I don't see how the object That we are checking to find Could ever really exist; Things do happen, but they happen From the mind; Things do fade away, But they fade into the emptiness, Fade into the mind itself. This famous triad that our life is made of: starting, being, and stopping, all comes from seed-pictures.  For all time, all things have flowed through the space created by the departure of anything that could not come from these pictures. The emptiness of teaching emptiness

gru.acip: ,THOS PA CAN GYIS KHYOD BSGOM ZER, ,YA MTHA' MA MTHA' BSGRUB BSGRUB DANG, ,DPYAD PA MANG PO BYED BYED NAS, ,SGOM LA SKYON NI 'TSOL 'TSOL ZAD,
gru.wylie: thos pa can gyis khyod bsgom zer, ,ya mtha' ma mtha' bsgrub bsgrub dang, ,dpyad pa mang po byed byed nas, ,sgom la skyon ni 'tshol 'tshol zad
gru.english: Those who do possess some training Say they're meditating on you, But spend their time trying to prove One thing or another. They analyze, and then they examine, Looking again and again For some problem in the way that others Try to meditate. Critiquing others' meditation is not alone an answer.

gru.acip: ,DE YI RGYU MTSAN CI STE NA, ,PHUNG PO TSOGS TZAM LA BRTEN NAS, ,NGA'O SNYAM PA'I BLO SKYE ZHING, ,NGA'O SNYAM PA'I BLO DES NI, ,DMIGS PA NGA LA DMIGS NAS NI, ,RNAM PA BDEN PAR GRUB PAR 'DZIN,
gru.wylie: de yi rgyu mtshan ci ste na, ,phung po tshogs tsam la brten nas, ,nga'o snyam pa'i blo skye zhing, ,nga'o snyam pa'i blo des ni, ,dmigs pa nga la dmigs nas ni, ,rnam pa bden par grub par 'dzin
gru.english: And why is that the case? The state of mind which thinks “That's me” comes up in us Based on nothing more Than the collection of our parts. And when the mind Then looks at this “me,” It believes it exists in truth.

gru.acip: ,DE NYID BDEN PA'I GCIG DANG NI, ,BDEN PA'I DU MAR MA GRUB PAR, ,NGES PA'I RTAGS LAS NGA NYID NI, ,BDEN PAR MED PAR NGES PA YI, ,NGES SHES DE YI 'DZIN STANGS DE'I, ,RGYUN NI SKYONG BA YIN ZHES KYANG, ,NGA LA GNOD PA CHUNG BAR NGES,
gru.wylie: de nyid bden pa'i gcig dang ni, ,bden pa'i du mar ma grub par, ,nges pa'i rtags las nga nyid ni, ,bden par med par nges pa yi, ,nges shes de yi 'dzin stangs de'i, ,rgyun ni skyong ba yin zhes kyang, ,nga la gnod pa chung bar nges
gru.english: That me cannot exist as either One thing that's real, Or things that are real And more than one; We prove this with some reasoning, And then we come to understand That I myself cannot be real; And then we focus upon The sustained flow of thought That holds things in this way. This is it, they say— And certainly this way of thinking Does some small damage to me. This word “real” can give us some trouble, if we don't think carefully.  On the one hand, we can say that a taxi cab which is pieced together by the mind from seed-pictures is not as “real” as we thought it was, before we heard about the pictures. On the other hand though, the taxi is quite certainly real enough to break our leg, if we suddenly step out in front of it.  In this case, the broken leg itself is coming from pictures planted when we hurt someone else in the past, in some grossly lesser way (all apple seeds are so much smaller than apple trees).  It just looks like the breaking of our leg is coming from the taxi car bumper. How do “I” relate to my body & my mind?

gru.acip: ,DE YI RGYU MTSAN CI STE NA, ,NGA NI PHUNG PO'I STENG DU NI, ,BDEN PAR KHEGS PA DGOS PA LA, ,PHUNG PO LA NI DMIGS PA YI, ,PHUNG PO'I STENG GI NGA NYID NI, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA MA KHEGS PAS, ,NGA NYID PHUNG PO'I STENG DU 'GYING,
gru.wylie: de yi rgyu mtshan ci ste na, ,nga ni phung po'i steng du ni, ,bden par khegs pa dgos pa la, ,phung po la ni dmigs pa yi, ,phung po'i steng gi nga nyid ni, ,bden par grub pa ma khegs pas, ,nga nyid phung po'i steng du 'gying
gru.english: And why is this the case? What you're supposed to be doing Is denying that the “me” Could apply to body & mind In a way that's really real. If you fail to prove That “me” is something That could ever apply To body & mind, Then what you end up with Is me, dancing atop The body and the mind. Again, the most difficult thing of all to recognize as an aggregate of seed-pictures is “we” ourselves.  Again, we are like the farmer riding on a donkey searching for his donkey—the “me” being the donkey.  But now imagine that the donkey is dancing on his head, as he looks for it.

gru.acip: ,NGA NI PHUNG PO LA DMIGS NAS, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PAR SNANG BA YI, ,SNANG BA DE LTAR MA GRUB PAR, ,TSAD MAS NGES SHES 'DRONGS NA NI, ,GNOD KYI GZHAN DU MA YIN NO,
gru.wylie: nga ni phung po la dmigs nas, ,bden par grub par snang ba yi, ,snang ba de ltar ma grub par, ,tshad mas nges shes 'drongs na ni, ,gnod kyi gzhan du ma yin no
gru.english: When you focus on the body & mind, The “me” you see appears to be Something that really exists. But if you reach a correct perception Which finally realizes that this “me” Cannot exist the way it seems, Only then have you really hurt me. And it cannot happen any other way.

gru.acip: ,PHUNG PO LA DMIGS NGA'O ZHES, ,DE YI BDEN GRUB BKAG TZAM GYI, ,MED DGAG 'DZIN STANGS YUL BYAS NAS, ,SHUGS MA NYAMS SHING GSAL NGAR LDAN,
gru.wylie: phung po la dmigs nga'o zhes, ,de yi bden grub bkag tsam gyi, ,med dgag 'dzin stangs yul byas nas, ,shugs ma nyams shing gsal ngar ldan
gru.english: You take as the object Of the way you look at things That absence of something there: The simple lack of anything Which could really exist When you look at body & mind And say “me.” You keep it up strong, Clear and vivid. Let's appreciate this expression, “simple lack.”  The suggestion is that emptiness is not all that complicated: just try to picture a “myself” which is not coming from my seed-pictures, and understand that this one thing does not, can not, and never did exist.

gru.acip: ,NGA NI BLO BDE BSAM GRUB YIN, ,LA LA NGA NI 'BUD DO ZER, ,RNAM BDUN RIGS PAS DPYAD RTAGS KYIS, ,PHUNG PO LA DMIGS NGA NYID NI, ,BDEN PAR MED PAR NGES PA YI, ,NGES SHES 'DZIN STANGS RGYUN SKYONG ZER,
gru.wylie: nga ni blo bde bsam grub yin, ,la la nga ni 'bud do zer, ,rnam bdun rigs pas dpyad rtags kyis, ,phung po la dmigs nga nyid ni, ,bden par med par nges pa yi, ,nges shes 'dzin stangs rgyun skyong zer
gru.english: I am in fact the easiest thing You could ever have to think about; Still, some people make the claim That they will drive me from their mind. They use the analysis Of the seven types of logic To come to the realization That the “me” you see When you look at your body & mind Was never something real. And then, they say, They will maintain This way of thinking, And stay in a stream Of that realization. The seven types of logic are not being questioned here; only the state of mind which examines them, without an awareness that this state itself “feels” as though it were coming from its own side, and not from pictures flying out of our seeds. The seven refer to the objects we are examining, to determine whether they come from their own side or not.  Those are composed first of all of the five classical parts to the person: physical form; feelings; capacity of discrimination; other factors that compose the individual; and then finally overall consciousness. These five are what in modern times we refer to simply as “body & mind.”  Mind in the five has been broken down into things like feelings and discrimination, since these two are the root of all trouble in the world: I like this or that, I like her or him; because they make me feel good, or not. To the examination of these five we then add an inquiry into whether the simple collection of the five itself is coming “towards” us from the other side; and the same for the physical outline of ourselves.

gru.english: It seems that what you mean When you say It's a thing that has No edges and no center, You are trying to say That it cannot exist As an object which is physical. But if a view isn't even Focused on what is “me,” Then how could the way it sees things Be opposed to the way I see? What you're describing Cannot be counted Among the things that hurt me. This useless meditation goes back to the idea that if we try to focus our mind on nothing at all, then somehow we are seeing emptiness.  Here the mistake is to believe that anything which has no edges or center is emptiness; but in that case, empty space itself (the absence of physical objects) would have to be emptiness (the absence of anything not flowing from our picture-seeds). Useless Meditation #23 The Idea That Endless Blue Is the Endless Absence Of Self-Existent Things

gru.english: What's happening in actual fact Is that the state of understanding As we described it above Takes as its object, Or has a way of looking at things, As it is sustained towards An absence of something Consisting of the simple cancellation Of anything that could really exist— And then we give that flow Of understanding a nickname of sorts: The “absence of a certain thing.” So far, so good.  The understanding is not the absence that the understanding understands, but conditionally we can refer to it as that absence.

gru.english: But suppose instead You make an effort— Whether it be in your thought explorations, Or else in your states of deep meditation— To focus in a sustained way On the thing it is which we truly deny When we speak of emptiness: On the “me” that comes up When you look at your body & mind— A “me” which has some real existence; And suppose you learn Never to lose sight of this thought. Again, we have to be careful how we use the word “real” during an emptiness meditation.  Our sense of “me” or ourselves certainly is real, and quite valid.  But if this sense is infected by the irrational belief that I exist out there, independent of my mental seeds, then it is the source of all pain and trouble—since we will be attempting to take care of a “me” who is not even there.

gru.english: There are only two kinds of people: Those who are studying spiritual ways, And those who have no study. Those who study are as many as The bloom of the fig, exceedingly rare; And they can be divided Into those on the path, and those who aren't— Those that are not the path Are infinitely more in number. When a fig tree blooms, the flower literally develops inside the fruit, rather than on the outside and only afterwards developing into the fruit.  As such, the bloom is very rarely visible.  People who meditate regularly are just as rare; and of those only a tiny percentage actually reach a “path,” which here refers to meditation on the most meaningful topics of life.

gru.english: There are, admitted, many schools Among those who've wandered off; But these come down to two: Thus who hold that things never change, And those who hold that things never were. Every single one of these groups, Except for the ones called “Outcasts,” Denies that past or future lives Can even be said to exist. None of them have freedom, And none of them Three Jewels, Nor anything of the like. There are extremely few people who understand how change happens in our life—how we get old, for example.  Good seeds, planted inside our mind by paying attention to what others around us need, by definition wear out as they push out images of youth and good looks.  Soon the beautiful pictures are replaced by ones that are more and more worn—weak, and then sick with age. And the vast majority of people alive and aging in our world today have not the slightest understanding of how they came here this once, and how it must logically happen yet again, and again.  And so they do nothing to prepare—and they will pay for it. Since almost every human alive in this world has no idea why or how they are here, they cannot even imagine what freedom from suffering would be like, or work towards it.  They have no concept at all of the Three Jewels of a person who is beyond all suffering and can help all beings; a teaching that can make this happen; and helpers available who have accomplished the core of this teaching: the direct perception of emptiness which the Angel is struggling to share with us he

gru.english: I'd have to say though that If you're able to master these meditations, It can accomplish one good thing for you: You start to feel some hope That you could see emptiness— As such, I would say You should go ahead and do them. Stay aware however That they themselves cannot Enable you to rid yourself Of this idea of mine: That things in themselves are real. It's sort of comforting that even the Devil admits that even just the habit of meditating regularly can indeed help get us on the right track, even if that meditation isn't perfect. gru.english: Now if you manage to reject That things themselves are real, But this takes you to a place Where you cannot see a way That things could work— Where some things could cause others— Then you have joined my school, And you have lost any hope at all Of doing me any damage. It may be true that the pen we see out there is not “real” in the sense that it comes towards us from its own side; but that doesn't mean that it can't work at all.  We need to remember that things all work just the way they're supposed to work; just that they're not doing that from their own side—but rather through seeds supplied from my own mind.  My seeds create the writing on the paper that seems to be coming from the tip of the pen.

gru.english: It would appear That those of the Mind-Only School And the Independent Group Hold presentations which say That the ideas that things Exist in and of themselves, Or exist by definition, Or exist through some nature of their own, Or exist substantially Are actually correct. The Mind-Only group is a step above both the Detailist and Sutrist schools, whom we've already heard from.  Their defining belief is that—when we are looking at a patch of blue—the blue which we see is not standing in the outside world; rather, we are watching a seed within our mind flower into a blue color which is also in our mind.  All of this seeing of the outside world is happening within a region of our own mind known as “storehouse consciousness.” The fourth and highest of the four schools of classical Buddhism is known as the “Middle Way.”  It is divided into two sections: the Independent Group, and the Consequence Group.  Members of the Independent Group believe that words, and logic, have an inborn capacity to express or prove things; which is to say, accurate words and correct logic should be perceived the same by any sane person. This then is what it means to say that these thinkers believe that some things could exist by definition, and so on—all the terms listed here refer to the same things.  Still though these opinions fail to allow for a world which is in every detail created by the seeds within our mind.

gru.english: If you don't know how To describe cause & effect With things that have no nature, You will never have two truths, And never see freedom either. On one hand, it's a little bit of a mental stretch for all of us to realize that both apple seeds and apple trees are coming from the same repository of mental seeds.  On the other hand, once we get there it feels very comfortable, since now we have an explanation for how one thing can trigger another even in a world where they never actually make contact with each other.

gru.english: The protector Nagarjuna Said things like: “For those on the outside, There is no means To reach Peace. They have lost the truths Of the deceptive and of suchness; And no one who loses these two truths Can ever be free.” Those books by the way Were dedicated to me! The phrase “on the outside” most often refers to anyone who cannot comprehend any of the four classical Buddhist ways of explaining the world.  Technically though any group except the higher half of the fourth school—the Consequence Group—will be unable to reach a genuine state of peace, since on some level they still cling to a thing which could even in some small way come from its own side. Reference is also made in these lines to the idea of two divisions to reality itself: a “deceptive” division, and an “ultimate” division, here referred to as “suchness.”  The former refers to things as observed from the viewpoint of appearing to come from their own side, even though in the end they cannot.  “Ultimate” reality then is the very fact that nothing could ever come from its own side. When we use the word “truth” as it is applied in these particular lines, we are not referring to a statement of fact—but rather to a division of reality itself. It's difficult to imagine that a book composed by Arya Nagarjuna—the most famous human emptiness explainer in history—could be “dedicated to the Devil.”  But if even as we read a great clarification of emptiness, we feel that it is coming from its own side (rather than from my si

gru.english: Now those of the Independent Group Within the Middle Way Would never accept the idea That things existed in truth. They'd say though nonetheless That if things did not exist By definition on a nominal level, Then we could never describe The working of things—cause & effect. Until the day though that you discard This viewpoint of reality, You will find it a difficulty To bring the path of the realized ones Into your heart, within any Of the three different ways. Why, as we mentioned above, is the highest of the four classical Buddhist schools of ancient India—the Middle Way School—divided into two different groups: the Independent Group and the Consequence Group? One useful way to answer this question is to approach if from the side of the “raw data” involved.  Here's how we can think of this in a clear and simple way. So consider how we put together an ice-cream sundae, on one of those rare days when we allow ourselves one.  First you take a container of vanilla ice cream out of the freezer, and scoop three or four balls of it into a bowl.  Then you get some chocolate sauce and maybe heat it up a bit. You spread the sauce over the top of the balls of ice cream, and then maybe sprinkle on some almond slices, and top the whole thing off with a maraschino cherry. Now let's apply this to the raw data of the pen.  Let's say the pen was sitting on top of a desk in an empty room, and then a person opened the door and walked in, along with their dog. gru.english: And even those great and holy beings— If they had gone no further than that— Would have been left, for the most part, Knowing nothing, and practicing meditations Where they learned nothing more. They would spend their time Practicing this state of mind, Pitch black misunderstanding, Trembling in the dark of a mousehole, Nothing to think about, And thinking on nothing That saw things any different Than the way I already do. gru.english: Listen to me now, Miss Wisdom. You can talk all you want About how people can tear A hole in the fabric Of this suffering life Simply by entertaining The suspicion that you might Be who you are; But the truth of it is That nobody believes In you at all— And let me give you Some proof of that! Your wise ones Run around selling the Dharma So they can feed their bellies; They abandon The monastery debate ground And focus on wandering Around the local towns. They abandon their vows And go find a girlfriend; They abandon morality And embrace desire. They abandon their Hermitages up in the mountains, And come down to run With the dogs. People who really understand emptiness understand the brother concept of emptiness—which is the principle of “dependent events”: the fact that all things are flowing out of those mental seeds we've planted by how we treat others. As such, a person who really understands emptiness would tend to be most careful to follow a moral code.  The Devil is poking fun here especially at ordained people who pretend to be great emptiness masters and at the same time misbehave around the principle of dependence: maintaining plain old good behavior.

gru.english: Neither is this present Moment of the mind Something that could transform Into the next moment of that mind. And none of those moments Is truly in The present moment— Don't you feel There's a contradiction here? If a thing were truly real, It could never change Into something else; If something could change Into something else, We could no longer say It was truly real. When we say that something is “real,” we tend to think of it as a discrete object, with edges in time: it is there in front of us, now.  It shouldn't change within the one present moment, since if it did then it would be two different things.  The great Arya Nagarjuna is the one who most enjoys pointing out strange little inconsistencies about our life and our world which just might indicate that something else is going on, than we always thought.

gru.english: If thus we cannot locate A moment of the mind That was ever a thing that could be, Could you please explain to me Where it is You claim to be in residence? Since the very first lines of our Cantos, the Devil has been claiming that he is the real landlord of the residential space of the mind. gru.english: Part of what you do Inside this mind Is to inspire the three different Kinds of mental poison. Let's say that first You decide to inspire The mind to thoughts of anger. This anger itself Is something that appears To exist in reality; And if it really were The way that it seems, Then its nature Could never be altered. The “three poisons” are three negative states of mind that we see drawn, for example, in the very center of the famous Buddhist painting of the Wheel of Life.  Here first we see depicted a pig, which represents misunderstanding the world around us, and even ourselves. Then we have a snake, which represents how we feel upset at someone whom we believe is preventing us from getting something we want—whereas really the one who is preventing us is always ourselves, the planter of the seeds. And then finally we see a rooster (or in the older paintings, a pigeon), which represents our desire—and more specifically our feeling that there has to be a way that we can get the things we want, without first assuring that those around us get what they want.  And then even these three kings of all the negative emotions—monarchs of misunderstanding our life—are themselves flowing from older situations when we ignored the needs of others.

gru.english: If the mind were to exist Through some nature of its own, Then you could never see Karma and its consequences— Good deeds or the bad— Accumulating inside of it; Nor could they lead To some personal experience. There would be no cycle of pain; There would be no nirvana Where we escaped from it— None of the 84,000 mountains Of Dharma teachings would even exist; And none of our places of shelter, None of the Three Jewels, Could be something existing either. None of the three poisons Of the mind could ever exist, And there would be none Of our 84,000 negative emotions. The Angel is sort of wrapping up the thoughts she's expressed in the immediately preceding lines; except now she has specifically confirmed for us that both sides of the grand division of the universe into pain and freedom from that pain are all produced by the power of seed-pictures.

gru.english: In a world that exists In reality, Nothing that exists exists. If anything of everything Existed, That would contradict Saying it all was real. Look— This round of suffering existence Has no starting point at all: Now suppose that Any particular mind Goes and takes a birth As a pleasure being; Suppose now further That it took a birth Within the formless realm. If the mind had nothing But the mind to focus on, And the mind held the mind To exist in reality, Then since that way of looking At the mind could never shift To another way of seeing things, That mind could never ever Take another form of birth After that one. According to the earliest literature of Buddhism in this world, our planet consists of three layers, like a triple-decker sandwich.  Every other planet has the same structure, and so the three layers of our world are combined with the corresponding three layers of every other planet in the universe to represent three all-encompassing realms of mortal existence. These three realms are referred to as the desire realm; the form realm; and the formless realm.  Those beings who reside in the desire realm are distinguished by constant thoughts of desire, for objects such as food or sex. If though people in the desire realm are able to cultivate deep states of meditative concentration (even if these don't happen to be focused on particularly helpful objects), the simple fact that there is a small blank spot in their life that they didn't have time to fill with distinctl
