gru.english: The lifetime of the pleasure being— And all their glory, And all their possessions, All the objects of their senses— Would appear to exist In reality. Those then for time With no beginning Would have to have existed Without depending On a single other thing. And that would make them Things that could never change; Things that remained there Forever the same. How then could it be possible For this person to ever die, Or move on to another life? A “pleasure being” is one of those superhero-like people we mentioned, in any of the three realms.  Again, if they existed from their own side—as we persist in believing pens do—then it could not be the case that all the realms of life available to all of us in our present level of understanding would be subject to inevitable suffering, death, and moving on one more time to terrors we never anticipated.  But in fact they are, even as we read these lines about them, right now.

gru.acip: ,'CHI DANG TSE 'PHO SRID ZER NA, ,RANG TSUGS THUB PAR MA GYUR PAS, ,'GYUR BA MED PA'I BDEN GRUB 'GAL,
gru.wylie: 'chi dang tshe 'pho srid zer na, ,rang tshugs thub par ma gyur pas, ,'gyur ba med pa'i bden grub 'gal
gru.english: And suppose you insist: “Yet it is a fact That people do die, And move on to Another birth.” Well since in that case They would no longer be Things that stand on their own, It would become a contradiction To continue to insist That they existed “in reality,” In a nature immutable. The fact that rebirth does indeed work doesn't prove that it comes from its own side.  Thinking that it does is a mistake that applies to everything in the world around us—as well as ourselves.

gru.acip: ,LHA LUS BDEN PAR GRUB PA NA, ,'GRO BA GZHAN DU SKYE BA'ANG MED, ,'DOD PA'I YON TAN LNGA PO YANG, ,LHA MO'I GZUGS LA CHAGS PA YI, ,CHAGS PA BDEN PAR SNANG BA YI, ,SNANG BA GZHAN DU MI 'GYUR BAS, ,SGRA SOGS 'DOD YON BZHI PO LA, ,CHAGS PA CI YI PHYIR NA SKYE, ,SKYE NA GZUGS LA BDEN GRUB 'GAL,
gru.wylie: lha lus bden par grub pa na, ,'gro ba gzhan du skye ba'ang med, ,'dod pa'i yon tan lnga po yang, ,lha mo'i gzugs la chags pa yi, ,chags pa bden par snang ba yi, ,snang ba gzhan du mi 'gyur bas, ,sgra sogs 'dod yon bzhi po la, ,chags pa ci yi phyir na skye, ,skye na gzugs la bden grub 'gal
gru.english: If the body of a pleasure being Really did exist in truth, Then they could never take A rebirth as another Type of being. And the five objects Of the senses— Appearing as they do To the attachment to Their heavenly form As if they existed in truth— Could never start appearing To be some other way. In that case then How could anyone Begin to feel attachment To the other four objects Of the senses— Sound and all the rest? If they did, then it Would clearly be a contradiction For the colors and shapes They'd already been focusing on To have existed in reality. These superhero-type beings enjoy massive amounts of pleasures of the senses, and develop strong attachment for them—these qualities quite nearly define them.  And yet an intense engagement with the outside world does not establish that this outside world is “real,” in the sense of coming from its own side.  Quite the opposite.

gru.acip: ,LHA YI BU MO LA DMIGS NAS, ,YID DU 'ONG BA'I BYAMS PA DE, ,LTOS MED BDEN PAR GRUB PAR SNANG, ,SNANG BA GZHAN 'GYUR MI SRID NA, ,LHA MA YIN DANG 'THAB PA'I TSE, ,ZHE SDANG SKYE BA DNGOS SU 'GAL, ,GAL TE ZHE SDANG SKYES PA NA, ,YID 'ONG BYAMS PA'I BDEN GRUB DE, ,LTOS MED 'GYUR BA MED PA 'GAL,
gru.wylie: lha yi bu mo la dmigs nas, ,yid du 'ong ba'i byams pa de, ,ltos med bden par grub par snang, ,snang ba gzhan 'gyur mi srid na, ,lha ma yin dang 'thab pa'i tshe, ,zhe sdang skye ba dngos su 'gal, ,gal te zhe sdang skyes pa na, ,yid 'ong byams pa'i bden grub de, ,ltos med 'gyur ba med pa 'gal
gru.english: And when the beings of pleasure Gazed upon their daughters With that version of love That sees them as so lovely, That love would see What it sees in a way That depended on nothing else— As something truly there. That way of things appearing Is something that could never Change to looking another way; And that would directly contradict The fact that—when these beings Of pleasure battle with their cousins— Their feelings change to hatred. If these pleasure beings Could begin to feel hate, Then that would contradict The idea that their lovely love Existed in reality, And depended on nothing else. When these temporarily god-like beings (who are, again, created by the karmic seeds of deep meditation, but without emptiness content) give birth to children in their realms, it should be a birth which does not cause them any kind of pain.  And so when a child arrives it simply appears in the lap of its mother—and these children are favored with the same affection that we give our own kids here in the world of humans. These beings are though divided into full pleasure beings and half pleasure beings; everything about the life of the latter is slightly less glorious than with the former.  This of course leads to intense feelings of jealousy between the two (as we ourselves might feel towards a fellow employee at work promoted to a position just above our own). These feelings of envy create intense feelings of hatred between the two races that are legendary; and this leads to legendary b

gru.acip: ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I LAG STABS 'DIS, ,CHOS RNAMS THAMS CAD MED PA 'DRA, ,BLO GCIG BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I NGOR, ,CHOS KUN SKYE 'GAG 'GRO 'ONG MED, ,THA SNYAD LAS 'BRAS THAMS CAD MED,
gru.wylie: bden par grub pa'i lag stabs 'dis, ,chos rnams thams cad med pa 'dra, ,blo gcig bden par grub pa'i ngor, ,chos kun skye 'gag 'gro 'ong med, ,tha snyad las 'bras thams cad med
gru.english: This method of implementing The concept that things Could exist in reality Is the same for every other Thing in the universe: They simply Could never exist! If a single state of our mind Existed in and of itself, Then none of the things In the whole universe That ever appeared to it Could ever start, or stop, Or go, or come. Nor could karma And its consequences Even exist, Even in name. This “in name” here is a little tricky.  It depends upon our understanding that names—words themselves—are a shorthand expression of the shining pictures coming out of the karmic seeds in our mind.  (In this sense, the famous Western phrase that “In the beginning was the Word” is very profound.) And so when we say in this context that things exist “in name” or “in name only,” what we're really saying, correctly, is that they are patchwork creations of our seed-pictures.  And this is the sister ultimate truth of things that we refer to as “dependence,” or “cause & effect.” Karma itself though, and its creations, could never exist at all in a world where the mind itself was anything other than a composite of karmic pictures—as the Devil would have it.

gru.acip: ,MDOR NA CHOS KUN MED PAR GO ,DE YI RGYU MTSAN CI STE NA, ,BDEN PAR 'DOD RNAMS CHOS KUN NI, ,LTOS MED GZHAN LA RAG MA LAS, ,KHO RANG NGO BOS GRUB PAR SNANG,
gru.wylie: mdor na chos kun med par go ,de yi rgyu mtshan ci ste na, ,bden par 'dod rnams chos kun ni, ,ltos med gzhan la rag ma las, ,kho rang ngo bos grub par snang
gru.english: To put it briefly, Please understand, Everything that exists Would cease to exist. And why is that? Once you say That a thing exists in truth, Then it cannot rely Upon any other thing; It could never Be relative To anything else. It would have to appear In the universe All on its own, in itself. If a changing thing could exist without causes, it would have no relation to any other thing: it would be truly “independent,” from its own side. Resolving the contradictions of life

gru.acip: ,'JIG RTEN THA SNYAD LA BSTUN PA'I, ,CHOS RNAMS THAMS CAD RGYU RKYEN DANG, ,PHAN TSUN LTOS BZHAG BLO BUR DU, ,RTOG PA'AM MING GIS BTAGS TZAM LA, ,GZHI GCIG STENG DU GNYIS KA NI, ,'DU BA'I SKABS CIG MA BYUNG BAS, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I PHYOGS LTAR NA, ,RKYEN LA LTOS PA'I CHOS KUN MED, ,DES NA CHOS KUN MED PA YIN,
gru.wylie: 'jig rten tha snyad la bstun pa'i, ,chos rnams thams cad rgyu rkyen dang, ,phan tshun ltos bzhag blo bur du, ,rtog pa'am ming gis btags tsam la, ,gzhi gcig steng du gnyis ka ni, ,'du ba'i skabs cig ma byung bas, ,bden par grub pa'i phyogs ltar na, ,rkyen la ltos pa'i chos kun med, ,des na chos kun med pa yin
gru.english: Consider now These two ideas— One, that things in the universe Generally match the way That they are spoken about In terms of the world at large: They rely on their causes, And they rely on comparison One to the other. Two, that they spring up All of a sudden; Products of nothing more Than mental pictures, And names. These two ideas Could never convene And cooperate With regard to any Single object in the world. If thinking thus we approach The position that things Exist with some reality Of their own, We would have to assert That there was no single thing In this entire universe That depended on conditions. And then we'd have To go further, And say that nothing Existed at all. The idea of pictures flowing from mental seeds explains—fully and logically—why anything ever happens at all.  If we think carefully, none of the other, “normal” explanations of our world makes any sense anyway.

gru.acip: ,KHA LA KUN RDZOB KHAS BLANGS KYANG, ,KUN RDZOB RGYU RKYEN LTOS GRUB YIN, ,KHYOD NI LTOS MED GRUB PAR 'DOD, ,DES NA KUN RDZOB KHYOD LA MED,
gru.wylie: kha la kun rdzob khas blangs kyang, ,kun rdzob rgyu rkyen ltos grub yin, ,khyod ni ltos med grub par 'dod, ,des na kun rdzob khyod la med
gru.english: You pay lip service To the idea That things are deceptive, But look— If something is deceptive, Then it has its own Causes and conditions too. You keep saying, instead, That things can exist Without relying on anything else. What you're really saying then Is that there's no such thing As a deceptive reality. It would seem to be a mistake to talk about a real reality which was—at the same time—deceptive; the terms appear to be contradictory.  But if we think carefully we can imagine a world which is real—where things like apple seeds and apple trees do things—but still is not what it seems: for it seems to us, on a normal day, that things have some existence from their own side, and not from ours.  This then would be a reality that was deceptive, but still real.

gru.acip: ,LHA MA YIN GYI BLO DE NI, ,LHA YI DPAL 'BYOR 'DOD YON LA, ,PHRAG DOG 'GRAN SEMS SKYES PA'I TSE, ,KHYOD RANG LHA RU SKYES PA NA, ,DPAL 'BYOR BDEN GRUB MI 'GYUR BAS, ,KHYOD DANG LHAN CIG GNAS PAR NGES, ,DES NA KHYOD KYIS KHYOD RANG LA, ,PHRAG DOG 'GRAN SEMS BYED DAM CI,
gru.wylie: lha ma yin gyi blo de ni, ,lha yi dpal 'byor 'dod yon la, ,phrag dog 'gran sems skyes pa'i tshe, ,khyod rang lha ru skyes pa na, ,dpal 'byor bden grub mi 'gyur bas, ,khyod dang lhan cig gnas par nges, ,des na khyod kyis khyod rang la, ,phrag dog 'gran sems byed dam ci
gru.english: Now there within the heart Of the lesser cousins Arise different thoughts Of envy and wanting To compete with those Higher pleasure beings In the treasures they possess, And the pleasures that they feel. If the lesser ones die And get reborn As one of those very beings, Remember— Those treasures existed In truth, and so They wouldn't have changed; And so these beings Would still now be Possessed of all of them. So answer me on this: What are they supposed to do? Should they be envious Of themselves? Should they each compete With themselves? What happens to envy in a world where everything everyone has is coming from how well they have always shared what they have—and everyone knows that?  If envy is coming from its own side, then even after I get what I was envious of I should still feel the same envy. How pleasure can change to pain

gru.acip: ,LHA YI BDEN GRUB ZHIG PA'I RJES, ,LHA MIN BDEN GRUB CES ZER NA, ,SKYE 'JIG BDEN GRUB YOD MIN PAS, ,BDEN GRUB GZHAN DU 'GYUR BAS NA, ,KHYOD KYI 'GYUR MED DON DE 'GAL,
gru.wylie: lha yi bden grub zhig pa'i rjes, ,lha min bden grub ces zer na, ,skye 'jig bden grub yod min pas, ,bden grub gzhan du 'gyur bas na, ,khyod kyi 'gyur med don de 'gal
gru.english: And suppose you say: “The way that it works Is that the true existence Of the pleasure being Comes to an end; And that is followed By the true existence Of their lesser cousin.” Well now since There could never exist A starting or a stopping That existed in truth, And it being the case then That something that existed In truth could never change To something else, Then you have neatly Contradicted Your own assertion That these things Could never change.

gru.acip: ,YI DVAGS LUS KYI BKRES SKOM DE, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I 'GYUR MED NA, ,SKYE NAS SKYE BA THAMS CAD DU, ,BKRES SKOM NYID KYI RANG BZHIN LAS, ,GZHAN DU 'GYUR BA MI SRID PAS, ,'O NI RGYUN PAR BRGYAL LO AANG, ,KHYOD NI DMYAL BAR SKYES PA'I TSE, ,SKYES PA NYID KYIS BDEN GRUB 'GAL, ,DMYAL BA TSA GRANG SDUG BSNGAL DE, ,GSAR DU MYONG BAS SKYE MED 'GAL,
gru.wylie: yi dvags lus kyi bkres skom de, ,bden par grub pa'i 'gyur med na, ,skye nas skye ba thams cad du, ,bkres skom nyid kyi rang bzhin las, ,gzhan du 'gyur ba mi srid pas, ,'o ni rgyun par brgyal lo aang, ,khyod ni dmyal bar skyes pa'i tshe, ,skyes pa nyid kyis bden grub 'gal, ,dmyal ba tsha grang sdug bsngal de, ,gsar du myong bas skye med 'gal
gru.english: And furthermore, it being the case That things exist in truth, And thus can never change, Then even if the hungry ghost Were feeling starved and parched, Then in all their future lives to live, In rebirth after rebirth, It would be an impossibility For that very hunger and thirst To change into something else, And thus waver from its nature. They would continue their collapsing To the ground in birth after birth, And eventually find themselves Born within the hells. This birth itself would contradict Your position that they'd been real; And it would further be a contradiction For them to have a new experience, Inside that hell, of the burning And freezing there. In discussing where reality really comes from, our beautiful author is strongly taking advantage of the opportunity to describe all the places that each one of us will inevitably end up in, as we age and die in lifetime after lifetime, in lives that flow naturally from the fact that how we treat others always ends up creating the place we live in next.  An extra incentive to figure out where things are really coming from, so we can avoid death and wandering again—creating an endless life of joy and service.

gru.acip: ,BDE SDUG GNYIS PO DNGOS 'GAL NA, ,GZHI GCIG STENG DU CI STE 'DU, ,KHYOD NI LHA LAS 'PHOS MA THAG ,LHA YI BDE BA GZHAN MI 'GYUR, ,LHA YI BDE BA'I RANG BZHIN LAS, ,'GYUR BA MED CING TSA BA YI, ,SDUG BSNGAL RANG BZHIN 'GYUR MED PA, ,PHYOGS GCIG 'DU BA MI SRID KYANG, ,BDEN GRUB KHYOD LA 'DU BA NI, ,SNYING TSIM SNYING TSIM DE RE KHYER, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I SKYON 'DI LA, ,YON TAN DU BZUNG SNYING RE TSIM,
gru.wylie: bde sdug gnyis po dngos 'gal na, ,gzhi gcig steng du ci ste 'du, ,khyod ni lha las 'phos ma thag ,lha yi bde ba gzhan mi 'gyur, ,lha yi bde ba'i rang bzhin las, ,'gyur ba med cing tsha ba yi, ,sdug bsngal rang bzhin 'gyur med pa, ,phyogs gcig 'du ba mi srid kyang, ,bden grub khyod la 'du ba ni, ,snying tshim snying tshim de re khyer, ,bden par grub pa'i skyon 'di la, ,yon tan du bzung snying re tshim
gru.english: Pleasure and pain Are mutually exclusive things; They cannot ever happen In one person in one moment. And according to you, The pleasure they were feeling As a being of pleasure Could not have changed Into something else As they moved to another Type of being. So here you have the pleasure Of a pleasure being Which can never be altered From its natural nature; And at the same time you have The torture of watching your body Burned within the hell— Again with a natural nature, Which cannot change Into something else. The two could never combine Within a single person Within a single moment, But yes I know You must hang on To your “truly exist” And claim they could combine. I truly pity you, That you have to carry the weight Of all these contradictions; I truly pity the fact That you feel you must consider All these different fallacies As being your badge of honor. It's our natural assumption, each of us, that the pleasure or pain which we feel from an object or another person is coming from them to us.  It would require a truly superhuman effort to come to the realization—on our own—that the pain or pleasure that we experience when we come in contact with another person or thing is actually flowing from our own mind. We enjoy some kind of supernatural good fortune that there have come before us people who have figured out how all this is happening.  To become one of those people, we would finally understand how it is that things feel to us cannot be coming from their side.  And

gru.acip: ,GZHI GCIG STENG DU JI LTAR 'DU, ,'GAL KHYAB THAMS CAD KHAS LEN PA'I, ,BDEN GRUB KHYOD LA SNYING RE TSIM, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I NYES PA'O,
gru.wylie: gzhi gcig steng du ji ltar 'du, ,'gal khyab thams cad khas len pa'i, ,bden grub khyod la snying re tshim, ,bden par grub pa'i nyes pa'o
gru.english: How on earth could the two Ever come together In a single place or time? It seems you will have To content yourself With this little “Really exists” of yours, And heartily embrace All the resulting contradictions Of believing in it; For such are the faults Of anything That could have this real existence. The greatest teachers of emptiness over the course of history—people like Arya Nagarjuna, for example—have often focused on teaching emptiness from the point of view of the many impossibilities we are surrounded with, in a world where things exist from their own side. It's a very common and wonderful Buddhist teaching technique then where—rather than handing the student the answers to conundra—we simply point out these contradictions, and encourage the pupil to do the heavy lifting of resolving them. And they can only be resolved by coming to the conclusion that things and people are flowing from us—from seeds planted by every second of our past behavior, up to the present moment. Rebirth as an impossibility

gru.acip: ,MA RIG PA YI DON GCIG TSANG, ,'KHOR BA 'DI LA MTHA' MED PAS, ,'GRO BA LNGA POR SKYES PA'I TSE, ,RE RE LTAR GYI PHUNG PO LA, ,DMIGS NAS BDEN PAR GRUB PA YI, ,'DZIN STANGS SO SOR SKYES PA DANG, ,DE YANG LTOS MED 'GYUR MED DANG, ,RAG MA LAS PAR KHYOD ZHEN PA'I, ,ZHEN PA GZHAN DU MI 'GYUR BZHIN,
gru.wylie: ma rig pa yi don gcig tshang, ,'khor ba 'di la mtha' med pas, ,'gro ba lnga por skyes pa'i tshe, ,re re ltar gyi phung po la, ,dmigs nas bden par grub pa yi, ,'dzin stangs so sor skyes pa dang, ,de yang ltos med 'gyur med dang, ,rag ma las par khyod zhen pa'i, ,zhen pa gzhan du mi 'gyur bzhin
gru.english: Where this one thing Stands complete— Where we misunderstand our world— The cycle of pain continues on, The cycle never-ending. And in it we each are born Into each of the five different Forms of life; And in each individual life We look upon Each body and mind And hold them to exist in truth. It seems as though The way you grasp to things— As depending on nothing else at all, As relying on nothing else there is— Is as well itself a belief That will have to be immutable! How we view our body and mind—in each lifetime we live—forces us to enter more & more bodies and minds of the same kind: suffering.  The cycle of these lifetimes is here described as “never-ending”; but this only applies when we are still misunderstanding where everything around us comes from. There will come a day—soon, if we work to understand the lines of The Cantos—that this otherwise never-ending cycle of pain will finally and perfectly end. The “five different forms of life” mentioned here are the five (and only five) choices of mind & body that we can ever be born into, so long as we misunderstand where things come from: human; animal; hungry ghost; hellbeing; and pleasure being—which would then include their “lesser cousin” pleasure beings. By the way, it's not at all that the Devil (nor we) specifically believe that nothing depends upon anything else.  The Devil knows, as we all do, that apple trees depend on apple seeds.  But remember that these are apple trees as we think of them; and apple seeds a

gru.acip: ,'DIR YANG PHUNG PO TSOGS TZAM LA, ,BRTEN NAS NGA'O SNYAM PA YI, ,BLO YI 'DZIN STANGS BDEN GRUB TU, ,SNANG BA LTAR DU KHYOD 'DOD PAS, ,'GRO BA DRUG PO RE RE LTAR, ,LUS KYI 'DZIN STANGS GZHI GCIG TU, ,'DU LUGS JI LTAR BYED NA AANG, ,PHAL CHER DNGOS 'GAL ZHUGS PA MANG,
gru.wylie: 'dir yang phung po tshogs tsam la, ,brten nas nga'o snyam pa yi, ,blo yi 'dzin stangs bden grub tu, ,snang ba ltar du khyod 'dod pas, ,'gro ba drug po re re ltar, ,lus kyi 'dzin stangs gzhi gcig tu, ,'du lugs ji ltar byed na aang, ,phal cher dngos 'gal zhugs pa mang
gru.english: What you believe then is that— When we look at the simple collection Of the parts that make us up, And hold it in our minds as “me”— Then this “me” exists as it seems to: As something truly there. How then can you assert That each of these six Different kinds of birth Can exist with a single instance Of a body as you hold it to be? Almost all of your ideas here Are simply complete contradictions. We all appreciate that things like our body are made up of multiple parts.  And we all appreciate that mentally we lump these parts together and call it “me.”  It's just that we misunderstand where these parts have come from.

gru.acip: ,RNAM PA'ANG PHAL CHER GA LA MTHUN, ,'GRO BA DRUG PO THAMS CAD KYI, ,SDUG BSNGAL TSA GRANG LTAR 'GAL BA'I, ,BZOD PAR DKA' BA'I SDUG BSNGAL RNAMS, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I LTOS MED DANG, ,GZHAN LA RAG NI MA LAS DANG, ,'GYUR MED RTAG BRTAN THEG {%THER} ZUG 'DI, ,KHYOD KYI MI LUS 'DI THOG TU, ,DUS GCIG LA NI JI LTAR MYONG,
gru.wylie: rnam pa'ang phal cher ga la mthun, ,'gro ba drug po thams cad kyi, ,sdug bsngal tsha grang ltar 'gal ba'i, ,bzod par dka' ba'i sdug bsngal rnams, ,bden par grub pa'i ltos med dang, ,gzhan la rag ni ma las dang, ,'gyur med rtag brtan theg {%ther} zug 'di, ,khyod kyi mi lus 'di thog tu, ,dus gcig la ni ji ltar myong
gru.english: And how could all their features then Ever coexist? All the unbearable sufferings Of all the six different forms That living beings take on— Sufferings that would be As contradictory in nature As feelings of hot and cold— Would be things with a real existence: Never depending, one on another; Immutable; never-shifting; Things both concrete and solid. How could it ever be That you experienced each of them then, Acting all together, In this one human form you have? Again, when we say “things with real existence” here, we're talking about a different kind of real; that is, something that could exist from its own side, without our having been kind or cruel to others in the past.  A pen made of luminous pictures from seeds in our mind quite certainly has real existence of a different kind: it works, but only if we have the seeds to see it work.

gru.acip: ,PHUNG PO TSOGS TZAM LA BRTEN NAS, ,NGA'O SNYAM PA'I BLO DE NI, ,DMIGS PA NGA LA DMIGS NAS NI, ,RNAM PA BDEN PAR GRUB PAR 'DZIN,
gru.wylie: phung po tshogs tsam la brten nas, ,nga'o snyam pa'i blo de ni, ,dmigs pa nga la dmigs nas ni, ,rnam pa bden par grub par 'dzin
gru.english: And so here is a state of mind Which considers the simple Combination of body & mind, And thinks of it as “me.” But when it gazes upon this “me,” It grasps to the perception That it is something that really exists. The key term here is the word “simple”; which in this context refers to a union of body & mind which is coming from its own side, and not resulting from seed-pictures.  No such “me” exists.

gru.acip: ,DE NI GANG ZAG BDAG 'DZIN YIN, ,DER ZHEN GANG ZAG BDAG ZHEN YIN, ,DE LTAR GRUB NA BDEN GRUB YIN,
gru.wylie: de ni gang zag bdag 'dzin yin, ,der zhen gang zag bdag zhen yin, ,de ltar grub na bden grub yin
gru.english: This is what it means When we say that a person Is grasping onto the self-existence Of the person. This is what it means When we say that a person Is attached to the idea Of a self-existent person. For something to exist this way Is what we mean When we say that a thing Has some true existence.

gru.acip: ,DE 'DRA'I BLO NI LHAN SKYES LA, ,PHUNG PO LA DMIGS NGA DE NI, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PAR SNANG BA DE, ,SNANG BA LTAR DU GRUB 'DUG NA, ,RTAG PA MTHA' BZUNG TSUL GYIS SU, ,DGAG BYA'I TSAD KYI DGAG RGYU DE, ,'KHRUL MED NGOS NI ZIN PA NA, ,DE NI DGAG RGYU'I GTZO BO YIN, ,DGRA YI GTZO BO'ANG DE YIN NO,
gru.wylie: de 'dra'i blo ni lhan skyes la, ,phung po la dmigs nga de ni, ,bden par grub par snang ba de, ,snang ba ltar du grub 'dug na, ,rtag pa mtha' bzung tshul gyis su, ,dgag bya'i tshad kyi dgag rgyu de, ,'khrul med ngos ni zin pa na, ,de ni dgag rgyu'i gtso bo yin, ,dgra yi gtso bo'ang de yin no
gru.english: And now suppose it were the case That the “me” we see When an inborn state of mind like this Gazes upon the body & mind And thinks they exist in truth Really did exist in truth. That thing then— This thing that could only exist In a theoretical sense— Is the thing we need to deny: This is the measure Of what we need to refuse. If we can identify, Without any error, This supposed thing, Then that itself is the main thing Which we must seek to deny. And it is as well The face of our true foe. This term, “the thing we need to deny,” is crucial in the study of emptiness.  When we do say “emptiness,” then what we mean is that something which we thought was there is not there at all. If we can correctly identify this thing we need to deny, then true emptiness is in our hand.  And what we deny—again—is anything in our world that is not flowing out of seeds in my mind, planted there by how I treat others. It's fun sometimes to get together with a pretty large group of people, and propose that we look for emptiness together.  One way to do this is to have everyone in the room raise their left hand, and stick out their index finger. Then ask everyone to point to just one thing in the room which is not flowing from their karmic seeds.  The fingers should wander around in the air for a while—and even descend to point to each person themselves—and then conclude in a shrug as no one finds anything. And what we have found then is emptiness.

gru.acip: ,DE LTAR GYUR PA'I NGA DE NI, ,PHUNG PO DANG NI RANG NGOS NAS, ,GRUB PA'I GCIG TU GRUB PA'AM, ,GRUB PA'I THA DAD GANG DU GRUB,
gru.wylie: de ltar gyur pa'i nga de ni, ,phung po dang ni rang ngos nas, ,grub pa'i gcig tu grub pa'am, ,grub pa'i tha dad gang du grub
gru.english: And let me ask you a question: Is this “me” that you believe in Something that exists, from its own side, As one and the same As body & mind? Or somehow separate from it? Again, if body and mind existed out there, from their own side—in & of themselves, as they seem to—then there would be no need for them ever to change, the least bit: they don't depend on anything else, and so they are not subject to change when things in their environs change.

gru.acip: ,GCIG TU GRUB PO ZER NA NI, ,THA DAD GTAN MED GCIG GRUB DANG, ,RANG BZHIN GZHAN DU MI 'GYUR DANG, ,GZHAN LA RAG NI MA LAS DANG, ,LTOS MED 'GYUR MED THER ZUG PAS,
gru.wylie: gcig tu grub po zer na ni, ,tha dad gtan med gcig grub dang, ,rang bzhin gzhan du mi 'gyur dang, ,gzhan la rag ni ma las dang, ,ltos med 'gyur med ther zug pas
gru.english: Ah!  You say this me Is the same as that body & mind? Then they must be A one & the same Which can never allow For any degree of separation; They must be a single thing; And its nature must never vary, Even the slightest bit; And it must never rely On anything other; It must be solid, Ever self-standing, Ever immutable. Again, all in a world where things are coming from their own side.

gru.acip: ,PHUNG PO DANG NI RANG NGOS NAS, ,GRUB PA'I 'GYUR BA GANG DU SONG, ,'GYUR BA 'GYUR BA'I 'GYUR MED MTSAR,
gru.wylie: phung po dang ni rang ngos nas, ,grub pa'i 'gyur ba gang du song, ,'gyur ba 'gyur ba'i 'gyur med mtshar
gru.english: Where then is it That the body & mind, And the change that they Have passed through— Coming as it does, From its very own side— Have all gone off to? This changeless Change of changing of yours Is truly a wondrous thing! Problems with the idea of aging & dying

gru.acip: ,YANG GCIG CHOS KUN MED PA KHYOD, ,SKYE 'CHI YOD NA BDEN GRUB MED, ,KHYOD KYI LUGS LA CHOS KUN NI, ,STOS {%LTOS} MED 'GYUR BA MED PAR GRUB, ,PHAN TSUN LTOS GRUB CHOS MED PAS, ,DES NA KHYOD LA CHOS KUN MED,
gru.wylie: yang gcig chos kun med pa khyod, ,skye 'chi yod na bden grub med, ,khyod kyi lugs la chos kun ni, ,stos {%ltos} med 'gyur ba med par grub, ,phan tshun ltos grub chos med pas, ,des na khyod la chos kun med
gru.english: And if this one-and-the-same me That was none of everything there is Could be born, and could then die, Then it wouldn't any more exist As that kind of real That you were talking about! According to your system, Every single thing in the universe Exists in a way where it need not depend On anything else in the universe— In a way where it never changes. According to you, there cannot exist Any objects which stand In dependence upon each other; And so what you're really saying Is that there cannot exist Any objects at all in the universe! If all the objects around us came from their own side, then they could never affect or be affected by anything else in the universe: there would be no interactions of anything.  Which means no universe could ever be experienced, since to experience is automatically to change.

gru.acip: ,KHYOD NI 'GRO BA GZHAN SKYES TSE, ,DE YI PHUNG DANG NGA GNYIS NI, ,BDEN PA'I GCIG TU GRUB DGOS PAS, ,PHUNG PO 'DI LA DMIGS NAS NI, ,'GRO BA GZHAN GYI PHUNG PO LA'ANG, ,NGA'O SNYAM PA'I BLO SKYE DGOS,
gru.wylie: khyod ni 'gro ba gzhan skyes tshe, ,de yi phung dang nga gnyis ni, ,bden pa'i gcig tu grub dgos pas, ,phung po 'di la dmigs nas ni, ,'gro ba gzhan gyi phung po la'ang, ,nga'o snyam pa'i blo skye dgos
gru.english: When the time comes for you To take your birth into a different life, Then your “me” and the body & mind That exist there in that new life Are going to have to exist As a single thing that is also real. And then even when you sit and look At this body & mind that belong To another world, another form of life, It's going to have to pop into Your thoughts: “Oh, that is me!” If our body & mind come from their own side (and not from our seed-pictures), then there would be no reason for them to change, even lifetime to lifetime.  And then every time we were reborn into a new world, another identical “me” would pop up there.  Pretty soon we would be enough to fill all the planets!

gru.acip: ,DE BZHIN ZHUGS PAR GYUR ZER KYANG, ,ZHUGS PA'I 'GYUR BA KHO NAS NI, ,BDEN GRUB 'GYUR BA MED PA 'GAL,
gru.wylie: de bzhin zhugs par gyur zer kyang, ,zhugs pa'i 'gyur ba kho nas ni, ,bden grub 'gyur ba med pa 'gal
gru.english: And suppose you claim That this exactly the way That you have entered there; Isn't it though the case That the change involved In having entered Contradicts your position Of immutable self-existence? Pushed into a logical corner, the Devil is willing to claim that the body & mind he picks up as he starts his new lifetime is exactly the same as the body & mind that he left off with, in this last life. Even if that could somehow be the case, this new version of the same old body and mind would now exist in a later time—which would be a change.

gru.acip: ,NGA PHUNG BDEN PA'I GCIG GRUB NA, ,NGA YI BA LA DMIGS PA YI, ,NGA YIR 'DZIN PA KHYOD LA MED,
gru.wylie: nga phung bden pa'i gcig grub na, ,nga yi ba la dmigs pa yi, ,nga yir 'dzin pa khyod la med
gru.english: If “me” is something that is Really one and the same With the body and the mind, Then according to you It would never be possible To hold to something as “mine” In the sense of focusing On those things that are mine. If I am my body and my mind—in a world where things come from themselves—then they cannot be “mine” at the same time, since they are already “me,” the one who by definition possesses them. Remember, we're not trying to be cute here or debate impossibles or irrelevants.  It's just that there's something fundamentally wrong with our old way of thinking about even things as basic as “me” and “mine.” If that thinking is entirely mistaken, then it's totally possible that there is something totally mistaken about how we take care of this “me”—how we go about getting anything at all in this entire life of ours which would make us happy or comfortable.

gru.acip: ,GAL TE NGA YIR 'DZIN ZHE NA, ,BDEN GRUB GZHAN DU 'GYUR BAS NA, ,'GYUR BA MED PA'I BDEN GRUB 'GAL,
gru.wylie: gal te nga yir 'dzin zhe na, ,bden grub gzhan du 'gyur bas na, ,'gyur ba med pa'i bden grub 'gal
gru.english: And if you say That it really is possible To hold to something as “mine,” Then a thing that exists as real Has changed into something else— Thus contradicting your idea Of a self-existent existence Impossible to change. First a thing is not mine and then we obtain it, and it becomes mine.  That means it has changed from not mine to mine.  And that means it cannot be coming from its own side, independent of everything and everybody around it.  This in turn draws into question the idea that the thing was coming from its own side in the first place.

gru.acip: ,NGA YI LAG PA LA DMIGS PA'I, ,NGA YI BA YI BDEN GRUB DE, ,'GYUR BA MED PA'I RTAG PAR DANG, ,LTOS MED GZHAN LA RAG MA LAS,
gru.wylie: nga yi lag pa la dmigs pa'i, ,nga yi ba yi bden grub de, ,'gyur ba med pa'i rtag par dang, ,ltos med gzhan la rag ma las
gru.english: The real existence of a mine Where you focus on my hand Would have to be unchanging; Something that never varied, Never depending, never relying On anything else at all. If on the inside a person or a thing could come from its own side, then on the outside it could never engage in a relationship with something else—since that would already change it.

gru.acip: ,NGO BOS GRUB PA'I 'GYUR MED DANG, ,NGA YI RKANG SOGS LA DMIGS PA'I, ,NGA YIR 'DZIN PA SKYE BA 'GAL,
gru.wylie: ngo bos grub pa'i 'gyur med dang, ,nga yi rkang sogs la dmigs pa'i, ,nga yir 'dzin pa skye ba 'gal
gru.english: A changelessness That existed in and of itself Would contradict the very idea Of a perception starting up That was focused upon my foot, Or anything else of the like. If we do come from our own side and therefore never change, then how could we even shift our focus from me to my foot for the amount of time it takes to put my socks on in the morning? Problems with the shifts in attraction

gru.acip: ,DE BZHIN CHAGS PA'I BDEN GRUB DE, ,GZHAN DU MI 'GYUR THER ZUG PAS, ,'DI MIN KUN LA 'GROS 'DI KHYER,
gru.wylie: de bzhin chags pa'i bden grub de, ,gzhan du mi 'gyur ther zug pas, ,'di min kun la 'gros 'di khyer
gru.english: So too, a real reality In the form of feeling attachment Would be something that was solid, And never open to change. You should think about The effect this would have On the idea that everyone Likes to talk about: “Freedom from attachment.” It's not wrong to have things—to enjoy owning things that we acquire honestly and which give us pleasure, and which also help us in our life-task of helping others. And it's not wrong to enjoy something we rightfully possess—in the end, we properly want to own the state of nirvana, and our own Buddhahood.  To do so, we are told, we must overcome our attachment to anything at all—even good things. It's important to realize that the “attachment” spoken of in this manner—as a negative thing—is one where we want to acquire and to keep things through any means other than sharing: helping others to get what they hope for.  Acquisition through sharing is in fact what has made all the Buddhas in the universe who they are!

gru.acip: ,BUD MED LTA BU LA DMIGS NAS, ,MIG GIS GZUGS LA CHAGS PA YI, ,YID 'ONG DNGOS PO GZHAN DAG LA, ,BDEN PA'I CHAGS PA SKYE BA 'GAL, ,GAL TE SKYE NA 'GYUR MED 'GAL, ,SKYE BA KHO NAS BDEN GRUB 'GAL,
gru.wylie: bud med lta bu la dmigs nas, ,mig gis gzugs la chags pa yi, ,yid 'ong dngos po gzhan dag la, ,bden pa'i chags pa skye ba 'gal, ,gal te skye na 'gyur med 'gal, ,skye ba kho nas bden grub 'gal
gru.english: It would be a contradiction then To say that a man had looked At something like a woman And felt attraction to her form, And then begun to feel as well An attraction that was real Towards any other Alluring object at all; If the attraction began to be felt, Then that would contradict The idea that it was real; If something even begins at all, Then that contradicts The idea that things are immutable; And so we can say That it takes no more Than something starting To contradict your idea That things could exist as real. Forget trying to discuss the ethics of one person being attracted to another—a discussion which first of all requires a lot more information about the situation at hand.  The real point here is the question of how that attraction could ever start in the first place, if the attraction existed from its own side. When a thing exists from its own side, it doesn't require any outside causes or conditions to first come into being, or to remain in existence.  The very fact that people fall in love then proves the Devil wrong.

gru.acip: ,DE BZHIN DBANG PO GZHAN DAG LA'ANG, ,SO SOR CHAGS YUL LA DMIGS PA'I, ,BDEN PA'I CHAGS PA SKYE BA 'GAL, ,GAL TE SKYE NA SKYE MED 'GAL, ,BDEN GRUB GZHAN DU 'GYUR BA'ANG 'GAL,
gru.wylie: de bzhin dbang po gzhan dag la'ang, ,so sor chags yul la dmigs pa'i, ,bden pa'i chags pa skye ba 'gal, ,gal te skye na skye med 'gal, ,bden grub gzhan du 'gyur ba'ang 'gal
gru.english: The same reasoning applies To a case where any other Organ of the sense might focus On an object of attraction: It would be a contradiction To say that the attraction was real. And if the attraction started up, Then that would contradict the idea That nothing could ever start: It would be a contradiction even if A thing that really existed Could change to something else. Romantic feelings in a situation which is ethical can only be described as “delightful.”  Portraying Buddhism or the spiritual life as something which denies romance and wonder in life as something wrong is like trying to convince people that the free blue color of the sky is a bad thing. Romance which hurts other people though is by definition self-defeating, since we can only enjoy a single moment of good feeling if we have helped and served others: if we have dedicated ourselves to their happiness. Forget worrying about whether a proper good feeling might go away, or not.  Even for it to deepen gradually, day by day, is something that can only come from the seeds of serving the hopes and wishes of others.

gru.acip: ,DANG PO THOG MA MED DUS NAS, ,MIG GI DBANG PO'I YUL DAG LA, ,BDEN PA'I CHAGS PA LTOS MED DU, ,GRUB GRUB PAR NI YOD ZER NA,
gru.wylie: dang po thog ma med dus nas, ,mig gi dbang po'i yul dag la, ,bden pa'i chags pa ltos med du, ,grub grub par ni yod zer na
gru.english: And suppose you say That it's the case That from the very beginning, From the very start of things, There have always been Feelings of attraction To the objects of The sense power of the eye Which were real; That since forever these feelings Have always existed, Without depending on anything else. Just because things have been around forever doesn't mean that they don't change as they are.  We see a seed become a sprout become a lovely flower and then wilted petals on the ground. But again, if they were “real” in the way that the Devil wants them to be, they would not go through their cycles.  And again, they are really real when—as things that come from their seeds—they do pass through these changes. Problems with kids & fogeys

gru.acip: ,YOD NA 'GRO BA GZHAN LNGA RU, ,SKYE BA MED PAS KHYOD LA 'GAL, ,MI LUS TSE 'DIR 'PHRAL BLANGS BZHIN, ,THOG MED GRUB PA'I KHAS LEN 'GAL,
gru.wylie: yod na 'gro ba gzhan lnga ru, ,skye ba med pas khyod la 'gal, ,mi lus tshe 'dir 'phral blangs bzhin, ,thog med grub pa'i khas len 'gal
gru.english: And if so, then since There should never have been Any births into any of the other Of the five different forms of life, You contradict yourself. You contradict the fact That for time without beginning We have taken on these births, In just the same way That in this present moment We have slipped on a human body Here within this life. Just by being alive in this world, we do things towards other people and are thus constantly planting more seeds in our mind.  As these seeds exceed a certain minimum and a certain maximum quality, we are born into forms of life other than the human. Some of these other forms of life—such as animals—we can see here in this world.  With our capacity of reasoning, we can deduce that there could well be other forms of life we cannot here observe.

gru.acip: ,BU CHUNG NAS NI RIM PAR NI, ,RGAN PO'I LUS SU GYUR BZHIN DU, ,THOG MED DUS NAS RGAN PO'I LUS, ,'DI GA BCOS MIN LTOS MED DU, ,GRUB PA'I KHAS LEN 'DI 'DRA AANG, ,MA RIG YIN KYANG GAD MO 'CHOR,
gru.wylie: bu chung nas ni rim par ni, ,rgan po'i lus su gyur bzhin du, ,thog med dus nas rgan po'i lus, ,'di ga bcos min ltos med du, ,grub pa'i khas len 'di 'dra aang, ,ma rig yin kyang gad mo 'chor
gru.english: Our bodies transform, Step by step, From the form of a child Into that of the aged. How then can you Take the position That this same body Of the elderly one Has existed for time Without a beginning, Never refreshed, Existing in and of itself? Yes, we know— It's just your misunderstanding, But how can we keep A burst of laughter From escaping out our lips? Middle age transforms into old age; what makes us think that old age itself will last forever?

gru.acip: ,AA MAR SKYES PA YIN BZHIN DU, ,'GYUR MED RGAN PO'I RANG BZHIN DU, ,GRUB GRUB 'DRA BA 'DI GAR NA, ,RGAN POR AA MA'I LUS SU NI, ,ZHUGS PA'I TSUL 'DI KHYOD KYIS SMROS,
gru.wylie: aa mar skyes pa yin bzhin du, ,'gyur med rgan po'i rang bzhin du, ,grub grub 'dra ba 'di gar na, ,rgan por aa ma'i lus su ni, ,zhugs pa'i tshul 'di khyod kyis smros
gru.english: On one hand then You have somebody Taking birth inside their mother; Who on the other hand Keeps going on In the form of a fogey unchanged. Tell us now Just how this works: Someone here who's elderly, And who's entered into The body of their mother! We see that life enters new wombs, all around us; we see those who pass away from this life, also all around.  Those who enter all have unique personalities and propensities, which logically they must have gained earlier on.  The two suggest at least a strong possibility. A list of different “mines”

gru.acip: ,NGA PHUNG BDEN PA'I GCIG GRUB NA, ,PHUNG PO LA CHAGS BDEN 'DZIN DE, ,'GYUR BA MED PAS SEMS LA NI, ,BDEN 'DZIN CI YI PHYIR NA SKYE,
gru.wylie: nga phung bden pa'i gcig grub na, ,phung po la chags bden 'dzin de, ,'gyur ba med pas sems la ni, ,bden 'dzin ci yi phyir na skye
gru.english: If the “me” really is One and the same With my body and mind In a way which is real, Then our habit of grasping To some true existence Of our body and our mind Would have to be unchangeable. How then could we ever begin To have in our mind fresh ideas Of holding things as true? Even the simple continuation of misunderstanding would entail shifting into an entity within a new time.  But just that much change is impossible for something that is coming from its own side—independently.

gru.acip: ,NGA DANG PHUNG PO BDEN PA YI, ,THA DAD DU NI GRUB PA NA, ,'BREL MED DON GZHAN YIN DGOS PAS, ,LAG PA NA YANG NGA NA ZHES, ,BDAG GIR BYED PA 'BREL MED YIN,
gru.wylie: nga dang phung po bden pa yi, ,tha dad du ni grub pa na, ,'brel med don gzhan yin dgos pas, ,lag pa na yang nga na zhes, ,bdag gir byed pa 'brel med yin
gru.english: And now suppose instead That the “me” existed as something Which was separate, in truth, From the body and the mind. In this case, this “me” And body & mind would have to be Completely unrelated, separate things. And then it would be Completely irrelevant To consider anything as my own: To say, when I hurt my hand, That I had hurt myself. Nobody would say that they were just their hand; but everybody says “I hurt myself” when they hurt their hand.  At the very least, this discrepancy is one of those situations that Arya Nagarjuna encourages us to look into, as a possible alert that things are not what we think they are.

gru.acip: ,NGA PHUNG BDEN PA'I DU MAR NI, ,GRUB NA NGA PHUNG BDEN PA YI, ,GCIG TU GRUB PAR 'GYUR BA YIN,
gru.wylie: nga phung bden pa'i du mar ni, ,grub na nga phung bden pa yi, ,gcig tu grub par 'gyur ba yin
gru.english: If what I consider “me” Is, in truth, the many parts Of my body & mind, Then my “me” must also be A single thing with body & mind. Do we count the whole of a thing as an additional thing, on top of the parts that make the whole?  If it becomes then another part, then where is the whole? Again, these are not just silly questions; they are danger signs that the way we think of things may be badly mistaken—which would make our life a little chaotic, since what we think makes things happen isn't what makes them happen, and we might not get what we want to get, very often. Some scripture in support

gru.acip: ,NGA PHUNG BDEN PA'I GCIG GRUB NA, ,PHUNG PO'I CHA SHAS KUN DANG NI, ,BDEN PA'I GCIG TU GRUB DGOS PAS, ,SHAR NUB LHO BYANG DBUS DBYE BA'I, ,PHYOGS NI GANG DU GCIG PAR 'GYUR,
gru.wylie: nga phung bden pa'i gcig grub na, ,phung po'i cha shas kun dang ni, ,bden pa'i gcig tu grub dgos pas, ,shar nub lho byang dbus dbye ba'i, ,phyogs ni gang du gcig par 'gyur
gru.english: If the “me” were, In reality, One with my body & mind, Then the “me” would have to be, In reality, One with each and every one Of the separate parts of body & mind. And then the “me” would be One with each of the separate Directions of east, and west, South, and north, and middle. If I am—from my own side—equivalent to the sum of the parts of my body and mind, then I should equally be equivalent to the sum of each of their parts: hands and feet, sadness and happiness. The physical parts of me have further divisions into those to the left, and those to the right; or, we can say, corresponding for example to north and south.  A whole which existed from its own side would also have to include the extent of all the parts of each of the directions—and thus be as large as the universe itself.

gru.acip: ,NGA PHUNG BDEN PA'I RANG BZHIN DU, ,'GYUR BA MED PA GANG DU SONG, ,'GYUR GYIN 'GYUR GYIN MI 'GYUR ZER, ,'DI 'DRA'I BDEN GRUB YA MTSAN CAN,,
gru.wylie: nga phung bden pa'i rang bzhin du, ,'gyur ba med pa gang du song, ,'gyur gyin 'gyur gyin mi 'gyur zer, ,'di 'dra'i bden grub ya mtshan can
gru.english: Where then would your “me” Run off to—the one That was unchangeable, And truly in nature body & mind? Oh this real existence of yours— The kind that's always changing, And then changing over again— But which still you say is changeless, Is truly something amazing! Twelfth Canto Everyone Is Too Busy For Wisdom Mr. Misunderstanding defends himself

gru.acip: ,DE YI RGYU MTSAN CI STE NA, ,SKYES PA BUD MED GANG YANG RUNG, ,SDOM PA GSUM PO GANG YANG RUNG, ,LEN YANG MI DGOS BSRUNG MI DGOS, ,DBANG BSKUR RNAM DAG MI DGOS SHING, ,DAM TSIG BSRUNG YANG MI DGOS LA, ,DGE BCU SGRUB KYANG MI DGOS SHING,
gru.wylie: de yi rgyu mtshan ci ste na, ,skyes pa bud med gang yang rung, ,sdom pa gsum po gang yang rung, ,len yang mi dgos bsrung mi dgos, ,dbang bskur rnam dag mi dgos shing, ,dam tshig bsrung yang mi dgos la, ,dge bcu sgrub kyang mi dgos shing
gru.english: And what, you ask, Is the reason for this? Whether we're talking about Women or men, And whichever one Of the three sets of vows We're talking about, These people take them, But they don't need them— They don't need To keep them. They have no need For an authentic empowerment Into the Way of the Diamond, And they have no need To keep their diamond pledges; They don't even Feel a need To keep the ten good deeds! The “three sets of vows” referred to here refer to the vows of ethical behavior; the vows of the bodhisattva; and the vows of the Diamond Way. The vows of ethical behavior are—most basically—the ten universal commitments that we listed above. The vows of the bodhisattva consist of 64 sacred commitments that we take when we have pledged ourselves to stop the suffering of every living being in the universe.  They begin with committing not to praise oneself, or denigrate others. The secret vows of the Diamond Way help us to maintain a sacred view of the people and events around us—which is the one way to reach total enlightenment within a single human lifetime.

gru.acip: ,CI YANG MED PA'I NGO SPROD BYED, ,YID LA CI YANG MI BSAM PAR, ,BSGOMS PAS TING 'DZIN 'PHRAL MANG SKYE, ,'DI NI NGA YI BSGOM SGRUB MKHAN,
gru.wylie: ci yang med pa'i ngo sprod byed, ,yid la ci yang mi bsam par, ,bsgoms pas ting 'dzin 'phral mang skye, ,'di ni nga yi bsgom sgrub mkhan
gru.english: Lead people By the hand To the nothing at all; Teach them Not to think Of anything. Make their concentration Filled with busyness Every time they meditate; Ah, these are The masters of meditation Inside my system! On the subject of fakes, we come back here to meditation instructors who have not the slightest clue about the genuine article. A fake yoga teacher we can tell simply from how they perform a few basic poses; but a fake meditation teacher is a little more difficult to detect, since the meditation is going on invisibly inside their head. We have to listen carefully and see if we hear the telltale references to ethical behavior and reality which proceeds from seeds in the mind—rather than from its own side.  Then we know we have met the real thing.

gru.acip: ,GZHAN LA RAG NI LAS PA DANG, ,RGYU DANG RKYEN LAS SKYES PA DANG, ,PHAN TSUN RTEN 'BREL LTOS GRUB PAS, ,DE RNAMS NGA YI GROGS YIN MOD,
gru.wylie: gzhan la rag ni las pa dang, ,rgyu dang rkyen las skyes pa dang, ,phan tshun rten 'brel ltos grub pas, ,de rnams nga yi grogs yin mod
gru.english: They all depend Upon something else; All of them are born From causes & conditions— They all come about Through a process Of mutual reliance; And every single One of them Is a companion to me. The way that the world flows in shining pictures from seeds in our mind has so far been an enemy to living kind—but our beautiful Angel is pointing out here that if we turn things around and practice constant kindness towards others, this same mechanism can be one that creates a perfect world, to be our ultimate friend. Friends who help each other

gru.acip: ,SNANG BA BRTEN NAS SKYES PA 'DIS, ,SNANG BA BDEN GRUB MTHA' NGE DANG, ,SNANG BA GTAN MED MTHA' GNYIS SEL, ,SNANG BA BDEN PAR MED PA 'DIS, ,SNANG BA BDEN GRUB MTHA' DE DANG, ,SNANG BA GTAN MED MTHA' GNYIS SEL,
gru.wylie: snang ba brten nas skyes pa 'dis, ,snang ba bden grub mtha' nge dang, ,snang ba gtan med mtha' gnyis sel, ,snang ba bden par med pa 'dis, ,snang ba bden grub mtha' de dang, ,snang ba gtan med mtha' gnyis sel
gru.english: The appearance of things Is the fact That things arise in dependence; The appearance of things Draws a line To stop things being real; The appearance of things Banishes the two extremes Where nothing exists at all; The appearance of things Proves that nothing is real; The appearance of things Destroys the extreme That anything is real; The appearance of things Banishes the two extremes Where nothing exists at all. “The appearance of things” has a very specific meaning in emptiness teachings: it refers to the reality which is glued together by those luminous images coming out of my karmic seeds. If this particular appearance really exists, then we can say that the “two extremes” are impossible: that things could exist (from their own side), or that things don't exist at all (if they are empty of a seed-picture reality).

gru.acip: ,RTEN 'BREL RGYU 'BRAS BSLU MED DES, ,RANG BZHIN GRUB PA'I NGES SHES KYI, ,'DZIN STANGS MA LUS KUN 'JIG PAR, ,MTHONG BA'I NGES PA BRTEN RNYED TSE, ,YI DAM RNAMS LA MCHOD DO GYIS,
gru.wylie: rten 'brel rgyu 'bras bslu med des, ,rang bzhin grub pa'i nges shes kyi, ,'dzin stangs ma lus kun 'jig par, ,mthong ba'i nges pa brten rnyed tshe, ,yi dam rnams la mchod do gyis
gru.english: This understanding Of interdependence— The fact that cause & effect Can never fail us— Destroys all the ways In which our certainty That things exist through Some nature of their own Holds things to be. When thus we have reached A reliance upon perceiving That this is how things are, Try your best to make then This excellent offering To every personal Angel there is. The old cause-and-effect in our life, the old version of dependence in our days, dictated that even tiny negative thoughts came back to us as grand disasters in our life.  Here the Angel proposes a new kind of dependence: let us rely more & more upon our understanding of where all these things are really coming from—those seed-pictures.

gru.acip: ,RGYU 'BRAS MI BSLU'I GTAN TSIGS KYIS, ,RTAGS GZHAN LA NI LTOS MED DU, ,YOD MTHA' BRAL BA'I STONG PAR NI, ,'GRUB PA'I TSUL LAS RANG RGYU LAS, ,RANG 'BRAS 'BYUNG BA BSLU MED LA, ,GTING NAS NGES SHES 'DRONGS PA'I TSE, ,ZHAL BZHI PA LA MCHOD DO GYIS,
gru.wylie: rgyu 'bras mi bslu'i gtan tshigs kyis, ,rtags gzhan la ni ltos med du, ,yod mtha' bral ba'i stong par ni, ,'grub pa'i tshul las rang rgyu las, ,rang 'bras 'byung ba bslu med la, ,gting nas nges shes 'drongs pa'i tshe, ,zhal bzhi pa la mchod do gyis
gru.english: The logical proof Which says that Cause & effect is infallible Establishes an emptiness Free of the extreme Of thinking that Things could exist, Even without our depending On any other reason. And then with this We elicit within ourselves A certainty, from the Very bottom of our heart, Of how it is infallible that A corresponding result Will come from A corresponding cause. Try your best to make then This excellent offering To the Four-Faced One. Just what does it mean when we speak of “the extreme that things exist”?  This is any “edge” in the universe out beyond the scope of the Middle Way, which itself says that everything exists (through seed-pictures) and at the same time nothing exists (independent of seed-pictures).  Here, the extreme—which could never itself exist—would be any object or person in our life which exists independent of our own seeds. The Four-Faced One is sometimes simply called “The Protector,” and is one of the principal supernatural beings who takes care that accurate teachings are not lost in this world.

gru.acip: ,NGES SHES YUL GYI 'DZIN STANGS KUN 'JIG NI, ,RANG BZHIN GRUB PA'I 'DZIN STANGS YIN PAR GO
gru.wylie: nges shes yul gyi 'dzin stangs kun 'jig ni, ,rang bzhin grub pa'i 'dzin stangs yin par go
gru.english: When this certainty Shatters all the ways In which we used to hold The objects around us, Then finally we grasp The way we always thought That things could exist Through some nature Of their own.

gru.acip: ,STONG NYID LA DMIGS ZHI GNAS SGRUBS, ,LHAG MTHONG BSGOM PA'I MAN NGAG NI, ,STONG PA NYID LA MNYAM PAR ZHOG
gru.wylie: stong nyid la dmigs zhi gnas sgrubs, ,lhag mthong bsgom pa'i man ngag ni, ,stong pa nyid la mnyam par zhog
gru.english: May we achieve That quietude which places Its focus on emptiness; May we sit in Balanced meditation Upon emptiness itself, Using the advices For meditating on insight. Another reference to the unbeatable combination of true insight into how emptiness works, together with the mental quietude which allows us to hold our thoughts upon that insight.

gru.acip: ,'JOG PAR MA BDE MNYAM GZHAG DUS, ,RNAM BDUN RIGS PAS MA DPYAD NA, ,LHAG MTHONG 'GRUB PAR GA LA 'GYUR,
gru.wylie: 'jog par ma bde mnyam gzhag dus, ,rnam bdun rigs pas ma dpyad na, ,lhag mthong 'grub par ga la 'gyur
gru.english: Suppose though it comes In our balanced meditation That it no longer feels comfortable To stay in that focus. How then could We ever achieve insight, If we didn't know how To use the reasoning In seven different parts, To accomplish our examination? The “reasoning in seven different parts” is explained in emptiness classics such as Master Chandrakirti's Entering the Middle Way.  Here we use the example of a wagon to examine emptiness.  An automobile works very well in modern times, since it is so ubiquitous—always around us to remind us of emptiness. A car (1) is not something other than its component parts.  (2) Neither though does it exist as something which is one and the same as those parts.  (3) We cannot say that the self is possessed of the parts to the person; (4) that it depends upon its component parts; or (5) that the component parts depend upon the self.  But at the same time (6) the car cannot be the simple collection of its component parts; nor (7) does it consist of the outline of those parts when they are put together. As we can see when we give these options some thought, all of them only make sense if we remember that they are referring for example to pieces of a wagon that could be coming from their own side—at us. The point of mentioning this technique of emptiness analysis is what the ancient books refer to as the “thousand good reasons” why emptiness is true.  It is said that the kindest and most intelligent of disciples seek a whole variety of ways to p

gru.acip: ,LTOS GRUB KHYOD KYIS KHAS LEN NA, ,NGA BDEN PAR 'DZIN LA LTOS NAS NI, ,KHYOD GNYEN PO SHES RAB ZHES BZHAG NA, ,NGA BDEN PA MED PA KHYOD LA 'GAL,
gru.wylie: ltos grub khyod kyis khas len na, ,nga bden par 'dzin la ltos nas ni, ,khyod gnyen po shes rab zhes bzhag na, ,nga bden pa med pa khyod la 'gal
gru.english: Given that you accept This idea of things Happening in reliance, Then the fact is That the spiritual antidote Which you yourself represent— The one called “wisdom”— Relies in the end On me, the habit Of holding things as real. So isn't the claim That I myself Am not something real A contradiction, In your own system? It is a cornerstone of emptiness philosophy that all things depend upon other things; in the end, this is a reference to the grand reliance of all people and things upon our seed-pictures. But if we take this reliance in the sense of things gaining their identity by comparison to what they are not, then even the figments of the Devil's imagination take on some reality, as the counterpoint to seed-picture productions. The solution here is to recognize the reality of misconceptions that things could exist from their own side; since those misconceptions do spring from their valid, infernal causes.

gru.acip: ,PHA RI'I BLO NA SKYE BA DE, ,TSU RI LA NI LTOS GRUB NA, ,GNYEN PO SHES RAB SKYE BA DE, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA LA LTOS NAS, ,BKAG PA'I SHES RAB SKYE'O ZHES, ,KUN GYIS GLENG BAS KHYOD LA 'GAL,
gru.wylie: pha ri'i blo na skye ba de, ,tshu ri la ni ltos grub na, ,gnyen po shes rab skye ba de, ,bden par grub pa la ltos nas, ,bkag pa'i shes rab skye'o zhes, ,kun gyis gleng bas khyod la 'gal
gru.english: The perception That a mountain Is over there Occurs in reliance Upon a mountain That is over here. The arisal of The antidote, wisdom, Is something that relies Upon things that Exist in reality. And so when everybody Runs around saying They are going to give birth To a wisdom that denies things, They are thus contradicting You yourself! Wisdom can't do what she does unless there is something negative that she has to overcome: some way of misunderstanding the world, a belief that things are coming from their own side. The Devil is saying that if we took away this misunderstanding and what it believes in forever, then Wisdom would no longer have anything around that could define its boundaries. But a Wisdom can also be infinite, reaching to all places of the universe.

gru.acip: ,NYON MONGS LA SOGS CHOS KUN NI, ,GRUB TZAM NYID NAS RANG RANG THOG ,BDEN GRUB RE RE SO SOR NI, ,DUS MNYAM LTOS MED RANG GRUB YIN,
gru.wylie: nyon mongs la sogs chos kun ni, ,grub tsam nyid nas rang rang thog ,bden grub re re so sor ni, ,dus mnyam ltos med rang grub yin
gru.english: Now whenever any Of all the things there are— Negative thoughts and the like— Simply comes into existence, There comes into existence Along with it its corresponding Existence in reality. These are simultaneous; They rely on nothing else, And they are self-created. It is indeed the case that the moment a thing comes into existence, it comes into existence with a state of existing in a certain way. But that “certain way” that the thing exists doesn't have to be existing from its own side.  The Devil is not admitting an alternative way of coming into existence—which is to come into existence along with a way of existing through seed-pictures.

gru.acip: ,GCIG NAS GCIG TU 'PHO BA MIN, ,NYON MONGS SKYE BZHIN PA LA YANG, ,BDEN GRUB KYIS KYANG DUS MNYAM SLEB, ,'PHO BA'I TSUL NI MA YIN CING,
gru.wylie: gcig nas gcig tu 'pho ba min, ,nyon mongs skye bzhin pa la yang, ,bden grub kyis kyang dus mnyam sleb, ,'pho ba'i tshul ni ma yin cing
gru.english: None of these Is something that shifts From one state to another. Even in the case Of negative thoughts That are in the act Of arising, This existence in truth Arrives simultaneously; It does not occur Through a process where Something has shifted its state. The Devil is absolutely right in saying that whatever is the true manner in which all things come into being, it must accompany even the most painful and wrong things in the world as they start and then grow.  But this is exactly what makes them fixable: the fact that they come from the seeds we have chosen to plant within our own mind, before.

gru.acip: ,NYON MONGS SKAD CIG SNGA MA NI, ,'GAG BZHIN PA LA'ANG NGA YOD MOD, ,SKAD CIG GNYIS PAR SKYE BZHIN LA'ANG, ,GRUB TZAM LTOS MED NGA YOD PAS,
gru.wylie: nyon mongs skad cig snga ma ni, ,'gag bzhin pa la'ang nga yod mod, ,skad cig gnyis par skye bzhin la'ang, ,grub tsam ltos med nga yod pas
gru.english: When an earlier instant Of a negative emotion Is in the process of stopping, Admittedly I Must still be there. And even as that of The second instant Is in the act of arising, I am still there too: I arrive from the very occurrence; And I rely on nothing. The Devil is failing here to make a distinction between the way that negative emotions start (through my own seed-pictures) and the solidity that they seem to have when I misunderstand where they have come from. Just because the Devil is “natural” to our mind, from the viewpoint of having always been there so far, doesn't mean that his own existence doesn't depend on anything.  In fact he depends upon the same kind of seed-pictures that everybody and everything else does. A great and total darkness

gru.acip: ,NGA NI BDEN PAR GRUB PA NI, ,KHAS NI MI LEN KHA MED DANG, ,MI BYED KA MED 'GRO DRUG GO ,SEMS CAN RNAMS KYIS BCOS PA YIN,
gru.wylie: nga ni bden par grub pa ni, ,khas ni mi len kha med dang, ,mi byed ka med 'gro drug go ,sems can rnams kyis bcos pa yin
gru.english: You have no choice But to accept the idea That I exist as real. Neither do the beings Of the six types of birth Have any choice, But to do the same. I am fact am a creation Of all those living beings. It is an irony that—as a Buddhist practitioner—we are actively trying to kill something that we ourselves originally gave life to: misunderstanding where the people and things around us have come from.  But there are lots of things in our life that at first we wanted, and later learned were not good for us.  And we learned to let them go.

gru.acip: ,GDAGS GZHI CHOS KUN LA DMIGS NAS, ,RTOG PAS PHAR LA BTAGS NAS NI, ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA 'DUG GO ZHES, ,KHO RANG TSO YIS BCOS PA YIN,
gru.wylie: gdags gzhi chos kun la dmigs nas, ,rtog pas phar la btags nas ni, ,bden par grub pa 'dug go zhes, ,kho rang tsho yis bcos pa yin
gru.english: They look at the thing To call a thing: At every existing thing. Their imagination Sends a name out to it, And then they say “This really exists.” And it is all a creation Of their own. It's true that everything around us—and in particular the things that give us pain or unhappiness—is a creation of our own: we chose to engage in the behavior that planted all these seeds in the first place. It is equally true that the pictures coming out of these seeds of our own planting have created something real.  The pain, for example, is undeniable. But the fact that the pain is real doesn't prove that it exists real-ly, or from its own side, from itself.  Pain is not unchangeable, because pain does not come from its own side.  Pain is created by our adamant refusal to take care of others around us—which means that we can choose not to make more pain for ourselves, any day we finally decide to.

gru.acip: ,BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I NGES SHES KYI, ,NGES NGO SNANG NGO GNYIS KA LA, ,SHES RAB KHYOD NI MI SNANG MOD, ,MED PAR SNANG BA GA NA YIN, ,MED PAR SNANG NA GTAN MED YIN,
gru.wylie: bden par grub pa'i nges shes kyi, ,nges ngo snang ngo gnyis ka la, ,shes rab khyod ni mi snang mod, ,med par snang ba ga na yin, ,med par snang na gtan med yin
gru.english: There is a state of mind Where we feel sure That things exist as real; Now admittedly, Miss Wisdom, Such things exist Neither in what you know Nor in what appears to you; But now how would things Ever appear to not exist? If they appeared to not exist, They wouldn't exist at all. Here the Devil is basically saying, “Look, we all know that the things in front of us cannot actually exist the way they seem to: it just wouldn't make sense.  But what alternative are you proposing?  What's the use of living a life full of things and people that we know aren't even there?” There is of course another option, where we cancel what is not there in front of us, and replace that with objects and persons made of seed-pictures.  Then we can really fix our life.

gru.acip: ,BDEN GRUB RDUL TZAM MED PA LA, ,YOD PA LTAR DU MA 'DZIN CIG ,
gru.wylie: bden grub rdul tsam med pa la, ,yod pa ltar du ma 'dzin cig
gru.english: And so my final advice To you is that you Should never consider Things that possess Not a single atom Of real existence As if they actually did. Here the Devil actually is giving us some invaluable advice.  In a way, we cannot clarify in our own minds what is true, if we are never inspired to give careful thought to what is not true.  The Devil can be extremely useful! Twenty-Second Canto How to Find the Diamond Way Learning about bliss & emptiness

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, CHOS DUNG DKAR PO'I KHA DOG CHOS CAN, KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, DKAR PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, chos dung dkar po'i kha dog chos can, kha dog yin par thal, dkar po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: In that case, I disagree that the color of a white seashell is a color. If you do disagree, let's consider once more the color of a white seashell.  It is too a color! Why do you say that? Because it's white!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, CHOS DUNG DKAR PO'I KHA DOG CHOS CAN, DKAR PO YIN PAR THAL, CHOS DUNG DKAR PO'I KHA DOG DANG GCIG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, chos dung dkar po'i kha dog chos can, dkar po yin par thal, chos dung dkar po'i kha dog dang gcig yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that it's white. If you do disagree, let's again consider the color of a white seashell. It is too white! Why do you say that? Because it's identical to the color of a white seashell!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, DKAR PO DANG DMAR PO GNYIS KYI GZHI MTHUN MED PAR THAL, DKAR PO DANG DMAR PO GNYIS 'GAL BA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, dkar po dang dmar po gnyis kyi gzhi mthun med par thal, dkar po dang dmar po gnyis 'gal ba yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that it is impossible for one thing to be entirely white and entirely red. Suppose you do disagree.  It is too impossible for one thing to be entirely white and entirely red at the same time. Why do you say that? Because being entirely white and being entirely red are two contradictory things.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SANGS RGYAS RIN CHEN 'BYUNG LDAN GYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, SER PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sangs rgyas rin chen 'byung ldan gyi kha dog chos can, kha dog yin par thal, ser po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that the color of the Buddha named “Source of Jewels” is a color. If you do disagree, then let's again consider the color of Source of Jewels. It is too a color! Why do you say that? Because it's yellow!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SANGS RGYAS RIN CHEN 'BYUNG LDAN GYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, SER PO YIN PAR THAL, SANGS RGYAS RIN CHEN 'BYUNG LDAN GYI KHA DOG DANG GCIG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sangs rgyas rin chen 'byung ldan gyi kha dog chos can, ser po yin par thal, sangs rgyas rin chen 'byung ldan gyi kha dog dang gcig yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that the color of this Buddha is yellow. If you do disagree, let's consider once again the color of Source of Jewels.  It is too yellow! Why do you say that? Because it's identical to the color of the Buddha named “Source of Jewels”!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SANGS RGYAS TSE DPAG MED KYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, DMAR PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sangs rgyas tshe dpag med kyi kha dog chos can, kha dog yin par thal, dmar po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Well then, I disagree that the color of Limitless Life is a color. If you do disagree, then let's consider again the color of the Buddha named “Limitless Life.” It is too a color. Why do you say that? Because it is red!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SANGS RGYAS TSE DPAG MED KYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, DMAR PO YIN PAR THAL, SANGS RGYAS TSE DPAG MED KYI KHA DOG GI LDOG PA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sangs rgyas tshe dpag med kyi kha dog chos can, dmar po yin par thal, sangs rgyas tshe dpag med kyi kha dog gi ldog pa yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that the color of this Buddha is red. Suppose you do disagree.  Consider once again the color of the Buddha, Limitless Life. It is too red! Why do you say that? Because it is the reverse of all that is not the color of Limitless Life!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SANGS RGYAS TSE DPAG MED KYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, KHYOD KHYOD KYI LDOG PA YIN PAR THAL, KHYOD GZHI GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sangs rgyas tshe dpag med kyi kha dog chos can, khyod khyod kyi ldog pa yin par thal, khyod gzhi grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that the color of this Buddha is the reverse of the reverse of their color. Suppose you do disagree.  Consider once more the color of the Buddha named “Limitless Life.”  It is too the reverse of its reverse. Why do you say that? Because it is an example of reality.

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG, SANGS RGYAS DON YOD GRUB PA'I KHA DOG CHOS CAN, DKAR PO YIN PAR THAL, KHA DOG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang, sangs rgyas don yod grub pa'i kha dog chos can, dkar po yin par thal, kha dog yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: We can also make this point another way. Consider the color of the Buddha named “Amogha Siddhi,” or Accomplishment. So, I suppose it's white? Why do you say that? Because it is a color.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SANGS RGYAS DON YOD GRUB PA'I KHA DOG CHOS CAN, KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, LJANG GU YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sangs rgyas don yod grub pa'i kha dog chos can, kha dog yin par thal, ljang gu yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that the color of this Buddha is a color. Suppose you do disagree.  Consider the color of the Buddha named “Accomplishment.”  It is too a color. Why do you say that? Because it is green.

gru.acip: RTZA BAR 'DOD NA, SANGS RGYAS DON YOD GRUB PA'I KHA DOG CHOS CAN, DKAR PO MA YIN PAR THAL, SANGS RGYAS DON YOD GRUB PA'I KHA DOG DANG GCIG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rtsa bar 'dod na, sangs rgyas don yod grub pa'i kha dog chos can, dkar po ma yin par thal, sangs rgyas don yod grub pa'i kha dog dang gcig yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I agree with your original statement: the color of this Buddha is white. If you do agree with our original statement, then consider once again the color of this particular Buddha. It is not white! Why do you say that? Because it is identical with the color of the Buddha named “Accomplishment”! 3 Colors & The Four Primary Colors

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, NAG PO CHOS CAN, RTZA BA'I KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, NAG PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, nag po chos can, rtsa ba'i kha dog yin par thal, nag po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that black is a primary color. Suppose you do disagree.  And yet black is a primary color. Why do you say that? Because it is black!

gru.acip: RTAGS DANG PO MA GRUB NA, NAG PO CHOS CAN, DKAR PO MA YIN PAR THAL, NAG PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rtags dang po ma grub na, nag po chos can, dkar po ma yin par thal, nag po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree to the first part of your reason: it's not true that black is not white. Suppose you do disagree to the first part of our reason.  Consider black.  It is not white. Why do you say that? Because it is black!

gru.acip: RTAGS GNYIS PA MA GRUB NA, NAG PO CHOS CAN, SER PO MA YIN PAR THAL, NAG PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rtags gnyis pa ma grub na, nag po chos can, ser po ma yin par thal, nag po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree with the second part of your reason: it's not true that black is not yellow. If you do disagree with this second part, then consider black once again. It is not yellow. Why do you say that? Because it is black!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, 'JAM DBYANGS DMAR SER GYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, YAN LAG GI KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, DMAR PO DANG SER PO GNYIS KYI YAN LAG GI KHA DOG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, 'jam dbyangs dmar ser gyi kha dog chos can, yan lag gi kha dog yin par thal, dmar po dang ser po gnyis kyi yan lag gi kha dog yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that the russet-gold color of Gentle Voice is a secondary color. If you do disagree, then consider again the russet-gold color of Gentle Voice.  It is so a secondary color. Why do you say that? Because it's the secondary color you get when you mix red and gold.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, 'JAM DBYANGS DMAR SER GYI KHA DOG CHOS CAN, DMAR PO DANG SER PO GNYIS KYI YAN LAG GI KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, DMAR SER YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, 'jam dbyangs dmar ser gyi kha dog chos can, dmar po dang ser po gnyis kyi yan lag gi kha dog yin par thal, dmar ser yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that that russet-gold is the color you get when you mix red and gold. If you do disagree, then consider once more this russet-gold color. It is too the secondary color you get when you mix red and gold. Why do you say that? Because it is russet-gold!

gru.acip: RTAGS RE RE NAS GRUB STE, 'JAM DBYANGS DMAR SER GYI KHA DOG DANG GCIG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rtags re re nas grub ste, 'jam dbyangs dmar ser gyi kha dog dang gcig yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Each of the reasons given is correct, because the russet-gold color of Gentle Voice is identical to the russet-gold color of Gentle Voice.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, LJANG GU CHOS CAN, YAN LAG GI KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, NAG PO DANG SER PO GNYIS KYI YAN LAG GI KHA DOG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, ljang gu chos can, yan lag gi kha dog yin par thal, nag po dang ser po gnyis kyi yan lag gi kha dog yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that green is a secondary color. Suppose you do disagree.  And yet green is a secondary color! Why do you say that? Because it is the secondary color that you get when you mix black and yellow.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, LJANG GU CHOS CAN, NAG PO DANG SER PO GNYIS KYI YAN LAG GI KHA DOG YIN PAR THAL, LJANG GU YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, ljang gu chos can, nag po dang ser po gnyis kyi yan lag gi kha dog yin par thal, ljang gu yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that green is the secondary color you get when you mix black and yellow. If you do disagree, then again consider green.  It is too the secondary color you get when you mix black and yellow. Why do you say that? Because it's green!

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, TZANDAN GYI DRI CHOS CAN, GZUGS YIN PAR THAL, GZUGS RUNG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, tsandan gyi dri chos can, gzugs yin par thal, gzugs rung yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree that the smell of sandalwood is a form. Suppose you do disagree.  Let's consider again the smell of sandalwood.  It is too a form! Why do you say that? Because it is something you can point to as being a form.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, TZANDAN GYI DRI CHOS CAN, DER THAL, DRI DANG KHA DOG GNYIS 'GAL BA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, tsandan gyi dri chos can, der thal, dri dang kha dog gnyis 'gal ba yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that there is no one thing which is both a smell and a color at the same time. If you do disagree, then let's again consider the smell of sandalwood.  It is so true that it cannot be a smell and a color at the same time! Why do you say that? Because being a smell and being a color are contradictory to one another. 6 Form & the Door of Sense Of Visible Form

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SGRA CHOS CAN, GZUGS YIN PAR THAL, BEM PO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sgra chos can, gzugs yin par thal, bem po yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that sound is form. Consider, once again, sound.  It is too form. Why do you say that? Because it is matter.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SGRA CHOS CAN, BEM PO YIN PAR THAL, RDUL DU GRUB PA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sgra chos can, bem po yin par thal, rdul du grub pa yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that sound is matter. If you do disagree, then consider sound.  It is too matter. Why do you say that? Because it is something made of tiny physical particles.

gru.acip: MA KHYAB NA KHYAB PA YOD PAR THAL, RDUL DU GRUB PA BEM PO'I MTSAN NYID YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma khyab na khyab pa yod par thal, rdul du grub pa bem po'i mtshan nyid yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Just because something is made of tiny physical particles, doesn't mean it's matter. But it does mean that, because “something made of tiny physical particles” is in fact the definition of matter.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SGRA CHOS CAN, MIG SHES KYI BZUNG BYA MA YIN PAR THAL, RNA SHES KYI MNYAN BYA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sgra chos can, mig shes kyi bzung bya ma yin par thal, rna shes kyi mnyan bya yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that sound is not that object which is perceived by the consciousness of the eye. If you do disagree, then consider sound once again.  It is not that object which is perceived by the consciousness of the eye. Why do you say that? Because it is that object which is heard by the consciousness of the ear.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, SGRA CHOS CAN, RNA SHES KYI MNYAN BYA YIN PAR THAL, SGRA'I SKYE MCHED YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, sgra chos can, rna shes kyi mnyan bya yin par thal, sgra'i skye mched yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that sound is that object which is heard by the consciousness of the ear. Let's consider, once more, sound.  It is so that object which is heard by the consciousness of the ear. Why do you say that? Because it is the door of sense of sound.

gru.acip: MA GRUB NA, BUM PA CHOS CAN, KHYOD KHYOD DANG THA DAD LAS LDOG PAR THAL, KHYOD BDAG MED YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: ma grub na, bum pa chos can, khyod khyod dang tha dad las ldog par thal, khyod bdag med yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that a coffee cup is the reverse of everything which is different from it. If you do disagree, then let's again consider the coffee cup.  It is too the reverse of everything which is different from it! Why do you say that? Because it is something in the universe which has no self-nature!

gru.acip: GONG GI MA KHYAB MTSAMS LA RTAGS MA GRUB ZER NA, GSER BUM ZANGS BUM GNYIS CHOS CAN, BUM PA DANG THA DAD LAS MI LDOG PAR THAL, BUM PA DANG THA DAD YIN PA'I PHYIR,

Because they are different from a coffee cup! 7 If Something Is the Reverse Of All That Is Different From a Coffee Cup, Does It Have to Be The Reverse of All That Is Not a Coffee Cup?
