gru.acip: DBANG SHES DE RNAMS LA YUL GZUGS SOGS RNAMS NGO BO DANG KHYAD PAR GYI THA SNYAD BTAGS PA'I GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG ZHING SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PAR 'DOD PAS, DER GRUB PA BKAG NAS BKAG PA DE CHOS KYI BDAG MED DU 'JOG GO ,
gru.wylie: dbang shes de rnams la yul gzugs sogs rnams ngo bo dang khyad par gyi tha snyad btags pa'i gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par snang zhing snang ba ltar grub par 'dod pas, der grub pa bkag nas bkag pa de chos kyi bdag med du 'jog go
gru.english: They would say that it appears to these sense consciousnesses that their objects—visible form and the rest—are such that they are by definition what the terms which describe their basic natures and various features refer to; and that they must indeed exist in the way that they appear to. And then the absence that we establish by disproving that they could exist this way is what we [here in the Mind Only School] say is the lack of a self-nature to things.

gru.acip: DES NA SNGON 'DZIN MIG SHES LA SNGON PO SNGON POR SNANG BA'I TSE MING BRDAS BZHAG TZAM MA YIN PAR RANG GI GNAS TSUL GYI NGOS NAS GRUB PAR SNANG BA'I SNANG TSUL YOD PAR SHES PAS,
gru.wylie: des na sngon 'dzin mig shes la sngon po sngon por snang ba'i tshe ming brdas bzhag tsam ma yin par rang gi gnas tshul gyi ngos nas grub par snang ba'i snang tshul yod par shes pas
gru.english: And so when blue appears to be blue to the visual consciousness which is apprehending blue, this appears to be happening through the very nature of the blue, and not through the application of certain names and terms. And at some point we realize that this is how things are appearing to us.

gru.acip: MIG SHES KYI NGO BOR SNGON PO SNGON PO ZHES PA'I THA SNYAD 'JUG PA'I 'JUG GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA'I DON NI DE YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: mig shes kyi ngo bor sngon po sngon po zhes pa'i tha snyad 'jug pa'i 'jug gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par snang ba'i don ni de yin no
gru.english: This then is what it means when we say that—to the visual consciousness—it appears that blue is, by definition, what the term “blue” refers to.

gru.acip: DON SMRA SDE GNYIS KYIS SNGON PO LA SNGON PO'O ZHES BRJOD PA'I SGRA'I BRJOD BYA'I RANG LDOG RTOG BTAGS YIN PAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB CES 'DOD KYANG, SNGON PO SNGON PO ZHES PA'I SGRA 'JUG PA'I GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR 'DOD PAS RNAM RIG PA DANG MI 'DRA BA'I KHYAD PAR CHE'O,,
gru.wylie: don smra sde gnyis kyis sngon po la sngon po'o zhes brjod pa'i sgra'i brjod bya'i rang ldog rtog btags yin pas rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub ces 'dod kyang, sngon po sngon po zhes pa'i sgra 'jug pa'i gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par 'dod pas rnam rig pa dang mi 'dra ba'i khyad par che'o
gru.english: The two Objectist schools would agree that when we call blue “blue,” the thing that we're referring to with our words, from a conceptual point of view, is something labeled in our thoughts—and thus not something that exists by definition. They do believe, however, that blue is—by definition—the thing that we refer to when we say “blue.” As such, there is a huge difference between their beliefs and those of the Mentalists.

gru.acip: RNAM RIG PA'I SKABS 'DIR GZUGS SOGS RANG 'DZIN RTOG PA'I ZHEN GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PAR 'DOD PA NI
gru.wylie: rnam rig pa'i skabs 'dir gzugs sogs rang 'dzin rtog pa'i zhen gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub par 'dod pa ni
gru.english: And why is that? Well, first of all, let's look at what they mean, here in the context of the Mentalist School, when they assert that things like visible form are not, by definition, what the thoughts that are holding them think they are.

gru.acip: RTOG PA'I ZHEN GZHI'I RANG LDOG TZAM LA MI BYED KYI, DE'I GZHI LDOG BAG CHAGS BRTAN BYUNG GI DBANG SHES LA GZUGS SOGS KYI THA SNYAD GANG LA 'JUG PA'I GZHIR SNANG BA'I SNANG TSUL LTAR GYI DON LA 'DOD CING, SNANG BA LTAR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PAR 'DOD LA,
gru.wylie: rtog pa'i zhen gzhi'i rang ldog tsam la mi byed kyi, de'i gzhi ldog bag chags brtan byung gi dbang shes la gzugs sogs kyi tha snyad gang la 'jug pa'i gzhir snang ba'i snang tshul ltar gyi don la 'dod cing, snang ba ltar rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub par 'dod la
gru.english: When the Mentalists speak this way, they are not just talking about what these thoughts think they see, in a conceptual form. Rather, they are referring to the actual manifestation: they are referring to the visual form which appears to the sense consciousness as it has arisen from a solid seed. And what they say is that it does not exist, as it appears to, by definition.

gru.acip: MDO SDE PAS NI SNGON PO LA GZUGS SO ZHES PA'I SGRA'I BRJOD BYA'I CHA LTA BU RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PAR 'DOD KYANG, BSHAD MA THAG PA'I SNANG TSUL LTAR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR 'DOD PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: mdo sde pas ni sngon po la gzugs so zhes pa'i sgra'i brjod bya'i cha lta bu rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub par 'dod kyang, bshad ma thag pa'i snang tshul ltar rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par 'dod pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: The Sutrists believe that when we say of blue that “it is physical form,” it is not something which exists by definition from the point of view of being something which is expressed in words; they do however believe that it is something which exists by definition from the point of view how it appears, as we have just described that.

gru.acip: DES NA, BAG CHAGS BRTAN BYUNG GI DBANG SHES GCIG LA'ANG SNGON PO SNANG BA'I TSE, SNGON PO SNGON POR SNANG BA DANG, SNGON PO PHYI ROL DON DU SNANG BA DANG, SNGON PO SNGON PO ZHES PA'I THA SNYAD 'JUG PA'I GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA GSUM
gru.wylie: des na, bag chags brtan byung gi dbang shes gcig la'ang sngon po snang ba'i tshe, sngon po sngon por snang ba dang, sngon po phyi rol don du snang ba dang, sngon po sngon po zhes pa'i tha snyad 'jug pa'i gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par snang ba gsum
gru.english: When thus blue appears to even a single moment of sense consciousness which has arisen from a solid seed, three different things are going on: [1] the blue is appearing as blue; [2] the blue is appearing to be an outer object; and [3] the blue is appearing to be what the term “blue” applies to, by definition.

gru.acip: DANG DES DRANGS PA'I RTOG PA'ANG GSUM YOD PA LAS, SNGA MA NI RIGS MTHUN PA'I BAG CHAGS KYIS SNANG BA YIN PAS MI 'GOG CING, PHYI MA GNYIS SU SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PA 'GOG PA YIN TE 'CHAD PAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: dang des drangs pa'i rtog pa'ang gsum yod pa las, snga ma ni rigs mthun pa'i bag chags kyis snang ba yin pas mi 'gog cing, phyi ma gnyis su snang ba ltar grub pa 'gog pa yin te 'chad par 'gyur ro
gru.english: There are also three different thoughts elicited by these three appearances. The first of the three appearances is occurring due to a seed of a consistent type; and so we don't deny it. But we do deny that the latter two exist in the way they appear to—this point I will cover below. The Three Reasonings of Master Asanga, on naming things

gru.acip: DE YANG, THEG BSDUS LAS, ,MING GI SNGA ROL BLO MED PHYIR, ,MANG BA'I PHYIR DANG MA 'DRES PHYIR, ,DE YI BDAG NYID BDAG MANG DANG, ,BDAG 'DRES 'GAL BAS GRUB PAR 'GYUR, ,ZHES RIGS PA GSUM BSTAN PA'I
gru.wylie: de yang, theg bsdus las, ,ming gi snga rol blo med phyir, ,mang ba'i phyir dang ma 'dres phyir, ,de yi bdag nyid bdag mang dang, ,bdag 'dres 'gal bas grub par 'gyur, ,zhes rigs pa gsum bstan pa'i
gru.english: The Summary of the Greater Way presents three different forms of reasoning here: The point is made Because of the contradictions That it would exist in itself; There would be many selves; And the selves would be mixed— Since there is no thought That could come before the name; And they would be multiple; And they cannot mix together.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, LTO LDIR BA SOGS LA RANG RANG GI MING 'JUG PA DE RANG GI GNAS TSOD KYIS DBANG GIS 'JUG CING 'JUG GZHI DER RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA YIN NA,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, lto ldir ba sogs la rang rang gi ming 'jug pa de rang gi gnas tshod kyis dbang gis 'jug cing 'jug gzhi der rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa yin na
gru.english: Here's how the first of these reasonings goes. Suppose that when someone gave a name to something with a rounded belly, or anything of the like, they thought that the name applied to the thing by the very nature of the thing; and that the thing which received the name existed by definition. 3) The Proof That Water Pitchers Don't Get Their Names by Definition

gru.acip: LTO LDIR BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD LA BUM PA ZHES PA'I THA SNYAD 'JUG PA DE BRDA LA MI BLTOS PAR THAL, KHYOD BUM PA'O ZHES BRJOD PA'I THA SNYAD KYI GZHIR DNGOS PO'I GNAS TSOD KYI NGOS NAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: lto ldir ba chos can, khyod la bum pa zhes pa'i tha snyad 'jug pa de brda la mi bltos par thal, khyod bum pa'o zhes brjod pa'i tha snyad kyi gzhir dngos po'i gnas tshod kyi ngos nas rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: In that case, we'd have to address them with this reasoning: Consider this thing here, with a rounded belly. Are you saying that—when we call it a “water pitcher”—this giving it a name doesn't depend upon any term at all? Why do you ask that? Because the thing with a rounded belly is called a “water pitcher” just by its very nature: it is a “water pitcher” by definition.

gru.acip: DES NA, LTO LDIR BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD BUM PA'O ZHES BRJOD PA'I THA SNYAD KYI GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB STE, KHYOD LA BUM PA'O ZHES MING MA BTAGS PA'I GONG ROL NAS DE'O SNYAM PA'I BLO SKYE BA MED PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: des na, lto ldir ba chos can, khyod bum pa'o zhes brjod pa'i tha snyad kyi gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub ste, khyod la bum pa'o zhes ming ma btags pa'i gong rol nas de'o snyam pa'i blo skye ba med pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: And so thus it is that we can say: Take this thing with a rounded belly. It is not the case that it is, by definition, the thing that we apply the name “water pitcher” to; Because no thought has come up, before we apply the name “water pitcher” to it, which says to itself, “Oh, this thing is a water pitcher.” 4) The Proof That No One Is Called Different Names by Nature

gru.acip: RIGS PA GNYIS PA NI, SKYES BU GCIG LA DBANG PO DANG BRGYA BYIN DANG MIG STONG CAN SOGS MING MI 'DRA BA DU MA BTAGS PA'I TSE MING DE DAG SKYES BU DE LA DNGOS PO'I DBANG GIS 'JUG PAR THAL, DON DE MING DE DAG 'JUG PA'I 'JUG GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rigs pa gnyis pa ni, skyes bu gcig la dbang po dang brgya byin dang mig stong can sogs ming mi 'dra ba du ma btags pa'i tshe ming de dag skyes bu de la dngos po'i dbang gis 'jug par thal, don de ming de dag 'jug pa'i 'jug gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's look next at the second reasoning. Now let's consider a case where we refer to a single being with a variety of different names, such as “The Powerful One,” or “Destroyer of a Hundred Cities,” or “One with a Thousand Eyes,” and so on. Are you saying that all these names apply to this being by the being's very nature? Why do you say that? Because the fact that the being given these names is the one given the names is something which exists by definition.

gru.acip: DE LTAR THAL BA LAS, DON GCIG MING DU MA'I 'JUG GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB STE, DON GCIG PO DE DU MAR MI 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar thal ba las, don gcig ming du ma'i 'jug gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub ste, don gcig po de du mar mi 'gyur ba'i phyir ro
gru.english: Seeing the absurd consequences that thinking the opposite would lead to, we can then say: It is not the case that when a single object serves as what we give multiple names to, it serves this way by definition; Because a single object couldn't then become many. 5) The Proof That One Name Is Never Applied to Different People by Nature

gru.acip: RIGS PA GSUM PA NI, SKYES BU MI 'DRA BA GNYIS LA BKRA SHIS ZHES MING 'DRA BA GCIG BTAGS PA'I TSE MING DE DON DE GNYIS LA DNGOS DBANG GIS 'JUG PAR THAL, DON MI 'DRA BA GNYIS PO DE MING GCIG PO 'JUG PA'I 'JUG GZHIR RANG GI GNAS LUGS KYI DBANG GIS GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rigs pa gsum pa ni, skyes bu mi 'dra ba gnyis la bkra shis zhes ming 'dra ba gcig btags pa'i tshe ming de don de gnyis la dngos dbang gis 'jug par thal, don mi 'dra ba gnyis po de ming gcig po 'jug pa'i 'jug gzhir rang gi gnas lugs kyi dbang gis grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Which brings us to the third reasoning: Let's consider a case where the same name, “Jon,” is applied to two different people. Are you saying that this name applies to the two different people by their very nature? Why do you say that? Because these two different people serve as what the single name applies to by their very nature.

gru.acip: DE LTAR THAL BA LAS DON GNYIS PO DE CHOS CAN, MING GCIG PO DE 'JUG PA'I 'JUG GZHIR RANG GIS MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB STE, KHYOD MI 'DRA BA'I THA DAD YIN PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar thal ba las don gnyis po de chos can, ming gcig po de 'jug pa'i 'jug gzhir rang gis mtshan nyid kyis ma grub ste, khyod mi 'dra ba'i tha dad yin pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Seeing the absurd consequence of this train of thinking, we can instead say: Let's consider these two people. The fact that the two of them are what the one name is given to cannot be something that exists by definition; Because they are in fact two different, separate people.

gru.acip: 'ON KYANG, MDO SDE PA LTAR NA BUM PA ZHES PA'I BRDA'I DNGOS KYI BRJOD BYA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB NA, BUM PA'O SNYAM PA'I BLO SKYE BA DE BRDA 'BREL BYAS PA LA MI BLTOS PA'I SKYON YOD KYANG,
gru.wylie: 'on kyang, mdo sde pa ltar na bum pa zhes pa'i brda'i dngos kyi brjod bya rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub na, bum pa'o snyam pa'i blo skye ba de brda 'brel byas pa la mi bltos pa'i skyon yod kyang
gru.english: But let's look at the Sutrist view here. They would agree that there is this problem that—if something were to exist, by definition, as the direct referent of the name “water pitcher”—then when the thought came up in our mind, “Oh, this is a water pitcher,” it would not have to rely on having made any connection between the term and the object.

gru.acip: DBANG SHES LA LTO LDIR BA DE BUM PA'I MING 'JUG PA'I GZHIR SNANG TSUL LTAR RANG GIS MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA LA DE LTA BU'I SKYON MED CES SMRA YANG,
gru.wylie: dbang shes la lto ldir ba de bum pa'i ming 'jug pa'i gzhir snang tshul ltar rang gis mtshan nyid kyis grub pa la de lta bu'i skyon med ces smra yang
gru.english: At the same time though they would say that the way in which the thing with the rounded belly appears to the sense consciousness as being the thing that the word “water pitcher” applies to is something that exists by definition; and so the problem would not apply, in this sense.

gru.acip: 'O NA, RIGS PA DE DAG GIS NGO BO DANG KHYAD PAR LA KUN BTAGS PA'I KUN BTAGS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PA RTOGS NUS KYANG, GZUGS SOGS PHYI ROL DON GYIS STONG PA JI LTAR RTOGS NUS ZHE NA,
gru.wylie: 'o na, rigs pa de dag gis ngo bo dang khyad par la kun btags pa'i kun btags rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub pa rtogs nus kyang, gzugs sogs phyi rol don gyis stong pa ji ltar rtogs nus zhe na
gru.english: One may now ask the following question: We can understand now, from the different forms of reasoning you've discussed, how it is that the process of attributing a basic nature, and various features, to things is something that can't be happening by definition. How next are we to understand the way it is that things like form are empty of being outer objects?

gru.acip: NUS TE, BSHAD MA THAG PA LTAR GZUGS SOGS RANG 'DZIN RTOG PA'I ZHEN GZHIR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR KHEGS PA NA, DE'I TSE SNANG BA LTAR ZHEN PA'I RTOG PA DE ZHEN YUL LA 'KHRUL PAR 'GRUB LA,
gru.wylie: nus te, bshad ma thag pa ltar gzugs sogs rang 'dzin rtog pa'i zhen gzhir rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par khegs pa na, de'i tshe snang ba ltar zhen pa'i rtog pa de zhen yul la 'khrul par 'grub la
gru.english: Here's how it's done. As I've just explained, we can disprove the way in which we tend to think that things like form exist, by definition, as the objects of our perceptions. And we thus further prove that these thoughts are mistaken towards what they are considering; believing that they exist as they appear to.

gru.acip: DE GRUB PA'I STOBS KYIS DE LTAR SNANG BA'I DBANG SHES RNAMS KYANG RANG GI SNANG YUL LA 'KHRUL PAR 'GRUB,
gru.wylie: de grub pa'i stobs kyis de ltar snang ba'i dbang shes rnams kyang rang gi snang yul la 'khrul par 'grub
gru.english: Proving that they are mistaken proves, in turn, that the sense consciousnesses are also mistaken, when things appear that way to them.

gru.acip: DE GRUB NA DBANG SHES LA SNGON PO SOGS KYI RNAM PA SHAR BA DE, PHYI ROL DON GYIS RANG 'DRA'I RNAM PA TSUR GTAD NAS SHAR BA MA YIN GYI,
gru.wylie: de grub na dbang shes la sngon po sogs kyi rnam pa shar ba de, phyi rol don gyis rang 'dra'i rnam pa tshur gtad nas shar ba ma yin gyi
gru.english: And once we establish that, we see that when things like blue make their appearance to the sense consciousness, it's not as though this appearing is something that happens through a process where an outer object is presenting a likeness of itself inwards, towards the consciousness.

gru.acip: RANG SNANG MKHAN GYI DBANG SHES RNAMS SNGO SOGS DE DANG DE'I BDAG NYID DU SKYES PAR RTOGS PAS, SNGO SOGS RANG SNANG MKHAN GYI SHES PA DANG RDZAS GCIG DU GRUB PO,,
gru.wylie: rang snang mkhan gyi dbang shes rnams sngo sogs de dang de'i bdag nyid du skyes par rtogs pas, sngo sogs rang snang mkhan gyi shes pa dang rdzas gcig du grub po
gru.english: Rather, we come to realize that the sense consciousness which is appearing blue is doing so because it has actually arisen itself as a blue entity. And then we are able to establish that things like blue are actually made of the same material as the awareness which is appearing blue.

gru.acip: DE GRUB NA, SNGO SOGS RANG SNANG BA'I SHES PA LAS RDZAS THA DAD KYIS STONG BAR 'GRUB PA'I PHYIR NA PHYI ROL GYI DON MED PAR KHONG DU CHUD PAR 'GYUR BA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: de grub na, sngo sogs rang snang ba'i shes pa las rdzas tha dad kyis stong bar 'grub pa'i phyir na phyi rol gyi don med par khong du chud par 'gyur ba yin no
gru.english: And once we establish that, we thereby establish that the blue or whatever it may be is actually empty of being any separate substance from the awareness which is appearing blue and so on. And with that, we finally grasp that there are no outer objects. What exactly is an “outer object”?

gru.acip: SPYIR DE GNYIS KYIS GZUGS 'DZIN PA'I SKYES BU LA GZUGS RGYANGS CHAD KYI TSUL DU SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PAS PHYI DON YOD CES 'DOD LA,
gru.wylie: spyir de gnyis kyis gzugs 'dzin pa'i skyes bu la gzugs rgyangs chad kyi tshul du snang ba ltar grub pas phyi don yod ces 'dod la
gru.english: Generally speaking, what these two groups call an “outer object” is one that does exist as it appears to, when for example a form appears to a person who is holding it as though it existed out there, to a distance.

gru.acip: MDO SDE PAS SNGON PO DANG SNGON 'DZIN DBANG SHES GNYIS RGYANGS CHAD DU SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PAR 'DOD CING DE LTAR SNANG BA DE, YUL GYI NGOS NAS RANG 'DRA'I RNAM PA TSUR GTAD NAS SHAR BA'I PHYI DON YIN PAR 'DOD DO,,
gru.wylie: mdo sde pas sngon po dang sngon 'dzin dbang shes gnyis rgyangs chad du snang ba ltar grub par 'dod cing de ltar snang ba de, yul gyi ngos nas rang 'dra'i rnam pa tshur gtad nas shar ba'i phyi don yin par 'dod do
gru.english: The Sutrists believe that—when blue and the sense consciousness which holds the blue appear to exist at a distance from each other—they actually do exist this way. They also believe that when things appear this way, what's happening is that the object of the perception is presenting a likeness of itself that goes from its side inwards, towards the consciousness. And this is what they would call an “outer” object.

gru.acip: RANG RGYUD PA DANG SEMS TZAM PA GNYIS KYI LUGS LA PHYI ROL GYI DON MED PAS, DE GNYIS KYIS TSUR MTHONG GI RGYUD KYI SNGON 'DZIN DBANG SHES LA SNGON PO RGYANGS CHAD DU SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB PAR 'DOD DE,
gru.wylie: rang rgyud pa dang sems tsam pa gnyis kyi lugs la phyi rol gyi don med pas, de gnyis kyis tshur mthong gi rgyud kyi sngon 'dzin dbang shes la sngon po rgyangs chad du snang ba ltar ma grub par 'dod de
gru.english: According to both members of the Independent branch of the Middle Way, and those of the Mind Only School, outer objects don't exist. They say that something like the blue cannot exist the way it seems to, to a person who holds that things are coming from their side. That is, when the blue appears to the sense consciousness holding to blue as though it existed at a distance, this is not the way things actually are.

gru.acip: DER THAL, DE YIN NA, PHYOGS CHA YOD DGOS PA'I PHYIR TE, DE YIN NA, GO SA MNON NUS SU YOD DGOS LA, DE LTA NA PHYOGS CHA DANG BCAS PAR 'GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, de yin na, phyogs cha yod dgos pa'i phyir te, de yin na, go sa mnon nus su yod dgos la, de lta na phyogs cha dang bcas par 'grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that if something is an atom, it's got to have parts. But it does, because if something is an atom, it must possess sides! Because if something is an atom, it's got to be something that can occupy a spot in space. And if something occupies a spot in space, that in itself proves that it must have sides!

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG, PHYI ROL GYI DON MED DE, SNGON 'DZIN DBANG PO'I MNGON SUM LA SNGON PO RGYANGS CHAD DU SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang, phyi rol gyi don med de, sngon 'dzin dbang po'i mngon sum la sngon po rgyangs chad du snang ba ltar ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: We can also say it this way: No outer objects exist. Because when it seems to the direct sense perception which holds to blue that the blue exists out there, at a distance, this is not in fact the case at all.

gru.acip: DE NI THEG BSDUS LAS, ,YI DVAGS DUD 'GRO MI RNAMS DANG, ,LHA RNAMS JI LTAR RIGS RIGS SU, ,DNGOS GCIG YID NI THA DAD PHYIR, ,DON MA GRUB PAR 'DOD PA YIN, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA'I RIGS PA'O,,
gru.wylie: de ni theg bsdus las, ,yi dvags dud 'gro mi rnams dang, ,lha rnams ji ltar rigs rigs su, ,dngos gcig yid ni tha dad phyir, ,don ma grub par 'dod pa yin, ,zhes gsungs pa'i rigs pa'o
gru.english: This source of this particular reasoning is a verse in A Summary of the Greater Way: We say that no such objects Even exist, for the reason that A single object is perceived In separate ways By a craving spirit, an animal, A human, and a worldly god— Each according to their kind. 10) The Kaleidoscope Proof That There Are No Outer Objects

gru.acip: DER THAL, LHAN CIG DMIGS NGES DE, SNGON PO DANG SNGON 'DZIN TSAD MA RDZAS GZHAN MA YIN PAR SGRUB PA'I RTAGS YANG DAG YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, lhan cig dmigs nges de, sngon po dang sngon 'dzin tshad ma rdzas gzhan ma yin par sgrub pa'i rtags yang dag yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that they are invariably found in conjunction. And yet they are, because “they are invariably found in conjunction” is a correct reason for proving that blue and an accurate perception holding to the blue are made of no different material.

gru.acip: RTAGS DE'I DON NGES DKA' BAS BZHED PA MI MTHUN PA MANG DU SNANG YANG, MKHAS GRUB RIN PO CHES BSHAD PA LTAR, 'DIR LHAN CIG NI YUL DUS GCIG PA DANG, DMIGS PA NI TSAD MAS DMIGS PA DANG, NGES PA NI KHYAB PA'I DON YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: rtags de'i don nges dka' bas bzhed pa mi mthun pa mang du snang yang, mkhas grub rin po ches bshad pa ltar, 'dir lhan cig ni yul dus gcig pa dang, dmigs pa ni tshad mas dmigs pa dang, nges pa ni khyab pa'i don yin no
gru.english: It's particularly difficult to grasp the meaning of this particular reason; and we see many different opinions about how to interpret it. Kedrup Je though explains it as follows. Found “in conjunction” means that the time period in which the object exists matches the period in which the perception exists. “Found” means “can be observed with an accurate perception.” And “invariably” means that these are always the case.

gru.acip: DE'I TSE DE GNYIS RDZAS GCIG YIN LA, SNGON 'DZIN TSAD MA LA SNGON PO RGYANGS CHAD KYI TSUL DU SNANG BA LTAR GRUB NA, DE GNYIS RDZAS THA DAD YIN PAR 'GYUR BAS LHAN CIG DMIGS MA YIN PAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: de'i tshe de gnyis rdzas gcig yin la, sngon 'dzin tshad ma la sngon po rgyangs chad kyi tshul du snang ba ltar grub na, de gnyis rdzas tha dad yin par 'gyur bas lhan cig dmigs ma yin par 'gyur ro
gru.english: When the blue is being focused upon by the apperception, we would have to say that it and the original accurate perception of it were made of the same thing; but if the blue did exist at a distance, as it appears to for the original accurate perception holding to blue, then the two would have to amount to two different things. And in that case the blue and the original perception of the blue could not be existing simultaneously, in conjunction. 12) The Ancient Habituation Proof for Why Objects Appear as Outer

gru.acip: SEMS TZAM PAS RIGS PAS BSGRUBS PA'I PHYI ROL DON GYIS STONG PA'I STONG NYID DE, THAL RANG GNYIS DANG SNGAGS KYI SKABS SU'ANG KHAS LEN DGOS PAR RJE YAB SRAS KYIS BSHAD DO,,
gru.wylie: sems tsam pas rigs pas bsgrubs pa'i phyi rol don gyis stong pa'i stong nyid de, thal rang gnyis dang sngags kyi skabs su'ang khas len dgos par rje yab sras kyis bshad do
gru.english: The Lord and his spiritual sons state that emptiness—in the form of the world being empty, as established by the proofs of the Mind Only School, of outer objects—is something that we can as well accept in the context of both branches of the Middle Way (the Consequence and Independent branches); and in the teachings of the secret way.

gru.acip: DE YANG THAL 'GYUR BAS NI SO SKYE'I RGYUD KYI GZUGS SGRA SOGS 'DZIN PA'I GNOD MED KYI BLO DON MTHUN RNAMS LA NI, YUL GZUGS SGRA SOGS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB BAR SNANG YANG SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB PAS, DE RNAMS SNANG YUL LA 'KHRUL BAR 'DOD LA,
gru.wylie: de yang thal 'gyur bas ni so skye'i rgyud kyi gzugs sgra sogs 'dzin pa'i gnod med kyi blo don mthun rnams la ni, yul gzugs sgra sogs rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub bar snang yang snang ba ltar ma grub pas, de rnams snang yul la 'khrul bar 'dod la
gru.english: Now the members of the Consequence branch of the Middle Way School begin with states of perception, within the mind of a normal person, which are free of any particular adventitious problems of perception and are nominally consistent with what they are considering—things like visible forms, sounds, and so on. These objects—the visible forms, sounds, and the rest—appear to those states of mind as if they existed by definition, whereas in fact they do not exist as they appear to. The followers of this branch then would say that these perceptions are mistaken towards the objects as they appear to the mind.

gru.acip: RANG RGYUD PAS NI, BLO DE RNAMS LA DE LTAR SNANG ZHING SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PAR 'DOD PAS, SNANG YUL LA MA 'KHRUL BAR BZHED DE, THAL RANG GNYIS KYI DGAG BYA LA PHRA RAGS KYI KHYAD PAR CHE'O,,
gru.wylie: rang rgyud pas ni, blo de rnams la de ltar snang zhing snang ba ltar grub par 'dod pas, snang yul la ma 'khrul bar bzhed de, thal rang gnyis kyi dgag bya la phra rags kyi khyad par che'o
gru.english: Followers of the Independent branch though would say that these objects are both appearing to these states of mind as we described, and at the same time actually existing the way they appear to. As such, they would assert that these perceptions are unmistaken towards their objects as these objects appear to the mind. There is a vast difference in subtlety then between how the Consequence and the Independent branches describe what it is that the concept of no-self denies.

gru.acip: DES NA 'DI PA'I LUGS LA CHOS THAMS CAD BLO DON MTHUN NAM GNOD MED LA SNANG BA'I DBANG GIS BZHAG PA TZAM DU BZHED PAS, BLO GNOD MED LA SNANG BA'I DBANG GIS BZHAG PA TZAM MIN PAR YUL RANG GI SDOD LUGS KYIS NGOS NAS GRUB PA NI RTAGS KYI DGAG BYA YIN LA,
gru.wylie: des na 'di pa'i lugs la chos thams cad blo don mthun nam gnod med la snang ba'i dbang gis bzhag pa tsam du bzhed pas, blo gnod med la snang ba'i dbang gis bzhag pa tsam min par yul rang gi sdod lugs kyis ngos nas grub pa ni rtags kyi dgag bya yin la
gru.english: And thus we can say that, according to those who follow the Independent Branch, every existing entity in the universe is established as existing by virtue of its having made its appearance to a consistent—or we can say, unaffected—state of mind. Thus too, in this sub-school, the thing that we deny with our reasoning on this topic is any object which could exist through its own way of being, rather than being established by virtue of having made its appearance to an unaffected state of mind.

gru.acip: DE LTAR GRUB PA ZHIG BYUNG NA, BDEN PAR GRUB PA DON DAM PAR GRUB PA SOGS SU 'GYUR BA YIN PAS, DE LTAR GRUB PAR 'DZIN PA NI BDEN 'DZIN LHAN SKYES SU 'DOD CING, BDEN 'DZIN LA SHES SGRIB KYIS KHYAB PAR BZHED DO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar grub pa zhig byung na, bden par grub pa don dam par grub pa sogs su 'gyur ba yin pas, de ltar grub par 'dzin pa ni bden 'dzin lhan skyes su 'dod cing, bden 'dzin la shes sgrib kyis khyab par bzhed do
gru.english: If a particular object were to exist through its own way of being, then it would be what we call “existing in truth,” or “existing in an ultimate sense,” and so on. And in this particular branch, holding things to exist this way is what our inborn tendency to see things as real does. They would further say that all forms of holding things as real are obstacles to omniscience.

gru.acip: DPE DE DON LA SBYAR NA, MIG BSLAD PA'I LTAD MO BA LA SGYU MA'I RTA GLANG JI LTAR SNANG BA DE BZHIN DU, MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA'I THA MAL BA'I SEMS CAN RNAMS LA CHOS 'DI DAG SNANG BA NA BLO LA SNANG BA'I DBANG GIS BZHAG PA MA YIN PAR RANG GI SDOD LUGS KYI NGOS NAS GRUB PAR SNANG NGO,,
gru.wylie: dpe de don la sbyar na, mig bslad pa'i ltad mo ba la sgyu ma'i rta glang ji ltar snang ba de bzhin du, ma rig pas bslad pa'i tha mal ba'i sems can rnams la chos 'di dag snang ba na blo la snang ba'i dbang gis bzhag pa ma yin par rang gi sdod lugs kyi ngos nas grub par snang ngo
gru.english: Now let's apply this metaphor to real life. Consider first how an illusory horse or elephant appears to an onlooker whose eyes are infected. This is how all the things around them appear to exist, to the average living being—to someone whose eyes are infected by misunderstanding. Things seem to exist from their own side, just from the way they are, and are not things which are established as existing due to their appearance to the mind.

gru.acip: ,MIG MA BSLAD PA LA RTA GLANG DU SNANG ZHEN GNYIS KA MED PA LTAR, JI LTA BA MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA'I 'PHAGS PA'I YE SHES KYI GZIGS NGOR BDEN GRUB KYI SNANG ZHEN GNYIS KA MED DO,,
gru.wylie: mig ma bslad pa la rta glang du snang zhen gnyis ka med pa ltar, ji lta ba mngon sum du rtogs pa'i 'phags pa'i ye shes kyi gzigs ngor bden grub kyi snang zhen gnyis ka med do
gru.english: Neither horses nor elephants appear to a person whose eyes are uninfected; nor is there any question of their believing in these particular creatures. This then stands as a metaphor for what happens in the perceptions of a realized being who is in the act of perceiving, directly, the real way things are. Nothing appears to these perceptions as existing in truth; and neither would they believe in such a thing even if it did. 14) The Proof of Neither One nor Many, Independent Style

gru.acip: DGAG BYA DE 'GOG PA'I GCIG DU BRAL GYI RIGS PA 'CHAD PA LA GNYIS, RTAGS 'GOD PA DANG, TSUL SGRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: dgag bya de 'gog pa'i gcig du bral gyi rigs pa 'chad pa la gnyis, rtags 'god pa dang, tshul sgrub pa'o
gru.english: Let's turn now to the reasoning that we use to disprove the existence of this unreal thing that emptiness is devoid of. This logic is known as “Neither One nor Many,” and we will cover it in two steps: setting forth the actual proof, and then demonstrating how the different necessary relationships required in a valid proof do hold true with it.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, MYU GU CHOS CAN, BDEN PAR MED DE, BDEN GRUB KYI GCIG DANG BDEN GRUB KYI DU MA GANG RUNG DU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR, DPER NA GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, myu gu chos can, bden par med de, bden grub kyi gcig dang bden grub kyi du ma gang rung du ma grub pa'i phyir, dper na gzugs brnyan bzhin
gru.english: Here is the first: Consider a sprout. It does not exist in truth, Because it is neither one thing which exists in truth, nor multiple things which exist in truth. It is, for example, similar to the reflection of an object in a mirror.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, KHYAB PA DANG PHYOGS CHOS SGRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa la gnyis, khyab pa dang phyogs chos sgrub pa'o
gru.english: The second part here has two sections of its own: first we establish that the relationships of necessity hold, and then we establish that the relationship between the subject and the reason holds.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, BDEN GRUB KYI GCIG DANG DE'I DU MA GANG RUNG DU MA GRUB NA, BDEN PAR MED PAS KHYAB STE, BDEN GRUB TU YOD NA, DE GNYIS GANG RUNG DU YOD DGOS PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, bden grub kyi gcig dang de'i du ma gang rung du ma grub na, bden par med pas khyab ste, bden grub tu yod na, de gnyis gang rung du yod dgos pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Here is the first: It is indeed the case that—if something is neither one thing which exists in truth, nor multiple things which exist in truth—then it cannot exist in truth. And that's true because—if something were to exist in truth—then it would necessarily have to exist as one or the other of those two. 15) The Proof of Not One, Because of Parts

gru.acip: GNYIS PA PHYOGS CHOS SGRUB PA LA GNYIS LAS DANG PO NI,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa phyogs chos sgrub pa la gnyis las dang po ni
gru.english: As for the second step, where we establish that the relationship between the subject and the reason holds, we proceed in two stages. Here is the first.

gru.acip: MYU GU CHOS CAN, BDEN GRUB KYI GCIG TU MED DE, CHA BCAS YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: myu gu chos can, bden grub kyi gcig tu med de, cha bcas yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Consider a sprout. It cannot exist as one thing which exists in truth, Because it is something which has its own parts.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, BDEN GRUB KYI GCIG YIN NA, CHA MED KYI GCIG YIN DGOS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, bden grub kyi gcig yin na, cha med kyi gcig yin dgos pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that it is necessarily the case that—if something has its own parts—it cannot exist as one thing which exists in truth. And yet it is necessarily the case; for if something were one thing which existed in truth, then it would have to be a singular object without any parts of its own.

gru.acip: DER THAL, CHA SHAS KYI DBYE BA YOD NA, PHAN TSUN BLTOS NAS GRUB PAS BDEN GRUB YIN PAR 'GAL BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, cha shas kyi dbye ba yod na, phan tshun bltos nas grub pas bden grub yin par 'gal ba'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that if something were one thing which existed in truth, then it would have to be a singular object without any parts of its own. And yet it would have to be, Because if a thing were divided into parts, then these parts would exist through relying on each other; and it would then be a contradiction to say that the thing existed in truth.

gru.acip: 'DOD NA, CHA BCAS SU GRUB PO,,
gru.wylie: 'dod na, cha bcas su grub po
gru.english: Well yes, I can agree to that: the atom in the middle has one part where the atom to the east is touching it, but where the atom to the west is not touching it. If you do agree, then it follows that the atom in the middle is something which has parts!

gru.acip: MYU GU CHOS CAN, BDEN GRUB KYI DU MAR MED DE, BDEN GRUB KYI GCIG MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: myu gu chos can, bden grub kyi du mar med de, bden grub kyi gcig med pa'i phyir
gru.english: The proof at this point goes like this: Consider a sprout; It cannot be multiple things which exist in truth, Because there is no such thing as one thing which exists in truth.

gru.acip: RTAGS NI CHA MED BKAG PAS 'GRUB PO,,
gru.wylie: rtags ni cha med bkag pas 'grub po
gru.english: I disagree that it does necessarily follow for the reason that wherever examples of multiple things exist, there must as well exist an example of one of those things. And yet this reason holds true, for the simple reason that we have already disproven the idea that anything could not have parts.

gru.acip: DE LTAR CHOS THAMS CAD CHA BCAS SU GRUB NA CHOS RE RE LA'ANG CHA DANG CHA CAN GNYIS RE YOD PAR 'GRUB BO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar chos thams cad cha bcas su grub na chos re re la'ang cha dang cha can gnyis re yod par 'grub bo
gru.english: And the reason for that is—once we have proven, in the way that we did, that every existing entity in the universe has parts—then we have by the way proven that for each one of these we can further find both the parts, and the whole which possesses these parts.

gru.acip: DE 'DRA BA DE NYID BLO LA SNANG BA'I DBANG BA'I BZHAG PA'I BRDZUN PA'I SDOD LUGS YIN GYI, BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I SDOD LUGS NI MA YIN TE, BDEN PAR GRUB NA SNANG TSUL DANG GNAS TSUL MTHUN DGOS PA'I PHYIR TE, MI MTHUN NA BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I DON MA TSANG BA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de 'dra ba de nyid blo la snang ba'i dbang ba'i bzhag pa'i brdzun pa'i sdod lugs yin gyi, bden par grub pa'i sdod lugs ni ma yin te, bden par grub na snang tshul dang gnas tshul mthun dgos pa'i phyir te, mi mthun na bden par grub pa'i don ma tshang ba'i phyir ro
gru.english: This kind of situation—this very situation—is a case where the way a thing exists is false: where it is established as false because of the way it appears to the mind. This is not a case where the way the thing exists is in truth—for if something were to exist in truth, then the way it appears to us and the way it really is would have to match. If they don't match, then the very criterion for something to exist in truth is missing.

gru.acip: PHYI MA GRUB STE, BUM 'DZIN DBANG SHES LA NI BUM PA'I MCHU ZHABS DANG LTO BA MGRIN PA SOGS KYI CHA RNAMS SO SOR SNANG BA GANG ZHIG, BUM PA DE NYID CHA CAN GCIG TU GNAS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: phyi ma grub ste, bum 'dzin dbang shes la ni bum pa'i mchu zhabs dang lto ba mgrin pa sogs kyi cha rnams so sor snang ba gang zhig, bum pa de nyid cha can gcig tu gnas pa'i phyir
gru.english: This latter proof is established as follows. The spout, belly, neck, and so forth of the water pitcher—its parts—appear to the sense perception holding the pitcher to be separate things; whereas the pitcher itself exists as a single whole.

gru.acip: GCIG DU BRAL GYI RTAGS 'DI KHYAB BYED MA DMIGS PA'I RTAGS YIN LA, CHA BCAS DANG RTEN 'BREL GYI RTAGS GNYIS NI, MYU GU BDEN MED DU SGRUB PA'I 'GAL ZLA DMIGS PA'I RTAGS YANG DAG YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: gcig du bral gyi rtags 'di khyab byed ma dmigs pa'i rtags yin la, cha bcas dang rten 'brel gyi rtags gnyis ni, myu gu bden med du sgrub pa'i 'gal zla dmigs pa'i rtags yang dag yin no
gru.english: The proof we call “One & Many” is the kind of logical statement in which the reason given is a negative where one thing that always implies another is missing. The two proofs based on having parts, and on being interdependent, employ correct reasons which prove that a sprout is devoid of reality due to the presence of something whose presence is always inconsistent with the presence of something else.

gru.acip: MTHUN DPE GZUGS BRNYAN LA BRTEN NAS BDEN MED NGES TSUL NI, BYAD BZHIN GYI GZUGS BRNYAN DE BYAD BZHIN DU SNANG YANG SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB PA NGES SLA BAS, DE NGES ZIN NAS DPE DE BZHIN DU, MYU GU LTA BU YANG RANG RE'I BLO NGOR BDEN PAR SNANG YANG SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB PA'O ZHES NGES PAR BYED PA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: mthun dpe gzugs brnyan la brten nas bden med nges tshul ni, byad bzhin gyi gzugs brnyan de byad bzhin du snang yang snang ba ltar ma grub pa nges sla bas, de nges zin nas dpe de bzhin du, myu gu lta bu yang rang re'i blo ngor bden par snang yang snang ba ltar ma grub pa'o zhes nges par byed pa yin no
gru.english: Let's do though talk a bit about how we can come to an understanding of how nothing exists in truth, by utilizing the combined example of a reflection in a mirror. The reflection of an object in a mirror may appear to actually be that object; and yet it does not exist in the way it seems to. This point is perceived easily; and then we go on from the example to see something similar: we come to an understanding of the idea that something like a sprout—despite the fact that it appears to our minds as though it exists in truth—does not exist in the way it seems to.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, 'DI PA'I LUGS LA CHOS RNAMS RTOG PA'I DBANG GIS 'JOG TSUL SHES DGOS TE, DE SHES NA, CHOS RNAMS RTOG PAS BTAGS TZAM DU 'GRUB LA, DE GRUB NA RTOG PAS BTAGS TZAM MA YIN PA'I CHOS MED PAR GO BAS SO,,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, 'di pa'i lugs la chos rnams rtog pa'i dbang gis 'jog tshul shes dgos te, de shes na, chos rnams rtog pas btags tsam du 'grub la, de grub na rtog pas btags tsam ma yin pa'i chos med par go bas so
gru.english: Here is the first. We must come to an understanding of how this particular system demonstrates that every existing thing in the universe is established through our conceptions. If we do, then we can confirm that all of these entities are simply projected by these conceptions; and once we do that, we can grasp that there is nothing in the universe which is not simply projected this way.

gru.acip: DE LTAR NA, RTOG PAS BTAGS TZAM MA YIN PA'I SDOD LUGS SU GRUB PA NI, RTAGS KYI DGAG BYA'I TSAD MTHAR THUG PA YIN LA,
gru.wylie: de ltar na, rtog pas btags tsam ma yin pa'i sdod lugs su grub pa ni, rtags kyi dgag bya'i tshad mthar thug pa yin la
gru.english: As such, we can say that the ultimate description of what we deny when we speak of no-self is something that exists in such a way that it is not simply projected by our conceptions.

gru.acip: DE DANG BRTEN NAS BZHAG PA MA YIN PA'I YOD PA DANG, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA, RANG NGOS NAS GRUB PA, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA, BDEN PAR GRUB PA RNAMS DON 'DRA'O,,
gru.wylie: de dang brten nas bzhag pa ma yin pa'i yod pa dang, rang bzhin gyis grub pa, rang ngos nas grub pa, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa, bden par grub pa rnams don 'dra'o
gru.english: We can then say as well that the point is similar whether we describe what we deny in that way; or by saying that it is anything that could exist in a way where it was not established as existing through things depending on other things; or which existed through some nature of its own; or existed from its own side; or existed by definition; or existed in truth.

gru.acip: RTOG PA YOD PA KHO NAS YOD PA NYID DANG, RTOG PAS MED PAR YOD PA NYID MED PA DE DAG NI GOR MA CHAG PAR THAG PA BSDOGS PA LA BTAGS PA'I SBRUL LTAR RANG GI NGO BOS MA GRUB PAR NGES SO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR CHOS THAMS CAD RTOG PAS BTAGS TZAM DU 'JOG GO
gru.wylie: rtog pa yod pa kho nas yod pa nyid dang, rtog pas med par yod pa nyid med pa de dag ni gor ma chag par thag pa bsdogs pa la btags pa'i sbrul ltar rang gi ngo bos ma grub par nges so, ,zhes gsungs pa ltar chos thams cad rtog pas btags tsam du 'jog go
gru.english: It is only when there is present a conception, that something exists; and where a conception is not responsible, we cannot say that a thing exists, at all. It is an absolute certainty—beyond any question—that nothing can exist through any nature of its own; for then it would be like a coiled rope that someone was thinking of as a snake. As the Master puts it here, we can say that every single object in the universe is established by nothing more than our conceptions.

gru.acip: NGA ZHES THA SNYAD BTAGS PA'I DON JI 'DRA ZHIG TU GRUB BTZAL NA MI RNYED KYANG, MA BRTAGS MA DPYAD PA'I TSE RTOG PAS BTAGS TZAM DU YOD PA
gru.wylie: nga zhes tha snyad btags pa'i don ji 'dra zhig tu grub btsal na mi rnyed kyang, ma brtags ma dpyad pa'i tshe rtog pas btags tsam du yod pa
gru.english: When we say “me,” and then we try to go find just how it is that what we call “me” exists, there's nothing there to find; nonetheless, we can say that the “me” does actually exist—but only in a way where we project it with our conceptions, and don't think about it too much, or look too closely.

gru.acip: MING GI THA SNYAD KYIS DBANG TZAM GYIS BZHAG PA MIN PA'I YOD PAR 'DZIN PA NI, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DANG, BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I 'DZIN TSUL YIN PAS, DE LTAR 'DZIN PA'I RTOG PA RNAMS BDEN 'DZIN YIN LA, DES BZUNG BA LTAR GRUB PA NI BRTAG PA MTHA' BZUNG GI BDEN TSAD DO,,
gru.wylie: ming gi tha snyad kyis dbang tsam gyis bzhag pa min pa'i yod par 'dzin pa ni, rang bzhin gyis grub pa dang, bden par grub pa'i 'dzin tshul yin pas, de ltar 'dzin pa'i rtog pa rnams bden 'dzin yin la, des bzung ba ltar grub pa ni brtag pa mtha' bzung gi bden tshad do
gru.english: Suppose though that we hold the belief that things can exist without being established as what they are by nothing more than terms. This then is what it would be for a thing to exist through some nature of its own; and this is what it would be to hold that something exists in truth. As such, thoughts where we hold things to exist this way are examples of what it is to hold that something exists in truth; and for a thing to actually exist in the way that these thoughts hold it to be is the measure of that only-hypothetical “in truth.”

gru.acip: THA SNYAD DU BRTEN NAS BZHAG PA NYID KYIS BTAGS YOD DANG, BTAGS YOD YIN PA NYID KYIS, RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA MED PA'I TSUL SNYING THAG PA NAS MA GO PHYIN CHAD RANG BZHIN GYIS MED, BDEN PAR MED CES CI TZAM SMRAS KYANG DON GTING NAS GO BA MA YIN PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: tha snyad du brten nas bzhag pa nyid kyis btags yod dang, btags yod yin pa nyid kyis, rang gi ngo bos grub pa med pa'i tshul snying thag pa nas ma go phyin chad rang bzhin gyis med, bden par med ces ci tsam smras kyang don gting nas go ba ma yin pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: What it means for something to exist nominally is the very fact that it has been established as existing through the use of terms. And the very fact that something exists nominally means that it does not exist through any identity of its own. Until such point as we understand this idea from the bottom of our heart, we can go around talking about how nothing exists through any nature of its own, or how nothing exists in truth; but no matter how many times we repeat it in words, we are not really grasping the concept at its very depths.

gru.acip: BDAG MED RIGS PAS SGRUB TSUL MDOR BSDUS BSHAD PA LA GNYIS, GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED DANG, CHOS KYI BDAG MED RIGS PAS SGRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: bdag med rigs pas sgrub tshul mdor bsdus bshad pa la gnyis, gang zag gi bdag med dang, chos kyi bdag med rigs pas sgrub pa'o
gru.english: Let us turn here to a brief explanation of how this group establishes the concept of no-self by using reasoning. I'll proceed in two steps: proving, with reasoning, that the person is not themselves; and then proving—also with reasoning—that things are not themselves.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, NGAR 'DZIN LHAN SKYES 'DIS PHUNG PO LNGA'I STENG DU DE LA MA BLTOS PA'I NGA TSANG BA ZHIG GAM, NGA DE RANG GI PHUNG PO'I STENG DU BTAGS PA TZAM MA YIN PAR PHUNG PO'I STENG DU GDOD MA NAS GRUB GRUB PA ZHIG TU 'DZIN TSUL YOD PAS DE NGES PAR BYA,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, ngar 'dzin lhan skyes 'dis phung po lnga'i steng du de la ma bltos pa'i nga tshang ba zhig gam, nga de rang gi phung po'i steng du btags pa tsam ma yin par phung po'i steng du gdod ma nas grub grub pa zhig tu 'dzin tshul yod pas de nges par bya
gru.english: Here is the first of these ideas. There is a certain way in which the automatic tendency to grasp to a “me” holds things to be. That is, it is where we believe, first of all, that there is a complete “me” which exists relative to the five parts to a person, but which does not rely upon those parts. Or you can say it is where we believe that there is a “me” which has beyond a doubt existed for time with no beginning relative to those parts of the person, but which is not simply something which exists in name. Your first job then is to sort out what it is we're denying in these two descriptions.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, SPYIR YOD NA, GCIG DANG DU MA GANG RUNG DU YOD DGOS PA'I KHYAB PA NGES PA LA BRTEN NAS 'GRUB BO,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, spyir yod na, gcig dang du ma gang rung du yod dgos pa'i khyab pa nges pa la brten nas 'grub bo
gru.english: Sorting this out depends on sorting out something else; which is the fact that—if, in general, something exists—then it must exist as one thing or as more than one thing. This is the second idea here: the necessary relationship.

gru.acip: 'DIR CHOS CAN DU 'DZIN TSUL GNYIS LAS, DANG PO NI, NGA CHOS CAN, RANG GI PHUNG PO'I STENG DU RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB TE, DE'I STENG DU DE DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GCIG DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS THA DAD GANG DU'ANG MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR, DPER NA, GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN NO,,
gru.wylie: 'dir chos can du 'dzin tshul gnyis las, dang po ni, nga chos can, rang gi phung po'i steng du rang bzhin gyis ma grub te, de'i steng du de dang rang bzhin gyis gcig dang rang bzhin gyis tha dad gang du'ang ma grub pa'i phyir, dper na, gzugs brnyan bzhin no
gru.english: There are two ways of looking at the subject under consideration here. Here is how we would express the first: Consider “me.” I am not something that exists, through some nature of my own, relative to the parts of me; Because the “me” does not exist—through any nature of its own—as one thing, relative to the parts of me; nor does it exist—through any nature of its own—as a separate thing, relative to these same parts. It is, for example, similar to the reflection of an object in a mirror.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GCIG DANG THA DAD GANG RUNG DU GRUB DGOS PA'I PHYIR TE, YOD NA GCIG DANG DU MA GANG RUNG DU YOD DGOS PA'I PHYIR TE, GCIG DANG DU MA GNYIS DNGOS 'GAL YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, rang bzhin gyis grub na, rang bzhin gyis gcig dang tha dad gang rung du grub dgos pa'i phyir te, yod na gcig dang du ma gang rung du yod dgos pa'i phyir te, gcig dang du ma gnyis dngos 'gal yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Just because the “me” does not exist—through any nature of its own—as one thing, relative to the parts of me; nor does it exist—through any nature of its own—as a separate thing, relative to these same parts, it's not necessarily the case that I am not something that exists, through some nature of my own, relative to the parts of me. And yet it is necessarily so; because if something did exist through some nature of its own, then it would have to exist either as one thing that existed through some nature of its own, or as a separate thing that existed through some nature of its own. And that's because—if something does exist—then it must either exist as a single thing, or more than one thing. That in turn is true because being one thing contradicts, directly, being more than one thing; and vice versa.

gru.acip: PHYOGS CHOS SGRUB PA LA GNYIS KYI, DANG PO NI,
gru.wylie: phyogs chos sgrub pa la gnyis kyi, dang po ni
gru.english: Let's look next at how we establish here the relationship between the subject under consideration and the quality expressed in the reason. I'll proceed in two parts; here is the first.

gru.acip: NGA CHOS CAN, PHUNG PO'I STENG DU DE DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GCIG TU MA GRUB STE, DE DANG CHA MED KYI GCIG TU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: nga chos can, phung po'i steng du de dang rang bzhin gyis gcig tu ma grub ste, de dang cha med kyi gcig tu ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Consider the “me.” It does not exist as one thing, through any nature of its own, relative to the parts of me; Because it does not exist, relative to these parts, as a single thing which has no parts of its own.

gru.acip: DER THAL, CHA BCAS YIN PA'I PHYIR, RTAGS SNGAR BZHIN BSGRUB BO,,
gru.wylie: der thal, cha bcas yin pa'i phyir, rtags sngar bzhin bsgrub bo
gru.english: I disagree that the “me” does not exist, relative to its parts, as a single thing which has no parts of its own. And yet it does not; for it does have parts. And that's true for the same reasons that we presented before, [when we demonstrated that every existing thing has parts].

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, DE CHOS CAN, PHUNG PO'I STENG DU DE DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS THA DAD DU MA GRUB STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS GCIG TU GRUB PA MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, de chos can, phung po'i steng du de dang rang bzhin gyis tha dad du ma grub ste, rang bzhin gyis gcig tu grub pa med pa'i phyir
gru.english: Which brings us to the second part of establishing the relationship between the subject under consideration and the quality expressed in the reason: Consider this same thing. It is indeed the case that this “me” does not exist—through any nature of its own—as a separate thing, relative to the parts of me; Because there is nothing in the universe that exists, through any nature of its own, as one thing.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB NA, PHUNG PO DANG MA 'BREL BAR LOGS SU BZUNG DU YOD DGOS PA'I PHYIR TE, PHUNG PO LA BLTOS PA'I RAG LAS PA YIN NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PAR GRUB PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, rang bzhin gyis grub na, phung po dang ma 'brel bar logs su bzung du yod dgos pa'i phyir te, phung po la bltos pa'i rag las pa yin na, rang bzhin gyis med par grub pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: I disagree that—just because the “me” does not exist as something other than the parts of me which has no relationship to them—it cannot exist, relative to the parts of me, as a separate thing. And yet then it cannot; for if the “me” existed through some nature of its own, there would have to be something here which we could consider as existing apart—with no connection to the parts of me. And that's true because if something were dependent here—if it relied upon the parts to me—then that would prove that it couldn't be existing through some nature of its own.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, NGAR 'DZIN LHAN SKYES KYIS BZUNG BA LTAR GRUB PA'I BDAG DE CHOS CAN, PHUNG PO'I STENG DU MED DE, PHUNG PO'I STENG DU DE DANG GCIG DANG DU MA GANG RUNG DU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, ngar 'dzin lhan skyes kyis bzung ba ltar grub pa'i bdag de chos can, phung po'i steng du med de, phung po'i steng du de dang gcig dang du ma gang rung du ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Which brings us to our second point from above: a second way of looking at the subject under consideration here. Let's consider a “me” which could actually exist in the way that our automatic tendency to grasp to a “me” holds it to be. No such thing exists relative to the parts of me; Because it exists neither as one thing relative to these parts, nor as more than one thing relative to these parts.

gru.acip: KHYAB PA SGRUB TSUL NI SNGAR LTAR RO,,
gru.wylie: khyab pa sgrub tshul ni sngar ltar ro
gru.english: Proving the fact that if the quality expressed in this reason holds true with a particular thing, then the quality asserted about our subject also holds true for it, is done in the same way as we did it above.

gru.acip: RTAGS SGRUB PA LA GNYIS KYI DANG PO NI,
gru.wylie: rtags sgrub pa la gnyis kyi dang po ni
gru.english: As for proving the reason, we also proceed in two parts; here is the first.

gru.acip: DE 'DRA'I BDAG DE PHUNG PO'I STENG DU DE DANG GCIG TU MA GRUB STE, GRUB NA RIGS PA GSUM GYIS GNOD PA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: de 'dra'i bdag de phung po'i steng du de dang gcig tu ma grub ste, grub na rigs pa gsum gyis gnod pa'i phyir te
gru.english: This kind of “me” does not exist as one thing relative to the parts of me; Because its being so is drawn into question by three different arguments.

gru.acip: DE 'DRA'I BDAG DE PHUNG PO'I STENG DU DE DANG GCIG TU GRUB NA, DBYER MED KYI GCIG TU 'GYUR BAS, DE'I TSE GANG GIS NYE BAR LEN PA PO DANG, GANG NYE BAR BLANG BAR BYA BA'I RNAM GZHAG MI 'THAD PA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: de 'dra'i bdag de phung po'i steng du de dang gcig tu grub na, dbyer med kyi gcig tu 'gyur bas, de'i tshe gang gis nye bar len pa po dang, gang nye bar blang bar bya ba'i rnam gzhag mi 'thad pa'i phyir te
gru.english: Now if this kind of “me” existed as a thing which were—relative to its parts—one with them, then these would have to exist as an indivisible one. And in that case, it would be incorrect to posit one thing here as having taken on the parts to the person at birth, and another thing as being what was taken on at birth.

gru.acip: BSDU NA BDEN GRUB KYI SKYE 'JIG BYED PAR SONG BA'I PHYIR SKYE BA LEN PA'I TSE NGO BO 'GYUR DU MI RUNG BAS 'GRO BA RIGS DRUG GI GZHI MTHUN PA YOD PAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: bsdu na bden grub kyi skye 'jig byed par song ba'i phyir skye ba len pa'i tshe ngo bo 'gyur du mi rung bas 'gro ba rigs drug gi gzhi mthun pa yod par 'gyur ro
gru.english: To summarize these, the exhibiting of a starting and stopping that the me was accomplishing would itself exist in truth. Because of that, when the “me” took a birth, it would have to be a single example of all six different forms of rebirth—since it would then be inappropriate to say its basic nature had undergone any kind of change.

gru.acip: RTAGS GNYIS PA NI, DE 'DRA'I BDAG DE PHUNG PO'I STENG DU DE DANG THA DAD DU MA GRUB STE, DE LTAR GRUB NA PHUNG PO LA BLTOS MED DU GRUB DGOS PAS, PHUNG PO LAS YAN GAR LOGS SU YOD DGOS PA LAS DE MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rtags gnyis pa ni, de 'dra'i bdag de phung po'i steng du de dang tha dad du ma grub ste, de ltar grub na phung po la bltos med du grub dgos pas, phung po las yan gar logs su yod dgos pa las de med pa'i phyir
gru.english: Which brings us to the second part from above, for proving the reason: It is not the case that a “me” like this could exist as something separate, relative to the parts of me; Because, if it did, then it would have to exist as something that no longer relied upon the parts of me; and then it would have to exist as a discrete entity apart from these parts—whereas there exists no such thing.

gru.acip: DANG PO DER THAL, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB NA, GZHAN LA RAG MA LAS PAR GRUB DGOS PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: dang po der thal, rang bzhin gyis grub na, gzhan la rag ma las par grub dgos pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: And the first part of this reason does hold true, for if something did exist through some nature of its own, then it would have to exist without relying on anything else.

gru.acip: DE LTAR BDAG RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB NA BDAG PHUNG PO DANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GCIG DANG THA DAD GANG RUNG DU GRUB DGOS PA DANG,
gru.wylie: de ltar bdag rang gi ngo bos grub na bdag phung po dang rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gcig dang tha dad gang rung du grub dgos pa dang
gru.english: As such, we can say that—if the “me” were to exist through some essence of its own—then this “me” would have to exist either as one thing which existed by definition, or else as more than one thing which existed by definition, both relative to the parts of me.

gru.acip: DE GNYIS KA LA'ANG RIGS PAS GNOD PAR MTHONG BA NA BDAG NI RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA CUNG ZAD KYANG MED DO SNYAM DU NGES PA RNYED PA NI,
gru.wylie: de gnyis ka la'ang rigs pas gnod par mthong ba na bdag ni rang gi ngo bos grub pa cung zad kyang med do snyam du nges pa rnyed pa ni
gru.english: Once we see that both of these options are drawn into question by proper reasoning, then we can discover that certainty which says to itself, “There is not the slightest thing about me that exists through some essence of its own.”

gru.acip: MKHAS GRUB NOR BZANG RGYA MTSOS KYANG, GCIG DU BRAL GYI RIGS PAS DE LTAR DPYAD PA LAS DPYAD DON LA NGES SHES TSAD MA SKYES PA DE'I TSE, DE'I DUS SU MYU GU SOGS RTEN 'BYUNG GI CHOS RNAMS RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR RTOGS PA YIN, ZHES GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: mkhas grub nor bzang rgya mtshos kyang, gcig du bral gyi rigs pas de ltar dpyad pa las dpyad don la nges shes tshad ma skyes pa de'i tshe, de'i dus su myu gu sogs rten 'byung gi chos rnams rang bzhin gyis ma grub par rtogs pa yin, zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: The wise and accomplished Norsang Gyatso also says: Suppose we do use the logic called “Neither One nor Many” to perform our examination; and then we reach a point where an accurate perception arises: one in which we reach a true understanding of the point we've been examining. At this juncture we have indeed had the realization that none of the things that occur through interdependence—neither sprouts nor anything of the like—can ever exist through some nature of their own. 18) The Seven-Part Reasoning

gru.acip: SHING RTA DE RANG GI YAN LAG RNAMS DANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GCIG DANG THA DAD SOGS BDUN PO GANG DU YANG MA GRUB STE,
gru.wylie: shing rta de rang gi yan lag rnams dang rang bzhin gyis gcig dang tha dad sogs bdun po gang du yang ma grub ste
gru.english: Now the wagon does not exist in any of these seven different ways: as something one with its parts; as something separate from is parts, and so on:

gru.acip: DE CHOS CAN, RANG GI YAN LAG RNAMS DANG NGO BOS GRUB PA'I SO SO BA MA YIN TE, YIN NA BUM PA DANG SNAM BU BZHIN DU KHYOD RANG GI YAN LAG LAS YAN GAR DU SO SOR DMIGS DGOS PA LAS DE MA MTHONG BA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de chos can, rang gi yan lag rnams dang ngo bos grub pa'i so so ba ma yin te, yin na bum pa dang snam bu bzhin du khyod rang gi yan lag las yan gar du so sor dmigs dgos pa las de ma mthong ba'i phyir ro
gru.english: Let's again consider the wagon. It is not an entity which exists through some essence of its own, and which is discrete from its parts; Because if it were, then it would have to be observed as a discrete object isolated from its parts—as separate as a water pitcher is from a bolt of cloth—whereas in fact it is not seen to be so.

gru.acip: ,DE NI DE NYID DU'AM 'JIG RTEN DU, ,RNAM PA BDUN GYIS 'GRUB 'GYUR MIN MOD KYI, ,RNAM DPYAD MED PAR 'JIG RTEN NYID LAS 'DI, ,RANG GI YAN LAG BRTEN NAS 'DOGS PA YIN, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de ni de nyid du'am 'jig rten du, ,rnam pa bdun gyis 'grub 'gyur min mod kyi, ,rnam dpyad med par 'jig rten nyid las 'di, ,rang gi yan lag brten nas 'dogs pa yin, ,zhes gsungs pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Admittedly it cannot exist in itself; Nor in the everyday world Would they ever say that the wagon Existed in any of these seven ways. Nonetheless, even in the world They would say that something Is called a wagon based on its parts— Without questioning the matter further.

gru.acip: RTAGS SNGA MA LNGA'I SGRUB BYED NI, SHING RTA LA BSHAD PA BZHIN BSGRUB PAR BYA ZHING, DER MA ZAD, GCIG DANG THA DAD KYI PHYOGS GNYIS SNGAR GCIG DU BRAL LA BSHAD PA BZHIN RIGS 'GRE SBYOR,
gru.wylie: rtags snga ma lnga'i sgrub byed ni, shing rta la bshad pa bzhin bsgrub par bya zhing, der ma zad, gcig dang tha dad kyi phyogs gnyis sngar gcig du bral la bshad pa bzhin rigs 'gre sbyor
gru.english: The justifications for the first five of the logical statements are something you can confirm as they have been explained with reference to the wagon. Not only that—the two aspects of the presentation which refer to being one and the same, or to being separate things, are something where you can apply the parallel arguments in the proof of “Neither One nor Many.”

gru.acip: GNYIS PA CHOS KYI BDAG MED RIGS PAS SGRUB TSUL LA, GCIG DU BRAL GYI GTAN TSIGS, RDO RJE GZEGS MA, YOD MED SKYE 'GOG ,MU BZHI SKYE 'GOG ,RTEN 'BREL GYI GTAN TSIGS DANG LNGA YOD PA LAS,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa chos kyi bdag med rigs pas sgrub tshul la, gcig du bral gyi gtan tshigs, rdo rje gzegs ma, yod med skye 'gog ,mu bzhi skye 'gog ,rten 'brel gyi gtan tshigs dang lnga yod pa las
gru.english: This brings us to our section from above: specific proofs for establishing that no things are themselves. Here there are five different logical statements: [a] Neither One nor Many; [b] The Sliver of Diamond; [c] The Denial that Things Can Start Either from Things that Exist, or from Things that Do Not Exist; [d] The Denial that Things Can Start through Any of the Four Possible Options; and [e] the Proof that Uses Interdependence. 19) The Proof of Neither One nor Many, Consequence Style, Applied to Things

gru.acip: GZUGS SOGS RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG YANG MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA'I SO SKYE'I DBANG PO'I SHES PA LNGA LA GZUGS SOGS SNANG BA NA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA MA GTOGS, SNANG TSUL GZHAN MI 'BYUNG BAS,
gru.wylie: gzugs sogs rang bzhin gyis stong yang ma rig pas bslad pa'i so skye'i dbang po'i shes pa lnga la gzugs sogs snang ba na rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par snang ba ma gtogs, snang tshul gzhan mi 'byung bas
gru.english: Things like physical objects are, in fact, empty of any nature of their own; but when they make their appearance to the sense awareness of a normal person—one whose mind is infected by misunderstanding—they seem as if they did exist by definition. There is in fact no other way that it could appear to them.

gru.acip: THAL 'GYUR BA'I SKABS 'DIR RANG CAG SO SKYE'I SHES NGOR GZUGS SGRA SOGS SNANG BA NI YOD MOD, SNANG TSUL LTAR GRUB PA 'DI KA RANG RTAGS KYI DGAG BYA YIN ZHES BZHED PAR SNANG BAS,
gru.wylie: thal 'gyur ba'i skabs 'dir rang cag so skye'i shes ngor gzugs sgra sogs snang ba ni yod mod, snang tshul ltar grub pa 'di ka rang rtags kyi dgag bya yin zhes bzhed par snang bas
gru.english: Here in the context of the Consequence branch of the Middle Way, we do admittedly accept that visible forms, sounds, and so on make their appearance to the senses of a normal person. It would appear though that what their reasoning seeks to deny is precisely the idea that these things could actually exist in the way that they appear to.

gru.acip: 'DI 'GOG PA'I TSE, BUM PA LA MTSON NA, DE CHOS CAN, SO SKYE'I SHES NGOR SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB STE, SNANG BA LTAR GCIG DANG SNANG BA LTAR THA DAD GANG RUNG DU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'di 'gog pa'i tshe, bum pa la mtshon na, de chos can, so skye'i shes ngor snang ba ltar ma grub ste, snang ba ltar gcig dang snang ba ltar tha dad gang rung du ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: And when they make this denial, they start for example with a water pitcher: Consider the water pitcher. It does not actually exist in the way that it appears to, to the senses of a normal person; Because it exists neither as a same thing that exists in the way it appears to; nor as a separate thing which exists in the way it appears to.

gru.acip: KHYAB PA SNGAR LTAR BSGRUB,
gru.wylie: khyab pa sngar ltar bsgrub
gru.english: The necessary relationship here—that if something exists neither as a same thing that exists in the way it appears to, nor as a separate thing which exists in the way it appears to, it does not then actually exist in the way that it appears to, to the senses of a normal person—is proven here in the same way that we did it before.

gru.acip: DE CHOS CAN, SNANG BA LTAR GCIG TU MA GRUB STE, RANG GI GDAGS GZHI LA BTAGS PA'I BTAGS CHOS TZAM YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: de chos can, snang ba ltar gcig tu ma grub ste, rang gi gdags gzhi la btags pa'i btags chos tsam yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Consider the water pitcher. It does not exist as a same thing which exists in the way it appears to, Because it is nothing more than a projected entity: the result of a name being applied to an object which receives the name.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, SO SKYE'I SHES NGOR BUM SOGS RANG GI GDAGS GZHI LA BTAGS PA'I BTAGS CHOS TZAM DU MI SNANG BAR GDAGS GZHI DANG BTAGS CHOS GNYIS MI PHYED PA'I TSUL GYIS RANG NGOS NAS GRUB PAR SNANG BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, so skye'i shes ngor bum sogs rang gi gdags gzhi la btags pa'i btags chos tsam du mi snang bar gdags gzhi dang btags chos gnyis mi phyed pa'i tshul gyis rang ngos nas grub par snang ba'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that—just because something is nothing more than a projected entity, the result of a name being applied to an object which receives the name—then it cannot exist as a same thing which exists in the way it appears to. And yet it cannot, since—first of all—things like water pitchers never appear to the senses of a normal person as if they were nothing more than a projected entity: the result of a name being applied to an object which receives the name. Rather, they appear to exist from their own side, in a way where what is given the name of “water pitcher” is not distinguished from the thing that results from the process of applying the name “water pitcher” to what receives this name.

gru.acip: DE CHOS CAN, SO SKYE'I SHES NGOR SNANG BA LTAR THA DAD DU MA GRUB STE, RANG GI GDAGS GZHI LA BLTOS NAS GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: de chos can, so skye'i shes ngor snang ba ltar tha dad du ma grub ste, rang gi gdags gzhi la bltos nas grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Now, once more, let's consider that water pitcher. It does not actually exist—in the way it appears to, to the senses of a normal person—as a separate thing; Because it exists through relying on the thing which is given its particular name.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, SNANG BA LTAR THA DAD DU GRUB NA, RANG GI GDAGS GZHI LA MA BLTOS PAR GRUB DGOS PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, snang ba ltar tha dad du grub na, rang gi gdags gzhi la ma bltos par grub dgos pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: I disagree that—just because something exists through relying on the thing which is given its particular name—it doesn't actually exist in the way it appears to—to the senses of a normal person—as a separate thing. And this necessarily is the case, since—if the water pitcher existed as a separate thing, as it appears to—then it would have to exist without relying on the thing which is given its particular name.

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG, SO SKYE'I DBANG PO'I SHES PA LA GZUGS SGRA SOGS SNANG TSUL LTAR MA GRUB PAR THAL, DE'I NGOR KUN RDZOB KYI CHOS RNAMS SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang, so skye'i dbang po'i shes pa la gzugs sgra sogs snang tshul ltar ma grub par thal, de'i ngor kun rdzob kyi chos rnams snang ba ltar ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: And isn't it, once again, the case that visible forms, sounds, and the like could never actually exist in the way that they appear to, to the sense perceptions of a normal person? Why do you say that? Because none of the deceptive objects in the universe actually exists in the way that it appears to, to those perceptions.

gru.acip: DER THAL, RANG RGYUD PA'I LUGS LA SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PA'I KUN RDZOB YOD PAS YANG DAG KUN RDZOB YOD CES 'DOD KYANG, THAL 'GYUR BA'I SKABS 'DIR SNANG BA LTAR GRUB PA'I KUN RDZOB MED PAS YANG DAG KUN RDZOB MI BZHED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, rang rgyud pa'i lugs la snang ba ltar grub pa'i kun rdzob yod pas yang dag kun rdzob yod ces 'dod kyang, thal 'gyur ba'i skabs 'dir snang ba ltar grub pa'i kun rdzob med pas yang dag kun rdzob mi bzhed pa'i phyir
gru.english: And this really is the case, for the following reason. Those who belong to the Independent branch of the Middle-Way School do, admittedly, accept the concept of objects which are “deceptive but correct”: which are deceptive, but which actually exist in the way that they appear to. Here in the Consequence branch of the same school, though, the idea of “deceptive but correct” is not accepted—since they would say that there is no such thing as an object which is deceptive, but which still actually does exist in the way that it appears to.

gru.acip: 'DI GNAD CHE BAS RGYAS PAR 'CHAD DGOS NA'ANG MANG DU DOGS LA, SO SKYE'I SHES DON SNANG BA LTAR MA GRUB CES PA 'DI DGAG BYA 'GOG TSUL SHIN TU PHRA BAS RANG CAG LTA BU'I BLO KHOG TU CHUD DKA' BA'I GNAS YIN TE ZHIB CHA 'BYED DGOS PA YOD DO,,
gru.wylie: 'di gnad che bas rgyas par 'chad dgos na'ang mang du dogs la, so skye'i shes don snang ba ltar ma grub ces pa 'di dgag bya 'gog tshul shin tu phra bas rang cag lta bu'i blo khog tu chud dka' ba'i gnas yin te zhib cha 'byed dgos pa yod do
gru.english: The points we have covered here are critical, and would certainly require a more detailed explanation—but again, I fear going on too long. Enough to note that—when we say that the things which a normal person perceives never actually exist in the same way that they seem to—this is an extremely subtle way of refusing that thing which the concept of no-self denies. It is a point which even we ourselves have difficulty digesting—and so we can say that you will have to learn to make some very subtle distinctions here. 20) The Sliver of Diamond

gru.acip: RANG RGYUD PA SOGS KYIS MYU GU LTA BU RANG GIS MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I RGYU GZHAN LAS SKYE BAS GZHAN SKYE YOD ZHES 'DOD,
gru.wylie: rang rgyud pa sogs kyis myu gu lta bu rang gis mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i rgyu gzhan las skye bas gzhan skye yod zhes 'dod
gru.english: What those who belong to the Independent branch of the Middle Way, and so on, believe in is a starting from something else—where something like a sprout starts from a cause which is something other than it, and which exists by definition.

gru.acip: DANG PO GRUB STE, RANG GI RGYU'I DUS NAS GRUB ZIN MI SKYE BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dang po grub ste, rang gi rgyu'i dus nas grub zin mi skye ba'i phyir
gru.english: The first point of our reason holds true because nothing which is already present in the time of its cause would ever then start.

gru.acip: DER THAL, DE'I DUS SU GRUB ZIN NA NI, SLAR YANG SKYE BA LA DGOS PA MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, de'i dus su grub zin na ni, slar yang skye ba la dgos pa med pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that nothing which is already present in the time of its cause would ever then start. And yet nothing would, for if by that time the thing were already present, then there would be no point in its starting over again.

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG, BDAG SKYE MED PAR THAL, RANG GI RGYU'I DUS SU GRUB ZIN 'GYUR MED DU SKYE BA MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang, bdag skye med par thal, rang gi rgyu'i dus su grub zin 'gyur med du skye ba med pa'i phyir
gru.english: We can also put it this way: Isn't it indeed the case that nothing ever starts from itself? Why do you say that? Because something that was already present during the time of its cause could never start, without changing.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, MYU GU CHOS CAN, GZHAN LAS MI SKYE STE, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I RGYU GZHAN LAS MI SKYE BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, myu gu chos can, gzhan las mi skye ste, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i rgyu gzhan las mi skye ba'i phyir
gru.english: Which brings us to our second point from above: Consider a sprout. It cannot start from something other than itself; Because it cannot start from a cause other than itself which exists by definition.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, RANG NGOS NAS GRUB NA, DUS GCIG GI TSE MED NA GTAN NAS MED DGOS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, rang ngos nas grub na, dus gcig gi tshe med na gtan nas med dgos pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that—just because something grows, from its own side, without existing at the time of its cause—it must start and be forever absent as well. And that is indeed the case, because—if something could exist from its own side—then if it were absent at any particular time then it would be forever absent.

gru.acip: DER THAL, RANG NGOS NAS GRUB NA GZHAN DU 'GYUR BA MI 'THAD PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: der thal, rang ngos nas grub na gzhan du 'gyur ba mi 'thad pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: I disagree that—if something could exist from its own side—then if it were absent at any particular time then it would be forever absent. And yet it would, for it is incorrect to say that something could change into something else, if it existed from its own side.

gru.acip: SGRUB TSUL GZHAN DU SHES,
gru.wylie: sgrub tshul gzhan du shes
gru.english: The way in which these different options are confirmed is something that you can learn from other sources. 23) The Proof That Uses Interdependence

gru.acip: THUN MONG MA YIN PA NI, THAL 'GYUR BA'I LUGS KYI RTOG PAS BTAGS TZAM DU GRUB PA'I TSUL SHES DGOS TE, SNGAR GYI RIGS PA DE DAG THAMS CAD KYANG MTHAR GTUGS NA RTEN 'BREL GYI RIGS PA LA THUG PAS SO,,
gru.wylie: thun mong ma yin pa ni, thal 'gyur ba'i lugs kyi rtog pas btags tsam du grub pa'i tshul shes dgos te, sngar gyi rigs pa de dag thams cad kyang mthar gtugs na rten 'brel gyi rigs pa la thug pas so
gru.english: As for the uncommon explanation, you will need to understand the presentation of the Consequence branch on how things exist as no more than projections of our conceptions. We can in fact say that the preceding proofs we've presented all come down to this one: to the proof based on interdependence.

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG, CHOS THAMS CAD RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB STE, SHES BYA, RTAG PA, DNGOS PO, BUM PA SOGS SPYI YIN PA RNAMS NI, RANG BZHIN GYIS MED, SPYI MA YIN PA'I CHOS BYE BRAG RNAMS KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang, chos thams cad rang bzhin gyis ma grub ste, shes bya, rtag pa, dngos po, bum pa sogs spyi yin pa rnams ni, rang bzhin gyis med, spyi ma yin pa'i chos bye brag rnams kyang rang bzhin gyis med pa'i phyir
gru.english: Here's another way we can say it: Nothing in the universe exists through any nature of its own, Because, first of all, none of those things which are qualities—whether we're talking about the total amount of knowable things; or the quality of existing without ever changing; or the quality of being a functioning thing; or “water pitchers,” or anything else of the like—exists through any nature of its own. And secondly, none of those things which are characteristic of those qualities—none of those existing things which we are not considering as a quality—exists through any nature of its own either.

gru.acip: SPYI MA YIN PA'I GZUGS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED DE, MDUN NA MNGON SUM DU YOD PA'I BUM PA GCIG LTA BU NI, RANG GI MCHU ZHABS SOGS LA BTAGS, RANG GI LUS LTA BU NI, YAN LAG GI STENG DU BTAGS, RI GCIG LTA BU NI SA RDO SOGS TSOGS PA'I STENG NAS BTAGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: spyi ma yin pa'i gzugs rang bzhin gyis grub pa med de, mdun na mngon sum du yod pa'i bum pa gcig lta bu ni, rang gi mchu zhabs sogs la btags, rang gi lus lta bu ni, yan lag gi steng du btags, ri gcig lta bu ni sa rdo sogs tshogs pa'i steng nas btags pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's look at the proofs here: Consider physical objects which are not general qualities. They cannot exist through any nature of their own; Because we can say the following about something like a single water pitcher which is immediately present, right in front of us. It is merely the result of a mental picture applied to its spout, its stand, and its other parts. The body of the pitcher itself is, further, merely the result of a mental picture applied to its own parts. A mountain standing there on its own is also nothing more than the result of a mental picture applied to the collection of earth and stone and so on, of which it is made.

gru.acip: SPYI MA YIN PA'I SHES PA NI RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED DE, DA LTA SKYE MA THAG PA'I RANG GI SHES RAB LTA BU NI SHES PA GZHAN LAS RAGS LAS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: spyi ma yin pa'i shes pa ni rang bzhin gyis grub pa med de, da lta skye ma thag pa'i rang gi shes rab lta bu ni shes pa gzhan las rags las pa'i phyir
gru.english: Consider, next, mental objects which are not general qualities. They also cannot exist through any nature of their own; Because we can take, for example, that state of wisdom which we just had come up in our own minds! It too is something which exists through dependence on mental entities that are distinct from it.

gru.acip: MDOR NA, RANG GI CHA SHAS DANG SGRA RTOG GIS BZHAG PA LA MA BLTOS PAR RANG DBANG DU GRUB PA'I CHOS MED PAS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA'I CHOS MED PA YIN TE,
gru.wylie: mdor na, rang gi cha shas dang sgra rtog gis bzhag pa la ma bltos par rang dbang du grub pa'i chos med pas rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i chos med pa yin te
