Concerning our original condition, we have already covered the majority of the beliefs of the Independent branch which are shared with those of the lower systems—particularly those shared with Mind Only belief system.  We can say however that here in this branch they do not accept the idea of anything that could exist in truth.  They do accept, however, that—in a nominal manner—things can exist in three other ways: they can exist by nature; they can exist by definition; and they can exist from their own side.

gru.acip: 'ON KYANG SEMS TZAM PAS SHES PA BDEN GRUB 'DOD CING 'DIS MI 'DOD PA BSHAD ZIN LA, PHYI DON 'DOD PA'I DBU MA PAS NI RANG RIG MI 'DOD CING, ZHI 'TSO'I RJES 'BRANG RNAMS KYIS RANG RIG KHAS LEN NO,,
gru.wylie: 'on kyang sems tsam pas shes pa bden grub 'dod cing 'dis mi 'dod pa bshad zin la, phyi don 'dod pa'i dbu ma pas ni rang rig mi 'dod cing, zhi 'tsho'i rjes 'brang rnams kyis rang rig khas len no
gru.english: We should say though that the Mind Only asserts that awareness itself exists in truth; whereas we have already noted how that would not be accepted in this system.  Adherents of the Middle Way system who do accept the existence of outside objects do not support the idea of apperception; but the followers of Shantarakshita do.

gru.acip: MTSAN NYID GSUM 'DOD TSUL NI SEMS TZAM PA DANG MTHUN TZAM YIN KYANG, MTSAN GZHI LA MI 'DRA BA YOD DE, 'DI BAS {%PAS} BUM PA BDEN STONG YONGS GRUB KYI MTSAN GZHI YIN PAR 'DOD CING, CIG SHOS KYIS MI 'DOD PAS SO,,
gru.wylie: mtshan nyid gsum 'dod tshul ni sems tsam pa dang mthun tsam yin kyang, mtshan gzhi la mi 'dra ba yod de, 'di bas {%pas} bum pa bden stong yongs grub kyi mtshan gzhi yin par 'dod cing, cig shos kyis mi 'dod pas so
gru.english: As far as how they see the three characteristics, the members of the Independent branch are fairly well in accord with those of the Mind Only.  These two systems would though disagree on how they describe the objects which possess these characteristics.  Followers of the Independent system would say that a prime example of totality would be the fact that a water pitcher is devoid of any true existence; whereas this would not be accepted by their counterparts.

gru.acip: MTSAN NYID GSUM NI, BUM PA LA SOGS PA'I 'DUS BYAS RNAMS NI GZHAN DBANG YIN LA, DE DAG LA BDEN PAR SGRA {%SGRO} BTAGS PA'I CHA NI KUN BTAGS DANG, BTAGS PA LTAR MA GRUB PA'I STONG NYID NI YONGS GRUB TU 'JOG GO
gru.wylie: mtshan nyid gsum ni, bum pa la sogs pa'i 'dus byas rnams ni gzhan dbang yin la, de dag la bden par sgra {%sgro} btags pa'i cha ni kun btags dang, btags pa ltar ma grub pa'i stong nyid ni yongs grub tu 'jog go
gru.english: As for how they identify the three characteristics, entities produced by causes & conditions—things like water pitchers or the like—would represent the characteristic known as “dominated things.”  Any aspect of these objects resulting from overrating their degree of reality—any aspect we might think is real—would represent the characteristic of “imaginary things.”  And then emptiness—in the sense of those objects not existing in the way we overrate them—this branch of the Middle Way would describe as the characteristic called “totality.” The path, according to the Independent branch within the Middle Way system

gru.acip: ,,GNYIS PA THAL 'GYUR BA'I LUGS LA GSUM, MTSAN NYID, SGRA DON, GRUB MTHA' 'O,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa thal 'gyur ba'i lugs la gsum, mtshan nyid, sgra don, grub mtha' 'o
gru.english: With this we have reached the second of the two branches within the belief system of the Middle Way—which is to say, the Consequence branch.  We will proceed in three sections devoted to the definition of a follower of this branch; the literal meaning of the word “Consequence” branch here; and then a description of their beliefs.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA THA SNYAD DU'ANG ZHAL GYIS MI BZHED PA'I DBU MA PA DE, DBU MA THAL 'GYUR BA'I MTSAN NYID DO,,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa tha snyad du'ang zhal gyis mi bzhed pa'i dbu ma pa de, dbu ma thal 'gyur ba'i mtshan nyid do
gru.english: Here is the first.  The definition of a follower of the Consequence branch of the Middle Way system of belief is as follows— A member of the Middle Way system who does not accept—even nominally—the idea that anything in the universe could exist by definition.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, THAL 'GYUR GYI SGO NAS PHYI RGOL GYI RGYUD LA BSGRUB BYA RTOGS PA'I RJES DPAG SKYE BAR 'DOD PA'I DBU MA PA YIN PAS NA, DBU MA THAL 'GYUR BA'O,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, thal 'gyur gyi sgo nas phyi rgol gyi rgyud la bsgrub bya rtogs pa'i rjes dpag skye bar 'dod pa'i dbu ma pa yin pas na, dbu ma thal 'gyur ba'o
gru.english: Here is our second point.  The word “Consequence” in the name of this branch of the Middle Way is meant to indicate the members of this group are followers of the Middle Way who believe that one can—through the use of a logical statement which points up the absurd consequences of an opponent's position—inspire in that opponent a deductive form of accurate perception which confirms the point we are trying to prove to them. The original condition, according to the Consequence branch within the Middle Way system

gru.acip: GSUM PA GRUB MTHA'I 'DOD TSUL LA GSUM, GZHI, LAM, 'BRAS BU'I RNAM GZHAG GO
gru.wylie: gsum pa grub mtha'i 'dod tshul la gsum, gzhi, lam, 'bras bu'i rnam gzhag go
gru.english: Here is our third point—on the beliefs held by the Consequence branch.  Once more we present their ideas on our original condition; the path we use to overcome this condition; and then what they see as the result of that path.

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG 'DI PA LA KHAS LEN TSUL DU MA YOD DE, RANG BZHIN GYIS STONG PA RTEN 'BREL GYI DON DU MTHONG NAS, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA KHAS MI LEN PA DANG,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang 'di pa la khas len tshul du ma yod de, rang bzhin gyis stong pa rten 'brel gyi don du mthong nas, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa khas mi len pa dang
gru.english: There are many other positions that this branch of the Middle Way takes.  For example, they view the fact that things are empty of any natural existence as the actual meaning of the idea of interdependence.  And then this leads them to refuse the idea that things could ever exist by definition.

gru.acip: GANG ZAG RDZAS YOD PA MI BZHED DE, GZHI GRUB NA BTAGS YOD YIN PAS KHYAB PAR BZHED PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: gang zag rdzas yod pa mi bzhed de, gzhi grub na btags yod yin pas khyab par bzhed pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Members of the Consequence branch do not agree that the person can exist in a substantial way.  This is because they hold the position that—if something is an existent entity—then it must be the creation of a labeling process.

gru.acip: ,,DNGOS PO BZHED KYANG RANG MTSAN MI 'DOD DE, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYI {%KYIS} GRUB PA MI BZHED PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: dngos po bzhed kyang rang mtshan mi 'dod de, rang gi mtshan nyid kyi {%kyis} grub pa mi bzhed pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: They do accept the concept of a functioning entity, but they would never agree that it could be a definitive expression of an archetype—since they deny that anything in the universe could exist by definition.

gru.acip: DE YANG GANG ZAG 'JOG 'BYED KYI BLO GNOD MED DES 'JOG RGYU'I GANG ZAG NI, BLO DE LA LTOS MED KYI TSUL GYIS DANG PO NYID NAS KYANG RANG GI NGOS NAS GRUB GRUB PA ZHIG LA 'DOD CING,
gru.wylie: de yang gang zag 'jog 'byed kyi blo gnod med des 'jog rgyu'i gang zag ni, blo de la ltos med kyi tshul gyis dang po nyid nas kyang rang gi ngos nas grub grub pa zhig la 'dod cing
gru.english: What these Independents have in mind here is that the person is somehow, surely, existing—from the very outset—as something from its own side.  It is not though something whose existence would have to be predicated solely on a certain state of mind—on an unaffected state of mind which was establishing its existence.

gru.acip: DE LTAR GRUB PA DE GANG ZAG RANG NGOS NAS SAM RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA'I DON YIN KYANG BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I DON YIN PAR MI 'DOD,
gru.wylie: de ltar grub pa de gang zag rang ngos nas sam rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i don yin kyang bden par grub pa'i don yin par mi 'dod
gru.english: They would further say that—although the situation just described would amount to the person existing from their own side, or existing by nature—it would not be so much as to say that they existed in truth.

gru.acip: THAL 'GYUR BA NI GANG ZAG DE KHO RANG 'JAL BYED KYI TSAD MA LA LTOS MED KYIS DANG PO {%NAS} MA GRUB PAR GANG ZAG DANG GANG ZAG 'JAL BYED KYI TSAD MA GNYIS PHAN TSUN BLTOS NAS GRUB PAS,
gru.wylie: thal 'gyur ba ni gang zag de kho rang 'jal byed kyi tshad ma la ltos med kyis dang po {%nas} ma grub par gang zag dang gang zag 'jal byed kyi tshad ma gnyis phan tshun bltos nas grub pas
gru.english: The Consequence branch, on the other hand, would say that it is not the case that the person could exist, from the very outset, as something that relied upon an accurate perception which was considering them.  They would assert, rather, that these two things—the person, and the accurate perception which is considering them—exist by means of a mutual dependence upon each other.

gru.acip: 'JOG BYED MING BRDA'AM RTOG PA'I BZHAG PA LAS {%LA} MA BLTOS PAR RANG GI NGOS NAS GRUB PA ZHIG BYUNG NA GANG ZAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DANG, RANG NGOS NAS GRUB PAR 'JOG LA,
gru.wylie: 'jog byed ming brda'am rtog pa'i bzhag pa las {%la} ma bltos par rang gi ngos nas grub pa zhig byung na gang zag rang bzhin gyis grub pa dang, rang ngos nas grub par 'jog la
gru.english: This branch would establish the person as existing by nature, or from its own side, if it could exist from its own side in the sense of not having to depend upon a process where it was established through names or thoughts which were positing its existence.

gru.acip: DER MA GRUB PA DE GANG ZAG GI BDAG MED MED {%GI BDAG MED} PHRA MOR BZHED, DE BZHIN DU CHOS GZHAN LA YANG RIGS PA SBYOR TE, PHUNG PO DANG BUM SOGS RANG BZHIN MED PA CHOS KYI BDAG MED PHRA MO YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: der ma grub pa de gang zag gi bdag med med {%gi bdag med} phra mor bzhed, de bzhin du chos gzhan la yang rigs pa sbyor te, phung po dang bum sogs rang bzhin med pa chos kyi bdag med phra mo yin no
gru.english: And the fact that the person cannot exist in this way is exactly what members of the Consequence branch describe as the subtle form of the lack of a self-nature to the person.  They then turn around and apply this same reasoning to other objects in the world; that is, the fact that things like the parts of a person, and water pitchers, have no nature of their own is what—according to them—the subtle lack of a self-nature to things refers to. What it means to say that something is empty of existing in a self-standing, substantial way

gru.acip: GANG ZAG RANG RGYA {%RKYA} THUB PA'I RDZAS YOD KYI 'DZIN TSUL DANG GRUB TSUL NI,
gru.wylie: gang zag rang rgya {%rkya} thub pa'i rdzas yod kyi 'dzin tshul dang grub tshul ni
gru.english: How do we describe then what it means to hold that the person exists in a self-standing, substantial manner?  How would the proof go here?

gru.acip: RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR 'DZIN PA'I STENG NAS GANG ZAG NI RANG GI PHUNG PO LA PHAR MI BLTOS PA'I DBANG SGYUR BA PO'I RJE BO LTA BU DANG,
gru.wylie: rang bzhin gyis grub par 'dzin pa'i steng nas gang zag ni rang gi phung po la phar mi bltos pa'i dbang sgyur ba po'i rje bo lta bu dang
gru.english: We would start with holding that the person existed by nature.  And then on top of that, for example, we would be holding that the person was some kind of director of the parts they were composed of—their heaps.  The parts would operate under the person's dictate, and the person would not be something that relied upon them.

gru.acip: GANG ZAG RANG RKYA THUB PA'I RDZAS YOD KYI 'DZIN TSUL DANG, DES BZUNG BA LTAR GRUB NA RANG RKYA THUB PA'I RDZAS YOD DU GRUB PAR 'JOG GO
gru.wylie: gang zag rang rkya thub pa'i rdzas yod kyi 'dzin tshul dang, des bzung ba ltar grub na rang rkya thub pa'i rdzas yod du grub par 'jog go
gru.english: This then is what it looks like when we say that the mind is holding the person to be self-standing, and substantial.  And this is what it would look like for the person to in fact actually exist, in some self-standing and substantial way.

gru.acip: RANG RGYUD PA SOGS RANG SDE GRUB MTHA' SMRA BA SHES SGRIB KHAS LEN PA DAG GIS NYON SGRIB LA KUN BTAGS DANG LHAN SKYES GNYIS YOD PA DE BZHIN DU SHES SGRIB LA YANG DE GNYIS YOD PAR 'DOD KYANG,
gru.wylie: rang rgyud pa sogs rang sde grub mtha' smra ba shes sgrib khas len pa dag gis nyon sgrib la kun btags dang lhan skyes gnyis yod pa de bzhin du shes sgrib la yang de gnyis yod par 'dod kyang
gru.english: Those of the Independent branch and so on—meaning those systems of our own tradition which accept the idea of obstacles to omniscience—say that there are two types of obstacles to nirvana: those which are learned in this life, and those which we already have as we come into this life.  And they would say that the same division applies to obstacles which prevent us from omniscience.

gru.acip: KUN BTAGS LHAN SKYES KYI KHYAD PAR YANG GRUB MTHAS BLO KHA BSGYUR BA LA MA BLTOS PAR, RANG GI NGANG GIS SKYE BA NI LHAN SKYES DANG, DES BLO KHA BSGYUR BA'I DBANG GIS BYUNG BA NI KUN BTAGS SO,,
gru.wylie: kun btags lhan skyes kyi khyad par yang grub mthas blo kha bsgyur ba la ma bltos par, rang gi ngang gis skye ba ni lhan skyes dang, des blo kha bsgyur ba'i dbang gis byung ba ni kun btags so
gru.english: We could clarify here, by the way, the difference between undesirable objects which are learned, and those which are inborn.  When one of these undesirables arises within us all of its own accord, without us having our mind influenced by some system of belief that we encounter in this life, then we describe it as “inborn.”  If such things arise as a result of our mind being influenced by any such system, then we say that they have been “learned.” A general presentation of the path, in the Consequence branch

gru.acip: 'DUN PA'I RDZUN {%RDZU} 'PHRUL GYI RKANG PA BRTZON 'GRUS KYI DE SEMS KYI DE DANG DPYOD PA'I RDZU 'PHRUL GYI RKANG PA STE BZHI,
gru.wylie: 'dun pa'i rdzun {%rdzu} 'phrul gyi rkang pa brtson 'grus kyi de sems kyi de dang dpyod pa'i rdzu 'phrul gyi rkang pa ste bzhi
gru.english: After that we have what are called (9–12) the “four strong legs of the miraculous”—referring to the miraculous legs of aspiration; the miraculous legs of effort; those of focus; and those of analytical discrimination.

gru.acip: DAD PA, BRTZON 'GRUS, DRAN PA, TING 'DZIN, SHES RAB KYI DBANG PO LNGA,
gru.wylie: dad pa, brtson 'grus, dran pa, ting 'dzin, shes rab kyi dbang po lnga
gru.english: Next are (13–17) the five powers of faith, effort, clear awareness, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

gru.acip: YANG DAD PA BRTZON 'GRUS DRAN PA TING 'DZIN SHES RAB KYI STOBS TE STOBS LNGA,
gru.wylie: yang dad pa brtson 'grus dran pa ting 'dzin shes rab kyi stobs te stobs lnga
gru.english: Following those we have (18–22) the five forces, again of faith, effort, clear awareness, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

gru.acip: DRAN PA YANG DAG BYANG CHUB KYI YAN LAG, CHOS RAB TU RNAM 'BYED YANG DAG BYANG CHUB KYI YAN LAG ,DE BZHIN DU BRTZON 'GRUS, DGA' BA, SHIN TU SBYANGS PA, TING NGE 'DZIN, BTANG SNYOMS YANG DAG BYANG CHUB KYI YAN LAG STE BYANG CHUB KYI YAN LAG BDUN,
gru.wylie: dran pa yang dag byang chub kyi yan lag, chos rab tu rnam 'byed yang dag byang chub kyi yan lag ,de bzhin du brtson 'grus, dga' ba, shin tu sbyangs pa, ting nge 'dzin, btang snyoms yang dag byang chub kyi yan lag ste byang chub kyi yan lag bdun
gru.english: After those come (23–29) the seven components of enlightenment: the component of enlightenment represented by clear awareness; the component of enlightenment represented by the ability to distinguish things; and then the same types of components for effort; joy; practiced ease; meditative concentration; and equanimity.

gru.acip: LHA MI PHAL PA LTA BU DANG, RI DVAGS DANG LJON SHING GRU ZAM SOGS SU SPRUL PA'I SKYE BA SPRUL SKU,
gru.wylie: lha mi phal pa lta bu dang, ri dvags dang ljon shing gru zam sogs su sprul pa'i skye ba sprul sku
gru.english: Then there is what we call (2) the “emanation in birth,” which could first of all look like a worldly god, or even an average human being.  But this type could also be emanating in the form of a wild animal in the forest; or even as a tree in that forest; or as a ship on the sea or a bridge over a river—and just about anything else!

whole_word_matches.context: lha mi phal pa lta bu dang, ri dvags dang ljon shing gru zam sogs su sprul pa'i skye ba sprul sku

gru.acip: MDZAD PA 'PHRIN LAS NI 'BAD MED LHUN GRUB TU 'BYUNG STE, YID BZHIN GYI NOR BU DANG, BUM PA BZANG PO, DPAG BSAM GYI SHING LAS RNAM RTOG DANG 'BAD PA MED PAR 'DOD RGU 'BYUNG BA LTAR RO,,
gru.wylie: mdzad pa 'phrin las ni 'bad med lhun grub tu 'byung ste, yid bzhin gyi nor bu dang, bum pa bzang po, dpag bsam gyi shing las rnam rtog dang 'bad pa med par 'dod rgu 'byung ba ltar ro
gru.english: These enlightened deeds of a Buddha, by the way, occur through a process of spontaneous manifestation, with never any effort or premeditation.  It's the same way that something like a wishing jewel, or a magic vase, or else a wish-giving tree gushes forth an unlimited supply of whatever a person might wish for, without any thought or effort from its own side.

gru.acip: ,DE LTAR THUN MONG GRUB MTHA'I RGYA MTSO LAS, ,CHA SHAS ZEGS MA TZAM ZHIG BKOD PA 'DI, ,RMA BYA'I MDONGS KYI KHA DOG SNA TSOGS LTAR, ,LEGS PA'I CHA BSAGS DU MAS RNAM PAR BKRA,
gru.wylie: de ltar thun mong grub mtha'i rgya mtsho las, ,cha shas zegs ma tsam zhig bkod pa 'di, ,rma bya'i mdongs kyi kha dog sna tshogs ltar, ,legs pa'i cha bsags du mas rnam par bkra
gru.english: Thus then have I set forth for you Just a tiny part—no more than a drop— From that veritable ocean of the systems Of belief, treated as a group. I selected for you the very best Of all the different parts, And what we ended up with then Blazed in brightness, like the rainbow Of hues we find on a peacock's plume.

gru.acip: ,LEGS PAR BSHAD LAS THOB PA'I DGE BA NI, ,GANGS RI'I TOG LTAR GANG ZHIG MCHIS PA DE, ,'GRO BLO'I YID KYI MUN PA SEL BA DANG, ,KUN MKHYEN YE SHES 'GRUB PA'I RGYUR BSNGO'O,,
gru.wylie: legs par bshad las thob pa'i dge ba ni, ,gangs ri'i tog ltar gang zhig mchis pa de, ,'gro blo'i yid kyi mun pa sel ba dang, ,kun mkhyen ye shes 'grub pa'i rgyur bsngo'o
gru.english: In short, it can be said That I must have attained Some bit of virtuous karma Through my careful explanations. I pray that all this goodness Stands high, like one of those peaks In the mountains covered with snow; And I dedicate this good As a cause which I hope begins The dispelling of any darkness In the minds of living beings, And their final achievement then Of the wisdom which knows all things.

gru.acip: (ZHES GRUB MTHA' KUN GYI SNYING PO'I DON BSDUS PA BLO GSAL 'JUG PA'I KHANG BZANG ZHES BYA BA
gru.wylie: (zhes grub mtha' kun gyi snying po'i don bsdus pa blo gsal 'jug pa'i khang bzang zhes bya ba
gru.english: This brings us to the end of that veritable palace built for the entertainment of those with clearest minds: A Brief Survey of the Essence of Every Existing Belief System.

gru.acip: 'DI LTA BU ZHIG GYI SA {%GYIS} DANG KHO BOS MTHUN RKYEN MTHA' DAG SBYAR NAS BAR DU BSGRUB BO ZHES
gru.wylie: 'di lta bu zhig gyi sa {%gyis} dang kho bos mthun rkyen mtha' dag sbyar nas bar du bsgrub bo zhes
gru.english: And he said to me, “We need you to write a book on this topic, of belief systems!  If you do, then I will take care of all the necessary expenses to get the book carved and printed.  And say, I know you're quite busy, but you can do it just in between your other things!”

gru.acip: BSKUL BA LA BRTEN NAS, GRUB MTHA'I KHYAD PAR DU MA RIGS {%RIG} PA SH'AKYA'I DGE SLONG GRAGS PA BSHAD SGRUB CES BYA BAS, CO NE'I GZIM KHANG NANG NYID DU NYE BAR SBYAR BA'O,,
gru.wylie: bskul ba la brten nas, grub mtha'i khyad par du ma rigs {%rig} pa shAkya'i dge slong grags pa bshad sgrub ces bya bas, co ne'i gzim khang nang nyid du nye bar sbyar ba'o
gru.english: And so based on this encouragement, the composition of this work has now been completed, here in his own humble quarters at Choney Monastery, by myself—that monk of the Shakya line who goes by the name of Drakpa Shedrup, and who does indeed understand no little detail on the topic of belief systems. Dedication of the Choney reprint

gru.acip: ^ ,,'DI'I GRUB MTHA'I GSUNG PAR CO NE DGON CHEN DU BZHUGS PA DUS 'GYUR DBANG GIS SNGAR NAS ME BZHES ZIN 'DUG PAS DA PHAN SLOB GNYER BA'I KHROD DU YIG CHA DKON GSHIS
gru.wylie: ^ ,,'di'i grub mtha'i gsung par co ne dgon chen du bzhugs pa dus 'gyur dbang gis sngar nas me bzhes zin 'dug pas da phan slob gnyer ba'i khrod du yig cha dkon gshis
gru.english: Now the woodblocks for this teaching on belief systems were originally stored at the great cloister of Choney, but they had—due to the vicissitudes of time—been damaged by fire, so that by our own days printed copies of this textbook of our monastery had become quite rare among those studying here.

gru.acip: BSHAD SGRUB DAR RGYAS YUN RING DU GNAS CHED SER SMAD GZHUNG BA {%PA} GRVA SKU BCAR MKHAN DRUNG T'A BLA MA RONG RNAM SRAS PA THUB BSTAN NOR BZANG SHAG TSANG NAS LHAG BSAM RNAM PAR DAG PAS RGYU SBYOR 'DU 'GOD KYIS
gru.wylie: bshad sgrub dar rgyas yun ring du gnas ched ser smad gzhung ba {%pa} grva sku bcar mkhan drung tA bla ma rong rnam sras pa thub bstan nor bzang shag tshang nas lhag bsam rnam par dag pas rgyu sbyor 'du 'god kyis
gru.english: And so—in order that this tradition of teaching and practice might continue to flourish, and remain long in this world—the necessary expenses for this new carving have been assembled, with the purest of intentions, taking on this personal responsibility, from the house of monks of myself, Tupten Norsang, Rong Namsepa of Ta Lama, high secretary of the Shungpa College of Sera Mey Monastery.

gru.acip: ,RGYU SBYOR NYID KYANG DENG NAS BYANG CHEN BAR, ,MKHAS DANG GRUB PA'I KHYU MCHOG RTEN BZANG BRGYUD, ,THUB BSTAN YANG SNYING 'JAM MGON LUGS BZANG 'DI, ,NAM YANG MI 'BRAL BYANG CHUB MYUR THOB SHOG ,,
gru.wylie: rgyu sbyor nyid kyang deng nas byang chen bar, ,mkhas dang grub pa'i khyu mchog rten bzang brgyud, ,thub bstan yang snying 'jam mgon lugs bzang 'di, ,nam yang mi 'bral byang chub myur thob shog
gru.english: And last we pray, that by the support Received to produce this text, Our sponsors may—in all the lives they live From today to their own enlightenment— Never live apart from the excellent way Of this Gentle Protector, itself the heart In the very heart of all the teachings Of the Able Ones themselves. May they pass from life to life In the excellent body and mind Of the head bull of the herd, Ever wise and ever accomplished, Achieving thus with greatest speed An enlightenment of their own.

gru.acip: (CES PA 'DI YANG DAD STABS {%STOBS} LHAG BSAM GYI RGYAN MDZES SER SMAD SPOM RA DGE BSHES CHOS MDZAD MKHAS GRUB THUB BSTAN NAS SER SMAD GRVA TSANG GI MTSAN NYID YIG CHA GSHAMS GSAL RNAMS KYI DPAR BSKRUN DGE BSNGO'I SMON TSIG TU YONGS 'DZIN KHRI BYANG SPRUL MING PAS SBYAR BA'O,,
gru.wylie: (ces pa 'di yang dad stabs {%stobs} lhag bsam gyi rgyan mdzes ser smad spom ra dge bshes chos mdzad mkhas grub thub bstan nas ser smad grva tshang gi mtshan nyid yig cha gshams gsal rnams kyi dpar bskrun dge bsngo'i smon tshig tu yongs 'dzin khri byang sprul ming pas sbyar ba'o
gru.english: These lines for dedicating the power of a good deed have been composed by myself, the one they call the emanation of Trijang, in honor of the publication of the above philosophical textbook of the Monastery of Sera Mey by the wise and accomplished Kedrup Tupten, a geshe and devotee of the Dharma from the Pomra College of Sera Mey, where he is indeed a jewel of the power of faith and personal responsibility for the happiness of others—a beautiful ornament who makes their college even more stunning.

gru.acip: SER SMAD MKHAN PO LAS 'DZIN RGYAL NGAG DBANG THEG MCHOG PAS BSTAN DON LHAG BSAM THUGS KHUR CHE BZHES BGYIS NGOR DAD GTONG LHAG BSAM YANGS PA SPOM RA DGE BSHES CHOS MDZAD MKHAS GRUB THUB BSTAN NAS
gru.wylie: ser smad mkhan po las 'dzin rgyal ngag dbang theg mchog pas bstan don lhag bsam thugs khur che bzhes bgyis ngor dad gtong lhag bsam yangs pa spom ra dge bshes chos mdzad mkhas grub thub bstan nas
gru.english: Grave responsibility for overseeing this publication was assumed by Ngawang Tekchok of Gyalrong College, who serves as the abbot of Sera Mey—a monk who is always ready to serve the teachings.  A major donation for the work was received from the aforementioned geshe and devotee of the Dharma from Pomra College, Kedrup Tupten—a practitioner of great faith and generosity who possesses himself a vast capacity to take on personal responsibility for the benefit of all beings.

gru.acip: DENG DUS KUN PHAN NYER MKHO'I RANG GZHUNG KUN GZHI SPYI MTHA', DON BDUN CU, RTAGS RIGS, GRUB MTHA' BCAS DANG, BSAM GZUGS SPYI MTHA', DGE NYI, DRANG NGES RTEN 'BREL MTHA' DPYOD BCAS KYI DPE BSKRUN LAS BYED,
gru.wylie: deng dus kun phan nyer mkho'i rang gzhung kun gzhi spyi mtha', don bdun cu, rtags rigs, grub mtha' bcas dang, bsam gzugs spyi mtha', dge nyi, drang nges rten 'brel mtha' dpyod bcas kyi dpe bskrun las byed
gru.english: We have a team of members of the monastery who have been currently working on producing new editions of major texts that are of great necessity and benefit to everyone.  These works include topics such as the overview and dialectic analysis of the Seventy Topics of the Jewel of Realizations; the science of reasoning; the current presentation of various belief systems; the overview and dialectic analysis of the study of the meditation levels of the form & formless realms; the twenty divisions of spiritual practitioners; and the overview and dialectic analysis on the art of interpretation.

gru.acip: ZHU DAG PA GTZANG THUB BSTAN RIN CHEN, SPOM RA BLO BZANG DNGOS GRUB, YIG BRIS PA MI GRANGS BCU GSUM NAS 'DI'I YIG BRIS TSVA RDOR THUB BSTAN BLO BZANG, DPAR RTZA BDAG SPROD PA MI NYAG BLO BZANG YON TAN SOGS LAS BYED 'BREL YOD
gru.wylie: zhu dag pa gtsang thub bstan rin chen, spom ra blo bzang dngos grub, yig bris pa mi grangs bcu gsum nas 'di'i yig bris tshva rdor thub bstan blo bzang, dpar rtsa bdag sprod pa mi nyag blo bzang yon tan sogs las byed 'brel yod
gru.english: The chief editors on our team are Tupten Rinchen of the Tsang College of Sera Mey, and Lobsang Ngudrup of Pomra College.  Some 13 different persons acted as scribes, and Tupten Lobsang of Tsador has taken on the task of storing and preserving the blocks.  And then we had numerous other assistants, such as Lobsang Yunten.

gru.acip: PHYI LO 1969 BOD RGYAL LO 2906 SA BYA ZLA GSUM PA'I YAR TSES LA GONG GSAL YIG CHA LE'U TSAN 'DI'I GRANGS NYIS BRGYA THAM PA RDO PAR GYIS LAM NAS DPAR 'DEBS LEGS BSGRUBS ZHUS PA'I
gru.wylie: phyi lo 1969 bod rgyal lo 2906 sa bya zla gsum pa'i yar tshes la gong gsal yig cha le'u tshan 'di'i grangs nyis brgya tham pa rdo par gyis lam nas dpar 'debs legs bsgrubs zhus pa'i
gru.english: And so it is, that in the modern year of 1969—corresponding to year 2906 of the Tibetan kings, or the earth bird year—during the rising moon in the third month, the printing of this particular text among the ones just listed has been completed, through the lithograph process.

gru.acip: [A41] DE LA BRTEN NAS DE DON GZHAN GYIS {%GYI} BDAG TU MA GRUB PAR RTOGS PAR 'GYUR BA YIN TE,
gru.wylie: [a41] de la brten nas de don gzhan gyis {%gyi} bdag tu ma grub par rtogs par 'gyur ba yin te
gru.english: And from that understanding you come to see that things have no nature of being separate.

gru.acip: [A77] SLOB DPON KLU SGRUB KYIS MDZAD PA'I PHYAG RGYA BZHI BSTAN PA CHOS 'BAR GYI 'GYUR, 'DI KLU SGRUB KYIS BYAS PA MIN PAR MAN SNYER BSHAD,
gru.wylie: [a77] slob dpon klu sgrub kyis mdzad pa'i phyag rgya bzhi bstan pa chos 'bar gyi 'gyur, 'di klu sgrub kyis byas pa min par man snyer bshad
gru.english: The Four Seals, attributed to Acharya Nagarjuna, was translated into Tibetan by Tenpa Chumbar: “Blaze of Dharma.”  According to The Golden Harvest of Advices, it was not written by Nagarjuna himself.

gru.acip: [A80] LTA BA BKA' BRTAGS KYI PHYAG RGYA BZHI KHAS MI LEN PA'I NANG PA'I GRUB MTHA' SMRA BA PO MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: [a80] lta ba bka' brtags kyi phyag rgya bzhi khas mi len pa'i nang pa'i grub mtha' smra ba po med pa'i phyir
gru.english: There is no one that belongs to an inner belief system—a Buddhist school of philosophy—who would ever deny the four seals that mark a view as the word of the Buddha.

gru.acip: [A91] DE YANG THOS PA DANG, BSAM PA DANG, SGOM PAS SHES KYI SGRAR BRJOD PA TZAM GYIS MA YIN TE, DE LTAR SHES NAS KYANG SNYING RJE'I SEMS BRTAN PA NYE BAR BZHAG STE SEMS CAN RNAMS KYI DON DU RTZOL ZHING 'DAB {%'BAD} LA BRTZON 'GRUS RTZOM MO,,
gru.wylie: [a91] de yang thos pa dang, bsam pa dang, sgom pas shes kyi sgrar brjod pa tsam gyis ma yin te, de ltar shes nas kyang snying rje'i sems brtan pa nye bar bzhag ste sems can rnams kyi don du rtsol zhing 'dab {%'bad} la brtson 'grus rtsom mo
gru.english: These things you will come to know by listening, contemplating, and meditating; but never just through the words themselves.  And then even once you do know, you must toil, struggle, and strive to reach unshakable compassion for the good of every living being. Appendix B Three presentations On the Numerist (Sankhya) School 1) Gelong Sherab Wangpo on the Numerist (Sankhya) School The following section is from The True Intent Made Even More Clear: A Treatment of Difficult Points in the Explanation of “Entering the Middle Way” Entitled “Illumination of the True Thought,” by Gelong Sherab Wangpo (1500–1586).

gru.acip: [B13] GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, BDAG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG PA DANG, BDAG GI BA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG PA'O,,
gru.wylie: [b13] gnyis pa la gnyis, bdag rang bzhin gyis grub pa dgag pa dang, bdag gi ba rang bzhin gyis grub pa dgag pa'o
gru.english: The second section has two parts: 1) Denying that a self could exist through some nature of its own; 2) Denying that anything belonging to the self could exist through some nature of its own.

gru.acip: [C7] ,'DI LA MTSAN NI GANG GANG GIS, ,SGRUB PAR BYED PA'I RGYU GANG YIN, ,DE DANG DE NI RAB RDZOGS PAS, ,MTSAN NI 'DI DAG YANG DAG 'GRUB,
gru.wylie: [c7] ,'di la mtshan ni gang gang gis, ,sgrub par byed pa'i rgyu gang yin, ,de dang de ni rab rdzogs pas, ,mtshan ni 'di dag yang dag 'grub
gru.english: Each of these signs has its own cause Which brings it about. When each of these causes is completed, Then each of the signs shows perfect.

gru.acip: [C8] ,BLA MA SKYEL LA SOGS PA DANG, ,YANG DAG BLANGS PA BRTAN PA DANG, ,BSDU BA BSTEN DANG GYA NOM PA'I, ,DNGOS PO SBYIN DANG GSAD BYA BA, ,THAR BAR BYED DANG DGE BA NI, ,YANG DAG BLANGS PA SPEL LA SOGS, ,SGRUB BYED RGYU YI MTSAN NYID DE, ,MDO LAS JI SKAD 'BYUNG BA BZHIN,
gru.wylie: [c8] ,bla ma skyel la sogs pa dang, ,yang dag blangs pa brtan pa dang, ,bsdu ba bsten dang gya nom pa'i, ,dngos po sbyin dang gsad bya ba, ,thar bar byed dang dge ba ni, ,yang dag blangs pa spel la sogs, ,sgrub byed rgyu yi mtshan nyid de, ,mdo las ji skad 'byung ba bzhin
gru.english: The details of the causes That bring about the signs Are as we find them in the sutras: Deeds such as transporting your Lama, Staying firm in the commitments you've made, Using the ways of gathering disciples, Giving exquisite gifts, And freeing animals meant to be killed— Taking up good deeds, Trying to make them more, And all such kinds of goodness.

gru.acip: [C37] RIN CHEN PHRENG BA DANG 'GRIG DKA' BAR SNANG BAS DPYAD BYA STE, RIN CHEN PHRENG BA LAS GSUNGS PA NI, BYANG SEMS MA GTOGS PA'I SEMS CAN THAMS CAD GYI BSOD NAMS JI SNYED YOD PA THAMS CAD BCUR BSGYUR BAS SANGS RGYAS KYI BA SPU'I BU GA GCIG 'GRUB, BA SPU'I BU GA THAMS CAD DE DANG 'DRA,
gru.wylie: [c37] rin chen phreng ba dang 'grig dka' bar snang bas dpyad bya ste, rin chen phreng ba las gsungs pa ni, byang sems ma gtogs pa'i sems can thams cad gyi bsod nams ji snyed yod pa thams cad bcur bsgyur bas sangs rgyas kyi ba spu'i bu ga gcig 'grub, ba spu'i bu ga thams cad de dang 'dra
gru.english: This point appears a little difficult to reconcile with what we see in the String of Jewels, and warrants further study.  What the String of Jewels says is that if you took all the good karma of every living being there is—excepting the bodhisattvas—and multiplied it times ten, then you would have enough to create a tiny hair in a single pore on the skin of an Enlightened Being.  And then you would need that same amount for every single one of the other tiny hairs on their skin.

gru.acip: [C38] BA SPU'I BU GA THAMS CAD 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS BRGYAR BSGYUR BAS DPE BYAD BZANG PO GCIG 'GRUB, ,DPE BYAD THAMS CAD DE DANG 'DRA,
gru.wylie: [c38] ba spu'i bu ga thams cad 'grub pa'i bsod nams brgyar bsgyur bas dpe byad bzang po gcig 'grub, ,dpe byad thams cad de dang 'dra
gru.english: If you took all the good karma needed to produce all of these tiny hairs, and multiplied that times a hundred, you would have enough to produce a single one of the minor marks.  And then you would need again that amount to produce every one of the remaining minor marks.

gru.acip: [C39] DPE BYAD BRGYAD CU THAMS CAD 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS BRGYAR BSGYUR BAS MDZOD SPU GTZUG TOR MA GTOGS PA'I MTSAN GCIG 'GRUB, MTSAN GZHAN THAMS CAD DE DANG 'DRA,
gru.wylie: [c39] dpe byad brgyad cu thams cad 'grub pa'i bsod nams brgyar bsgyur bas mdzod spu gtsug tor ma gtogs pa'i mtshan gcig 'grub, mtshan gzhan thams cad de dang 'dra
gru.english: If you took all of the good karma needed to produce all 80 of the minor marks, and multiplied it times a hundred, you would have enough to produce just one of the major signs—except for the treasure-hair or the crown ridge.  And you would need again that same amount for every one of the remaining major signs.

gru.acip: [C40] MTSAN SUM CU 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS STONG BSGYUR GYIS MDZOD SPU 'GRUB, MDZOD SPU 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS 'BUM BSGYUR GYIS GTZUG TOR 'GRUB,
gru.wylie: [c40] mtshan sum cu 'grub pa'i bsod nams stong bsgyur gyis mdzod spu 'grub, mdzod spu 'grub pa'i bsod nams 'bum bsgyur gyis gtsug tor 'grub
gru.english: If you took all the good karma needed to produce all of these 30 major signs and multiplied it times a thousand, you would have enough karma to produce the treasure-hair.  If you took all the good karma necessary to produce this treasure-hair, and multiplied it times a hundred thousand, then you would have enough to produce the crown ridge.

gru.acip: [C41] GTZUG TOR 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS GRANGS MED PHRAG BCUS GSUNG DBYANGS YAN LAG DRUG CU 'GRUB PAR GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR RO,
gru.wylie: [c41] gtsug tor 'grub pa'i bsod nams grangs med phrag bcus gsung dbyangs yan lag drug cu 'grub par gsungs pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: If you took all the good karma needed to produce the crown ridge, it is said, and multiplied it times 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000, then you would have enough to produce the 60 high qualities of a Buddha's speech. What causes the signs, and what they mean Here is some information about what causes the signs and marks, and what they mean.  It's from A Lamp Which Illuminates the Hidden Meaning, composed of notes to a teaching by the great Konchok Tenpay Drunme of Gungtang (1762–1823), an illustrious thinker from East Tibet.  Please note that the version of this text that we have is obviously corrupt, and some words cannot be discerned, although almost all the points are clear.  He is obviously though referencing the great commentary on the Jewel written by the Indian sage Haribhadra, which helps to decipher the carving. Above, the realized being Ananda

gru.acip: [C51] DED DPON DU GYUR BA'I TSE BYIS PA CHUNG NGU'I DUS NAS SROG CHAGS GROGS SBUR SOGS KYI'ANG SROG GCOD PA SPANGS BA'I BDEN TSIG GIS RGYA MTSOR GRU BO CHE MI MTHUN PA'I RLUNG GIS BSKYOD PA'I 'JIGS PA LAS GROL BAR BYAS PA LTA BU SOGS KYIS SKU CHE ZHING DRANG BA NYID DANG,
gru.wylie: [c51] ded dpon du gyur ba'i tshe byis pa chung ngu'i dus nas srog chags grogs sbur sogs kyi'ang srog gcod pa spangs ba'i bden tshig gis rgya mtshor gru bo che mi mthun pa'i rlung gis bskyod pa'i 'jigs pa las grol bar byas pa lta bu sogs kyis sku che zhing drang ba nyid dang
gru.english: (S8) There was a lifetime when our Teacher was the captain of a ship.  Even as a child, he had given up the act of taking life—even the lives of creatures like ants and other insects.  As an adult, he was in charge of a great sailing ship which one day encountered a terrible hurricane.  He performed an act of truth based on how he had protected life his entire life; and everyone was saved from the threat.  Because of deeds such as this, he came to have a body which was large and straight.

whole_word_matches.context: ng srog gcod pa spangs ba'i bden tshig gis rgya mtshor gru bo che mi mthun pa'i rlung gis bskyod pa'i 'jigs pa la

gru.acip: [C87] ,ZHES SOGS LTAR NYAN RANG DANG 'JIG RTEN DANG 'JIG RTEN LAS 'DAS PA'I BSOD NAMS GCIG TU BSDUS PA BCUR BSGRES PAS SANGS RGYAS KYI BA SPU'I KHUNG BU GCIG 'GRUB, BA SPU NYI KHRI CHIG STONG GI BAR DE DANG 'DRA'O,,
gru.wylie: [c87] ,zhes sogs ltar nyan rang dang 'jig rten dang 'jig rten las 'das pa'i bsod nams gcig tu bsdus pa bcur bsgres pas sangs rgyas kyi ba spu'i khung bu gcig 'grub, ba spu nyi khri chig stong gi bar de dang 'dra'o
gru.english: What this is saying is that you could lump together all the good karma accumulated by all the listeners, and all the self-made buddhas—and all the good karma that belongs to the world, or has gone beyond the world—and multiply it all by ten, and you would just have enough karma to produce a single fine hair growing out of a single pore on the skin of a Buddha.  And it would be the same for every one of the 21,000 tiny hairs that grow on a typical body.

gru.acip: [C88] BA SPU'I BU GA THAMS CAD BSKYED PA'I BSOD NAMS GCIG TU BSDUS PA BRGYAR BSGRES PAS DPE BYAD BZANG PO GCIG 'GRUB, DPE BYAD BRGYAD CU'I BAR DE DANG 'DRA'O,,
gru.wylie: [c88] ba spu'i bu ga thams cad bskyed pa'i bsod nams gcig tu bsdus pa brgyar bsgres pas dpe byad bzang po gcig 'grub, dpe byad brgyad cu'i bar de dang 'dra'o
gru.english: If you took all the good karma needed to produce all of these fine hairs in all of those pores of the skin, and rolled it into one, and multiplied that times a hundred, then you would have enough karma to produce a single one of the lovely marks on a Buddha's body.  And you would have to repeat the same, for each and every one of these 80 minor marks.

gru.acip: [C89] DPE BYAD BRGYAD CU 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS GCIG TU BSDOMS PA BRGYAR BSGRES PAS MTSAN BZANG GCIG 'GRUB, MTSAN SO GNYIS KYI BAR DE DANG 'DRA,
gru.wylie: [c89] dpe byad brgyad cu 'grub pa'i bsod nams gcig tu bsdoms pa brgyar bsgres pas mtshan bzang gcig 'grub, mtshan so gnyis kyi bar de dang 'dra
gru.english: If you combined all the good karma it would take to produce all 80 of the minor marks, and multiplied that by a hundred, you'd have enough karma to produce a single one of the exquisite signs.  And you'd have to repeat that for all 32.

gru.acip: [C90] MTSAN BZANG DE DAG 'GRUB PA'I BSOD NAMS THAMS CAD STONG DU BSGYUR BAS ZLA BA NYA 'DRA'I MDZOD SPU GCIG 'GRUB,
gru.wylie: [c90] mtshan bzang de dag 'grub pa'i bsod nams thams cad stong du bsgyur bas zla ba nya 'dra'i mdzod spu gcig 'grub
gru.english: If you took all the good karma needed to produce all these beautiful signs and multiplied that by a thousand, you'd have enough to produce the treasure-hair, which resembles the moon in full.

gru.acip: [C91] MDZOD SPU'I BSOD NAMS DAG STONG PHRAG BRGYAR BSGYUR BAS SANGS RGYAS KYI GTZUG TOR 'GRUB,
gru.wylie: [c91] mdzod spu'i bsod nams dag stong phrag brgyar bsgyur bas sangs rgyas kyi gtsug tor 'grub
gru.english: If you took the good karma required to produce the treasure-hair and multiplied it by a hundred thousand, you'd have enough to produce the crown ridge atop a Buddha's skull.

gru.acip: [C92] GTZUG TOR BSKYED PA'I BSOD NAMS BYE BA GRANGS MED BCU YIS YAN LAG DRUG CU'I GSUNGS DBYANGS 'GRUB STE,
gru.wylie: [c92] gtsug tor bskyed pa'i bsod nams bye ba grangs med bcu yis yan lag drug cu'i gsungs dbyangs 'grub ste
gru.english: If you took the good karma required to produce the crown ridge, and multiplied it by ten million multiplied by 10 to the 60th power, then you'd have enough karma to produce the Buddha's speech, replete with 60 high qualities.

gru.acip: [C104] RIGS MCHOG LAS SKYES PA SEN MO MTHO BA'I RGYUR 'ONG DON MED PAS DPE BYAD KYI SKABS KYI 'DI DAG MTSAN BZANG GI SKABS LTAR RGYUS 'BRAS BU SGRUB PA MA YIN GYI, DE'I TSE YOD PA'I PHYI ROL GYI RTAGS 'DI DAG NI NANG GI YON TAN DE DAG DPOG BYED KYI RANG BZHIN GYI RTAGS LTA BU ZHIG YIN GSUNG,
gru.wylie: [c104] rigs mchog las skyes pa sen mo mtho ba'i rgyur 'ong don med pas dpe byad kyi skabs kyi 'di dag mtshan bzang gi skabs ltar rgyus 'bras bu sgrub pa ma yin gyi, de'i tshe yod pa'i phyi rol gyi rtags 'di dag ni nang gi yon tan de dag dpog byed kyi rang bzhin gyi rtags lta bu zhig yin gsung
gru.english: Our Lama noted though that it makes no sense to say our Teacher's being born into the highest caste was the reason why he had raised fingernails; but that here in the discussion of the marks, we are not talking about qualities which are results produced by certain causes as in the case of the exquisite signs.  In this case, these outer manifestations are signs in the sense that they allow us to deduce certain internal, fine qualities.

gru.acip: [C130] SANGS RGYAS KYIS GSUNGS PA LTAR NYAMS SU BLANGS NA NAM ZHIG GTAN GYI 'DUN MA GRUB PAR 'GYUR BAS NA PHYI RJES SU YONGS SU DAG PA'I CHOS YIN LA DE STON PAR MDZAD PAS PHYAG GI RI MO RING BA NYID DANG,
gru.wylie: [c130] sangs rgyas kyis gsungs pa ltar nyams su blangs na nam zhig gtan gyi 'dun ma grub par 'gyur bas na phyi rjes su yongs su dag pa'i chos yin la de ston par mdzad pas phyag gi ri mo ring ba nyid dang
gru.english: (M46) If a person puts into practice what a Buddha teaches, then at some point they will realize their ultimate dreams; and so what comes later proves out that this is a perfectly pure teaching—and when we give people that teaching, the result is that the lines cut into our palms are long.

gru.acip: [C143] THAMS CAD LA PHAN PA KHO NA SGRUB PA'I 'BRAS RTAGS SU THUGS KA NA BKRA SHIS BA'I DPAL BE'U DANG, MGRIN PA NA DUNG GA-YAS 'KHYIL GYI RI MO YOD PA SOGS BKRA SHIS PA'I DGE MTSAN GYIS BRGYAN PA YIN GSUNG NGO,
gru.wylie: [c143] thams cad la phan pa kho na sgrub pa'i 'bras rtags su thugs ka na bkra shis ba'i dpal be'u dang, mgrin pa na dung ga-yas 'khyil gyi ri mo yod pa sogs bkra shis pa'i dge mtshan gyis brgyan pa yin gsung ngo
gru.english: (M80) As a sign that we work at nothing other than the benefit of every living being, there are the outlines of knots of glory upon the skin at our heart; and the outlines of a conch shell, spiraling to the right, at our throat—and so on.  And thus, said our Lama, are we adorned with the signs of auspicious goodness. Appendix D The 64 enlightened qualities Of a Buddha's speech There are a number of different presentations of the 64 enlightened qualities of the speech of an Enlightened Being.  Perhaps the earliest version may be found in a sutra by the name of the Inconceivable Secret of Those Gone Thus.  Another wonderful source is the great Master Vasubandhu, who has covered the 64 in his commentary to Lord Maitreya's Jewel of the Sutras. Our favorite version though is that by the great Quicksilver Lama, Ngulchu Dharma Bhadra.  It is found in his Key to the Door of Faith: A Short Work Relating the Fine Qualities of the Victorious Ones.  Here is a modernish translation.

gru.acip: [D21] GSUNG GI DON BSGRUBS PA LA SLAR 'GYOD PA MI 'BYUNG BAS GDUNG BA MED PA DANG,
gru.wylie: [d21] gsung gi don bsgrubs pa la slar 'gyod pa mi 'byung bas gdung ba med pa dang
gru.english: (20) A Buddha's speech removes all torment, because we never again feel any doubt about whether we will be able to carry out what she or he has taught us.

gru.acip: [D39] DON THAMS CAD 'GRUB PA'I BKRA SHIS KYI SNGA LTAS YIN PAS NA BYA SHANG SHANG TE'U'I DBYANGS LTA BU DANG,
gru.wylie: [d39] don thams cad 'grub pa'i bkra shis kyi snga ltas yin pas na bya shang shang te'u'i dbyangs lta bu dang
gru.english: (38) A Buddha's speech is like the song of a pheasant, for it is an auspicious portent, that all goals will be attained.

gru.acip: [E29] DE'I 'OG TU DE LTAR YONGS SU RTOG PA LA ZHUGS PA LA BRTZON 'GRUS 'BYUNG BAS RTZOL BA LAS BYUNG PA'I LAM 'CHAD LA,
gru.wylie: [e29] de'i 'og tu de ltar yongs su rtog pa la zhugs pa la brtson 'grus 'byung bas rtsol ba las byung pa'i lam 'chad la
gru.english: Subsequent to what we have just described, we gain a special form of effort towards these different types of deep consideration; this is explained as being a “path that arises through exerting ourselves.”

gru.acip: [E30] DE YANG TSOGS LAM 'BRING GIS BSDUS PA'I YANG DAG PAR SPONG PA BZHI CHOS CAN{%,} RTZOL BA LAS BYUNG PA'I LAM YIN TE, MI DGE BA SKYES PA DANG, MA SKYES BA {%PA} DAG LA DMIGS NAS GO RIM BZHIN DU YANG DAG PAR SPONG BA DANG, MI SKYE BA DANG, DGE BA SKYES PA DANG, MA SKYES PA DAG LA DMIGS NAS GO RIM BZHIN DU 'PHEL PA DANG BSKYED PA'I RGYU BLANG DOR LA SPRO BA'I BRTZON 'GRUS YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: [e30] de yang tshogs lam 'bring gis bsdus pa'i yang dag par spong pa bzhi chos can{%,} rtsol ba las byung pa'i lam yin te, mi dge ba skyes pa dang, ma skyes ba {%pa} dag la dmigs nas go rim bzhin du yang dag par spong ba dang, mi skye ba dang, dge ba skyes pa dang, ma skyes pa dag la dmigs nas go rim bzhin du 'phel pa dang bskyed pa'i rgyu blang dor la spro ba'i brtson 'grus yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let us consider, then, these four perfect abandonments, as they are taken in by the medium form of the path of accumulation. They constitute a path which arises through exerting ourselves; Because they consist of a kind of effort where we take delight in either taking up or giving up the following, as the case may be.  That is, we focus upon non-virtues which we have already given rise to, or those that we have yet to give rise to, and respectively either (5) abandon them perfectly, or (6) strive to never give them rise.  And then as far as virtues, we focus upon those which we have already given rise to, or not yet given rise to, and respectively either (7) try to increase them, or (8) try to give rise to them—focusing on the necessary causes.

gru.acip: [E31] BSGOM TSUL NI DE LTAR BLANG DOR BYA BA'I PHYIR DU 'DUN PA BSKYED, 'BAD PA BRTZON 'GRUS RTZOM, SEMS RAB TU 'DZIN, RAB TU 'JOG PAR BYED PA YIN LA,
gru.wylie: [e31] bsgom tshul ni de ltar blang dor bya ba'i phyir du 'dun pa bskyed, 'bad pa brtson 'grus rtsom, sems rab tu 'dzin, rab tu 'jog par byed pa yin la
gru.english: The method of practice we use here is that—first of all—we build up within ourselves a real aspiration to both take up what we need to, and give up what we need to, with regard to those virtues and non-virtues.  After that we redouble all our attempts & efforts.  We keep our thoughts strong, and then work to make them incredibly firm.

gru.acip: [E33] GSUM PA TING NGE 'DZIN YONGS SU SBYONG BA'I LAM NI, BLANG DOR BYED PA'I BRTZON 'GRUS DANG LDAN PA NI SEMS LAS SU RUNG PA NYID DU BYED PAS DE'I 'OG TU TING NGE 'DZIN YONGS SU SBYONG BA'I LAM 'CHAD DO,,
gru.wylie: [e33] gsum pa ting nge 'dzin yongs su sbyong ba'i lam ni, blang dor byed pa'i brtson 'grus dang ldan pa ni sems las su rung pa nyid du byed pas de'i 'og tu ting nge 'dzin yongs su sbyong ba'i lam 'chad do
gru.english: This brings us to our third sub-group, which consists of a path for perfecting our meditative concentration.  Once we are possessed of that kind of effort towards taking up what we need to, and giving up what we need to, then our mind has—in a sense—been put into good shape for the work ahead.  And with that, we are ready for what has been explained as a path for perfecting that concentration.

gru.acip: [E34] DE YANG TSOGS LAM CHEN POS BSDUS PA'I RDZU 'PHRUL GYI RKANG PA'I RNAM PA CHOS CAN, TING NGE 'DZIN YONGS SU SBYONG BA'I LAM YIN TE, TING NGE 'DZIN GYIS GRUB PA'I BYA BA SPRUL BSGYUR SOGS LA DMIGS NAS SPONG BA'I 'DU BYED BRGYAD DANG LDAN PA'I SGO NAS SGOM PA'I TING NGE 'DZIN MTSUNGS LDAN DANG BCAS PA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: [e34] de yang tshogs lam chen pos bsdus pa'i rdzu 'phrul gyi rkang pa'i rnam pa chos can, ting nge 'dzin yongs su sbyong ba'i lam yin te, ting nge 'dzin gyis grub pa'i bya ba sprul bsgyur sogs la dmigs nas spong ba'i 'du byed brgyad dang ldan pa'i sgo nas sgom pa'i ting nge 'dzin mtshungs ldan dang bcas pa yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Consider then the aspect of omniscience known as “strong legs of the miraculous,” taken in as it is by the greater form of the path of accumulation. This is indeed a path where we perfect our meditative concentration, Because it is a kind of concentration, involving a mental link, in which we focus upon skills—such as emanating forms and transforming objects—which must be attained through the use of meditative focus.  And we must practice that focus through a familiarity with the eight different counteragents used to combat typical problems in our meditation.

gru.acip: [E36] 'DUN PA'I TING NGE 'DZIN NI GUS SBYOR DANG, BRTZON 'GRUS KYI TING NGE 'DZIN NI RTAG SBYOR DANG, SEMS KYI TING NGE 'DZIN NI SNGON GOMS PA'I SA BON BRTAS PA DANG, DPYOD PA'I TING NGE 'DZIN NI GZHAN GYIS BSTAN PA'I CHOS RAB TU RNAM 'BYED RNAMS LA BRTEN NAS RIM BZHIN SEMS RTZE GCIG PA NYID LA RIG PA'O,,
gru.wylie: [e36] 'dun pa'i ting nge 'dzin ni gus sbyor dang, brtson 'grus kyi ting nge 'dzin ni rtag sbyor dang, sems kyi ting nge 'dzin ni sngon goms pa'i sa bon brtas pa dang, dpyod pa'i ting nge 'dzin ni gzhan gyis bstan pa'i chos rab tu rnam 'byed rnams la brten nas rim bzhin sems rtse gcig pa nyid la rig pa'o
gru.english: First here is (9) “aspirational concentration” [or “strong legs” of aspiration], which is adjoined by feelings of respect for the art of meditation; (10) “effortful concentration,” which is adjoined by constant persistence; (11) “mental focus,” which is adjoined by the great strengthening of mental seeds, due to constant past practice; and (12) “analytical concentration,” where we undertake deep explorations of the teachings we have been granted by others.  You can think of these four as incremental steps in the pursuit of complete, single-pointed focus.

gru.acip: [E45] BLANG DOR BYED PAR SPRO BA'I BRTZON 'GRUS DANG,
gru.wylie: [e45] blang dor byed par spro ba'i brtson 'grus dang
gru.english: (14) Effort then is a feeling of joy in the hard work of taking up what we need to take up, and giving up what we need to give up.

gru.acip: [E52] DE YANG BZOD PA DANG CHOS MCHOG GANG RUNG GI TING NGE 'DZIN DANG, DAD PA DANG, BRTZON 'GRUS DANG, DRAN PA DANG, ,SHES RAB RNAMS CHOS CAN, BDEN PA MNGON PAR RTOGS PA DANG 'BREL PA'I LAM YIN TE, RANG RANG GI MI MTHUN PHYOGS KYIS BRDZI BAR MI NUS PA'I STOBS SU GYUR BA'I SGOM BYUNG GI DAD SOGS YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: [e52] de yang bzod pa dang chos mchog gang rung gi ting nge 'dzin dang, dad pa dang, brtson 'grus dang, dran pa dang, ,shes rab rnams chos can, bden pa mngon par rtogs pa dang 'brel pa'i lam yin te, rang rang gi mi mthun phyogs kyis brdzi bar mi nus pa'i stobs su gyur ba'i sgom byung gi dad sogs yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: And so— Consider the (18) meditative concentration; (19) faith; (20) effort; (21) clear awareness; and (22) wisdom at the levels of warmth or “highest thing,” whichever it may be. They represent a path which connects to an extraordinary realization of the truth; Because they consist of faith—or whichever other one it may be—which is a sufficiently powerful force to resist being crushed by the powers that work against it. F. The seven components of enlightenment (aspects 23–29)

gru.acip: [E55] DE YANG BDEN PA'I RANG BZHIN LA DMIGS NAS, DE LAS SEMS MI G-YENG BAR BYED PA'I GNAS KYI YAN LAG DRAN PA DANG, RANG BZHIN GYI YAN LAG CHOS RAB TU RNAM PAR 'BYED PA DANG, MTHONG SPANGS LAS NGES PAR 'BYUNG BA'I YAN LAG BRTZON 'GRUS DANG, PHAN YON GYI YAN LAG DGA' BA DANG, NYON MONGS PA MED PA'I GZHI GNAS DANG NGO BO'I YAN LAG SHIN TU SBYANGS PA DANG, TING NGE 'DZIN DANG, BTANG SNYOMS YANG DAG BYANG CHUB YAN LAG GI RNAM PA BDUN CHOS CAN, MNGON PAR RTOGS PA'I LAM YIN TE, BDEN PA MNGON SUM DU GSAR DU MTHONG BA'I YE SHES YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: [e55] de yang bden pa'i rang bzhin la dmigs nas, de las sems mi g-yeng bar byed pa'i gnas kyi yan lag dran pa dang, rang bzhin gyi yan lag chos rab tu rnam par 'byed pa dang, mthong spangs las nges par 'byung ba'i yan lag brtson 'grus dang, phan yon gyi yan lag dga' ba dang, nyon mongs pa med pa'i gzhi gnas dang ngo bo'i yan lag shin tu sbyangs pa dang, ting nge 'dzin dang, btang snyoms yang dag byang chub yan lag gi rnam pa bdun chos can, mngon par rtogs pa'i lam yin te, bden pa mngon sum du gsar du mthong ba'i ye shes yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: And so let us consider now those aspects which consist of the seven components of enlightenment: [First,] a “component of fixation,” which keeps the mind from wandering off its object—which is to say, (23) clear awareness; [Second,] a “component of essential nature”—which refers to (24) the ability to make final distinctions about reality; [Third,] a “component of total release” from the undesirable qualities we eliminate when we reach the path of seeing—a reference to (25) effort; [Fourth,] a “component of benefit,” referring to the emotion of (26) joy; and then [Fifth through seventh,] the (27) practiced ease; (28) meditative concentration; and (29) equanimity which constitute elements free of negativities and represent, respectively, components of “foundation”; “residing”; and “essence.” Together, these seven are a path of extraordinary realization; Because they represent a wisdom with which we directly see—for the first time, and directly—ultimate reality.

gru.acip: [E132] DBU MA PA YIN PAS KUN GZHI KHAS MI LEN DGOS PA'I NGES PA MED DE, RNAL 'BYOR SPYOD PA'I DBU MA PA NI THA SNYAD DU SEMS TZAM PA DANG MTHUN PAR GRUB PA'I MTHA' RNAM PAR 'JOG PA'I PHYIR DANG,
gru.wylie: [e132] dbu ma pa yin pas kun gzhi khas mi len dgos pa'i nges pa med de, rnal 'byor spyod pa'i dbu ma pa ni tha snyad du sems tsam pa dang mthun par grub pa'i mtha' rnam par 'jog pa'i phyir dang
gru.english: And yet just because someone belongs to the Middle Way system it is not necessarily the case that they cannot accept the concept of a foundation consciousness.  After all, those members of the Middle Way school who lean towards the beliefs of those who follow precise practice are considered to follow a system of belief which is, nominally, consistent with that of the Mind Only.

gru.acip: [E133] NYI KHRI SNANG BAR, SLOB DPON BZANG SKYONG GIS SKABS SU BAB PA KUN GZHI'I RNAM PAR SHES PA LA SOGS PA SHES BYA RNAM PA BCUS BSDUS PA'I SNYING PO MKHYEN PA YIN PA'I PHYIR RNAM PA THAMS CAD MKHYEN PA NYID DO ZHES BYA BA 'DI NI CHES LEGS TE, YONGS SU GRUB PA LA DMIGS PA'O,,
gru.wylie: [e133] nyi khri snang bar, slob dpon bzang skyong gis skabs su bab pa kun gzhi'i rnam par shes pa la sogs pa shes bya rnam pa bcus bsdus pa'i snying po mkhyen pa yin pa'i phyir rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa nyid do zhes bya ba 'di ni ches legs te, yongs su grub pa la dmigs pa'o
gru.english: And we see the following section in the Illumination of the Twenty Thousand— Master Bhadrapala says that, “When something is a kind of knowledge which as its essence is taken in by the ten aspects of knowable things—that is, by things like the foundation consciousness being discussed here—then we can say it is, precisely, the state of omniscience.”  This presentation is exceedingly excellent, for we are focused upon the characteristic of totality.

gru.acip: [E167] GZHAN DON LA 'DUN PA DANG, DE LA SBYOR BA'I BRTZON 'GRUS DANG, DE'I THABS MA BRJOD {%BRJED} PA'I DRAN PA DANG CHOS NYID LA RTZE GCIG PA'I TING NGE 'DZIN DANG, MKHYEN PA ZANG {%ZAD} MI SHES PA'I SHES RAB DANG, 'KHOR BA JI SRID PAR RNAM PAR GREL {%GROL} BA NYAMS PA MI MNGA' BA'I RNAM PA DRUG CHOS CAN, RTOGS PA MA 'DRES PA YIN TE, KHYOD KYI RIGS SANGS RGYAS KHO NA LA MNGA' BA'I RTOGS PA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: [e167] gzhan don la 'dun pa dang, de la sbyor ba'i brtson 'grus dang, de'i thabs ma brjod {%brjed} pa'i dran pa dang chos nyid la rtse gcig pa'i ting nge 'dzin dang, mkhyen pa zang {%zad} mi shes pa'i shes rab dang, 'khor ba ji srid par rnam par grel {%grol} ba nyams pa mi mnga' ba'i rnam pa drug chos can, rtogs pa ma 'dres pa yin te, khyod kyi rigs sangs rgyas kho na la mnga' ba'i rtogs pa yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: And then consider these six aspects of enlightenment: (96) the fact that a Buddha never loses their aspiration to be of service to others; (97) the fact that they never lose joyful effort in carrying out this service; (98) the fact that they never lose their awareness, in the sense of never losing sight of the methods to remain joyful in that service; (99) and never fall out of their meditative concentration, staying single-pointed on the true nature of things; (100) and never fall out of that wisdom which understands that their knowledge is now never-ending; (101) and, finally, never fall out of their total liberation, for as long as the cycle of suffering may remain. These then are unmixed sorts of realization, Because their type of realization is a kind that is possessed only by a Buddha.

gru.acip: ,BLO GROS ZAB MOS GZHUNG BZANG DON, ,MCHOG TU JI BZHIN GZIGS PA YIS, ,DON GNYIS LHUN GRUB SEMS DPA' CHE, ,BLA MA DE LA GUS BTUD NAS,
gru.wylie: blo gros zab mos gzhung bzang don, ,mchog tu ji bzhin gzigs pa yis, ,don gnyis lhun grub sems dpa' che, ,bla ma de la gus btud nas
gru.english: With your intellect deep, You have seen the beautiful meaning Of the great books, Just as it is, And as high as it is. You are the great spiritual warrior Who without any effort at all Accomplishes both all you need, And all that others need— My Lama, I bow to you.

gru.acip: ,GDUL BYA RNAMS LA NGO BO MA NOR BA DANG KHYAD PAR MA 'DRES PAR YONGS SU RDZOGS PAR STON PAR MDZAD PA'I, ,MKHAS PA'I NANG NAS KYANG MKHAS PA'I MCHOG TU GYUR PA CHOS RJE DON GRUB RIN CHEN, RJE RED MDA' BA LA SOGS PA'I RJE RANG GI YONGS 'DZIN DE RNAMS LA MGO BOS PHYAG 'TSAL ZHES SHIN TU GUS PA STON PA'O,
gru.wylie: gdul bya rnams la ngo bo ma nor ba dang khyad par ma 'dres par yongs su rdzogs par ston par mdzad pa'i, ,mkhas pa'i nang nas kyang mkhas pa'i mchog tu gyur pa chos rje don grub rin chen, rje red mda' ba la sogs pa'i rje rang gi yongs 'dzin de rnams la mgo bos phyag 'tshal zhes shin tu gus pa ston pa'o
gru.english: And these people are the highest of sages even among sages in general; they have shared this path and these teachings with their own disciples in a complete way—and without erring in any way about the very essence of this knowledge, without adulterating any of its many particulars.  What this is all referring to is Je Tsongkapa's own mentors: teachers such as Chujey Dundrup Rinchen and Lord Rendawa.  He “bows his head low” to them—an indication of the extreme respect in which he holds them. A promise to write

gru.acip: ,GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, GANG LAS BYUNG BA'I GRUB MTHA' BSHAD PA, DE LAS BYUNG BA'I KUN GZHI DANG NYON YID BSHAD PA'O,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa la gnyis, gang las byung ba'i grub mtha' bshad pa, de las byung ba'i kun gzhi dang nyon yid bshad pa'o
gru.english: This brings us to the second of our three major sections—the actual composition of Je Tsongkapa's text.  We proceed in two steps: an explanation of the school from which the concepts of foundation consciousness and negative consciousness come; and then an explanation of these two concepts which are drawn from this school.

gru.acip: ,DANG PO NI, CI KUN GZHI DANG NYON YID 'DOD PA'I GRUB MTHA' SMRA BA DE SU ZHIG YIN, DUS NAM GYI TSE BYUNG ZHE NA,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, ci kun gzhi dang nyon yid 'dod pa'i grub mtha' smra ba de su zhig yin, dus nam gyi tshe byung zhe na
gru.english: Here's the first step.  One may ask: Just who are the philosophers who believe in foundation and negative consciousnesses?  And when was it that their school arose?

gru.acip: MDO LANGARKA {%LANGKAR} GSHEGS PA DANG, 'JAM DPAL RTZA RGYUD SOGS NAS THEG PA 'OG MA GNYIS LAS MCHOG TU GYUR PA'I, ,THEG PA CHEN PO'I BSTAN PA 'DZIN PAR LUNG BSTAN PA'I 'PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS,
gru.wylie: mdo langarka {%langkar} gshegs pa dang, 'jam dpal rtsa rgyud sogs nas theg pa 'og ma gnyis las mchog tu gyur pa'i, ,theg pa chen po'i bstan pa 'dzin par lung bstan pa'i 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis
gru.english: And this teacher—in both The Journey to Langka and in The Root Secret Teaching of Gentle Voice, as well as in other scriptures—predicted the coming of one who would preserve the teachings of the greater way: a way which is highest, relative to the two lower ways.   And this person was the realized one, Nagarjuna.

gru.acip: RJES SU, ,'JAM DPAL RTZA RGYUD SOGS NAS DRANG NGES 'BYED PAR LUNG BSTAN BRNYES PA'I 'PHAGS PA THOGS MED KYIS, ,RJE BTZUN BYAMS PA BSGRUB PAS ZHAL GZIGS TE
gru.wylie: rjes su, ,'jam dpal rtsa rgyud sogs nas drang nges 'byed par lung bstan brnyes pa'i 'phags pa thogs med kyis, ,rje btsun byams pa bsgrub pas zhal gzigs te
gru.english: After this came the one who had received his prediction, in holy books such as the Root Secret Text of Gentle Voice, that he would distinguish between those teachings of the Buddha which are to be taken literally, and those to be taken as figurative.  This was Master Asanga, himself a realized being, who for years performed special practices in order to make contact with Loving One, Lord Maitreya, himself; and then finally succeeded—meeting him face-to-face.

gru.acip: DE'I SNGON DU 'PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS SROL PHYE BA'I DBU MA PA NYID LAS GZHAN PA'I THEG PA CHEN PO'I GRUB MTHA' SMRA BA SU'I GSAL KHA MED DO,
gru.wylie: de'i sngon du 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis srol phye ba'i dbu ma pa nyid las gzhan pa'i theg pa chen po'i grub mtha' smra ba su'i gsal kha med do
gru.english: There is no clear record of a proponent of any school of the greater way prior to Master Asanga—except for the system founded by the Realized One, Nagarjuna; which is to say, before that, there was just the Middle Way. Strategies for understanding

gru.acip: ,MTSAN NYID SGRUB PAR BYED PA DANG, ,DGU DANG GCIG PUR 'DOD PA DGAG ,DON RNAM BZHI YIS KUN GZHI DANG, ,NYON MONGS CAN YID SHES PAR BYA,
gru.wylie: mtshan nyid sgrub par byed pa dang, ,dgu dang gcig pur 'dod pa dgag ,don rnam bzhi yis kun gzhi dang, ,nyon mongs can yid shes par bya
gru.english: Use four different strategies to understand Foundation and negative consciousnesses: Definitions; arguments for their existence; Refuting the belief that consciousness Can be grouped into nine; and the belief That they can be put in a single group.

gru.acip: ,GNYIS PA NI, 'O NA SEMS TZAM PA'I GRUB MTHA' DE LAS BYUNG BA'I KUN GZHI DANG NYON YID DE RGYU GANG GIS SHES PAR BYA SNYAM NA,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, 'o na sems tsam pa'i grub mtha' de las byung ba'i kun gzhi dang nyon yid de rgyu gang gis shes par bya snyam na
gru.english: This brings us to our second step from above—an explanation of the two concepts which are drawn from this school: foundation consciousness and negative consciousness.  What strategies will we use for coming to an understanding of them?

gru.acip: MTSAN NYID DANG SGRUB PAR BYED PA DANG, ,RNAM SHES TSOGS DGUR 'DOD PA DGAG PA DANG TSOGS GCIG PUR 'DOD PA DGAG PA STE, ,DON TSAN RNAM PA BZHI YI SGO NAS KUN GZHI DANG, ,NYON MONGS CAN GYI YID SHES PAR BYA'O,,
gru.wylie: mtshan nyid dang sgrub par byed pa dang, ,rnam shes tshogs dgur 'dod pa dgag pa dang tshogs gcig pur 'dod pa dgag pa ste, ,don tshan rnam pa bzhi yi sgo nas kun gzhi dang, ,nyon mongs can gyi yid shes par bya'o
gru.english: We will use four different strategies to understand foundation consciousness and negative consciousness: we will [1] examine their definitions and [2] arguments for their existence; we will [3] refute the belief that consciousness can be grouped into nine; and [4] we will also refute the belief that the different kinds of consciousness can be put into a single group. Defining the basis part of foundation consciousness: an introduction

gru.acip: ,BAG CHAGS BSGO GZHI YIN PHYIR DANG, ,DGE DANG MI DGE MNGON GYUR DANG, ,RGYUD GCIG LA NI 'JUG PA'I PHYIR, ,MA BSGRIBS LUNG MA BSTAN DU GRUB,
gru.wylie: bag chags bsgo gzhi yin phyir dang, ,dge dang mi dge mngon gyur dang, ,rgyud gcig la ni 'jug pa'i phyir, ,ma bsgribs lung ma bstan du grub
gru.english: We can establish that Foundation consciousness Is karmically neutral, Since it is the foundation Upon which karmic seeds Are imprinted, And because it manifests, Within a single mindstream, As both virtue and non-virtue.

gru.acip: DGE MI DGE'I BAG CHAGS BSGO GZHI YIN PA'I PHYIR DANG, ,DGE BA DANG MI DGE BA GANG DANG YANG CIG CHAR DU MNGON GYUR DU, ,RGYUD GCIG STE GANG ZAG BYE BRAG PA GCIG GI RGYUD LA NI 'JUG PA'I PHYIR NA, ,'CHAD 'GYUR LTAR MA SGRIB LUNG MA BSTAN DU RIGS PAS GRUB BO,
gru.wylie: dge mi dge'i bag chags bsgo gzhi yin pa'i phyir dang, ,dge ba dang mi dge ba gang dang yang cig char du mngon gyur du, ,rgyud gcig ste gang zag bye brag pa gcig gi rgyud la ni 'jug pa'i phyir na, ,'chad 'gyur ltar ma sgrib lung ma bstan du rigs pas grub bo
gru.english: We can establish, logically, that foundation consciousness itself is karmically neutral—since first of all it is the foundation upon which karmic seeds, whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous, are imprinted.  This is also because foundation consciousness manifests, within a single mindstream (meaning, within the mind of any particular person), as both virtue and non-virtue; that is, it could come up with either of them.  This point will be explained further below. Which mental functions can be adjunct to foundation consciousness?

gru.acip: GANG GIS BSGO BAR BYED PA TSOGS BDUN 'KHOR BCAS KYIS GANG LA BSGO BAR BYA BA'I GZHI KUN GZHI'I RNAM SHES LA, ,BSGO BYED RANG NYID 'GAG PA LA MNGON DU PHYOGS PA'I TSE, ,BZHAG PA'I DGE MI DGE LUNG MA BSTAN CI RIGS KYI BAG CHAGS PHYIS SU RKYEN DANG 'PHRAD NAS SMIN PA LAS RIGS 'DRA PHYI MA 'GRUB RUNG GI NUS PA STE,
gru.wylie: gang gis bsgo bar byed pa tshogs bdun 'khor bcas kyis gang la bsgo bar bya ba'i gzhi kun gzhi'i rnam shes la, ,bsgo byed rang nyid 'gag pa la mngon du phyogs pa'i tshe, ,bzhag pa'i dge mi dge lung ma bstan ci rigs kyi bag chags phyis su rkyen dang 'phrad nas smin pa las rigs 'dra phyi ma 'grub rung gi nus pa ste
gru.english: Now certain parts of the mind—the group of seven types of consciousness, along with their attendants—act to make an imprint upon foundation consciousness; that is, upon the foundation where seeds are imprinted.  As these states of mind—the ones that are doing the imprinting—draw to a close themselves, the seeds are planted. These seeds may be virtuous, non-virtuous, or neutral.  Later on, when they encounter the necessary conditions, they ripen and create a result of the same general content.  They may thus be described as the potential which results in this creation.

gru.acip: GZHAN DBANG YONGS GRUB GNYIS BDEN PAR GRUB PA NANG SHES PA BDEN PAR GRUB PA LA RAG LAS PAS NA NANG GI SA BON LA DAM PA'I DON GYI SA BON GYI MING BTAGS TE
gru.wylie: gzhan dbang yongs grub gnyis bden par grub pa nang shes pa bden par grub pa la rag las pas na nang gi sa bon la dam pa'i don gyi sa bon gyi ming btags te
gru.english: Two types of entities which exist in truth—contingents and culminations—depend upon awareness; which is something inside of us, and which also exists in truth.  As such, inner seeds are also given the name of [6] “ultimate” seeds.

gru.acip: ,SNOD KYI 'JIG RTEN 'GRUB PA'I THUN MONG GI SA BON DANG, BCUD KYI 'JIG RTEN 'GRUB PA'I THUN MONG MA YIN PA'I SA BON DANG, ,YANG BDE SDUG GI RTEN DU GYUR CING SEMS KYIS ZIN PAS NA BCUD KYI 'JIG RTEN 'GRUB PA'I TSOR BA DANG BCAS PA DANG DES MA ZIN PAS NA SNOD KYI 'JIG RTEN 'GRUB PA'I TSOR BA MED PA'I, ,SA BON TE DBYE TSUL RNAM PA BZHI DANG,
gru.wylie: snod kyi 'jig rten 'grub pa'i thun mong gi sa bon dang, bcud kyi 'jig rten 'grub pa'i thun mong ma yin pa'i sa bon dang, ,yang bde sdug gi rten du gyur cing sems kyis zin pas na bcud kyi 'jig rten 'grub pa'i tshor ba dang bcas pa dang des ma zin pas na snod kyi 'jig rten 'grub pa'i tshor ba med pa'i, ,sa bon te dbye tshul rnam pa bzhi dang
gru.english: The types of mental seeds can also be presented as four different types: [1] Mental seeds “for the communal,” which bring about the great vessel of the world. [2] Mental seeds “for the unique,” which bring about the individual beings who inhabit this vessel. [3] Or else we can list the mental seeds that bring about the beings who inhabit the vessel in the sense of being the basis for pleasure and pain; as well as for what is “held” by consciousness—that is, seeds that involve the capacity of feeling; and [4] Mental seeds which bring about the outer vessel of the world in the sense of what is not held by consciousness—which is to say, seeds that have no involvement with the capacity of feeling. Another set of four mental seeds

gru.acip: ,DGE DANG MI DGE MTSAN NYID PAR, ,'DOD LA SGRUB PAR BYED PA MED,
gru.wylie: dge dang mi dge mtshan nyid par, ,'dod la sgrub par byed pa med
gru.english: There is nothing that constitutes Proof for positions that Seeds can consist of Definitive virtue or non-virtue.

gru.acip: KUN BTUS LAS, DGE BA'I BAG CHAGS RJES 'BREL GYI DGE BAR BSHAD PA'I LUNG DANG, RNAM SMIN GYI RGYU MI BYED PAR THAL BA DANG, RGYU MTHUN GYI 'BRAS BU MI BSKYED PAR THAL BA DANG, SDOM PA THOB NAS MA BTANG GI BAR DU DGE BA RGYUN CHAGS SU MI 'BYUNG BAR THAL BA'I RIGS PAS DGE BA DANG MI DGE BA MTSAN NYID PAR, ,BSGRUB NAS DE LTAR 'DOD PA DAG GI DAM BCA' BA'I DON LA LUNG DANG RIGS PA DE RNAMS SGRUB PAR BYED PA YANG DAG TU SONG BA MED DO,,
gru.wylie: kun btus las, dge ba'i bag chags rjes 'brel gyi dge bar bshad pa'i lung dang, rnam smin gyi rgyu mi byed par thal ba dang, rgyu mthun gyi 'bras bu mi bskyed par thal ba dang, sdom pa thob nas ma btang gi bar du dge ba rgyun chags su mi 'byung bar thal ba'i rigs pas dge ba dang mi dge ba mtshan nyid par, ,bsgrub nas de ltar 'dod pa dag gi dam bca' ba'i don la lung dang rigs pa de rnams sgrub par byed pa yang dag tu song ba med do
gru.english: We do however see attempts to prove that the nature of the seeds can consist of definitive virtue, or non-virtue.  These arguments cite The Compendium, where it states that virtuous seeds are virtue by association.  Further, they say, these seeds could never act as causes for karmic ripenings, if they were truly this type of neutral entity. Neither could they ever produce a result of the type which stems from a cause of the same general type.  And finally, it would not then be the case that—once we have taken spiritual vows—our good karma continues on in an unbroken stream, until such time as we give them up. The scriptural references and logic for the points in the assertions of people who take such positions though are nothing that constitutes valid proof for these ideas.

gru.acip: DBANG {%DPANG} LO DANG SA BZANG LO CHEN GYIS, DANG PO ZLA SKYONG DANG YANG DAG BDEN, GNYIS PA DGA' BO DANG MCHOG GI SDE, GSUM PA SLOB DPON CHOS SKYONG SOGS KYIS 'DOD GSUNGS KYANG SHES BYED MA MTHONG ZHES GRUB MTHA' CHEN MO LAS SO,,
gru.wylie: dbang {%dpang} lo dang sa bzang lo chen gyis, dang po zla skyong dang yang dag bden, gnyis pa dga' bo dang mchog gi sde, gsum pa slob dpon chos skyong sogs kyis 'dod gsungs kyang shes byed ma mthong zhes grub mtha' chen mo las so
gru.english: The master translator from Pang, as well as the great translator Sasang, are said to hold the opinion that the first position is accepted by Masters Chandrapala and Samyaksatyavadi; the second by Masters Nanda and Paramasena; and the third by Master Dharmapala and others.  The author of the great book on philosophical systems though states that he has been unable to locate any corroboration of this attribution.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA LA GNYIS, LUNG RIGS LA BRTEN NAS LUGS 'DIR KUN GZHI DANG NYON YID YOD PAR SHES DGOS PAR GDAMS PA DANG, SGRUB BYED DNGOS SO,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa la gnyis, lung rigs la brten nas lugs 'dir kun gzhi dang nyon yid yod par shes dgos par gdams pa dang, sgrub byed dngos so
gru.english: This brings us to the second of the four strategies we began with: arguments for the existence of foundation consciousness and negative consciousness.  This section proceeds in two steps: advice that we should come to an understanding of how—based on both scriptural authority and logic—foundation consciousness and negative consciousness actually do, in this school, exist; and then a presentation of the actual support for these two.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA LA GNYIS KUN GZHI DANG, NYON YID SGRUB BYED DO,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa la gnyis kun gzhi dang, nyon yid sgrub byed do
gru.english: This brings us to our second step: the actual support for these two.  Here we'll first present support for foundation consciousness, and then support for negative consciousness.

gru.acip: DANG PO LA GNYIS, RIGS PA DANG, LUNG GIS SGRUB BYED DO,,
gru.wylie: dang po la gnyis, rigs pa dang, lung gis sgrub byed do
gru.english: We'll cover the first of these in two steps: support in the form of logic, and then support in the form of scriptural authority.

gru.acip: ,RNAL 'BYOR SPYOD PA'I GZHUNG LUGS NAS, ,SGRUB BYED RIGS PA MTHA' YAS PA, ,GSUNGS KYANG LEN DANG DANG PO GSAL, ,SA BON LAS DANG LUS TSOR DANG, ,SNYOMS 'JUG 'CHI 'PHO MI RUNG BA, ,BRGYAD DU 'DUS PHYIR 'DI BSHAD BYA,
gru.wylie: rnal 'byor spyod pa'i gzhung lugs nas, ,sgrub byed rigs pa mtha' yas pa, ,gsungs kyang len dang dang po gsal, ,sa bon las dang lus tshor dang, ,snyoms 'jug 'chi 'pho mi rung ba, ,brgyad du 'dus phyir 'di bshad bya
gru.english: Limitless reasoning Is spoken in the scriptural tradition Of the way of deep practice. Nonetheless, these can be summarized In eight arguments concerning Problems with taking birth; Engaging first; the clarity; The seeds; the operating; Feeling and the body; Deep meditation; And dying and moving on. These I will now explain.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, RNAM {%RNAL} 'BYOR GYI SA BZHI'I SGO NAS, SPYOD PA NYAMS LEN GTAN LA 'BEBS PA SEMS TZAM PA'I GZHUNG LUGS THEG BSDUS SOGS NAS, ,KUN GZHI DANG NYON YID SGRUB BYED KYI RIGS PA MTHA' YAS PA, ,GSUNGS KYANG KUN GZHI SGRUB BYED KYI GNAD BSDU NA,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, rnam {%rnal} 'byor gyi sa bzhi'i sgo nas, spyod pa nyams len gtan la 'bebs pa sems tsam pa'i gzhung lugs theg bsdus sogs nas, ,kun gzhi dang nyon yid sgrub byed kyi rigs pa mtha' yas pa, ,gsungs kyang kun gzhi sgrub byed kyi gnad bsdu na
gru.english: Here is the first.  The scriptural tradition of the Mind Only School—contained in works like A Summary of the Greater Way—sets forth endeavors of the spirit, spiritual activity, through a presentation on four levels of deep practice.  In these works, limitless reasoning is spoken to support both foundation and negative consciousnesses.  Nonetheless, the crucial points for proving the existence of foundation consciousness may be summarized as follows.

gru.acip: DE'I SGRUB BYED 'DI DAG DKA' 'GREL LAS GSUNGS PA'I TSIG CUNG ZAD GSAL DU BTANG NA,
gru.wylie: de'i sgrub byed 'di dag dka' 'grel las gsungs pa'i tshig cung zad gsal du btang na
gru.english: These arguments on foundation consciousness are covered in Je Tsongkapa's Autocommentary on the Difficult Points, and I would like at this point to clarify some of the wording there for our readers. First argument: How could we take birth?

gru.acip: GNYIS PA GRUB STE, DE LNGA'I RGYU YID BYED SOGS KYI NUS PA LA KHYAD PAR CUNG ZAD KYANG MED PA'I PHYIR, /2\
gru.wylie: gnyis pa grub ste, de lnga'i rgyu yid byed sogs kyi nus pa la khyad par cung zad kyang med pa'i phyir, /2\
gru.english: Then I disagree to the second possibility: that they could never arise one by one. But the second possibility is also true, because neither is there the slightest difference in strength between the ideas and such that act as the cause for the five. Third argument: How could there be clarity?

gru.acip: GRUB MTHA' RTZA BA LAS, ,MA BSHAD RTOG GNYIS CIG CHAR MIN SOGS PHYIR, ,BRGYAD MIN TSOGS DRUG SDE BDUN RJES 'BRANG LUGS, ,ZHES SO,, /5\
gru.wylie: grub mtha' rtsa ba las, ,ma bshad rtog gnyis cig char min sogs phyir, ,brgyad min tshogs drug sde bdun rjes 'brang lugs, ,zhes so,, /5\
gru.english: As the root text on comparative philosophy puts it: It is not explained that way, For the reason that, for example, Two thoughts cannot occur Simultaneously. Thus this is a system Which follows the Seven Books, Speaking of the collection Of six different kinds of consciousness, And not of a collection of eight. Sixth argument: How could feeling extend over the entire body?

gru.acip: 'DI'I DANG PO, BZHI PA, DRUG PA, BDUN PA, BRGYAD PA RNAMS NI SGRUB BYED DNGOS DANG, LHAG MA GSUM NI RTZOD SPONG DU GSUNGS SO,,
gru.wylie: 'di'i dang po, bzhi pa, drug pa, bdun pa, brgyad pa rnams ni sgrub byed dngos dang, lhag ma gsum ni rtsod spong du gsungs so
gru.english: It is stated that the first, fourth, sixth, seventh, and eighth of these arguments are the actual proofs for the existence of foundation consciousness; whereas the remaining three are refutations of the position that it does not exist. Scriptural authority for foundation consciousness

gru.acip: LUNG GIS KYANG GRUB STE, KUN GZHI RNAM PAR SHES PA DE, ,DKA' 'GREL DU DRANGS PA'I DGONGS 'GREL SOGS THEG CHEN GYI MDO LAS GSUNGS PAR MA ZAD, THEG DMAN GYI GTZUG LAG STE SDE SNOD RNAMS SU YANG, , BSTAN TE,
gru.wylie: lung gis kyang grub ste, kun gzhi rnam par shes pa de, ,dka' 'grel du drangs pa'i dgongs 'grel sogs theg chen gyi mdo las gsungs par ma zad, theg dman gyi gtsug lag ste sde snod rnams su yang, , bstan te
gru.english: Now the idea of a consciousness of the foundation also finds support in the scriptures.  This consciousness is, first of all, described in sutras of the greater way, such as the one called What I Really Meant, as this teaching is quoted in Je Tsongkapa's Commentary on the Difficult Points.  And not only that; it is presented even in “the books”—meaning the collection of scriptures—of the lower way.

gru.acip: MING GI RNAM GRANGS GZHAN DANG GZHAN DAG GIS BSTAN PAS NA LUNG GIS GRUB PO,
gru.wylie: ming gi rnam grangs gzhan dang gzhan dag gis bstan pas na lung gis grub po
gru.english: Thus, foundation consciousness is referred to with a whole variety of synonymous names; and as such we can say its existence is established by scripture. Other interpretations of the authority

gru.acip: KUN GZHI DANG NYON YID KYI SGRUB BYED 'DI NI PHYOGS TZAM MTSON PA STE, RGYAS PAR DKA' 'GREL LAS SHES PAR BYA'O,,
gru.wylie: kun gzhi dang nyon yid kyi sgrub byed 'di ni phyogs tsam mtshon pa ste, rgyas par dka' 'grel las shes par bya'o
gru.english: The arguments that we have presented here in support of the concepts of both foundation consciousness and negative consciousness are just a small, representative example of all the arguments that there are.  If you would like to learn more about this reasoning, I suggest that you refer to Je Tsongkapa's autocommentary. The position which says there are nine

gru.acip: ,BRGYAD PA KUN GZHI RNAM SHES LA YANG NGO BO NYID KYI KUN GZHI ZHES SANGS RGYAS 'GRUB PA'I DON DANG LDAN PA ZHIG DANG, RNAM SMIN GYI KUN GZHI ZHES KHAMS BCO BRGYAD LA DMIGS PA ZHIG DANG, KUN NAS NYON MONGS PA'I KUN GZHI ZHES CHOS KYI BDAG 'DZIN ZHIG STE, GSUM DU 'CHAD PA DANG,
