gru.english: The other kind of negation is where we deny identity. In this case, an additional phenomenon is implied, or established, when the mind excludes what the negation denies. Suppose for example that we want to indicate that a particular person belongs to the class of commoners, and so we say of them, “He or she is not a Brahmin.” This is not a simple denial that the person is of the Brahmin class; rather, it is also a positive assertion that the person belongs to the commoner class—that he or she is something other than the Brahmin class, and is somehow inferior to them in education or the like.

gru.acip: CHOS GZHAN 'PHEN PA LA DNGOS DANG SHUGS DANG SKABS KYIS 'PHANGS PA GSUM STE, DANG PO NI, BDAG MED PA YOD CES PA LTA BU STE DGAG BYA GCOD PA DANG, CHOS GZHAN 'PHEN PA GNYIS KA TSIG GCIG GIS SGRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: chos gzhan 'phen pa la dngos dang shugs dang skabs kyis 'phangs pa gsum ste, dang po ni, bdag med pa yod ces pa lta bu ste dgag bya gcod pa dang, chos gzhan 'phen pa gnyis ka tshig gcig gis sgrub pa'o
gru.english: When we say that “some other phenomenon is implied,” there are three different ways in which this implication can occur: directly, by intimation, or from context. An example of the first would be something like the statement that “There does exist a lack of a self-nature to things.” In this case, a single phrase serves both to exclude what it denies, and to imply another phenomenon.

gru.acip: ,DGAG PA DON GYIS BSTAN PA DANG, ,TSIG GCIG SGRUB PAR BYED PA DANG, ,DE LDAN RANG TSIG MI STON PA, ,MA YIN GZHAN PA GZHAN YIN NO, ZHES SO,,
gru.wylie: dgag pa don gyis bstan pa dang, ,tshig gcig sgrub par byed pa dang, ,de ldan rang tshig mi ston pa, ,ma yin gzhan pa gzhan yin no, zhes so
gru.english: A negation can imply Something else by intimation; A single phrase can also Function to assert; Both; or be insufficient, In the wording alone, To do the indicating. This then is the other kind, Where we deny Some other identity.

gru.acip: KHA CIG GZHI SGRUB PA DANG TSOGS NA MED DGAG MIN PAR SMRA BA MI 'THAD DE, BRAM ZE SGRUB PA YIN PAS BRAM ZES CHANG MI 'THUNG BA DGAG BYA BCAD TZAM YIN PA MI 'GOG PA'I PHYIR TE, DPER NA SGRA MNGON GYUR YIN PAS SGRA MI RTAG PA LKOG GYUR YIN PA MI 'GOG PA BZHIN NO,,
gru.wylie: kha cig gzhi sgrub pa dang tshogs na med dgag min par smra ba mi 'thad de, bram ze sgrub pa yin pas bram zes chang mi 'thung ba dgag bya bcad tsam yin pa mi 'gog pa'i phyir te, dper na sgra mngon gyur yin pas sgra mi rtag pa lkog gyur yin pa mi 'gog pa bzhin no
gru.english: Some say that it is incorrect to mention a negation which is not the absence of something in the same phrase with something that does in fact exist. A Brahmin for example is a positive entity, and so when you say “Brahmins don't drink alcohol,” you are not denying something in the sense of simply excluding what you mean to deny. Saying that sound exists at the manifest level of reality doesn't deny, for example, that the fact that sound is a changing thing exists at the recondite level of existence.

gru.acip: DE LTAR 'PHAGS PA'I DAM BCA' GZHI 'DIR BKOD PA NI, 'BRAS BU DE NYID DE'I NGO BO NYID LAS 'BYUNG BA MIN PA DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I RGYU GZHAN DAG LAS LTA 'BYUNG BA GA LA ZHIG STE DE MED PA DANG, RANG GZHAN GNYIS KA LAS KYANG 'BYUNG BA MA YIN PA DANG, RGYU MED PAR NI 'BYUNG BA GA LA YOD DE MED DO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar 'phags pa'i dam bca' gzhi 'dir bkod pa ni, 'bras bu de nyid de'i ngo bo nyid las 'byung ba min pa dang, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i rgyu gzhan dag las lta 'byung ba ga la zhig ste de med pa dang, rang gzhan gnyis ka las kyang 'byung ba ma yin pa dang, rgyu med par ni 'byung ba ga la yod de med do
gru.english: And so the assertion that the Realized One is setting forth at this point is that this result cannot occur through “that”—through some essential nature of its own. And how could it occur (meaning, it could never occur) through something other than itself which also existed by definition? Nor could the result occur through both itself and something other than it. How as well could it occur (meaning, it could never occur) without a cause at all?

gru.acip: DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YOD NA MTHA' BZHI'I SKYE BA GANG RUNG GIS KHYAB STE, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA LA RGYU YOD MED GNYIS SU KHA TSON CHOD CING, RGYU YOD PA LA RANG GZHAN RE RE BA DANG GNYIS KA TSOGS PA LAS SKYE BA GSUM DU KHA TSON CHOD PAS DAM BCA' BZHIS CHOG GO ,,
gru.wylie: dngos po rang bzhin gyis grub pa yod na mtha' bzhi'i skye ba gang rung gis khyab ste, rang bzhin gyis skye ba la rgyu yod med gnyis su kha tshon chod cing, rgyu yod pa la rang gzhan re re ba dang gnyis ka tshogs pa las skye ba gsum du kha tshon chod pas dam bca' bzhis chog go
gru.english: And if there were such a thing as something existing through some nature of its own, then it would necessarily have to grow in one of these four ways. This is because for a thing to grow through some nature of its own, it would either have to have a cause, or have no cause: there are only two choices. And if it did have a cause, then that cause would have either to be the thing itself, or something other than the thing itself; or else both of these two options together—there are only these three choices. As such, a total of four assertions is sufficient to make the point. Nothing grows in either reality

gru.acip: DANG PO LA GSUM, DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PAR 'DOD PA'I GRUB MTHA' MKHAN GYI LUGS DGAG PA, GRUB MTHAS BLO MA BSGYUR BA'I THA SNYAD DU YANG MED PAR BSTAN PA, DE LTAR BKAG PA RNAMS KYI DON BSDU BA'O,,
gru.wylie: dang po la gsum, de kho na nyid rtogs par 'dod pa'i grub mtha' mkhan gyi lugs dgag pa, grub mthas blo ma bsgyur ba'i tha snyad du yang med par bstan pa, de ltar bkag pa rnams kyi don bsdu ba'o
gru.english: The first of these, in turn, comes in three sections: denying the system of those who believe they have perceived some actual nature; demonstrating that things could not be said to grow from themselves even in the parlance of those who have not been influenced by any particular school of philosophy; and finally a summary of these denials. Denying ideas of those who think they perceive some actual nature

gru.acip: DE LTAR MYU GU'I NGO BO'AM RANG BZHIN GANG YIN THAMS CAD SA BON GYI DUS SU YOD NA, MYU GU'I NGO BO LAS DON GZHAN PA'I MYU GU GSAL BA NYID KYANG MI SRID PAS RGYU DUS NAS MYU GU'I RANG BZHIN NAM NGO BOR MA ZAD, MYU GU NYID KYANG YOD DGOS PAS, DE'I TSE DE GRUB PA'I 'OG TU SLAR YANG SKYE BA LA DON GTAN MED DO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar myu gu'i ngo bo'am rang bzhin gang yin thams cad sa bon gyi dus su yod na, myu gu'i ngo bo las don gzhan pa'i myu gu gsal ba nyid kyang mi srid pas rgyu dus nas myu gu'i rang bzhin nam ngo bor ma zad, myu gu nyid kyang yod dgos pas, de'i tshe de grub pa'i 'og tu slar yang skye ba la don gtan med do
gru.english: Thus we can say that—if every form of some essence or nature which the sprout possesses is present at the same time as the seed—then it is impossible for there to be any particular of a sprout which is a different entity from the essential nature of the sprout. Not only that, but since the sprout itself must also be present already, then at that point—when it has already come into being—there is absolutely no point to its growing once again, after that time. Things grown need not grow again

gru.acip: 'DI 'DRA BA'I GNOD PA MTHONG YANG MI LDOG PA NI, MYU GUS SA BON 'JIG PA NI RNAM 'GYUR GYI STENG NAS YIN PAS, RANG GIS RANG 'JIG PA DANG GA NA 'DRA SNYAM DU RGOL BA BLUN PAS YIN LA, NGO BO'AM RANG BZHIN THAMS CAD PHAR YIN TSUR YIN DU SONG NA RNAM 'GYUR SO SOR YANG MI 'GRUB PAS GNOD PA SPANG MI NUS SO,,
gru.wylie: 'di 'dra ba'i gnod pa mthong yang mi ldog pa ni, myu gus sa bon 'jig pa ni rnam 'gyur gyi steng nas yin pas, rang gis rang 'jig pa dang ga na 'dra snyam du rgol ba blun pas yin la, ngo bo'am rang bzhin thams cad phar yin tshur yin du song na rnam 'gyur so sor yang mi 'grub pas gnod pa spang mi nus so
gru.english: The opponent here can see this kind of problem coming up, and refuses to change their position, saying that when the sprout destroys the seed it happens only at the level of the manifestation—and thus there's no way that it's as if the sprout had destroyed itself. This kind of thinking though is foolish, for it cannot avoid the problem that—if all the essences or natures are such that to be one is to be the other, and vice versa—then you could never say on top of that that the manifestations were different from each other. Seed & sprout all the same

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, DE'I PHYIR DE LTAR DE KHO NA NYID RTOGS PAR 'DOD PA'I GRANGS CAN GYI LUGS, SANGS RGYAS PA'I LUGS LAS GZHAN DU BRTAGS PA'I BDAG SKYE BKAG NAS, GRUB MTHA'I LUGS GZHAN DU BLO MA SBYANGS PA'I 'JIG RTEN PA'I THA SNYAD DU YANG, BDAG LAS SKYE BAR RTOG PA 'DI MI 'THAD DO ZHES STON PA NI,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, de'i phyir de ltar de kho na nyid rtogs par 'dod pa'i grangs can gyi lugs, sangs rgyas pa'i lugs las gzhan du brtags pa'i bdag skye bkag nas, grub mtha'i lugs gzhan du blo ma sbyangs pa'i 'jig rten pa'i tha snyad du yang, bdag las skye bar rtog pa 'di mi 'thad do zhes ston pa ni
gru.english: This brings us to the second point from above: demonstrating that things could not be said to grow from themselves even in the parlance of those who have not been influenced by any particular school of philosophy. And so we have denied, as explained, the system of the Numerists, who believe they have realized the true nature of things; and yet it is nothing but what the Buddhists would describe as things coming from themselves: nothing but a figment of these other thinkers' minds. Here next then we describe how—even in the language of the everyday world, among people who have had no training in any specific school of thought—this idea that things could grow from themselves is an incorrect one. The root text covers it in these lines:

gru.acip: SDE PA KHA CIG NI, SGRUB PAR BYED PA NI RGYU YIN ZHES MTSAN NYID BSTAN PA LAS NA, GANG ZHIG GANG GI SKYED BYED SA BON GYI NGO BOR GNAS PA DE NI DE'I RGYU'I RKYEN NO,,
gru.wylie: sde pa kha cig ni, sgrub par byed pa ni rgyu yin zhes mtshan nyid bstan pa las na, gang zhig gang gi skyed byed sa bon gyi ngo bor gnas pa de ni de'i rgyu'i rkyen no
gru.english: Certain schools of thought give the definition of a cause as “anything which brings about another thing”; and so we can say that they view a causal condition as any entity whose nature is to be a seed which functions to produce any particular object.

gru.acip: DE LA RIGS PA'I DBANG DU BYAS NAS BRJOD PA, GAL TE RANG GIS NGO BOS GRUB PA'I RGYU GZHAN LA BRTEN NAS RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA'I 'BRAS BU GZHAN ZHIG 'BYUNG BAR 'GYUR NA NI,
gru.wylie: de la rigs pa'i dbang du byas nas brjod pa, gal te rang gis ngo bos grub pa'i rgyu gzhan la brten nas rang gi ngo bos grub pa'i 'bras bu gzhan zhig 'byung bar 'gyur na ni
gru.english: Turning now to the logic here, suppose it were indeed the case that a result which was something other than the cause—and which existed in & of itself—could grow based on a cause which was something other than the result, and which also existed in & of itself.

gru.acip: GANG GI PHYIR 'BRAS BU DE SKYED PAR BYED PA MA YIN PA MA LUS PA LA'ANG RGYU 'BRAS SU 'DOD PA GNYIS DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN NYID MTSUNGS PAR YOD PA'I PHYIR RO, ZHES GZHAN GYIS KHAS BLANGS PA'I GTAN TSIGS LA BRTEN PA'I HA CANG THAL BA GNYIS SO,,
gru.wylie: gang gi phyir 'bras bu de skyed par byed pa ma yin pa ma lus pa la'ang rgyu 'bras su 'dod pa gnyis dang, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan nyid mtshungs par yod pa'i phyir ro, zhes gzhan gyis khas blangs pa'i gtan tshigs la brten pa'i ha cang thal ba gnyis so
gru.english: They would be this way for the reason that each & every thing that did not act to produce a result would also be exactly the same, in being different from what we agreed to be the two of cause & effect. And so we come up with two completely absurd consequences that arise from the argument accepted by the other party here.

gru.acip: THAL BA DE GNYIS BSHAD NA JI LTAR SA LU SKYED PA'I SA BON RANG 'BRAS SA LU'I MYU GU LAS, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN YIN PA DE BZHIN DU, SA LU'I MYU GU SKYED BYED MA YIN PA ME DANG SOL BA DANG, NAS KYI SA BON LA SOGS PA YANG SA LU'I MYU GU LAS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN YIN PA NI GZHAN SKYE SMRA BA RNAMS KYI 'DOD TSUL LO,,
gru.wylie: thal ba de gnyis bshad na ji ltar sa lu skyed pa'i sa bon rang 'bras sa lu'i myu gu las, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan yin pa de bzhin du, sa lu'i myu gu skyed byed ma yin pa me dang sol ba dang, nas kyi sa bon la sogs pa yang sa lu'i myu gu las rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan yin pa ni gzhan skye smra ba rnams kyi 'dod tshul lo
gru.english: Let's look into these two absurdities. Suppose that the seed which produced a sprout of rice were, by definition, something other than the sprout which was its result. Things that were not agents in the production of a rice sprout then—things like a fire, or a lump of coal, or a barley seed—would also be, according to our other party here, objects which were, by definition, other than the rice sprout. This is what those who support the idea of things growing from things that are other than them are agreeing to.

gru.acip: YANG BOD MANG POS RTOG GE BAS DU BA KHYAD PAR BA YOD PA LA ME YOD PAS KHYAB PA DANG, BYAS PA LA MI RTAG PAS KHYAB PA SGRUB PA NA, YUL DUS THAMS CAD DU MI 'KHRUL PA SGRUB PA YIN LA,
gru.wylie: yang bod mang pos rtog ge bas du ba khyad par ba yod pa la me yod pas khyab pa dang, byas pa la mi rtag pas khyab pa sgrub pa na, yul dus thams cad du mi 'khrul pa sgrub pa yin la
gru.english: There are other Tibetan thinkers, logicians, who would make yet another claim: There are cases where we establish that—whenever a particular instance of smoke is present—then fire must also be there; or that whenever something is a thing that was created, then it must also be a changing thing. And when we do establish these facts, then we establish that they they necessarily hold true in all places, and all times.

gru.acip: DE SGRUB PA'I TSE NI TSANG MANG DANG BUM PA LTA BU NYI TSE BA GCIG GI STENG DU BSGRUBS NAS, DE NAS DE DANG YUL DUS GZHAN GYI KHYAB PA GNYIS RIGS MTSUNGS PA'I RGYU MTSAN GYIS,
gru.wylie: de sgrub pa'i tshe ni tshang mang dang bum pa lta bu nyi tshe ba gcig gi steng du bsgrubs nas, de nas de dang yul dus gzhan gyi khyab pa gnyis rigs mtshungs pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis
gru.english: And when we establish that, then we establish in turn that these relationships must hold true in every single random case, or point in time: in the kitchen, or with water pot. Again, when they hold in a single case, then by reason of logical equivalence they would hold as well in every other place or time.

gru.acip: KHYAB PA DE GNYIS YUL DUS THAMS CAD KYI STENG DU MI 'KHRUL BAR SGRUB PAR 'DOD PA LA, DE LTA NA GZHAN TZAM DU MTSUNGS PA'I RTAGS KYIS HA CANG THAL BA 'PHEN TE, 'DI 'DRA BA NI LDOG PA GCIG PA'I DPUNG 'PHUL LO, ZHES ZER RO,,
gru.wylie: khyab pa de gnyis yul dus thams cad kyi steng du mi 'khrul bar sgrub par 'dod pa la, de lta na gzhan tsam du mtshungs pa'i rtags kyis ha cang thal ba 'phen te, 'di 'dra ba ni ldog pa gcig pa'i dpung 'phul lo, zhes zer ro
gru.english: But it would be absurd then to say that—just because these necessary relationships would hold true in every single location or moment—they would hold equally true for any other two objects we chose, simply because they were different from each other. In that case you'd simply piling up logically necessary opposites.

gru.acip: 'DI YANG GZHUNG GI DON MA NGES SHING RTOG GE'I 'JUG PA LA RNAM PA MA SHAR BA'I GTAM YIN TE, DU BA KHYAD PAR BA DANG BYAS PA GNYIS YUL DUS KYIS KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PAR, SPYIR ME DANG MI RTAG PA LA MI 'KHRUL BAR BSGRUBS PAS,
gru.wylie: 'di yang gzhung gi don ma nges shing rtog ge'i 'jug pa la rnam pa ma shar ba'i gtam yin te, du ba khyad par ba dang byas pa gnyis yul dus kyis khyad par du ma byas par, spyir me dang mi rtag pa la mi 'khrul bar bsgrubs pas
gru.english: This kind of talk though simply reflects a failure to grasp the point of the scripture here; and an inability to adhere to logical form. Even if we fail to specify a particular location or point in time for a particular instance of smoke, or for the quality of being made, it still holds true that they will always imply—in general—fire; or the quality of being changing.

gru.acip: 'O NA 'DI JI LTAR YIN ZHE NA, TSIG GSAL LAS, RKYEN NYID 'DI PA TZAM GYIS KUN RDZOB GRUB PAR KHAS LEN GYI, PHYOGS BZHI KHAS BLANGS PA'I SGO NAS NI MA YIN TE, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR THAL BAR 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR DANG, DE YANG RIGS PA MA YIN PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: 'o na 'di ji ltar yin zhe na, tshig gsal las, rkyen nyid 'di pa tsam gyis kun rdzob grub par khas len gyi, phyogs bzhi khas blangs pa'i sgo nas ni ma yin te, dngos po rang bzhin dang bcas par thal bar 'gyur ba'i phyir dang, de yang rigs pa ma yin pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: “Well then,” one may ask, “what does the absurdity actually turn upon?” Let's begin with a reference from A Clarification of the Verses: What we say is that something is established as being deceptive reality simply by reason of this dependence upon conditions—it's not that we say it's due to accepting these four possibilities. Because if that were the case, then working things would have to possess some nature of their own; whereas that is something illogical.

gru.acip: RKYEN NYID 'DI PA TZAM ZHIG KHAS BLANGS NA NI, RGYU DANG 'BRAS BU GNYIS PHAN TSUN LTOS BA'I PHYIR NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA YOD PA MA YIN PAS, DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BAR 'GYUR BA MA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: rkyen nyid 'di pa tsam zhig khas blangs na ni, rgyu dang 'bras bu gnyis phan tshun ltos ba'i phyir ngo bo nyid kyis grub pa yod pa ma yin pas, dngos po rang bzhin dang bcas par smra bar 'gyur ba ma yin no
gru.english: And if we do accept this idea of depending upon conditions, then these two—causes & effects—would have to be interdependent. In that case, they could no longer exist in & of themselves; and it would not be the case that we would then become thinkers who assert that these working things have some nature of their own.

gru.acip: DE LTAR NA GZHAN SKYE'I GZHAN NI GZHAN TZAM ZHIG MIN GYI, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN YIN PAS DE KHAS LEN PA LA HA CANG THAL BA 'PHEN GYI, GZHAN TZAM KHAS BLANGS PA LA 'PHEN PA GTAN MIN NO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar na gzhan skye'i gzhan ni gzhan tsam zhig min gyi, rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i gzhan yin pas de khas len pa la ha cang thal ba 'phen gyi, gzhan tsam khas blangs pa la 'phen pa gtan min no
gru.english: We can thus say that the phrase “something other than itself” in the expression “the idea that something could grow from something other than itself” doesn't just refer to something other. Rather, it's a reference to something other which could exist through some nature of its own; and thus we can build a statement of complete absurdity based on accepting it. It is not at all the case though that you could build this absurdity based on the other party accepting that things could grow from something that was simply other.

gru.acip: 'OG NAS KYANG SKAD CIG SNGA PHYI THA DAD KYANG RGYUD GCIG TU 'DOD PA LA, ,GANG DAG RANG MTSAN NYID KYIS SO SO BA, ,DE DAG RGYUD GCIG GTOGS PAR RIGS MA YIN, ZHES RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I SO SO BA YIN NA, SNGA PHYI RGYUD GCIG TU GTOGS PA MI RIGS PAR GSUNGS PA DANG 'DI GNYIS RIGS PA 'DRA'O,,
gru.wylie: 'og nas kyang skad cig snga phyi tha dad kyang rgyud gcig tu 'dod pa la, ,gang dag rang mtshan nyid kyis so so ba, ,de dag rgyud gcig gtogs par rigs ma yin, zhes rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i so so ba yin na, snga phyi rgyud gcig tu gtogs pa mi rigs par gsungs pa dang 'di gnyis rigs pa 'dra'o
gru.english: Further on we'll be agreeing, in addition, to the idea that successive moments in the flow of a thing—despite the fact that they are distinct from one another—can nonetheless together constitute a flow of the thing. As the text puts it, It would be incorrect to say That two parts which were separate Through some nature of their own Could ever be included Into the flow of a single thing. This statement—that if successive moments of a thing were distinct from one another through some nature of their own, then it would be illogical to say that they were included into the flow of a single thing—is based upon the same sort of reasoning that we see here with something “other.”

gru.acip: DE YANG RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN YIN NA LTOS PA'I 'BREL BA 'GOG NUS LA, 'BREL MED DON GZHAN DU SONG NA 'BRAS BU GCIG RANG GI RGYU LAS SKYE NA, RGYU MIN PA THAMS CAD LAS KYANG SKYE BA DANG, RGYU GCIG GIS RANG GI 'BRAS BU SKYED NA RANG GI 'BRAS BU MIN PA'I 'BRAS BU'I DNGOS PO THAMS CAD SKYED PAR HA CANG THAL BA 'JUG PA'O,,
gru.wylie: de yang rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan yin na ltos pa'i 'brel ba 'gog nus la, 'brel med don gzhan du song na 'bras bu gcig rang gi rgyu las skye na, rgyu min pa thams cad las kyang skye ba dang, rgyu gcig gis rang gi 'bras bu skyed na rang gi 'bras bu min pa'i 'bras bu'i dngos po thams cad skyed par ha cang thal ba 'jug pa'o
gru.english: Further, if something really were something other than something else through some nature of its own, then that would thereby have the power to disprove the concept of a dependent relationship, and the two objects involved would come to be things that were disparate entities with no connection at all. And in that case, whenever a particular result grew from its particular cause, it would as well grow from each & every object in the universe that was not its particular cause. It would also then be the case that—whenever a particular cause produced its particular result—then it would as well produce all resulting entities that were not that particular result. Thus this position would indeed lead to certain complete absurdities.

gru.acip: RANG BZHIN MED PAR SMRA BAS RANG BZHIN DANG BCAS PAR SMRA BA LA THAL BA BSGRUBS PA NA, THAL BA LAS BZLOG PA'I DON CAN DU THAL BAR GA LA 'GYUR TE, ZHES DANG,
gru.wylie: rang bzhin med par smra bas rang bzhin dang bcas par smra ba la thal ba bsgrubs pa na, thal ba las bzlog pa'i don can du thal bar ga la 'gyur te, zhes dang
gru.english: And how can the work further then state, “Why on earth would it be the case that—when those who deny that things have any nature of their own demonstrate an absurd consequence of the beliefs of those who say that things do have such a nature—they would then necessarily have to be thinkers who support the point which is the opposite of this absurdity?”

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR THAL BA SGRUB PA NI PHA ROL PO'I DAM BCA' BA 'GOG PA TZAM GYI 'BRAS BU CAN YIN PA'I PHYIR, THAL BA LAS BZLOG PA'I DON DU 'GYUR BA YOD PA MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PA RNAMS JI LTAR DRANG SNYAM NA,
gru.wylie: de'i phyir thal ba sgrub pa ni pha rol po'i dam bca' ba 'gog pa tsam gyi 'bras bu can yin pa'i phyir, thal ba las bzlog pa'i don du 'gyur ba yod pa ma yin no, zhes gsungs pa rnams ji ltar drang snyam na
gru.english: How finally can the same text say, “As such the demonstration of absurdity here is meant only to have the effect of denying the position of the other party; it is not the case that there is some point which is the opposite of the absurdity and which is meant to be included into this effect.”

gru.acip: DE'I THAL CHOS NI SKYE BA DON MED DANG THUG MED DU THAL BA TZAM MIN GYI, SLAR YANG SKYE BA DON MED DANG THUG MED YIN LA, THAL CHOS DE BZLOG PA'I DON SLAR YANG SKYE BA DON BCAS DANG THUG BCAS NI GRANGS CAN KHO NA 'DOD KYI, RANG LA DE'I DAM BCA' BA MED PA'I RGYU MTSAN GYIS, DE KHAS BLANGS PA'I GRUB MTHA' DANG 'GAL BA MED CES PA'I DON TE LUNG DANG PO'I DON NO,,
gru.wylie: de'i thal chos ni skye ba don med dang thug med du thal ba tsam min gyi, slar yang skye ba don med dang thug med yin la, thal chos de bzlog pa'i don slar yang skye ba don bcas dang thug bcas ni grangs can kho na 'dod kyi, rang la de'i dam bca' ba med pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis, de khas blangs pa'i grub mtha' dang 'gal ba med ces pa'i don te lung dang po'i don no
gru.english: The point of the absurdity is not solely to say that the growing of things would then have to be pointless, and endless; but rather to say that their repeated growth would be pointless and endless. The idea that would be the opposite of these two absurdities would be that the repeated growth of things did have a point, and did come to an end—and that would be accepted only by the Numerists. What the first citation you've given then is actually saying is that—because we ourselves take no position on this matter—there is no danger of our contradicting the other position that our school does take.

gru.acip: LUNG GSUM PA'I DON NI THAL BA GNYIS KYI THAL CHOS BZLOG PA'I DON SLAR YANG SKYE BA DON BCAS DANG THUG BCAS KYI RTAGS KYIS BDAG SKYE MED PA MI SGRUB KYANG DGOS PA MED PA MIN TE, GRANGS CAN MI 'DOD PA'I SKYE BA DON MED DANG THUG MED BSGRUBS PAS, GRANGS CAN GYIS DAM BCAS PA'I BDAG LAS SKYE BA RNAM PAR BCAD PA TZAM ZHIG SGRUB PA'I DGOS PA CAN YIN PA'I PHYIR RO ZHES PA'I DON NO,,
gru.wylie: lung gsum pa'i don ni thal ba gnyis kyi thal chos bzlog pa'i don slar yang skye ba don bcas dang thug bcas kyi rtags kyis bdag skye med pa mi sgrub kyang dgos pa med pa min te, grangs can mi 'dod pa'i skye ba don med dang thug med bsgrubs pas, grangs can gyis dam bcas pa'i bdag las skye ba rnam par bcad pa tsam zhig sgrub pa'i dgos pa can yin pa'i phyir ro zhes pa'i don no
gru.english: What the third citation is saying is the following. The opposites of the quality being expressed in the two absurdities are (1) that there would be some point to things growing once again after they had already grown once; and (2) that such repeated growing would not be endless. Presented as reasons, they cannot, admittedly, establish that the growth of things does not occur through any kind of self-nature. But neither do they serve no purpose; for they do have the benefit of establishing that something which the Numerists would not want to accept—that the growth of something was pointless, and that it would be repeated endlessly—would have to be the case. And as such, they do disallow the growth through some self-nature which the Numerists do assert.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, 'DIR SMRAS PA RGYU 'BRAS GNYIS LA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN NYID KYANG YOD LA, THAMS CAD LAS THAMS CAD 'BYUNG BA YANG MIN TE, RGYU 'BRAS SO SOR NGES PA MTHONG BA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, 'dir smras pa rgyu 'bras gnyis la rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan nyid kyang yod la, thams cad las thams cad 'byung ba yang min te, rgyu 'bras so sor nges pa mthong ba'i phyir ro
gru.english: Here is the first. Now suppose someone comes and says the following: First of all, it is certainly the case that there is a difference—and a difference which exists in & of itself—between a cause and its result, where one is something other than the other. Even so, it is not the case that all objects would then arise from all other objects. And this is because we can see with our own eyes that certain causes are always connected to certain results.

gru.acip: RGYU GANG ZHIG 'BRAS BU DE SKYED PAR NUS PA DE NI NGO BOS GRUB PA'I GZHAN YIN NA'ANG RGYU YIN LA, DE'I PHYIR RGYU NGES SO,,
gru.wylie: rgyu gang zhig 'bras bu de skyed par nus pa de ni ngo bos grub pa'i gzhan yin na'ang rgyu yin la, de'i phyir rgyu nges so
gru.english: They continue with: And anything which is a cause and which is capable of producing a result is a cause, even if it happens to be something which exists by its own essence, and is other than the result; as such, the cause is specific.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA NI, SA LU'I SA MYUG SO SOR NGES PA 'DI GO RGYU MTSAN GANG LAS YIN ZHES RGYU 'BRAS NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SMRA BA 'DI LA 'DRI BAR BYA'O,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa ni, sa lu'i sa myug so sor nges pa 'di go rgyu mtshan gang las yin zhes rgyu 'bras ngo bo nyid kyis grub par smra ba 'di la 'dri bar bya'o
gru.english: This brings us to the second step from above, where we deny this response. Here we ask the following question to those who say that causes and results exist in & of themselves: “What exactly is the reason you give for this position you've expressed—that the seeds and the sprouts of rice are specific to each other?”

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN NYID RGYU 'BRAS YIN MIN KUN LA THUN MONG BA KHYAD PAR DU YONGS SU MA BCAD PA SHIN TU GRAGS PA 'DI NYID, PHYIR RGOL 'DI'I 'DOD PA LA GNOD BYED DO ZHES BSHAD PA NI,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang rang mtshan gyis grub pa'i gzhan nyid rgyu 'bras yin min kun la thun mong ba khyad par du yongs su ma bcad pa shin tu grags pa 'di nyid, phyir rgol 'di'i 'dod pa la gnod byed do zhes bshad pa ni
gru.english: Moreover, it is absolutely common knowledge that if two things were other than each other in a way that existed by definition, then that difference could not be denied in the specific instance of the common group of each & every other object, whether they were cause & effect or not. This fact, the root text says next, draws into question the entire position here of the other party.

gru.acip: DE BZHIN DU, SA LU'I SA BON YANG NI SA LU'I MYU GU DE LA LTOS PA YI KHYAD PAR BZHI DANG LDAN PA MIN TE, RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN NYID YIN PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de bzhin du, sa lu'i sa bon yang ni sa lu'i myu gu de la ltos pa yi khyad par bzhi dang ldan pa min te, rang gi ngo bo nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan nyid yin pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Just so, neither is the rice seed something which possesses these four qualities relative to it—to the rice sprout—because it is, in & of itself, something entirely other than the sprout.

gru.acip: ,MYU GU SA BON DANG NI DUS MNYAM YOD PA MA YIN TE, ,GZHAN NYID MED PAR LA {%SA} BON GZHAN PA NYID DU GA LA 'GYUR, ,DES NA MYU GU SA BON LAS SKYE 'GRUB PAR [205a] 'GYUR MIN PAS, ,GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YIN ZHES BYA BA'I PHYOGS 'DI GTANG BAR BYOS,
gru.wylie: myu gu sa bon dang ni dus mnyam yod pa ma yin te, ,gzhan nyid med par la {%sa} bon gzhan pa nyid du ga la 'gyur, ,des na myu gu sa bon las skye 'grub par [205a] 'gyur min pas, ,gzhan las skye ba yin zhes bya ba'i phyogs 'di gtang bar byos
gru.english: It is not the case That the sprout and seed Exist at the same time; If they cannot be Totally other, Then how could the seed Be something entirely other? Neither, therefore, Is it the case That the birth of a sprout From a seed could be [f. 205a]. As such, we implore you To relinquish this position, Where you claim that things Grow from something other.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, DE LTAR RE ZHIG PHYIR RGOL GZHAN LA GRAGS PA'I RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN GRUB GRUB LTAR BRJOD NAS SUN 'BYIN BYAS SO, ,DE NI RGYU 'BRAS GNYIS LA NGO BOS GRUB PA'I GZHAN MI SRID PAR BSHAD PA,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, de ltar re zhig phyir rgol gzhan la grags pa'i rang gi ngo bo nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan grub grub ltar brjod nas sun 'byin byas so, ,de ni rgyu 'bras gnyis la ngo bos grub pa'i gzhan mi srid par bshad pa
gru.english: Here's the first; we will begin with describing how, as if it were possible, things could exist as something other than other things, in a way which existed in & of itself—as the other party here declares it would be. And then we'll demolish this idea. That in itself would involve explaining why it's impossible for causes and their results to be, through some essence of their own, other than each other.

gru.acip: SA BON LA MYU GU LAS NGO BOS GRUB PA'I GZHAN NYID MED LA, DE MED PAR SA BON MYU GU LAS GZHAN PA NYID DU GA LA 'GYUR TE MI 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: sa bon la myu gu las ngo bos grub pa'i gzhan nyid med la, de med par sa bon myu gu las gzhan pa nyid du ga la 'gyur te mi 'gyur ro
gru.english: As for the seed as well, there exists none which is something totally other than the sprout, in a way where this is true in & of itself. And if that cannot be, then how on earth could the seed ever be something entirely other than the sprout? Meaning—it could never be so.

gru.acip: NGO BOS GRUB PA'I GZHAN NYID MED PA DES NA MYU GU SA BON LAS SKYES PA NGO BO NYID KYIS 'GRUB PAR 'GYUR BA MIN PAS DNGOS PO RNAMS GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YIN ZHES BYA BA'I PHYOGS 'DI GTANG BAR BYOS SHIG
gru.wylie: ngo bos grub pa'i gzhan nyid med pa des na myu gu sa bon las skyes pa ngo bo nyid kyis 'grub par 'gyur ba min pas dngos po rnams gzhan las skye ba yin zhes bya ba'i phyogs 'di gtang bar byos shig
gru.english: And since there could never be any quality where things were other than each other in a way that existed in & of itself, it is therefore neither the case that the birth of a sprout from a seed could be something that existed through some essential nature of its own. As such, we would implore you to relinquish this position, where you claim that things are such that they grow from something other than themselves.

gru.acip: ,'DI NI SA BON MYU GU LAS THA DAD PA DE RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA YIN NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA LA DUS NAM YANG LDOG PA MED PAS, SA BON GYI DUS NA'ANG MYU GU LAS RDZAS THA DAD DU 'GYUR LA, DE LTAR DE GNYIS DUS MNYAM DU 'GYUR BA LAS DE MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'di ni sa bon myu gu las tha dad pa de rang bzhin gyis grub pa yin na, rang bzhin gyis grub pa la dus nam yang ldog pa med pas, sa bon gyi dus na'ang myu gu las rdzas tha dad du 'gyur la, de ltar de gnyis dus mnyam du 'gyur ba las de med pa'i phyir
gru.english: The point being made here is this. Suppose that the fact that a seed was distinct from a sprout were something that existed through some nature of its own. Now a thing that existed through its own nature could never be stopped; as such, even in the seed's time it would be substantially distinct from the sprout—whereas if that were the case, then the seed & sprout would have to be simultaneous, while in fact they are not.

gru.acip: DE GNYIS LA NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GZHAN MED CES STON PA YIN GYI, RGYU 'BRAS GNYIS THA SNYAD DU NGO BO THA DAD DU 'DOD PA 'GOG PA MIN TE, DGAG BYA LA GTUG PA SHES DGOS SO,,
gru.wylie: de gnyis la ngo bo nyid kyis grub pa'i gzhan med ces ston pa yin gyi, rgyu 'bras gnyis tha snyad du ngo bo tha dad du 'dod pa 'gog pa min te, dgag bya la gtug pa shes dgos so
gru.english: All this is teaching us that—with regard to these two—there is no quality of being other than each other, in a way which exists through some essence of its own. What we are not denying here though is the belief that causes & effects are, in name only, entities that are discrete from each other. You need to try understand here that the argument is meant to address that non-existent thing which emptiness is empty of. The mistaken metaphor of the arms of a scale

gru.acip: DE DAG GIS NI BYA BA GNYIS DUS GCIG PAS SA MYUG GNYIS KYANG DUS GCIG PA DANG, DE'I DPER SRANG MDA'I MTHO DMAN GNYIS BKOD PA'I DPE MA GRUB PAR BSTAN GYI, BYA BA GNYIS LA DUS GCIG PA SRID NA DUS DER CHOS GNYIS KYANG NGES PAR DUS MNYAM ZHES STON PA MIN NO,,
gru.wylie: de dag gis ni bya ba gnyis dus gcig pas sa myug gnyis kyang dus gcig pa dang, de'i dper srang mda'i mtho dman gnyis bkod pa'i dpe ma grub par bstan gyi, bya ba gnyis la dus gcig pa srid na dus der chos gnyis kyang nges par dus mnyam zhes ston pa min no
gru.english: What the lines here are indicating is only the incorrectness of the ideas that—just because the two actions are simultaneous—then the pair of the seed & the sprout must also be simultaneous; and that the metaphor of the arms of a scale rising & dropping could apply here. They are not making the assertion that—if it is possible for two actions to be simultaneous—then the two objects involved must also be simultaneous.

gru.acip: DE YANG MI RUNG STE RGOL BA DE DAG GIS CHOS LAS BYA BA DON GZHAN DU KHAS MA BLANGS PA'I PHYIR DANG, 'DI NI BYA BA GNYIS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA 'GOG PA'I SKABS YIN PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: de yang mi rung ste rgol ba de dag gis chos las bya ba don gzhan du khas ma blangs pa'i phyir dang, 'di ni bya ba gnyis rang bzhin gyis grub pa 'gog pa'i skabs yin pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: This too though is mistaken, since these particular disputants do not accept the idea that action has an existence separate from the objects involved in the action; and, after all, this is a section of the text where we are disproving the idea that the two actions could exist through some nature of their own.

gru.acip: BKOD PA NI BDEN MOD KYI DE NI GZHAN SKYE DANG, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE BA BSTAN PA'I PHYIR YANG MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PAS, GAL TE SKYE BA 'DI NI ZHES PAS SKYE BA BKAG PA NI RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA'I SKYE BA TZAM BKAG GI ,SA BON LAS MYU GU SKYE BA TZAM 'GOG PA GTAN MIN NO,,
gru.wylie: bkod pa ni bden mod kyi de ni gzhan skye dang, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis skye ba bstan pa'i phyir yang ma yin no, zhes gsungs pas, gal te skye ba 'di ni zhes pas skye ba bkag pa ni rang gi ngo bos grub pa'i skye ba tsam bkag gi ,sa bon las myu gu skye ba tsam 'gog pa gtan min no
gru.english: We would have to admit that the metaphor is, in truth, presented in that sutra. Remember though that “this is speaking neither of things growing from something other than themselves; nor is it speaking of growth which occurs by definition.” As such, when the part about “suppose this growing” denies that things grow, it is only denying that things could grow through some essential nature of their own. We are absolutely not denying that, in general, sprouts grow from seeds.

gru.acip: 'GREL PAR CIG CAR DU BRTEN NAS 'BYUNG BA MA BRTAGS PAR GRUB PA SGYU MA LTA BU GSAL BAR BYA BA'I PHYIR DU GSUNGS PAR BSHAD PA'I CIG CAR DU BRTEN NAS 'BYUNG BA ZHES PA NI, BYA BA GNYIS CIG CAR DU YOD PA LA BYA DGOS TE, MDO DER SRANG MDA'I MTHO DMA'I DPES DUS MNYAM PA GCIG STON DGOS PA LA, SO {%SA} MYUG GNYIS DUS MNYAM PA LA BSHAD DU MI RUNG BA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: 'grel par cig car du brten nas 'byung ba ma brtags par grub pa sgyu ma lta bu gsal bar bya ba'i phyir du gsungs par bshad pa'i cig car du brten nas 'byung ba zhes pa ni, bya ba gnyis cig car du yod pa la bya dgos te, mdo der srang mda'i mtho dma'i dpes dus mnyam pa gcig ston dgos pa la, so {%sa} myug gnyis dus mnyam pa la bshad du mi rung ba'i phyir ro
gru.english: Remember that the autocommentary goes on to say, “It is so that people can come to see clearly that—when these things occur altogether, and we choose not to examine how they occur altogether in a dependent relationship—then they exist in the same way that an illusion does.” This statement must be read as describing how the two actions occur altogether. That is, while it is true that the sutra must be explained as using the metaphor of the arms of a scale to describe a type of simultaneity, it would be mistaken to describe it as explaining why the two of seed and sprout were simultaneous.

gru.acip: DES NA BYA BA GNYIS GCIG PA BKAG BA NI, RANG MTSAN GYIS GRUB PA'I BYA BA GNYIS YIN GYI, BYA BA GNYIS SPYIR DUS MNYAM PA YOD PA BKAG PA MIN NO,,
gru.wylie: des na bya ba gnyis gcig pa bkag ba ni, rang mtshan gyis grub pa'i bya ba gnyis yin gyi, bya ba gnyis spyir dus mnyam pa yod pa bkag pa min no
gru.english: Therefore the denial that the two actions occur at the same time is made with reference to the two as existing by definition; it is not the case that—in general—the idea that the two actions could be happening simultaneously is being refused.

gru.acip: RTEN BRTEN PA DON DAM PAR GRUB NA NI RANG BZHIN GZHAN DU 'GYUR BA MI 'THAD PAS, DUS NAM GYI TSE YANG BYA BA RTEN DGOS PAS MYU GU SOGS SKYE BA LA PHYOGS PA'I DUS SU YANG, SKYE BA'I BYA BA'I RTEN DU MYU GU YOD DGOS PAS RGYU 'BRAS GNYIS DUS MNYAM DU 'GYUR BA SOGS KYIS GNOD PAS MI 'THAD DO,,
gru.wylie: rten brten pa don dam par grub na ni rang bzhin gzhan du 'gyur ba mi 'thad pas, dus nam gyi tshe yang bya ba rten dgos pas myu gu sogs skye ba la phyogs pa'i dus su yang, skye ba'i bya ba'i rten du myu gu yod dgos pas rgyu 'bras gnyis dus mnyam du 'gyur ba sogs kyis gnod pas mi 'thad do
gru.english: If the basis and what rests upon this basis existed in an ultimate way, then it would be incorrect to say that they possessed a nature which was different from each other. Therefore, at the point in time when the action had to rely upon its own basis, then even at the juncture where the sprout or such was approaching its growth, there would have to be a sprout there to act as the basis which supported the action of growing. This model would be drawn into question by a situation where, for example, the cause and its result were thus simultaneous; as such, it would have to be incorrect.

gru.acip: CI STE SKYE BA MED PA'I SKYON SPANG BAR 'DOD NAS RGYU DUS SU 'BRAS BU DE MED DO ZHE NA, DE'I TSE SNGA PHYI BA 'DI LA NGO BOS GRUB PA'I GZHAN MED PA'I NYES PA SNGAR BSHAD ZIN TO,,
gru.wylie: ci ste skye ba med pa'i skyon spang bar 'dod nas rgyu dus su 'bras bu de med do zhe na, de'i tshe snga phyi ba 'di la ngo bos grub pa'i gzhan med pa'i nyes pa sngar bshad zin to
gru.english: Suppose then that the other party, hoping to avoid this problem that the awareness wouldn't grow, says that there is no result in the time of the cause. In that case there would come the problem that we already described earlier—with the case of a cause & result which were sequential—where there were no things that were other than each other, in a way where they existed through some essence of their own.

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, GAL TE GZHAN SKYE GRUB PA'I PHYIR DU RIGS PA GANG SMRAS PA DE NI, BUD SHING SKAM PO MAR GYIS BRAN PA LTAR KHYOD KYI BLO GROS KYI MES MA LUS PAR BSREGS PAS, KHYOD KYI SHES RAB KYI ME SBOR BA'I RIGS PA'I BUD SHING BSKUL BA DES CHOG GI DA DE BSKUL MI DGOS SO,,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, gal te gzhan skye grub pa'i phyir du rigs pa gang smras pa de ni, bud shing skam po mar gyis bran pa ltar khyod kyi blo gros kyi mes ma lus par bsregs pas, khyod kyi shes rab kyi me sbor ba'i rigs pa'i bud shing bskul ba des chog gi da de bskul mi dgos so
gru.english: Here is the first. The other party may come and make the following statement: Any argument that someone could present to prove the idea that things grow from something other than themselves is like pouring ghee on dry wood: the flames of your intellect consume everything. It's enough that you have the fuel of the firewood of clear thinking, to feed the fire of wisdom; we need no further fuel than that.

gru.acip: 'O NA RIGS PA MA BSTAN PAR GZHAN SKYE 'DOD PA'I DON MI 'GRUB PA MA YIN NAM ZHE NA,
gru.wylie: 'o na rigs pa ma bstan par gzhan skye 'dod pa'i don mi 'grub pa ma yin nam zhe na
gru.english: And you may ask us: “But if you cannot present any logic to help, how are you going to prove this idea—the belief you have that things could grow from something other than themselves?”

gru.acip: DE NI MA YIN TE GANG ZHIG 'JIG RTEN LAS GRUB PA DER NI, RIGS PA GZHAN GYIS CI YANG BYA BA MED DE, 'JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA NI SHIN TU STOBS DANG LDAN PA'I PHYIR RO ZHES BSHAD PA,
gru.wylie: de ni ma yin te gang zhig 'jig rten las grub pa der ni, rigs pa gzhan gyis ci yang bya ba med de, 'jig rten gyi mthong ba ni shin tu stobs dang ldan pa'i phyir ro zhes bshad pa
gru.english: The fact is that no such logic is needed. Once something has been established in the everyday world, there's nothing else to be achieved throught the use of further reasoning. And that's because what the world sees with its own eyes has overwhelming authority. And so the purpose of the lines that come next in the root text is to express this sentiment.

gru.acip: GANG GIS 'JIG RTEN PA THAMS CAD RANG GI LTA BA KHO NA LA GNAS NAS, 'JIG RTEN GYI MTHONG BA TSAD MAR 'DOD PAS NA SHIN TU STOBS DANG LDAN ZHING, NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I RGYU GZHAN LAS 'BRAS BU GZHAN 'BYUNG BA YANG 'JIG RTEN PA RNAMS KYIS MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PAR 'GYUR TE,
gru.wylie: gang gis 'jig rten pa thams cad rang gi lta ba kho na la gnas nas, 'jig rten gyi mthong ba tshad mar 'dod pas na shin tu stobs dang ldan zhing, ngo bo nyid kyis grub pa'i rgyu gzhan las 'bras bu gzhan 'byung ba yang 'jig rten pa rnams kyis mngon sum du rtogs par 'gyur te
gru.english: Suppose then that someone comes & says, Those—meaning all the people of the everyday world—who remain only with their own viewpoints consider what the world sees as accurate perception; that is, this is what they consider authoritative. And what people of the world perceive, directly, is that results issue from causes which are other than them, and which exist in & of themselves.

gru.acip: RIGS PA'I 'THAD PA YANG NYE BAR 'GOD PA NA, MNGON SUM DU GYUR MA GYUR GNYIS LAS GNYIS PA LA 'GOD PA YIN LA, DANG PO NI, MNGON SUM TSAD MAS GRUB PA'I PHYIR DE LA 'THAD PA 'GOD PA MA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: rigs pa'i 'thad pa yang nye bar 'god pa na, mngon sum du gyur ma gyur gnyis las gnyis pa la 'god pa yin la, dang po ni, mngon sum tshad mas grub pa'i phyir de la 'thad pa 'god pa ma yin no
gru.english: When a person presents a justification utilizing logic, this could either be done in a case where direct perception is involved, or where it is not. In the first of these two choices, things have already been established by virtue of a direct form of accurate perception; as such, we do not in this case present logical justifications.

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR GZHAN SKYE YOD PA 'DIR NI, DE YOD PAR SGRUB PA'I RIGS PA GZHAN SMRAS PA NYID KYIS LTA KO CI ZHIG BYA,
gru.wylie: de'i phyir gzhan skye yod pa 'dir ni, de yod par sgrub pa'i rigs pa gzhan smras pa nyid kyis lta ko ci zhig bya
gru.english: Given that—here in this exercise of establishing the existence of things growing from things that are other than themselves—what could possibly be the use of articulating the point with this additional logic for its existence?

gru.acip: DES NA GZHAN SKYE'I SGRUB BYED KYI 'THAD PA GZHAN MED PAR YANG, DNGOS PO RNAMS GZHAN LAS SKYE BA 'GRUB PAS, GZHAN LAS SKYE BA YOD PA 'DIR NI RIGS PA GZHAN BSTAN PAS DGOS PA CI ZHIG YOD DE MED DE, MNGON SUM GYIS GRUB PA'I PHYIR RO ZHE NA,
gru.wylie: des na gzhan skye'i sgrub byed kyi 'thad pa gzhan med par yang, dngos po rnams gzhan las skye ba 'grub pas, gzhan las skye ba yod pa 'dir ni rigs pa gzhan bstan pas dgos pa ci zhig yod de med de, mngon sum gyis grub pa'i phyir ro zhe na
gru.english: As such—even though there is no other justification used to establish, logically, the fact that things grow from things other than themselves—we nonetheless establish that entitites do, indeed, grow from other entities. What purpose then would be served by presenting any further logic for this—for the fact that things do grow from things other than themselves? There would be no such purpose, for this fact is established by our own direct perception. Contradicting what the world says—or not

gru.acip: DE LTAR BYAS NA NGO BO MED PA'I CHOS MI SRID PAS, GZHI GRUB PA YIN NA NGO BO GCIG DANG THA DAD LAS MI 'DA' LA, NGO BO YOD PA KHAS LEN KYANG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA'I NGO BO MED PA MI 'GAL LO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar byas na ngo bo med pa'i chos mi srid pas, gzhi grub pa yin na ngo bo gcig dang tha dad las mi 'da' la, ngo bo yod pa khas len kyang rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i ngo bo med pa mi 'gal lo
gru.english: Given all this, then—since an existing entity without any essential nature at all is an impossibility—we can say that once a thing exists, it possesses either one single essential nature, or else some separate natures: there is no other possibility. At the same time, it is no contradiction to say that an object possesses an essential nature, but lacks any essential nature which exists through some nature of its own.

gru.acip: DE LA MYU GU LA SOGS PA'I DNGOS PO'I NGO BO DON DAM PA NI, YANG DAG PA'I DON MNGON SUM DU MTHONG BA RNAMS KYI YE SHES KYI KHYAD PAR GYI YUL NYID KYIS BDAG GI RANG GI NGO BO RNYED PA YIN GYI, RANG GI BDAG NYID KYIS GRUB PA NI MA YIN TE, 'DI NI NGO BO GNYIS BSHAD PA'I GCIG YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: de la myu gu la sogs pa'i dngos po'i ngo bo don dam pa ni, yang dag pa'i don mngon sum du mthong ba rnams kyi ye shes kyi khyad par gyi yul nyid kyis bdag gi rang gi ngo bo rnyed pa yin gyi, rang gi bdag nyid kyis grub pa ni ma yin te, 'di ni ngo bo gnyis bshad pa'i gcig yin no
gru.english: Let's look at the ultimate nature possessed by objects such as a sprout. This is an essential nature of these objects which is discovered by the exceptional wisdom of those who see, directly, pure reality: and it is discovered through a self-nature of this one object. Even given that, this ultimate nature though is not something which exists in & of itself. This then is one of the two natures we've alluded to.

gru.acip: YE SHES DES RNYED PA'AM GRUB PAR BSTAN PA NA DES GRUB RGYU ZHIG BYUNG NA BDEN GRUB BO ZHES 'DZIN PA DGAG PA'I PHYIR, RANG GI BDAG NYID KYIS GRUB PA NI MA YIN NO, ZHES GSUNGS PAS
gru.wylie: ye shes des rnyed pa'am grub par bstan pa na des grub rgyu zhig byung na bden grub bo zhes 'dzin pa dgag pa'i phyir, rang gi bdag nyid kyis grub pa ni ma yin no, zhes gsungs pas
gru.english: When we say that this nature is “discovered” or established by this wisdom, we say in the same breath that it is not something which exists in & of itself; this is to prevent the idea that—if there is some way of establishing it—then this nature should exist in truth.

gru.acip: 'PHAGS PA'I MNYAM GZHAG GI YE SHES KYIS DON DAM BDEN PA GZHAL NA, BDEN GRUB TU 'GYUR BAS DE SHES BYA MA YIN PA SLOB DPON 'DI'I LUGS SU SMRA BA NI,
gru.wylie: 'phags pa'i mnyam gzhag gi ye shes kyis don dam bden pa gzhal na, bden grub tu 'gyur bas de shes bya ma yin pa slob dpon 'di'i lugs su smra ba ni
gru.english: Some people say that—if a realized being in a meditation on emptiness is able to bring ultimate reality under their consideration—then this reality would then have to exist truly; and that therefore it is not something which can ever be known. They say that this is the position being taken by the master here.

gru.acip: LUGS 'DIS MNYAM GZHAG GIS RNYED KYANG BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR BSHAD PA'I DON YE MA RTOGS BZHIN DU MKHAS PA'I LUGS NYAMS SU 'JUG PA'O,,
gru.wylie: lugs 'dis mnyam gzhag gis rnyed kyang bden par ma grub par bshad pa'i don ye ma rtogs bzhin du mkhas pa'i lugs nyams su 'jug pa'o
gru.english: People who describe it this way have failed, totally, to realize the point of the explanation that something can be discovered by this particular meditation and yet still not exist in truth; and in the midst of this failure, they are actually undermining the ways of the wise.

gru.acip: BYIS PA RNAMS KYI MTHONG BA'I YUL DU RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA DE BZHIN DU RANG GI NGO BO YOD PA NI MIN TE NGO BO GNYIS KYI GCIG YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: byis pa rnams kyi mthong ba'i yul du rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par snang ba de bzhin du rang gi ngo bo yod pa ni min te ngo bo gnyis kyi gcig yin no
gru.english: And so this is another one of the two natures we've been talking about: as an object being perceived by those who are still infants, it appears to exist by definition; and yet at the very same moment, it is anything but something which could possess some essential nature of its own.

gru.acip: GZHI DE KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR GRUB NA BRDZUN PAR 'GRUB DGOS SHING, BRDZUN PAR DNGOS SU 'GRUB PA LA GZHI DE LA SNGON DU BDEN GRUB TSAD MAS KHEGS DGOS PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: gzhi de kun rdzob bden par grub na brdzun par 'grub dgos shing, brdzun par dngos su 'grub pa la gzhi de la sngon du bden grub tshad mas khegs dgos pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Establishing that any particular object belongs to deceptive reality requires that it be established as something which is a lie; and to establish, directly, that something is a lie requires having denied—earlier, and through the use of an accurate perception—that it exists in truth.

gru.acip: DES NA BRDZUN PA MTHONG BA'I STOBS LAS ZHES PA NI, GANG ZAG RANG DGA' BA DE RNAMS KYIS BRDZUN PA MTHONG YANG DE DAG GIS BRDZUN PAR 'GRUB MI DGOS TE,
gru.wylie: des na brdzun pa mthong ba'i stobs las zhes pa ni, gang zag rang dga' ba de rnams kyis brdzun pa mthong yang de dag gis brdzun par 'grub mi dgos te
gru.english: And so in the expression above about the power of perceiving that something is deceptive making something else happen, it's not necessarily the case that—when some average person perceives something which is deceptive—they thereby establish that it is deceptive.

gru.acip: DPER NA SGYU MA'I LTAD MO BAS SGYU MA'I RTA GLANG MTHONG BA NA BRDZUN PAR MTHONG YANG, SNANG BA DE BRDZUN PAR 'GRUB MI DGOS PA BZHIN NO,,
gru.wylie: dper na sgyu ma'i ltad mo bas sgyu ma'i rta glang mthong ba na brdzun par mthong yang, snang ba de brdzun par 'grub mi dgos pa bzhin no
gru.english: A person watching a magic show, for example, can see an illusory horse or elephant, and are thus seeing something deceptive; but that doesn't necessarily mean that they thereby establish that what appears to them is deceptive.

gru.acip: CHOS CAN RNAMS BDEN STONG LAS NGO BO THA DAD NA BDEN GRUB TU 'GYUR PA'I PHYIR, NGO BO GCIG LA LDOG PA THA DAD PA BYAS PA DANG MI RTAG PA LTA BU STE, BYANG CHUB SEMS 'GREL LAS,
gru.wylie: chos can rnams bden stong las ngo bo tha dad na bden grub tu 'gyur pa'i phyir, ngo bo gcig la ldog pa tha dad pa byas pa dang mi rtag pa lta bu ste, byang chub sems 'grel las
gru.english: Now if certain given objects were such that to be them were not to be empty of any true nature, they would perforce have to exist in reality. As such, we would have to say that the two realities share the same nature, but in different manifestations—they are, for example, like being a thing which is made, and being a changing thing. As A Commentary on the Wish for Enlightenment puts it,

gru.acip: RKANG PA SNGA MAS DON DAM BDEN PA BLO'I YUL MIN PAR DAM BCAS PA RKANG PA PHYI MAS SGRUB PAR 'DOD PA NI, GZHUNG DE DAG GI DON DU GTAN MI SNANG NGO,,
gru.wylie: rkang pa snga mas don dam bden pa blo'i yul min par dam bcas pa rkang pa phyi mas sgrub par 'dod pa ni, gzhung de dag gi don du gtan mi snang ngo
gru.english: The belief that the first part of the verse presents an assertion that the ultimate could never be an object perceived by the mind; and that this assertion is somehow proven by the latter part of the verse, doesn't in my opinion represent the point of these lines in any conceivable way at all.

gru.acip: DE YIN NA NI SHES BYA THAMS CAD LA KHYAB PAR BYED PAS GNYIS DANG GNYIS MA YIN GYI PHUNG GSUM SEL BA YIN TE DBU MA SNANG BA LAS, PHAN TSUN SPANGS TE GNAS PA'I MTSAN NYID KYI CHOS DAG NI, CIG SHES {%SHOS} DGAG PA GZHAN SGRUB PA MED NA MED PA YIN PA'I PHYIR, GNYIS KA MA YIN PA'I PHYOGS SU RTOG PA YANG RIGS PA MA YIN NO, ZHES DANG,
gru.wylie: de yin na ni shes bya thams cad la khyab par byed pas gnyis dang gnyis ma yin gyi phung gsum sel ba yin te dbu ma snang ba las, phan tshun spangs te gnas pa'i mtshan nyid kyi chos dag ni, cig shes {%shos} dgag pa gzhan sgrub pa med na med pa yin pa'i phyir, gnyis ka ma yin pa'i phyogs su rtog pa yang rigs pa ma yin no, zhes dang
gru.english: And if something is this way, then it subsumes all the perceivable things there are; being either the two, or not the two, eliminates any third possibility between them. As Light on the Middle Way puts it, When two things are characterized by existing in a mutually exclusive relationship, then there exists no case where—if you eliminate the one—you do not establish the other. As such, it would further be illogical to imagine that there existed an option where something were neither.

gru.acip: PHUNG GSUM SEL BA'I DNGOS 'GAL CIG STON RGYU MED NA NI, YOD MED DAM GCIG DANG DU MA SOGS GANG 'DOD CES MTHA' GNYIS SU KHA TSON BCAD PA'I BRTAG PA BYAS NAS 'GOG SA MED LA, YOD NA DNGOS 'GAL GCIG 'GOG PA NI CIG SHOS SGRUB PA MED NA MED PA YIN PAS, DBU MA THAL 'GYUR BA LA DNGOS 'GAL MED ZER BA NI, DGAG GZHAG GI RNAM GZHAG MA CHAGS PA'O,,
gru.wylie: phung gsum sel ba'i dngos 'gal cig ston rgyu med na ni, yod med dam gcig dang du ma sogs gang 'dod ces mtha' gnyis su kha tshon bcad pa'i brtag pa byas nas 'gog sa med la, yod na dngos 'gal gcig 'gog pa ni cig shos sgrub pa med na med pa yin pas, dbu ma thal 'gyur ba la dngos 'gal med zer ba ni, dgag gzhag gi rnam gzhag ma chags pa'o
gru.english: If we were unable to demonstrate this principle of mutual exclusion—where all third possibilities are eliminated—then we could never reach a place where we denied an idea by using an examination where we divided things into two opposing possibilities: existing or not existing; one or many; and so on. And if we were able to show this exclusion, then there would be no possibility where if we denied one part of a direct of some mutual exclusion, we established its pair. And if there were no such possibility, then the claim that those of the Consequence branch had no case of mutual exclusion here would represent a failure to follow the principles of denial or assertion.

gru.acip: DNGOS 'GAL GCIG RNAM PAR BCAD NA CIG SHOS YONGS SU GCOD PA DANG, GCIG 'GOG NA CIG SHOS SGRUB DGOS PA LA DBU MA THAL RANG LA KHYAD PAR YOD PA MA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: dngos 'gal gcig rnam par bcad na cig shos yongs su gcod pa dang, gcig 'gog na cig shos sgrub dgos pa la dbu ma thal rang la khyad par yod pa ma yin no
gru.english: If two things stand in direct contradiction to one another and eliminating one of the two possibilities eliminates the other; or if disproving one had to establish the other; then we would have to say that there was no distinction between the Consequence and Independent groups within the Middle Way school. Deception within deception

gru.acip: YID KYI DBANG PO'I GNOD PA NI SNGAGS DANG SMAN LA SOGS PA DE DAG DANG GRUB MTHA' LOG PA DANG, GTAN TSIGS LTAR SNANG DANG GNYID KYI GNOD PA SOGS SO,,
gru.wylie: yid kyi dbang po'i gnod pa ni sngags dang sman la sogs pa de dag dang grub mtha' log pa dang, gtan tshigs ltar snang dang gnyid kyi gnod pa sogs so
gru.english: Conditions which can adversely affect the power of the thought would be things like the spells, potions, and such just mentioned—as well as mistaken schools of thought; false logic; or the mental hindrance caused by sleep.

gru.acip: 'PHAGS PA LA LTOS NAS NI YANG LOG GNYIS SU MED DE, JI LTAR GZUGS BRNYAN LA SOGS SNANG BA LTAR GYI DON DU MED PA BZHIN DU, MA RIG PA DANG LDAN PA RNAMS LA SNGON PO LA SOGS PA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR SNANG BA YANG, SNANG BA LTAR GYI DON DU MED PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: 'phags pa la ltos nas ni yang log gnyis su med de, ji ltar gzugs brnyan la sogs snang ba ltar gyi don du med pa bzhin du, ma rig pa dang ldan pa rnams la sngon po la sogs pa rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par snang ba yang, snang ba ltar gyi don du med pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: There is no such division in this case of correct & mistaken perceptions when the reference is, rather, to how a realized being sees things. Objects such as those reflected in a mirror, for example, do not exist in reality as they do in appearance; just so, it is the case that objects such as blue appear, to those who still possess misunderstanding, as though they existed by definition—but these things do not in fact exist the way they appear.

gru.acip: PHYIN CI LOG YIN PAR, 'JIG RTEN PA'I BLO RANG DGA' BAS KYANG RTOGS MOD KYANG, YID LA GRUB MTHA' NGAN PA'I GNOD PA YOD PAS LOG PAR BZUNG BA'I DON RNAMS, 'JIG RTEN PA'I BLO RANG DGA' BAS PHYIN CI LOG TU MI RTOGS PAS, 'JIG RTEN NYID LAS LOG PAR JI LTAR BZHAG CE NA,
gru.wylie: phyin ci log yin par, 'jig rten pa'i blo rang dga' bas kyang rtogs mod kyang, yid la grub mtha' ngan pa'i gnod pa yod pas log par bzung ba'i don rnams, 'jig rten pa'i blo rang dga' bas phyin ci log tu mi rtogs pas, 'jig rten nyid las log par ji ltar bzhag ce na
gru.english: We can admittedly come to realize, even just with some random state of mind from the everyday world, that things like these are mistaken. In the case though where we take particular objects in the wrong way because our mind is adversely affected by mistaken schools of thought, it is not that we can realize—with just such a random state of mind from the everyday world—that such objects are mistaken. How then can we say of these particular objects that, even just from the viewpoint of the everyday world, they are mistaken?

gru.acip: 'DIR GNOD PA YOD MED DPYOD PA'I GNOD PA NI, LHAN SKYES KYIS PHYIN CI LOG TU 'DZIN PA'I GNOD PA LA MI BYED PAS, GRUB MTHA' NGAN PAS BTAGS PA NI GRUB MTHAS BLO BSGYUR BA KHO NAS LOG PAR BTAGS PA'I GTZO BO SOGS YIN LA,
gru.wylie: 'dir gnod pa yod med dpyod pa'i gnod pa ni, lhan skyes kyis phyin ci log tu 'dzin pa'i gnod pa la mi byed pas, grub mtha' ngan pas btags pa ni grub mthas blo bsgyur ba kho nas log par btags pa'i gtso bo sogs yin la
gru.english: The answer is that—when we are looking into the question of whether or not there is some adverse effect going on—we are not referring to an adverse effect in the sense of an inborn state of mind holding to an object in a mistaken way. When we speak of an object which is imputed by the ideas of a mistaken school, we are speaking for example primarily of an object imputed only by the thoughts of those who have been influenced by some school of thought.

gru.acip: KUN RDZOB NI THA SNYAD PA'I TSAD MAS 'JOG DGOS PA'I PHYIR LOG PA'I KUN RDZOB 'JOG NA YANG DE LA BLTOS NAS 'JOG DGOS NA, MA RIG PA'I BAG CHAGS KYIS BSLAD PA NI 'KHRUL PAR THA SNYAD PA'I TSAD MAS MI 'GRUB PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: kun rdzob ni tha snyad pa'i tshad mas 'jog dgos pa'i phyir log pa'i kun rdzob 'jog na yang de la bltos nas 'jog dgos na, ma rig pa'i bag chags kyis bslad pa ni 'khrul par tha snyad pa'i tshad mas mi 'grub pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: Deceptive reality is something which must be established by a nominal form of accurate perception; as such, if we were to establish a mistaken form of deceptive reality, that too would have to be established relative to this type of perception. It is not the case then that we could ever use a nominal form of accurate perception to determine that something infected by deep seeds of misunderstanding was mistaken. Views inspired by sleep

gru.acip: MI SHES PA'I GNYID KYIS YID RAB TU BSKYOD PA'I MU STEGS CAN YID LA PHYIN CI LOG GI GRUB MTHA' NGAN PA DANG, GTAN TSIGS LTAR SNANG GI GNOD PA YOD PA 'DI DAG NI, DE KHO NA NYID LA 'JUG PAR 'DOD PAS SKYE BO MA BYANG BA GNAG RDZI DANG BUD MED LA SOGS PA YAN CHAD LA GRAGS PA'I SKYE BA DANG, 'JIG PA LA SOGS PA PHYIN CI MA LOG PA MA BZUNG BAR, 'JIG RTEN PA RNAMS LAS PHUL DU BYUNG BAR 'GRO BAR 'DOD PAS,
gru.wylie: mi shes pa'i gnyid kyis yid rab tu bskyod pa'i mu stegs can yid la phyin ci log gi grub mtha' ngan pa dang, gtan tshigs ltar snang gi gnod pa yod pa 'di dag ni, de kho na nyid la 'jug par 'dod pas skye bo ma byang ba gnag rdzi dang bud med la sogs pa yan chad la grags pa'i skye ba dang, 'jig pa la sogs pa phyin ci ma log pa ma bzung bar, 'jig rten pa rnams las phul du byung bar 'gro bar 'dod pas
gru.english: Consider now those of lower views, whose minds are inspired by the sleep of misunderstanding—those with minds adversely affected by mistaken, undesirable schools of thought, or false forms of logic. They wish to rise above the everyday world: they hope to engage in the way things really are. But they want to do so without recognizing things like starting & stopping—in the way these are understood among those who have not applied themselves formally to philosophy, beginning for example from cowherds or women—as being unmistaken.

gru.acip: DE LTAR NA THA SNYAD DU YOD PA LA NI TSAD MAS GRUB PA ZHIG DGOS SO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar na tha snyad du yod pa la ni tshad mas grub pa zhig dgos so
gru.english: As such, for a thing to exist nominally, it must be something which is confirmed by an accurate perception.

gru.acip: DA LTA GZUGS SGRA SOGS LNGA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR DBANG SHES LA SNANG BA NI, MA RIG PAS BSLAD PA YIN PAS SHES PA DE DANG, GZUGS BRNYAN DANG BRAG CHA SOGS SNANG BA'I DBANG SHES RNAMS LA, PHRA RAGS TZAM MA GTOGS PA SNANG YUL LA 'KHRUL MA 'KHRUL LA KHYAD PAR MED CING, SNGO SOGS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA DANG, GZUGS BRNYAN BYAD BZHIN DU YOD PA MI SRID KYANG,
gru.wylie: da lta gzugs sgra sogs lnga rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par dbang shes la snang ba ni, ma rig pas bslad pa yin pas shes pa de dang, gzugs brnyan dang brag cha sogs snang ba'i dbang shes rnams la, phra rags tsam ma gtogs pa snang yul la 'khrul ma 'khrul la khyad par med cing, sngo sogs rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa dang, gzugs brnyan byad bzhin du yod pa mi srid kyang
gru.english: Right now the five types of objects which include visible & audible forms are assuming an aspect—within our sense consciousnesses—where it seems as though they existed by definition. This is something that is happening because these states of mind are infected by misunderstanding. As such, when we compare these mental states to forms of sense consciousness which are assuming the aspect of things like a reflection in a mirror, or an echo, there is no difference between them where one is mistaken and the other is not—only some distinction of relative subtlety. It is impossible for things like the color blue to exist by definition; and it is impossible for reflections to be the things standing before the mirror.

gru.acip: BYAD BZHIN DU MED PA'I GZUGS BRNYAN YOD PA BZHIN DU, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA MIN KYANG SNGO SOGS YOD DGOS LA, DE YANG PHYI ROL GYI DON DU YOD PA BZHIN DU GZUGS BRNYAN YANG GZUGS KYI SKYE MCHED DU BZHED PA YIN TE, 'OG NAS GZUGS BRNYAN GYIS DE SNANG BA'I DBANG SHES SKYED PAR YANG GSUNGS SO,,
gru.wylie: byad bzhin du med pa'i gzugs brnyan yod pa bzhin du, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa min kyang sngo sogs yod dgos la, de yang phyi rol gyi don du yod pa bzhin du gzugs brnyan yang gzugs kyi skye mched du bzhed pa yin te, 'og nas gzugs brnyan gyis de snang ba'i dbang shes skyed par yang gsungs so
gru.english: And yet there can still exist a reflection in the mirror which does not exist as the object placed before the mirror; just so, blue & the like—despite the fact that they do not exist by definition—must still exist. Moreover, we take the position that the reflection, just as it exists as an outer object, belongs to the door of sense composed of visible objects. That is, it will be stated—further on—that the reflection acts to produce a sense consciousness which assumes its aspect.

gru.acip: DON DAM PAR GZHAN SKYE BKAG PA LA 'JIG RTEN PA'I NGOR GZHAN SKYE GRUB TU CHUG KYANG MI GNOD DO,,
gru.wylie: don dam par gzhan skye bkag pa la 'jig rten pa'i ngor gzhan skye grub tu chug kyang mi gnod do
gru.english: As such, when we undertake to deny that things could grow—in an ultimate sense—from things other than themselves, it would not draw our position into question even if we allowed that the growth of things from things other than themselves were confirmed in the eyes of the everyday world.

gru.acip: KUN RDZOB BDEN 'DZIN DE'I MTHUS SNGON PO LA SOGS PA GANG ZHIG ,RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED BZHIN DU DER SNANG BAR BCOS PA'I BCOS MA SEMS CAN RNAMS LA BDEN PAR SNANG BA DE NI,
gru.wylie: kun rdzob bden 'dzin de'i mthus sngon po la sogs pa gang zhig ,rang bzhin gyis grub pa med bzhin du der snang bar bcos pa'i bcos ma sems can rnams la bden par snang ba de ni
gru.english: Due to the power of this deception, in the form of our tendency to believe that things are real, there comes a construct where things like the color blue appear to exist through some nature of their own—in the very moment that they cannot. This false construct is something which appears, to living beings, as though it were real.

gru.acip: GZUGS BRNYAN SOGS BRDZUN YANG SNANG BA NI BRDZUN PAR SNANG BA YIN LA, DE NI BYAD BZHIN DU SNANG BA DANG DES STONG PA GNYIS TSOGS PA'I BRDZUN PA YIN PAS, DE'I BDEN STONG NI BYAD BZHIN DU BDEN PAS STONG PA YIN GYI, GZUGS BRNYAN RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I BDEN STONG GI DON MED DO,,
gru.wylie: gzugs brnyan sogs brdzun yang snang ba ni brdzun par snang ba yin la, de ni byad bzhin du snang ba dang des stong pa gnyis tshogs pa'i brdzun pa yin pas, de'i bden stong ni byad bzhin du bden pas stong pa yin gyi, gzugs brnyan rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i bden stong gi don med do
gru.english: Reflections & the like can lie to us; but still they do make their appearance, in a lying way. This is a kind of lie where there is a combination of two things: something appearing to be the object which was placed in front of the mirror; and this something's being void of actually existing as that object. As such, when we speak of “voidness of reality” here what we are talking about is the fact that the reflection is void of any existing, in reality, as the object reflected. We are not referring here to a voidness of reality in the sense of the reflection being empty of any true existence, in the form of existing by definition.

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR GZUGS BRNYAN BYAD BZHIN GYIS STONG PAR GRUB KYANG, GZUGS BRNYAN RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR 'DZIN PA'I KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR BDEN PA YIN PA LA 'GAL BA CI YANG MED PA'I DNGOS PO YIN PAS KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: de'i phyir gzugs brnyan byad bzhin gyis stong par grub kyang, gzugs brnyan rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par 'dzin pa'i kun rdzob kyi ngor bden pa yin pa la 'gal ba ci yang med pa'i dngos po yin pas kun rdzob kyi bden pa yin no
gru.english: As such, we can establish that the reflection is devoid of being the object placed before the mirror; but this is a case of a thing where there is absolutely no contradiction for this object to exist as real in the perceptions of a deception which holds that the reflection exists by definition. As such, this thing then is, as well, a case of deceptive reality.

gru.acip: DE LTA MA YIN PAR KUN RDZOB TU BDEN PAR MED NA KUN RDZOB BDEN PA YIN PAR 'GAL NA, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA THA SNYAD DU YANG MED PAR GSUNGS PA DANG, BDEN GRUB 'GEGS PA DANG BDEN MED SGRUB PA THAMS CAD THA SNYAD DU BYED PA'I RNAM GZHAG THAMS CAD DANG 'GAL BAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: de lta ma yin par kun rdzob tu bden par med na kun rdzob bden pa yin par 'gal na, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa tha snyad du yang med par gsungs pa dang, bden grub 'gegs pa dang bden med sgrub pa thams cad tha snyad du byed pa'i rnam gzhag thams cad dang 'gal bar 'gyur ro
gru.english: If it were not this way, and if there were nothing at all that constituted reality in a deceptive form, then it would be a contradiction for the reflection to be an instance of deceptive reality. And if that were the case, it would contradict the entire structure of things existing in name: everything about statements that things which existed by definition could never exist even nominally; the denial of things existing in truth; and the proof that nothing exists in truth.

gru.acip: DES NA PHYI NANG GI CHOS RNAMS GANG ZAG GSUM PO DE'I KUN RDZOB KYI NGOR BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR SGRUB PA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: des na phyi nang gi chos rnams gang zag gsum po de'i kun rdzob kyi ngor bden par ma grub par sgrub pa yin no
gru.english: Thus it is then that we establish that—to the perceptions of the deceptive state of mind of these three individuals—outer & inner phenomena cannot be determined to be real.

gru.acip: DE LTAR 'GREL PAS DE RNAMS KYI NGOR KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MIN PAR YE MA BSGRUBS PAR BDEN PA MIN ZHES BSGRUBS PA LA, KUN RDZOB BDEN PA MIN PAR BSGRUBS PAR 'DZIN PA NI, HA CANG YANG BLO'I 'JUG PA RTZINGS PAS SLOB DPON GYI DGONGS PA RANG GI BLO'I DRI MAS SBAGS NAS 'CHAD PA'I LUGS NGAN PA'O,,
gru.wylie: de ltar 'grel pas de rnams kyi ngor kun rdzob bden pa min par ye ma bsgrubs par bden pa min zhes bsgrubs pa la, kun rdzob bden pa min par bsgrubs par 'dzin pa ni, ha cang yang blo'i 'jug pa rtsings pas slob dpon gyi dgongs pa rang gi blo'i dri mas sbags nas 'chad pa'i lugs ngan pa'o
gru.english: Let's look then at the conclusion drawn in the autocommentary that these things are not real, in not being established in any way—to their perceptions—as not being deceptive reality. Taking this to be an assertion that what they see is not deceptive reality represents a total insensitivity to the actual meaning; it is a distasteful system of explanation where people have polluted the true intent of this master with the stench of their own way of thinking.

gru.acip: DE LTAR SGRUB PA YANG GANG ZAG DE GSUM LA MIN GYI, DE GSUM GYI NGOR BDEN PA MIN PA GANG ZAG GZHAN BDAG CAG RNAMS LTA BU LA SGRUB PA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar sgrub pa yang gang zag de gsum la min gyi, de gsum gyi ngor bden pa min pa gang zag gzhan bdag cag rnams lta bu la sgrub pa yin no
gru.english: How we establish things as we said is not that we refer to these three individuals themselves, but rather to something not being real to the perceptions of the three. It is determining the case for other persons—such as you & me.

gru.acip: GANG ZAG DE GSUM MIN PA'I 'OG MA RNAMS LA NI LHAN SKYES KYI BDEN 'DZIN YOD PAS, DE RNAMS KYI KUN RDZOB GANG YIN THAMS CAD KYI NGOR GANG YANG BDEN PAR MA GRUB PAR SGRUB MI NUS SO,,
gru.wylie: gang zag de gsum min pa'i 'og ma rnams la ni lhan skyes kyi bden 'dzin yod pas, de rnams kyi kun rdzob gang yin thams cad kyi ngor gang yang bden par ma grub par sgrub mi nus so
gru.english: People other than these three types—those at lower levels—still possess the inborn form of the tendency to believe that things are real. We would never be able to establish that the things that are deceptive for them lacked any true existence, to anyone's perceptions at all.

gru.acip: SNGAR BSHAD PA DE LTA MIN PAR DE DAG GI NGOR KUN RDZOB KYI BDEN PA MIN PA BSGRUB NA NI, SHIN TU MA 'BREL BA'I SGRUB BYED DU 'GYUR TE, BLO DE'I NGOR GZHI DE KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR 'GRUB PA LA GZHI DE BRDZUN PAR 'GRUB DGOS PAS DE LA BDEN ZHEN MED PA RGYU MTSAN DU 'GOD PA NI BZHAD GAD KYI GNAS SO,,
gru.wylie: sngar bshad pa de lta min par de dag gi ngor kun rdzob kyi bden pa min pa bsgrub na ni, shin tu ma 'brel ba'i sgrub byed du 'gyur te, blo de'i ngor gzhi de kun rdzob bden par 'grub pa la gzhi de brdzun par 'grub dgos pas de la bden zhen med pa rgyu mtshan du 'god pa ni bzhad gad kyi gnas so
gru.english: Suppose it were not the way we've explained it up to here: suppose to their perceptions things that were not deceptive reality could be established. The assertion then would lose any pertinence to anything at all. That is, in order to establish—to such a state of mind—that any particular object belonged to deceptive reality, we would have to prove that the object was lying to us. As such, positing—as our reason here—the idea that such individuals have no belief in reality deserves no more than our laughter.

gru.acip: BLO DE'I NGOR GZHI DE KUN RDZOB BDEN PAR 'GRUB PA LA GZHI DE BRDZUN PAR 'GRUB DGOS PA'I RGYU MTSAN NI, BUM SOGS LA KUN RDZOB BDEN PA ZHES PA'I TSIG ZUR GYI BDEN PA 'JOG PA NA BLO DANG DON GNYIS LAS, DON LA BDEN PAR MI 'JOG PAR, BDEN 'DZIN KUN RDZOB PA'I NGO BO NYID DU BDEN PAR GZHAG DGOS PAR MTHONG BA NA, KHYAD PAR DE MA SBYAR NA BDEN PAR MI 'GRUB CING BRDZUN PA YIN PAR MTHONG DGOS PA'I GNAD KYIS YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: blo de'i ngor gzhi de kun rdzob bden par 'grub pa la gzhi de brdzun par 'grub dgos pa'i rgyu mtshan ni, bum sogs la kun rdzob bden pa zhes pa'i tshig zur gyi bden pa 'jog pa na blo dang don gnyis las, don la bden par mi 'jog par, bden 'dzin kun rdzob pa'i ngo bo nyid du bden par gzhag dgos par mthong ba na, khyad par de ma sbyar na bden par mi 'grub cing brdzun pa yin par mthong dgos pa'i gnad kyis yin no
gru.english: Now what is the reason that—in order to establish that a certain object is, to this particular state of mind, deceptive reality—we would have to establish that the object was lying to us? Consider how we establish the word “reality,” in the expression “deceptive reality,” in the case of something like a water pitcher. Does it refer to the state of mind, or to the object of this mind? We are not in fact establishing the object as reality; rather, we need to establish reality here in the sense of establishing that the tendency to believe that things are real itself constitutes the essence of the deception. Once we see the need to do so, we can perceive that—without applying this distinction—the object does not exist in reality, and is lying to us. The need is the key here. A unique presentation on the negative emotions

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA NI, BDAG MED PA'I DE KHO NA NYID RIG PA'I MI MTHUN PHYOGS DANG, DE YANG RIG PA DE MED PA TZAM DANG, DE LAS GZHAN PA TZAM LA MI BYED KYI, 'GAL ZLA MI MTHUN PHYOGS GANG ZAG DANG CHOS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR SGRO 'DOGS PA'O,,
gru.wylie: de'i phyir nyon mongs can gyi ma rig pa ni, bdag med pa'i de kho na nyid rig pa'i mi mthun phyogs dang, de yang rig pa de med pa tsam dang, de las gzhan pa tsam la mi byed kyi, 'gal zla mi mthun phyogs gang zag dang chos rang bzhin gyis grub par sgro 'dogs pa'o
gru.english: As such, the form of misunderstanding which is involved with negative emotions represents the opposite of understanding where we grasp suchness, in the form of things not being themselves. This “misunderstanding” refers not to a simple lack of understanding, nor even something other than understanding—but constitutes a direct and contradictory opposite to understanding. Which is to say, this state of mind sees things where they are not: it believes that the person, and things, exist through some nature of their own.

gru.acip: DE LTAR BYAS NA CHOS KYI BDAG TU SGRO 'DOGS PA NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PAR 'JOG PA DANG, NGA DANG NGA YI BA RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PAR 'DZIN PA GNYIS 'JIG LTAR 'JOG PA RNAMS MNGON PA BA DANG MI MTHUN NO,,
gru.wylie: de ltar byas na chos kyi bdag tu sgro 'dogs pa nyon mongs can gyi ma rig par 'jog pa dang, nga dang nga yi ba rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub par 'dzin pa gnyis 'jig ltar 'jog pa rnams mngon pa ba dang mi mthun no
gru.english: As such, we can here establish “misunderstanding involved with negative emotions” as being the tendency to see a self-nature to entities which they don't in fact possess. And then we can establish, as being the view of destruction, the two tendencies to see “me” and “mine” as existing by definition. This way of doing it is not shared with the presentation of the Higher Knowledge schools.

gru.acip: GANG ZAG RANG RKYA THUB PA'I RDZAS YOD DU 'DZIN PA NI GRUB MTHAS BLO MA BSGYUR BA LA YANG YOD MOD KYANG, GANG ZAG PHUNG PO DANG MTSAN NYID MI MTHUN PA'I GZHAN DU YOD PAR 'DZIN PA NI GRUB MTHAS BLO MA BSGYUR BA LA MED DO,,
gru.wylie: gang zag rang rkya thub pa'i rdzas yod du 'dzin pa ni grub mthas blo ma bsgyur ba la yang yod mod kyang, gang zag phung po dang mtshan nyid mi mthun pa'i gzhan du yod par 'dzin pa ni grub mthas blo ma bsgyur ba la med do
gru.english: Now we would admit that the tendency to hold the person as being substantial, in the sense of being self-standing, can also be possessed by a person whose mind has not been influenced by the teachings of some particular school of thought. It is not the case though that someone whose mind has not been influenced in this way would ever hold that the person is other than the parts to the person, in the sense of being an entity with characteristics inconsistent with those of these parts.

gru.acip: GAL TE GANG ZAG DANG CHOS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA YOD PAR 'DOD PA'I PHYOGS LA, DE LTAR 'DZIN PA DE RNAMS NYON MONGS CAN GYI MA RIG PA DANG, BDAG 'DZIN GNYIS SU JI LTAR SGRUB CE NA,
gru.wylie: gal te gang zag dang chos rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa yod par 'dod pa'i phyogs la, de ltar 'dzin pa de rnams nyon mongs can gyi ma rig pa dang, bdag 'dzin gnyis su ji ltar sgrub ce na
gru.english: One may ask the following question: Let's look at systems of thought which accept the idea that there do exist a person, and things, which exist by definition. How do people who hold such views establish misunderstanding which is involved with negative emotions, and the two ways of holding that things are themselves?
