And this is because the state of mind which realizes the truth of a statement arises from a realization of the reason presented.

gru.acip: 'PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS NI ,GAL TE 'DI KUN MI STONG NA, ,'PHAGS PA'I BDEN PA BZHI PO RNAMS, ,KHYOD LA MED PAR THAL BAR 'GYUR, ZHES RANG LA BDEN BZHI MI 'THAD PA'I NYES PA MED PAR BSTAN LA,
gru.wylie: 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis ni ,gal te 'di kun mi stong na, ,'phags pa'i bden pa bzhi po rnams, ,khyod la med par thal bar 'gyur, zhes rang la bden bzhi mi 'thad pa'i nyes pa med par bstan la
gru.english: The Realized One, Nagarjuna, composed the following verse to show how he himself was free of this problem, of believing that the four truths were mistaken- If all of this Were not empty, Then for you The four higher truths Could not exist at all.

gru.acip: RANG GI GDAGS GZHI DANG, DE NYID DANG GZHAN GANG YANG MA GRUB PAS, MI BLUN PO LA BA LANG DU BTAGS PA NA RVA RING THUNG GI DPYAD PA MI 'JUG PA BZHIN DU, RGYU 'BRAS DE NYID DANG GZHAN GYI DPYAD PA MI 'JUG PA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: rang gi gdags gzhi dang, de nyid dang gzhan gang yang ma grub pas, mi blun po la ba lang du btags pa na rva ring thung gi dpyad pa mi 'jug pa bzhin du, rgyu 'bras de nyid dang gzhan gyi dpyad pa mi 'jug pa yin no
gru.english: The thing that we are giving the name "snake" here is actually no more that than anything else; once somebody has referred to an animal as a "cow," fools wouldn't think of measuring its horns to see how short or long they might be. Neither would they think to examine whether cause & effect were just that, or something else too.

gru.acip: YANG DE TZAM LA 'KHRUL NAS DPYAD PA BYAS PA NA KUN RDZOB MED PAR 'GYUR SNYAM DU MI BSAM STE, RIGS NGOR MA GRUB PA YIN GYI, KUN RDZOB KYI THUN MONG MIN PA'I GO BA NI SPROS PA MTHA' DAG BKAG RJES SU RNYED PA'I PHYIR TE, RTEN 'BYUNG SGYU MAR GO BA NI, BDEN PA'I SPROS PA KHEGS PA LA BLTOS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: yang de tsam la 'khrul nas dpyad pa byas pa na kun rdzob med par 'gyur snyam du mi bsam ste, rigs ngor ma grub pa yin gyi, kun rdzob kyi thun mong min pa'i go ba ni spros pa mtha' dag bkag rjes su rnyed pa'i phyir te, rten 'byung sgyu mar go ba ni, bden pa'i spros pa khegs pa la bltos pa'i phyir
gru.english: We can also say that-if we make an error just on this much but then continue our examination-we could avoid thinking that there was no such thing as deceptive reality. That is, we could say that a deceptive object fails to stand up in the face of proper reasoning; but the fact is that, once we have managed to block all elaborations of things existing in & of themselves, we gain a truly unique understanding of this deceptive reality. And that's because really understanding how dependence resembles an illusion relies upon the ability to block all these elaborations of things existing in reality.

gru.acip: YOD PA SGRUB MI DGOS, MED PA SGRUB MI NUS ZHES PA'I TSIG RIGS LA BRTEN NAS, TSAD MA'I DGAG SGRUB SPANG BAR MI BYA STE,
gru.wylie: yod pa sgrub mi dgos, med pa sgrub mi nus zhes pa'i tshig rigs la brten nas, tshad ma'i dgag sgrub spang bar mi bya ste
gru.english: I advise you not to rely upon statements like "If it were really there, you wouldn't have to prove it; if it weren't really there, it's not something that you could prove." That is, I advise you not to abandon the process of disproving or proving ideas by using the process of accurate perception.

gru.acip: DE NI DGAG SGRUB DON LA YOD PA 'GOG PA YIN GYI, TSAD MA'I DGAG SGRUB 'GAG PA MA YIN TE, DE LTA NA RIGS PA'I BSTAN BCOS BRTZAMS PAS CI BYA,
gru.wylie: de ni dgag sgrub don la yod pa 'gog pa yin gyi, tshad ma'i dgag sgrub 'gag pa ma yin te, de lta na rigs pa'i bstan bcos brtsams pas ci bya
gru.english: If you approach disproving or proving things the way they describe it there, you're going to end up denying something which is, in fact, actually here. It is not that what we're denying is the process itself of using accurate perception to establish that something either doesn't or does exist; if that were the case, then why would so many masters have expended such effort to compose the great classics on logical thinking?

gru.acip: DES KYANG YE MED PA DES MED DU RTOGS PA TSAD MA'I DGAG SGRUB KYI DON DU MA GO BAR ZAD DE, BDEN ZHEN 'GOG PA LA DE'I ZHEN YUL YE MED DU RTOGS DGOS PAS SO,,
gru.wylie: des kyang ye med pa des med du rtogs pa tshad ma'i dgag sgrub kyi don du ma go bar zad de, bden zhen 'gog pa la de'i zhen yul ye med du rtogs dgos pas so
gru.english: People like this have simply failed to understand that something which was never there in the first place is exactly what we either deny or establish when we talk about using accurate perception to come to an understanding that something doesn't exist. That is, when we undertake to stop our tendency to grasp to things as real, we have to do so by coming to the realization that what this tendency thinks is there was never there in the first place.

gru.acip: CI'I PHYIR CE NA, RGYU'I SNGAR YOD NA RGYU LA MI LTOS LA, SKYE BA'I SNGAR MED NA SKYES PA'I DUS NA YANG GZUGS BRNYAN BZHIN DU BCOS MAR 'GYUR GYI, RANG GI MTSAN NYID DU GRUB PAR GA LA 'GYUR,
gru.wylie: ci'i phyir ce na, rgyu'i sngar yod na rgyu la mi ltos la, skye ba'i sngar med na skyes pa'i dus na yang gzugs brnyan bzhin du bcos mar 'gyur gyi, rang gi mtshan nyid du grub par ga la 'gyur
gru.english: And why is that? If something were present even before its cause, then it wouldn't be dependent upon that cause. And if it didn't exist at all before it started, then at the point when it did start, it would have to be an artificial construction-similar to the reflection of an image in a mirror. And then how on earth could we say that it somehow existed through some nature of its own?

gru.acip: SKYE BA DANG 'JIG PA RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB NAS GSUNGS PA MA YIN GYI, 'JIG RTEN DAM PA MA YIN PA'I LAM DU 'GRO BA 'DI DE KHO NA NYID LA SBYOR BAR 'DOD PAS
gru.wylie: skye ba dang 'jig pa rang gi ngo bos grub nas gsungs pa ma yin gyi, 'jig rten dam pa ma yin pa'i lam du 'gro ba 'di de kho na nyid la sbyor bar 'dod pas
gru.english: Lord Buddha was not though saying here that starting & ending existed through any essential nature of their own. Rather, he was simply hoping to take those of the world who were travelling on a path which was not the highest one, and lead them to the concept of suchness.

gru.acip: DE DAG NI RTAG CHAD KYI LTA BAR GYUR PA NYID SRID PA'I RGYA MTSO YIN PAS NA LTA BAR GYUR PA'I SRID PA'I RGYA MTSO LAS STONG NYID RTOGS PA'I GRUS NGES PAR BRGAL BAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: de dag ni rtag chad kyi lta bar gyur pa nyid srid pa'i rgya mtsho yin pas na lta bar gyur pa'i srid pa'i rgya mtsho las stong nyid rtogs pa'i grus nges par brgal bar 'gyur ro
gru.english: People like this then have used the ship of realizing emptiness in order to cross over-completely, and with certainty-the ocean of this suffering life: an ocean which consists of how we view things. And that's because the ocean of pain actually consists of viewing things as either being unchanging, or stopping altogether. Clinging prevents realizations

gru.acip: GRUB PA RANG BZHIN MED PAR BSTAN PA'I PHYIR THOG MAR RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DANG DBUS SU GNAS PA DANG, MTHA' MAR 'JIG PA RNAMS SPANGS SHING DE DANG BRAL LO ZHES PA'I DON TO,,
gru.wylie: grub pa rang bzhin med par bstan pa'i phyir thog mar rang bzhin gyis skye ba dang dbus su gnas pa dang, mtha' mar 'jig pa rnams spangs shing de dang bral lo zhes pa'i don to
gru.english: The fact that things' having come into existence has no nature of its own is expressed in the following words of the root text: they have "left behind"-meaning they are devoid of-any starting (through any nature of their own); any such staying, in the middle of the process; and any ending, at the finish.

gru.acip: DE KHO NA NYID KYI RTOGS PA TSOL BA'I SLOB MA LA BLA MA 'GRO BA'I DON BSGRUB PA LA MKHAS SHING PHAN PAR 'DOD PAS THOG MA KHO NAR NI PHUNG PO DANG KHAMS DANG SKYE MCHED THAMS CAD YOD DO ZHES BRJOD PAR BYA'O,,
gru.wylie: de kho na nyid kyi rtogs pa tshol ba'i slob ma la bla ma 'gro ba'i don bsgrub pa la mkhas shing phan par 'dod pas thog ma kho nar ni phung po dang khams dang skye mched thams cad yod do zhes brjod par bya'o
gru.english: And so what we have here are sages who are masters at accomplishing the goals of living beings: teachers for those students who seek to reach a realization of suchness. Out of nothing less than a desire to help these students, such teachers will (though only at the beginning) make statements about how all these things-the parts to a person; the categories of existence; and the doors of sense-do in fact exist.

gru.acip: YOD PA YANG RING PO LA BRTEN NAS THUNG NGUR 'DOGS PA BZHIN DU GZUGS SOGS LA BRTEN NAS PHUNG POR 'DOGS PA DANG, MAR ME LAS 'OD 'BYUNG BA BZHIN DU RGYU LA BLTOS NAS 'BRAS BU RNAM PAR BZHAG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS MA GRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: yod pa yang ring po la brten nas thung ngur 'dogs pa bzhin du gzugs sogs la brten nas phung por 'dogs pa dang, mar me las 'od 'byung ba bzhin du rgyu la bltos nas 'bras bu rnam par bzhag gi ngo bo nyid kyis ma grub pa'o
gru.english: The way in which entities are established is that we call something "parts to a person" based on the presence of the physical form that makes up the first part; this is the same as when we call something "short" in comparison to something which is "long." Or sometimes we establish something which is a result based upon its cause, as when we talk about "the light that is coming from a lamp." These things do not though have any existence in & of themselves.

gru.acip: 'BRAS BU RE RE LA YANG RKYEN DU MA CAN YIN PA'I PHYIR DANG, RKYEN RE RE LA YANG MTHA' MED PA SKYE BA NA 'BAD PA DU MAS SGRUB DGOS SHING 'JIG PA NA 'BAD PA MED PAR RANG GI NGANG GIS 'JIG PAR
gru.wylie: 'bras bu re re la yang rkyen du ma can yin pa'i phyir dang, rkyen re re la yang mtha' med pa skye ba na 'bad pa du mas sgrub dgos shing 'jig pa na 'bad pa med par rang gi ngang gis 'jig par
gru.english: All the separate results there are in the universe have multiple factors that make them occur. And each one of these factors can bear limitless results; we just have to make it happen, by putting forth many efforts. But when these things come to an end, they tend to end all of their own accord-we need not put forth any effort for that to occur.

gru.acip: SHES PAS YUL RIG PA GRUB PA RIG PA TZAM GRUB ZIN PAS RIG PA GRUB PAR BYA BA'I PHYIR TU RANG GI {%GIS?} RIG GAM GZHAN GYIS RIG DPYOD PAR MI RIGS TE, DE LTAR NA SHES PA BEM POR 'GYUR TE, SGRON MES BUM PA GSAL DGOS PA BZHIN,
gru.wylie: shes pas yul rig pa grub pa rig pa tsam grub zin pas rig pa grub par bya ba'i phyir tu rang gi rig gam gzhan gyis rig dpyod par mi rigs te, de ltar na shes pa bem por 'gyur te, sgron mes bum pa gsal dgos pa bzhin
gru.english: When we know an object with our awareness, then this knowing itself is already established! It's not necessary that we go from further from there, and in order to establish that there was a knowing, examine the question of whether the knowing is done through a process of the mind being known by itself or through a process of the mind being known by something other than itself. In such a case then awareness itself would become a physical thing-something that had to be illuminated, in the way that a lamp illuminates a water pitcher. Scriptural support for saying there was something else in mind

gru.acip: 'JIG RTEN NYE BAR LEN PA'I PHUNG PO LNGA GANG LA MA RIG PA RKYEN DU YOD PAS MA RIG PA'I RKYEN CAN DU GRUB BO,,
gru.wylie: 'jig rten nye bar len pa'i phung po lnga gang la ma rig pa rkyen du yod pas ma rig pa'i rkyen can du grub bo
gru.english: Any time the world-referring to the five parts to the person that we have taken on at our birth-has misunderstanding as a contributing factor, then we can say that it is rooted in misunderstanding.

gru.acip: RANG GI RTZA BA'I GRUB MTHA'I LAM DE NYID LA MI 'GAL BAS GNAS PA STE DE LA NGO MTSAR CUNG ZAD KYANG MED DE,
gru.wylie: rang gi rtsa ba'i grub mtha'i lam de nyid la mi 'gal bas gnas pa ste de la ngo mtshar cung zad kyang med de
gru.english: In a way then they are simply remaining on their very own path-in the fundamentals of their own school of thought-since this idea in no way contradicts that path. And so there's not the slightest thing amazing about it: about their accepting this concept.

gru.acip: GRANGS CAN SOGS GANG DAG GIS RGYU RKYEN LA MA BRTEN PAR BDAG GAM RTAG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DANG 'JIG RTEN PHUNG PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR MNGON PAR ZHEN PA DE DAG LA NI
gru.wylie: grangs can sogs gang dag gis rgyu rkyen la ma brten par bdag gam rtag pa rang bzhin gyis grub pa dang 'jig rten phung po rang bzhin gyis grub par mngon par zhen pa de dag la ni
gru.english: Let's consider first the Numerists, and other such groups: those who refuse to rely upon ideas of causes & conditions, and who instead have a strong attraction to the idea that the self-or an unchanging thing-could exist through some nature of its own; or that the world (here a reference to the parts to a person) could exist through the same sort of nature.

gru.acip: YANG NA RANG SDE GANG DAG PHUNG PO LNGA GZUGS BRNYAN LTAR RANG BZHIN MED PA LA BDAG TU MING 'DOGS KYI, SEMS KYI RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA LA BDAG TU 'JOG PA DE DAG LTA BA'I CHU BOS KHYER TE,
gru.wylie: yang na rang sde gang dag phung po lnga gzugs brnyan ltar rang bzhin med pa la bdag tu ming 'dogs kyi, sems kyi rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa la bdag tu 'jog pa de dag lta ba'i chu bos khyer te
gru.english: Or we could put it this way, as referring to how some members of our own group have chosen to refer to the five parts of a person-which, after all, are similar to a reflection in a mirror in that they have no nature of their own-as being the "self." Or else those who assert that the mind (which they see as something that exists through some nature of its own) is the "self." All of these people have been swept away on the mighty current of wrong views.

gru.acip: SEMS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DE 'GYUR NA CHAD PAR 'GYUR MI 'GYUR NA RTAG PAR 'GYUR ZHES SBYAR TE, SNGA MA MDZES SAM BLA MA GSUNGS,
gru.wylie: sems rang bzhin gyis grub pa de 'gyur na chad par 'gyur mi 'gyur na rtag par 'gyur zhes sbyar te, snga ma mdzes sam bla ma gsungs
gru.english: At this point you could also say it as someone has fallen into the extreme of holding that nothing exists at all, when they say that the mind exists through some nature of its own and can change. And then when you say that the mind exists and cannot change, you have fallen into the extreme of holding that nothing can ever change. My own Lama once said though that he thought expressing this idea as we did above might be more elegant. Our own stolen away

gru.acip: GANG DAG BRTEN NAS DNGOS PO RNAMS, DE NYID DU NI GRUB 'DOD PA, DE DAG LA YANG RTAG SOGS SKYON, DE DAG JI LTAR 'BYUNG MI 'GYUR,
gru.wylie: gang dag brten nas dngos po rnams, de nyid du ni grub 'dod pa, de dag la yang rtag sogs skyon, de dag ji ltar 'byung mi 'gyur
gru.english: The problems that come up With these others- Things unchanging, or the like- Don't occur with those Who hold things as dependent, As being inside suchness.

gru.acip: GANG DAG DNGOS PO RNAMS BRTEN NAS 'BYUNG BAR KHAS LEN BZHIN DU YANG DE KHO NA NYID DU GRUB PAR 'DOD PA DE DAG LA YANG RTAG PAR LTA BA LA SOGS KYIS {%KYI} SKYON DE DAG JI LTAR 'BYUNG BAR MI 'GYUR TE,
gru.wylie: gang dag dngos po rnams brten nas 'byung bar khas len bzhin du yang de kho na nyid du grub par 'dod pa de dag la yang rtag par lta ba la sogs kyis skyon de dag ji ltar 'byung bar mi 'gyur te
gru.english: The problems that come up with these others-seeing things as unchanging, or the like-don't occur with those who, even as they accept the idea that things have come about through a process of dependence, at the same time hold that these entities still happen inside suchness.

gru.acip: RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA'I DNGOS PO KHAS BLANGS BAR 'GYUR NA CHAD PA DANG, MI 'GYUR NA RTAG PAR LTA BAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i dngos po khas blangs bar 'gyur na chad pa dang, mi 'gyur na rtag par lta bar 'gyur ro
gru.english: If you accept that things exist through some nature of their own, you're a nihilist; while if you don't, you're of the viewpoint that things are unchanging. The opposite, with emptiness

gru.acip: ,DBU MA PA GANG DAG BRTEN NAS BYUNG BA'I DNGOS PO RNAMS CHU YI NANG GI ZLA BA'I GZUGS BRNYAN LTA BUR NI YANG DAG PA BDEN PAR GRUB PA YANG MA YIN LA, LOG PA GTAN MED KYANG MA YIN PAR SNANG LA
gru.wylie: dbu ma pa gang dag brten nas byung ba'i dngos po rnams chu yi nang gi zla ba'i gzugs brnyan lta bur ni yang dag pa bden par grub pa yang ma yin la, log pa gtan med kyang ma yin par snang la
gru.english: These of the Middle Way though understand those entities which occur through a process of dependence, and so resemble a reflection of the moon in a body of water. That is, these things do not appear to them to exist purely, or in truth; but at the same time neither do they see them as having stopped: as things that do not exist at all.

gru.acip: DBU MA SPROS BRAL RTOGS PA'I YON TAN GYIS CHE BA'I BDAG NYID CAN DE DAG RNAMS LA RANG PHYOGS YOD NA DE SGRUB PA'I PHYIR GZHAN RNAMS DANG LHAN CIG RTZOD PAR 'GYUR NA
gru.wylie: dbu ma spros bral rtogs pa'i yon tan gyis che ba'i bdag nyid can de dag rnams la rang phyogs yod na de sgrub pa'i phyir gzhan rnams dang lhan cig rtsod par 'gyur na
gru.english: Now let's consider what happens when those who are great beings (by virtue of their having realized the Middle Way, free of all elaborations of self-existence) take on their part a valid position, and to prove it to others engage in philosophical dispute with those who hold opposing views.

gru.acip: PHYOGS RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA ZHIG YOD NA RANG PHYOGS SAM GZHAN PHYOGS ZHIG TU 'GYUR NA,
gru.wylie: phyogs rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa zhig yod na rang phyogs sam gzhan phyogs zhig tu 'gyur na
gru.english: Suppose then that there were a position that anyone took, which existed in & of itself. Necessarily, it would have to be either the position of our group, or the position of the other group.

gru.acip: DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN MED PAR RTOGS PAS GNAS MED PAR MTHONG BA'I BDAG NYID CHEN PO 'PHAGS PA RNAMS NI SDUG PA LAS CHAGS PA MED CING MI SDUG PAR GZUNG BAS CHAGS PA DANG BRAL TE, GTI MUG GIS GNAS PA YANG MIN TE, GNAS PA'I RGYU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dngos po rang bzhin med par rtogs pas gnas med par mthong ba'i bdag nyid chen po 'phags pa rnams ni sdug pa las chags pa med cing mi sdug par gzung bas chags pa dang bral te, gti mug gis gnas pa yang min te, gnas pa'i rgyu ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: And think then of those great beings, those realized beings, who have realized that things have no nature of their own; who have seen what cannot be real. They no longer have attachment to what is attractive: they hold things as unattractive, and thus are freed of that attraction. Neither is it the case that they live there in dark ignorance, for the causes that would make them remain here are gone. A final word

gru.acip: , RIGS PA'I DBANG PHYUG 'PHAGS CHEN KLU SGRUB KYIS, ,RTEN BYUNG MTHA' BRAL STON GZHUNG RGYA MTSO LAS, ,RIGS PA'I RJES 'BRANG BLO GROS BSRUBS SHING GIS, ,RO BRGYA LDAN PA'I MAR GYI NYID {%NYING} KHU BLANGS,
gru.wylie: rigs pa'i dbang phyug 'phags chen klu sgrub kyis, ,rten byung mtha' bral ston gzhung rgya mtsho las, ,rigs pa'i rjes 'brang blo gros bsrubs shing gis, ,ro brgya ldan pa'i mar gyi nyid khu blangs
gru.english: The God of Reasoning, That mighty realized being, Nagarjuna, Went to the ocean Of the great books that teach Dependence, Free of all extremes. He took up The stirring stick Of that wisdom Which follows reasoning, And drew from the sea The very essence, A butter possessed Of a thousand flavors.

gru.acip: ,DNGOS ZHEN SRID PA'I MTSO CHEN LAS 'ONGS PA, ,RTAG CHAD MTHAR LTA'I CHU BO LEGS BRGAL NAS, ,YANG DAG LTA BA'I THANG LA 'BYIN 'DOD NA, ,GZHUNG LUGS GRU CHEN 'DI NANG 'JUG PAR BYOS,
gru.wylie: dngos zhen srid pa'i mtsho chen las 'ongs pa, ,rtag chad mthar lta'i chu bo legs brgal nas, ,yang dag lta ba'i thang la 'byin 'dod na, ,gzhung lugs gru chen 'di nang 'jug par byos
gru.english: If you hope to step forth Out of that massive sea Of suffering life, where you Still believe that things exist; If you hope to cross Safely over that treacherous Body of water where you Still hold to the extremes- That either things can never change, Or else cannot exist at all; If you ever hope To extract yourself, And walk upon that dry land Of the purest view of things, Then come, I beg you, and board The mighty ship Of this scriptural tradition.

whole_word_matches.context: yang dag lta ba'i thang la 'byin 'dod na, ,gzhung lugs gru chen 'di nang 'jug par byos

gru.acip: ,BDAG NYID CHEN PO 'PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS MDZAD PA'I DBU MA RIGS PA DRUG CU PA'I t'IKKA MU COR SMRA BA RNAM PAR 'THAG PA ZHES BYA BA 'DI NI
gru.wylie: bdag nyid chen po 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis mdzad pa'i dbu ma rigs pa drug cu pa'i TIkka mu cor smra ba rnam par 'thag pa zhes bya ba 'di ni
gru.english: And so there it is: Crushing the Words of the Impudent, a commentary upon the Sixty Verses of that great being, Nagarjuna-The Arya.

gru.acip: ,PHAN BDE'I 'BYUNG GNAS RGYAL BSTAN YONGS 'DU'I LJON, ,RAB RGYAS 'GRO KUN THAR MCHOG 'BRAS BZANG LA, ,SPYOD PHYIR BKRA SHIS LHUN GRUB CHOS GRVA CHER, ,CHOS SBYIN 'DZAD MED DAL 'GRO'I RGYUN 'DI SPEL,,
gru.wylie: phan bde'i 'byung gnas rgyal bstan yongs 'du'i ljon, ,rab rgyas 'gro kun thar mchog 'bras bzang la, ,spyod phyir bkra shis lhun grub chos grva cher, ,chos sbyin 'dzad med dal 'gro'i rgyun 'di spel
gru.english: This book has been printed At the great monastery Of Tashi Hlunpo, So that the orchard garden- The teachings of the Victors, Source of all help & happiness- Might flourish, and every being Come to take their fill Of the finest fruits that grow there: That highest liberation; We pray That the river flow Of this gift of the Dharma Might forever swell, Unending.

gru.acip: MGON PO KLU SGRUB CHOS CAN, BSTAN BCOS RTZOM PA'I THOG MAR STON PA LA BSTOD PHYAG MDZAD PA LA RGYU MTSAN YOD DE, THUB PA SANGS RGYAS BCOM LDAN 'DAS DES RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA DANG 'GAG PA SPONG BA'I RTEN CING 'BREL 'BYUNG RANG DBANG DU GSUNGS PA'I RGYU MTSAN GYIS DE LA BSTOD PA YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: mgon po klu sgrub chos can, bstan bcos rtsom pa'i thog mar ston pa la bstod phyag mdzad pa la rgyu mtshan yod de, thub pa sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das des rang bzhin gyis skye ba dang 'gag pa spong ba'i rten cing 'brel 'byung rang dbang du gsungs pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis de la bstod pa yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider the protector, Nagarjuna. There is a specific reason why he sings the praises of, and bows down to, the Teacher-here as he first begins the composition of this classical commentary; Because he wishes to sing his praises to the Able One, the Buddha, for the reason that this Conqueror has described, independently, that principle of dependent relationship which serves to overthrow the idea that the starting & stopping of things could occur through some nature of their own.

gru.acip: MGON PO KLU SGRUB CHOS CAN, SKABS 'DIR NYAN THOS SDE PA'I NGOR YON TAN 'GRIB CING, NYES PA KUN GYI 'BYUNG GNAS MED LTA 'GOG PA'I RIGS PA RGYAS PAR MI STON PA'I RGYU MTSAN YOD DE, NYAN THOS KYI SDE SNOD RANG LAS MED LTA 'GOG PA'I RIGS PA RGYAS PAR GSUNGS SHING, DE LA BRTEN NAS NYAN THOS DE DAG GIS KYANG MED LTA BKAG PA'I RGYU MTSAN GYIS 'DIR MA BSHAD PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: mgon po klu sgrub chos can, skabs 'dir nyan thos sde pa'i ngor yon tan 'grib cing, nyes pa kun gyi 'byung gnas med lta 'gog pa'i rigs pa rgyas par mi ston pa'i rgyu mtshan yod de, nyan thos kyi sde snod rang las med lta 'gog pa'i rigs pa rgyas par gsungs shing, de la brten nas nyan thos de dag gis kyang med lta bkag pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis 'dir ma bshad pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider then our protector, Nagarjuna. There is a reason why, at this point in the text, he does not present-to those who belong to the listener group-any detailed presentation of the reasoning needed to deny that view that nothing could exist (a view which blocks the development of all good qualities, and serves as a source for every fault); Because this reason is that the logic for denying the view that nothing could exist is something which has already been described, at length, in the body of scriptures belonging to these listeners themselves; and because of that, these listeners already deny the view that nothing could exist. Advice to listen about how things are not as they seem

gru.acip: DNGOS SMRA BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD KYI LUGS LA BYIS PA SO SO SKYE BO THAMS CAD PHUNG PO'I DNGOS PO PHYIS LEN PA MED PA'I MYANG 'DAS THOB ZIN PA'I BDAG NYID DU RGYU MTSAN CIS MI 'DOD NAS 'DOD RIGS PAR THAL, KHYOD KYI LUGS LA BYIS PA RNAMS KYI DNGOS PO BDEN PAR BTAGS PA BZHIN DU DE DNGOS PO'I DE KHO NA NYID DU GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dngos smra ba chos can, khyod kyi lugs la byis pa so so skye bo thams cad phung po'i dngos po phyis len pa med pa'i myang 'das thob zin pa'i bdag nyid du rgyu mtshan cis mi 'dod nas 'dod rigs par thal, khyod kyi lugs la byis pa rnams kyi dngos po bden par btags pa bzhin du de dngos po'i de kho na nyid du grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider those who assert that things which perform a function have some existence of their own. Why-for what reason-wouldn't they agree, in their system, that each & every infant (every ordinary person, who had not seen emptiness directly) was a special being who had already attained nirvana; a state where, after that, they would no longer have to take on those entities which are parts of a person? Because it would certainly make sense for them to do so! Because, according to their system, these same infants would be functioning things that we could label as being real; which means that they would have to be examples of the very suchness of functioning things. Pain will come so long as we hold the extremes

gru.acip: DE KHO NA NYID GZIGS PA'I MNYAM GZHAG LA LTOS TE 'KHOR 'DAS SPANG BLANG DU BSTAN PA MIN PAR THAL, BLO DE'I NGOR DE GNYIS SPANG BLANG THA DAD DU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: de kho na nyid gzigs pa'i mnyam gzhag la ltos te 'khor 'das spang blang du bstan pa min par thal, blo de'i ngor de gnyis spang blang tha dad du ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: But it is not the case that what we are indicating here is that the cycle of suffering, and nirvana, are-respectively-something that we seek to give up, and something that we seek to take up, all relative to that deep meditation in which we see suchness. And that's because these two cannot exist, to the perceptions of that state of mind, as things to give up or take up which are distinct from each other.

gru.acip: DER THAL, SRID PA DANG MYANG 'DAS RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, srid pa dang myang 'das rang bzhin gyis ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: And that certainly is the case, because neither this suffering life nor nirvana is a thing which exists through any nature of its own. Getting used to wisdom

gru.acip: GNYIS PA LA 'GAG PA RDZAS GRUB DGAG ,SGYU MA LTA BU'I 'GOG PA SGRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa la 'gag pa rdzas grub dgag ,sgyu ma lta bu'i 'gog pa sgrub pa'o
gru.english: This brings us to our second point in this discussion on nirvana, which is showing how our own position on the question is correct. Here we proceed in two steps of (1) denying that there could be such a thing as a cessation which existed in a substantial way; and (2) proving the idea of a cessation that is similar to a magical illusion.

gru.acip: 'KHOR BA CHOS CAN, KHYOD LA SNGON DANG PHYI MA'I MTHA' RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, RTEN 'BREL YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'khor ba chos can, khyod la sngon dang phyi ma'i mtha' rang bzhin gyis ma grub par thal, rten 'brel yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider then the cycle of pain. Its first earlier parts and its later parts cannot exist through any nature of their own, Because it exists in dependence.

gru.acip: KHYAB PAR THAL, SNGON SKYES RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB NA, SLAR DE LDOG TU MI RUNG BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: khyab par thal, sngon skyes rang bzhin gyis grub na, slar de ldog tu mi rung ba'i phyir
gru.english: And our reason here does indeed establish our assertion, Because if the parts that started earlier existed through some nature of their own, then it would not make sense to say that-at some later point-they had stopped.

gru.acip: NYAN THOS SDE BA DE DAG CHOS CAN, RTEN CING 'BREL PAR 'BYUNG BA YAN LAG BCU GNYIS KYI 'KHOR LO SNGON GYI MTHA' DANG PHYI MA'I MTHA' RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA'I 'KHOR TSUL JI LTA BA BZHIN MI SHES PAR THAL, 'DUS BYAS THAMS CAD RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS SKYE 'JIG BYED PAR RTOGS {%RTOG} PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: nyan thos sde ba de dag chos can, rten cing 'brel par 'byung ba yan lag bcu gnyis kyi 'khor lo sngon gyi mtha' dang phyi ma'i mtha' rang bzhin gyis ma grub pa'i 'khor tshul ji lta ba bzhin mi shes par thal, 'dus byas thams cad rang gi mtshan nyid kyis skye 'jig byed par rtogs pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider those who belong to the listener group. They certainly do not understand, correctly, the wheel of life, with its twelve different links describing how things occur in a dependent relationship; that is, they certainly do not understand how the earlier parts and the later parts of this wheel spin in a circle, with no nature of their own. And that's because they still imagine that each & every produced entity there is goes about starting & stopping through some quality of its own. A denial of starting

gru.acip: 'DUS BYAS RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PAR BSTAN PA DANG, DE GZHAN LA JI LTAR 'CHAD PA'I TSUL, DE RGYAL BA'I DGONGS PAR BSGRUB PA, ZHAR LA LTOS PA'I DBYE BA BSTAN PA'O,,
gru.wylie: 'dus byas rang bzhin gyis med par bstan pa dang, de gzhan la ji ltar 'chad pa'i tshul, de rgyal ba'i dgongs par bsgrub pa, zhar la ltos pa'i dbye ba bstan pa'o
gru.english: We'll cover this point in four steps. (1) First we'll demonstrate how it is that produced things cannot exist through any nature of their own; (2) then describe how we explain this point with other things; (3) next prove how this is actually the true intent of the Victors; and (4) finally present, as an incidental point, the different divisions of the concept of reliance.

gru.acip: DANG PO LA SKYE 'JIG RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DGAG ,SKYE 'JIG GSUNGS PA'I DGOS PA, DON DE NYID NGES PAR BYA BA'O,,
gru.wylie: dang po la skye 'jig rang bzhin gyis grub pa dgag ,skye 'jig gsungs pa'i dgos pa, don de nyid nges par bya ba'o
gru.english: We'll treat the first of those three steps in three parts of its own: (1) denying that starting & stopping could occur through any nature of their own; (2) explaining the purpose why statements were made about starting & stopping; and (3) confirming certain points about this subject.

gru.acip: 'DOD NA, RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE BA MED PAR THAL, RANG GI NGO BO DANG GZHAN GYI NGO BO'I RANG BZHIN DU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'dod na, rang bzhin gyis skye ba med par thal, rang gi ngo bo dang gzhan gyi ngo bo'i rang bzhin du ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: Suppose you agree to that idea. Can't we say, then, that there is no such thing as something arising through any nature of its own? Because isn't it true that they exist neither as something with an essence of its own, nor as something with some other kind of essence? A denial of stopping

gru.acip: 'DU BYED SOGS KYI ZHIG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, 'DU BYED SOGS KYI ZHIG PA DE 'DU BYED SOGS KYI RGYU ZAD PA LAS,{%no ,} 'BYUNG BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'du byed sogs kyi zhig pa rang bzhin gyis ma grub par thal, 'du byed sogs kyi zhig pa de 'du byed sogs kyi rgyu zad pa las, 'byung ba'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider the ending of fresh karma, and the rest. It must not be something which occurs through any nature of its own, Because that ending of things like fresh karma is something that comes about through the wearing out of its causes.

gru.acip: 'DU BYED SOGS KYI ZHIG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, RANG GI NGO BO DE GZHAN GYI NGO BO'I RANG BZHIN DU MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'du byed sogs kyi zhig pa rang bzhin gyis ma grub par thal, rang gi ngo bo de gzhan gyi ngo bo'i rang bzhin du ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: And it must so be the case that the ending of things like fresh karma cannot be something which comes about through any nature of its own, Because its own essence cannot exist as the nature of the essence of something else. A summary on starting & stopping

gru.acip: SKYE 'GAG GNYIS KA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PAR THAL, DE GNYIS KA RGYU LA BRTEN NAS BYUNG BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: skye 'gag gnyis ka rang bzhin gyis ma grub par thal, de gnyis ka rgyu la brten nas byung ba'i phyir
gru.english: And so let's consider starting & stopping. The fact is that neither one of them can exist through any nature of its own; Because both of them come about through dependence on their causes. Why did The Buddha even mention starting & stopping?

gru.acip: DNGOS PO RANG GI NGO BOS GRUB PA'I BDAG NYID CAN DU ZHEN PA'I SO SO SKYE BO RNAMS CHOS CAN, RANG GI SEMS KYIS BSLUS NAS 'KHOR BAR 'GYUR TE, CHAGS SOGS NYON MONGS PA'I,{% no ,} GZHAN DBANG DU GYUR PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dngos po rang gi ngo bos grub pa'i bdag nyid can du zhen pa'i so so skye bo rnams chos can, rang gi sems kyis bslus nas 'khor bar 'gyur te, chags sogs nyon mongs pa'i, gzhan dbang du gyur pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider those individual, ordinary people who are so strongly attached to the idea that entities possess a nature which occurs of its own accord. They are deceived by their own mind, and so continue to circle inside the cycle of pain; Because they have fallen under the power of attachment and everything else involved with the negative emotions.

gru.acip: GSUM PA LA, MDZAD PA MTHAR PHYIN PA'I 'PHAGS PA RNAMS KYIS GZIGS TSUL, MGON PO KLU SGRUB NYID KYIS GZIGS PA'I TSUL,
gru.wylie: gsum pa la, mdzad pa mthar phyin pa'i 'phags pa rnams kyis gzigs tshul, mgon po klu sgrub nyid kyis gzigs pa'i tshul
gru.english: Which then takes us to our third step from above; about the way in which realized beings see these things in specific stages. We'll cover this in two sections: (1) the way in which realized beings-those who have come to the final completion of all the deeds they had to do-see things; and then (2) how our protector, Nagarjuna, sees things himself.

gru.acip: RKANG PA THA MA GNYIS LA, MGON PO KLU SGRUB CHOS CAN, 'DU BYED RANG BZHIN MTHA' DAG GIS DBEN PAR MNGON SUM DU MTHONG STE, RMONGS PA'I GRONG KHYER MI ZAD PA'I 'GRO BA MTHA' DAG SGYU MA DANG 'DRA BAR MNGON SUM DU GZIGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rkang pa tha ma gnyis la, mgon po klu sgrub chos can, 'du byed rang bzhin mtha' dag gis dben par mngon sum du mthong ste, rmongs pa'i grong khyer mi zad pa'i 'gro ba mtha' dag sgyu ma dang 'dra bar mngon sum du gzigs pa'i phyir
gru.english: And then finally, let's take the final two lines here- Let's consider our protector, Nagarjuna. He has seen, directly, that fresh karma is devoid of every kind of a self-nature; Because he has seen, directly, how the City of the Ignorant-filled with an endless number of suffering beings-is like a magical illusion. Scriptural support for the stages of sight

gru.acip: DE RGYAL BA'I DGONGS PAR BSGRUB PA LA, PHUNG SOGS GSUNGS PA DRANG DON DU BSTAN, SKYE MED GSUNGS PA NGES DON DU BSGRUB PA'O,,
gru.wylie: de rgyal ba'i dgongs par bsgrub pa la, phung sogs gsungs pa drang don du bstan, skye med gsungs pa nges don du bsgrub pa'o
gru.english: Next is our third step from before: proving how this way of teaching is actually the true intent of the Victors. We'll proceed in two sections: (1) showing how statements about the parts to the person and so forth were actually meant to be figurative; and then (2) proving that when Lord Buddha described how nothing ever arises on its own, he was being literal.

gru.acip: PHUNG KHAMS SKYE MCHED DE KHO NAR MA GRUB KYANG STON PAS GSUNGS PA LA DGOS PA YOD DE, DE KHO NA NYID LA DRANG BA'I PHYIR TU GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: phung khams skye mched de kho nar ma grub kyang ston pas gsungs pa la dgos pa yod de, de kho na nyid la drang ba'i phyir tu gsungs pa'i phyir
gru.english: And so let's consider the parts to the person; the categories of existence; and the doors of sense. Even though they do not exist as that alone, nonetheless there was a specific purpose for the Teacher to describe them that way. And that's because he taught them as a means to leading people on to suchness.

gru.acip: PHYI MA BSGRUB PA, KHYOD 'JIG PAR 'GYUR BA RKYEN LA LTOS TE, KHYOD GNAS BYED KYI RKYEN ZAD PA DE KHYOD 'JIG PA'I RKYEN YIN PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: phyi ma bsgrub pa, khyod 'jig par 'gyur ba rkyen la ltos te, khyod gnas byed kyi rkyen zad pa de khyod 'jig pa'i rkyen yin pa'i phyir
gru.english: We can put a proof for the last of the three in the following way: It is the case that the stopping of a thing depends upon factors, Because the wearing out of the factors that serve to sustain a thing is itself the factor that leads to its stopping. Mistaken positions amount to the same thing

gru.acip: DANG PO LA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHAS BLANGS PAS GZHAN SDE LAS RANG GI RTZA BA'I GRUB MTHA' DANG 'GAL BA MED PAR THAL BA, RANG SDES KHAS LEN PA CHES MI RIGS PA DANG, DE'I 'THAD PA'O,,
gru.wylie: dang po la, rang bzhin gyis grub pa khas blangs pas gzhan sde las rang gi rtsa ba'i grub mtha' dang 'gal ba med par thal ba, rang sdes khas len pa ches mi rigs pa dang, de'i 'thad pa'o
gru.english: The presentation itself has three sections: (1) how it is that people's own most basic position in no way contradicts that of the others, given that they accept the idea that things exist through some nature of their own; (2) how it is that it would be incorrect in the extreme for our own groups to accept that idea; and (3) why this idea is itself quite correct.

gru.acip: DNGOS PO RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PAR KHAS BLANGS PA'I STOBS KYIS GZHAN SDE LA RANG DBANG GI RTZA BA'I GRUB MTHA' DANG 'GAL BA MED PAR THAL, GRANGS CAN BYE BRAG PA SOGS GZHAN SDE RNAMS DNGOS PO RTAG SOGS SU ZHEN PA'I LAM LA GNAS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dngos po rang bzhin gyis grub par khas blangs pa'i stobs kyis gzhan sde la rang dbang gi rtsa ba'i grub mtha' dang 'gal ba med par thal, grangs can bye brag pa sogs gzhan sde rnams dngos po rtag sogs su zhen pa'i lam la gnas pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider those who accept the idea that entities could exist through some nature of their own. Can't we say that-since they do accept this idea-these people in no way contradict those other, non-Buddhist groups, whose basic tenet is that things exist through some power of their own? Because aren't they, essentially, then following the path of non-Buddhist groups like the Numerists, and the Detailers, who are attracted to ideas such as saying that a functional thing could be unchanging? Something we could never accept

gru.acip: GNYIS PA LA, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA KHAS BLANGS PA LA MTHAR LTA'I GZHAN DBANG DU 'GYUR BA DANG, RANG BZHIN MED PAR SMRA BA LA DE'I DBANG DU MI 'GYUR BAR BSTAN PA'O,,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa la, rang bzhin gyis grub pa khas blangs pa la mthar lta'i gzhan dbang du 'gyur ba dang, rang bzhin med par smra ba la de'i dbang du mi 'gyur bar bstan pa'o
gru.english: And so now we have reached our second part from above-a discussion of how things are or are not under the sway of extreme views. We proceed in two parts: (1) showing how those who have accepted the idea that things could exist through some nature of their own have fallen under the power of extreme views; and (2) demonstrating that those who profess that nothing has any nature of its own do not fall under this power.

gru.acip: GANG DAG BRTEN NAS DNGOS PO RNAMS, DE NYID DU NI GRUB 'DOD PA, DE DAG LA YANG RTAG SOGS SKYON, DE DAG JI LTAR 'BYUNG MI 'GYUR,
gru.wylie: gang dag brten nas dngos po rnams, de nyid du ni grub 'dod pa, de dag la yang rtag sogs skyon, de dag ji ltar 'byung mi 'gyur
gru.english: The problems that come up With these others- Things unchanging, or the like- Don't occur with those Who hold things as dependent, As being inside suchness.

gru.acip: DNGOS POR SMRA BA'I RANG SDE RNAMS RTAG CHAD KYI MTHAR LTA'I GZHAN DBANG DU 'GYUR BAR THAL, DNGOS PO RNAMS DE KHO NA NYID DU GRUB PAR KHAS BLANGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dngos por smra ba'i rang sde rnams rtag chad kyi mthar lta'i gzhan dbang du 'gyur bar thal, dngos po rnams de kho na nyid du grub par khas blangs pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider then those of our own group who assert that functioning things exist in & of themselves. It is indeed the case that they fall under the power of the extreme views of holding either that things are never-changing; or that they have stopped altogether; Because they accept the idea that functioning things exist through some kind of essential nature of their own.

gru.acip: KHYAB PAR THAL, RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA DE PHYIS YOD NA RTAG PA DANG MED NA CHAD PAR 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: khyab par thal, rang bzhin gyis grub pa de phyis yod na rtag pa dang med na chad par 'gyur ba'i phyir
gru.english: And the reason we've given here does indeed prove our assertion, Because if something that existed through some nature of its own still existed later, then it would have to be never-changing; whereas if it did not exist later on, it could never have existed at all. How those who see nothing never fall

gru.acip: RANG BZHIN MED PAR THAL, BYA BYED {%RANG BZHIN MED PAR BYA BYED} 'THAD PAR RTOGS PA'I GANG ZAG CHOS CAN, MTHAR LTA'I DBANG DU MI 'GYUR BAR THAL, DNGOS PO YANG DAG PAR GRUB PA YANG MIN LOG PA GTAN MED KYANG MIN PAR RTOGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rang bzhin med par thal, bya byed 'thad par rtogs pa'i gang zag chos can, mthar lta'i dbang du mi 'gyur bar thal, dngos po yang dag par grub pa yang min log pa gtan med kyang min par rtogs pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider those individuals who realize that-even if things have no nature of their own-the way that everything in the world works is still perfectly alright. It certainly then is the case that they cannot fall under the power of those extreme views; Because they realize that things neither exist in any pure way on their own; and yet neither are they missing: nor are they something that cannot exist at all.

gru.acip: BDAG NYID CHEN PO 'PHAGS PA RNAMS CHOS CAN, RANG PHYOGS RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA SGRUB PA'I SGO NAS RTZOD PA MI MDZAD DE, RTEN 'BREL RANG BZHIN GYIS SKYE 'GAG MED PAR MNGON SUM DU RTOGS PA'I PHYIR{%,}
gru.wylie: bdag nyid chen po 'phags pa rnams chos can, rang phyogs rang bzhin gyis grub pa sgrub pa'i sgo nas rtsod pa mi mdzad de, rten 'brel rang bzhin gyis skye 'gag med par mngon sum du rtogs pa'i phyir
gru.english: Let's consider those great beings-those realized beings. They no longer engage in dispute over what they believe to be true, in a way in which those beliefs exist through some nature of their own; Because they have realized, directly, the way that nothing which occurs in dependence could ever start or stop through any nature of its own.

gru.acip: PHYI MA GNYIS LA, GZHAN PHYOGS BKAG PA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA MED DE, RANG PHYOGS BSGRUB PA RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: phyi ma gnyis la, gzhan phyogs bkag pa rang bzhin gyis grub pa med de, rang phyogs bsgrub pa rang bzhin gyis ma grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: And what the last two lines [in the Tibetan, the last four in the English] are saying is- Let's consider the exercise of disproving the positions that others have taken. It cannot exist through any nature of its own; Because the exercise of proving our own positions cannot exist through any nature of its own. How we disengage, according to our focus

gru.acip: ,PHAN BDE'I 'BYUNG GNAS RGYAL BSTAN YONGS 'DU'I LJON, ,RAB RGYAS 'GRO KUN THAR MCHOG 'BRAS BZANG LA, ,SPYOD PHYIR BKRA SHIS LHUN GRUB CHOS GRVA CHER, ,CHOS SBYIN 'DZAD MED DAL 'GRO'I RGYUN 'DI SPEL,,
gru.wylie: phan bde'i 'byung gnas rgyal bstan yongs 'du'i ljon, ,rab rgyas 'gro kun thar mchog 'bras bzang la, ,spyod phyir bkra shis lhun grub chos grva cher, ,chos sbyin 'dzad med dal 'gro'i rgyun 'di spel
gru.english: This book has been printed At the great monastery Of Tashi Hlunpo, So that the orchard garden- The teachings of the Victors, Source of all help & happiness- Might flourish, and every being Come to take their fill Of the finest fruits that grow there: That highest liberation; We pray That the river flow Of this gift of the Dharma Might forever swell, Unending.

gru.acip: ,GANG DAG BRTEN NAS DNGOS PO RNAMS, ,DE NYID DU NI GRUB 'DOD PA, ,DE DAG LA YANG RTAGS LCOGS SKYON, ,DE DAG JI LTAR 'BYUNG MI 'GYUR,
gru.wylie: gang dag brten nas dngos po rnams, ,de nyid du ni grub 'dod pa, ,de dag la yang rtags lcogs skyon, ,de dag ji ltar 'byung mi 'gyur
gru.english: The problems that come up With these others- Things unchanging, or the like- Don't occur with those Who hold things as dependent, As being inside suchness.

gru.acip: ,RIGS PA DRUG CU PA'I TSIG LE'UR BYAS PA ZHES BYA BA SLOB DPON 'PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYI ZHAL SNGA NAS MDZAD PA RDZOGS SO,,
gru.wylie: rigs pa drug cu pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa zhes bya ba slob dpon 'phags pa klu sgrub kyi zhal snga nas mdzad pa rdzogs so
gru.english: This concludes The Sixty Verses on Reasoning, Set in Verse, which was composed by that holy master, the Realized One, Nagarjuna.

gru.acip: 'JIG RTEN PA'I CHOS DANG CHOS MTSUNGS PAR MI RIGS PA'I PHYIR ZHES BYA BA NI 'JIG RTEN PA'I CHOS RNAMS NI 'JIG RTEN PA'I RJES SU 'BRANGS NAS GRUB PA YIN GYI, MI RTAG PA NYID DANG, STONG PA NYID DANG, BDAG MED PA NYID DANG LA SOGS PA NI 'JIG RTEN PA NYID LAS GRUB PA MA YIN NO,,
gru.wylie: 'jig rten pa'i chos dang chos mtshungs par mi rigs pa'i phyir zhes bya ba ni 'jig rten pa'i chos rnams ni 'jig rten pa'i rjes su 'brangs nas grub pa yin gyi, mi rtag pa nyid dang, stong pa nyid dang, bdag med pa nyid dang la sogs pa ni 'jig rten pa nyid las grub pa ma yin no
gru.english: Here is what Master Chandrakirti means when he states that "it would be illogical to say that these things which are beyond the world are equivalent to things of the world." The expression "things of the world" refers to things which are established following the way this is done in the normal world. But there are things which cannot be established using this same way of the world: things like the impermanence of things; emptiness; and the fact that things are not themselves.

gru.acip: (7) RANG LUGS MI SGRUB PAR GZHAN GYI PHYOGS 'GOG PA TZAM DU KHAS LEN MI LEN DANG,
gru.wylie: (7) rang lugs mi sgrub par gzhan gyi phyogs 'gog pa tsam du khas len mi len dang
gru.english: (7) Do they or do they not accept the idea of simply refuting an opponent's position, without establishing ones own?

gru.acip: DANG PO GRUB STE, SNGA RGOL LA LTOS NA YANG DGOS PA MED, PHYI RGOL LA LTOS NAS KYANG DGOS PA MED, 'JIG RTEN PA LA LTOS NAS KYANG DGOS PA MED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dang po grub ste, snga rgol la ltos na yang dgos pa med, phyi rgol la ltos nas kyang dgos pa med, 'jig rten pa la ltos nas kyang dgos pa med pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that there is no need to apply the phrase "in an ultimate sense" to the quality we're trying to prove. And yet there is no need, Because, first of all, there is no need for it relative to the person presenting the argument. Neither is there any need relative to the person to whom the argument is being presented. And finally, even in terms of the everyday world, there is no need.

gru.acip: DANG PO GRUB STE, SNGA RGOL DBU MA PAS BDAG SKYE KUN RDZOB TU YANG KHAS MA BLANGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: dang po grub ste, snga rgol dbu ma pas bdag skye kun rdzob tu yang khas ma blangs pa'i phyir
gru.english: I disagree that-relative to the person presenting the argument-there is no need to add the expression "in an ultimate sense." And yet there is no need, Because where the person presenting the argument is a member of the Middle Way School, the idea of something growing from itself would never be accepted, even if we were just speaking of it happening in a deceptive way, and not an ultimate way.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA GRUB STE, BDEN PA GNYIS LAS NYAMS PA'I MU STEGS NI BDEN PA GNYIS CHAR 'GOG PAR RIGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa grub ste, bden pa gnyis las nyams pa'i mu stegs ni bden pa gnyis char 'gog par rigs pa'i phyir
gru.english: Well then I disagree to the second part of your reason. I disagree that-relative to the person to whom the argument is being presented-there is no need to add the expression "in an ultimate sense." And yet even in this second context there is no need for it; Because in a case where the opponent is a follower of a non-Buddhist school and has failed even to grasp the concept of two realities-deceptive & ultimate-it is appropriate to make our refutation from the point of view of both of those realities at once.

gru.acip: GSUM PA GRUB STE, 'JIG RTEN PAS NI RGYU LAS 'BRAS BU 'BYUNG BA TZAM ZHIG 'DOD KYI, BDAG DANG GZHAN GANG LAS SKYE ZHES MI DPYOD PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gsum pa grub ste, 'jig rten pas ni rgyu las 'bras bu 'byung ba tsam zhig 'dod kyi, bdag dang gzhan gang las skye zhes mi dpyod pa'i phyir
gru.english: Then I disagree to the third part of your reason. I disagree that-even in terms of the everyday world-there is no need to add the expression "in an ultimate sense." And yet there is no need to add "in an ultimate sense" even in this third context; Because people in the everyday world simply accept a scenario where results come from causes; they don't dig deeper into it, to see whether those results came from causes that were the results themselves, or from causes that were something other than those results.

gru.acip: RTZA RTAGS GNYIS PA GRUB STE, DON DAM PA'I KHYAD PAR CHOS CAN LA SBYOR NA, SNGA RGOL LA LTOS TE CHOS CAN MA GRUB PA'I SKYON DU 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: rtsa rtags gnyis pa grub ste, don dam pa'i khyad par chos can la sbyor na, snga rgol la ltos te chos can ma grub pa'i skyon du 'gyur ba'i phyir
gru.english: Well then, I disagree with the reason you've given in the second case above; that is, I disagree that-in a case where the opponent is a follower of a non-Buddhist school and has failed even to grasp the concept of two realities, deceptive & ultimate-then it is appropriate to make our refutation from the point of view of both of those realities at once. And yet this second reason we've given is correct; Because if you do decide to apply the qualification "in an ultimate sense" to the subject under consideration here, you will incur the fault that the subject under consideration will no longer be valid, with respect to the opponent.

gru.acip: DE YANG MI RIGS TE, DE SKAD DU MA SMRAS PA'I PHYIR DANG, SMRAS NA'ANG PHYI RGOL LA CHOS CAN MA GRUB PA'I SKYON DU 'GYUR BA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: de yang mi rigs te, de skad du ma smras pa'i phyir dang, smras na'ang phyi rgol la chos can ma grub pa'i skyon du 'gyur ba'i phyir te
gru.english: But you are mistaken in saying this, since nobody here has spoken of the eye or such in this way. And even if they had, you would still incur that fault that the subject under consideration would be invalid for the opponent.

gru.acip: LEGS LDAN NA RE, DPER NA SANGS RGYAS PAS BYE BRAG PA LA SGRA MI RTAG PAR SGRUB PA NA, 'BYUNG 'GYUR GYI SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA BYE BRAG BA {%PA} LA MI 'GRUB, NAM MKHA'I YON TAN GYI SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA SANGS RGYAS PA LA MI 'GRUB PO,,
gru.wylie: legs ldan na re, dper na sangs rgyas pas bye brag pa la sgra mi rtag par sgrub pa na, 'byung 'gyur gyi sgra chos can du bzung na bye brag ba la mi 'grub, nam mkha'i yon tan gyi sgra chos can du bzung na sangs rgyas pa la mi 'grub po
gru.english: Master Bhavaviveka would make the following claim: It's similar, for example, to the case where someone from a Buddhist school is proving, to a member of the Detailer school, that sound is impermanent. If they take, as the subject under consideration, sound as a product of the elements, then this subject will not be acceptable to the Detailer. If they take as this subject sound as a quality of space, then it will not be acceptable to the Buddhist.

gru.acip: DE BZHIN DU BYE BRAG PAS GSAL BYED PA LA SGRA MI RTAG PAR DAM 'CHA' BA NA, BYAS BA'I SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA GSAL BYED BA {%PA} LA MI 'GRUB, SNGAR YOD RKYEN GYIS GSAL BA'I SGRA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA BYE BRAG BA {%PA} LA MI 'GRUB BO,,
gru.wylie: de bzhin du bye brag pas gsal byed pa la sgra mi rtag par dam 'cha' ba na, byas ba'i sgra chos can du bzung na gsal byed ba la mi 'grub, sngar yod rkyen gyis gsal ba'i sgra chos can du bzung na bye brag ba la mi 'grub bo
gru.english: And let's consider a similar case, where a Detailer is asserting to one of the Manifestors that sound is impermanent. If they consider sound as something made, then the subject under consideration will not be valid to the Manifestor. But if they consider sound from the point of view of something which is already present in the cause, and then later becomes manifest, then this subject won't be valid for the Detailer.

gru.acip: DE BZHIN DU SANGS RGYAS PAS BYE BRAG PA LA SGRA MI RTAG PAR SGRUB PA NA, 'JIG PA PHYIS 'BYUNG GI RGYU DON GZHAN LA MI LTOS PA'I MI RTAG PA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA BYE BRAG PA LA MI 'GRUB, DE LA LTOS PA'I MI RTAG PA CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA SANGS RGYAS PA LA MI 'GRUB BO,
gru.wylie: de bzhin du sangs rgyas pas bye brag pa la sgra mi rtag par sgrub pa na, 'jig pa phyis 'byung gi rgyu don gzhan la mi ltos pa'i mi rtag pa chos can du bzung na bye brag pa la mi 'grub, de la ltos pa'i mi rtag pa chos can du bzung na sangs rgyas pa la mi 'grub bo
gru.english: For yet another case, suppose a Buddhist is undertaking to prove to a Detailer that sound is impermanent. If they take, as part of the subject under their consideration, a kind of impermanence where the later destruction of the sound depends on no separate, later factor, then this subject will not be acceptable to the Detailer. And yet if they take, as part of this subject, a kind of impermanence where that later destruction does depend on a separate, later factor, then the subject under consideration will be unacceptable to the Buddhist.

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR RGOL BA SO SO'I 'DOD PA THUN MONG MA YIN PAS KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PAR, SNGA RGOL PHYI RGOL GNYIS KA LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I SPYI TZAM ZHIG CHOS DANG CHOS CAN DANG DPER BZUNG DGOS SO,,
gru.wylie: de'i phyir rgol ba so so'i 'dod pa thun mong ma yin pas khyad par du ma byas par, snga rgol phyi rgol gnyis ka la mthun snang du grub pa'i spyi tsam zhig chos dang chos can dang dper bzung dgos so
gru.english: We can conclude then that we must select-as the quality we are attempting to prove; and as our subject under consideration; and as our parallel example-a general form of things which appears the same way to both the proponent and the opponent in an argument; we should never qualify any of these in a way which is unique to the beliefs of either debater.

gru.acip: DE BZHIN DU DBU MA PAS MIG SOGS BDAG DANG GZHAN LAS SKYE BA MED PAR GRANGS CAN PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA LA SGRUB PA NA,
gru.wylie: de bzhin du dbu ma pas mig sogs bdag dang gzhan las skye ba med par grangs can pa dang dngos smra ba la sgrub pa na
gru.english: Still another example is offered when a member of the Middle Way School seeks to prove, to either a Numerist or a Functionalist, that things like the sense power of the eye arise neither from themselves, nor from other things.

gru.acip: BDEN PAR GRUB PA'I MIG SOGS CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA DBU MA PA LA MI 'GRUB, BRDZUN PAR GRUB PA'I MIG SOGS CHOS CAN DU BZUNG NA DNGOS SMRA BA LA MI 'GRUB PAS NA,
gru.wylie: bden par grub pa'i mig sogs chos can du bzung na dbu ma pa la mi 'grub, brdzun par grub pa'i mig sogs chos can du bzung na dngos smra ba la mi 'grub pas na
gru.english: If they take, as their subject under consideration, an eye or other sense power which exists in truth, then the subject would not be valid for the follower of the Middle Way. And yet if they took as their subject an eye or such which existed in a deceptive way, it would not be valid for the Functionalist.

gru.acip: BDEN BRDZUN GANG GIS KYANG KHYAD PAR DU MA BYAS PAR DBU MA PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA GNYIS KA LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I MIG SOGS TZAM PO CHOS CAN DU BZUNG DGOS TE,
gru.wylie: bden brdzun gang gis kyang khyad par du ma byas par dbu ma pa dang dngos smra ba gnyis ka la mthun snang du grub pa'i mig sogs tsam po chos can du bzung dgos te
gru.english: As such, they should take-as the subject of their debate-the simple eye, or whatever, itself: the one which appears in the same way to both the proponent of the Middle Way and to the Functionalist; without specifying whether they are talking about an eye which exists either in truth or in a deceptive manner.

gru.acip: DBU MA PA DANG DNGOS SMRA BA GNYIS KYIS KHYAD PAR GYI CHOS DPYOD PA'I GZHI YIN PAS GNYIS KA'I MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB DGOS PA'I PHYIR, ZHES ZER RO,,
gru.wylie: dbu ma pa dang dngos smra ba gnyis kyis khyad par gyi chos dpyod pa'i gzhi yin pas gnyis ka'i mthun snang du grub dgos pa'i phyir, zhes zer ro
gru.english: This then would be correct; for what we need here is a single object which both the follower of the Middle Way and the Functionalist can examine, to see whether or not it possesses a specific characteristic: we need a subject under consideration which appears the same to both parties.

gru.acip: MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I DON YANG PHYI RGOL LA TSAD MA JI LTA BA ZHIG GIS GRUB PA'I TSAD MA DE 'DRA BA ZHIG GIS SNGA RGOL LA YANG GRUB BA'O,,
gru.wylie: mthun snang du grub pa'i don yang phyi rgol la tshad ma ji lta ba zhig gis grub pa'i tshad ma de 'dra ba zhig gis snga rgol la yang grub ba'o
gru.english: Now what does it mean when we say that "the object must appear the same to the two parties"? It means that the perception of the object which is considered accurate by the opponent must also be accepted as accurate by the proponent. Why Master Bhavaviveka's points on the subject under consideration are incorrect

gru.acip: DANG PO NI, SKABS 'DIR SNGA RGOL PHYI RGOL GNYIS KA'I MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I CHOS CAN BZHAG TU MI RUNG STE,
gru.wylie: dang po ni, skabs 'dir snga rgol phyi rgol gnyis ka'i mthun snang du grub pa'i chos can bzhag tu mi rung ste
gru.english: Here is the first, in classic debate form: It is, in the current context, incorrect to posit a subject under consideration which could appear in the same way to both the proponent and the opponent.

gru.acip: KHYAB STE, SNGA RGOL PHYI RGOL GNYIS KA LA MTHUN SNANG BA YIN NA, PHYI RGOL GYI LUGS LA TSAD MA JI LTA BU ZHIG GIS GRUB PA'I TSAD MA DE 'DRA BA ZHIG GIS SNGA RGOL GYI LUGS LA YANG GRUB DGOS PA'I PHYIR TE, MTHUN SNANG BA'I DON DE LTAR LAM RIM LAS GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR RO, ,
gru.wylie: khyab ste, snga rgol phyi rgol gnyis ka la mthun snang ba yin na, phyi rgol gyi lugs la tshad ma ji lta bu zhig gis grub pa'i tshad ma de 'dra ba zhig gis snga rgol gyi lugs la yang grub dgos pa'i phyir te, mthun snang ba'i don de ltar lam rim las gsungs pa'i phyir ro,
gru.english: That doesn't prove that it would be incorrect, in the current context, to posit a subject under consideration which could appear in the same way to both the proponent & the opponent. And yet it does. If the subject under consideration here did appear in the same way to both the proponent & the opponent, then the version of accurate perception accepted in the system of the opponent as one with which we could establish things would also have to be accepted as the same kind of accurate perception in the system of the proponent. And that certainly is the case, because this is how the literature on the steps of the path to enlightenment describes what it is for an object to appear the same way to both parties.

gru.acip: RTAGS PHYI MA GRUB STE, DNGOS SMRA BA'I LUGS LA, DON DAM PA'I KHYAD PAR DOR BA'I MIG SOGS SPYI TZAM BLOS GZUNG DU MI RUNG BA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: rtags phyi ma grub ste, dngos smra ba'i lugs la, don dam pa'i khyad par dor ba'i mig sogs spyi tsam blos gzung du mi rung ba'i phyir te
gru.english: And the latter reason we have given here holds true, because it would not be correct-in the Functionalist system-to take into consideration a general form of the eye or the rest, without regard to the distinction of existing in an ultimate way.

gru.acip: GZHAN YANG RGOL BA GNYIS KA'I LUGS LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I CHOS CAN MED DE, RGOL BA GNYIS KA'I LUGS LA MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I CHOS CAN SGRUB BYED KYI TSAD MA MED PA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: gzhan yang rgol ba gnyis ka'i lugs la mthun snang du grub pa'i chos can med de, rgol ba gnyis ka'i lugs la mthun snang du grub pa'i chos can sgrub byed kyi tshad ma med pa'i phyir te
gru.english: Beyond all this, we can say that there can be no subject under consideration which appears, according to the systems of the two debaters, in the same way to both parties.

gru.acip: CHOS CAN SGRUB BYED TSAD MA DE SNGA RGOL DBU MA BAS {%PAS} YUL GYI RANG BZHIN LA 'KHRUL BA'I TSAD MAR 'DOD, PHYI RGOL DNGOS SMRA BAS DE LA MA 'KHRUL BA'I TSAD MAR 'DOD PA'I PHYIR RO,,
gru.wylie: chos can sgrub byed tshad ma de snga rgol dbu ma bas yul gyi rang bzhin la 'khrul ba'i tshad mar 'dod, phyi rgol dngos smra bas de la ma 'khrul ba'i tshad mar 'dod pa'i phyir ro
gru.english: And that's because the accurate perception which establishes the existence of the subject under consideration is-according to the proponent, the follower of the Middle Way-an accurate perception which is mistaken about the nature of its object; whereas the opponent, the Functionalist, would assert that it is an accurate perception which is unmistaken about this nature.

gru.acip: DE NI DE LTAR MA YIN TE, 'DI LTAR GANG GI TSE 'DIR SKYE BA BKAG BA BSGRUB PAR BYA BA'I CHOS SU 'DOD PA DE'I TSE, DE KHO NAR DE'I RTEN CHOS CAN PHYIN CI LOG TZAM GYIS BDAG GI NGO BO RNYED PA NI NYAMS PAR GYUR PAR 'DIS RANG NYID KYIS KHAS BLANGS PA NYID DO,,
gru.wylie: de ni de ltar ma yin te, 'di ltar gang gi tshe 'dir skye ba bkag ba bsgrub par bya ba'i chos su 'dod pa de'i tshe, de kho nar de'i rten chos can phyin ci log tsam gyis bdag gi ngo bo rnyed pa ni nyams par gyur par 'dis rang nyid kyis khas blangs pa nyid do
gru.english: But that's not the way it is; and here's why. Suppose we have a case where we've accepted-as the quality we are trying to prove about a particular subject that we have under consideration-the absence of the starting of a thing. We entirely accept that, with nothing more than that, the tendency of a state of mind which is nothing but mistaken to see some self-nature in the subject under consideration-that which acts as the basis of this quality-is undermined.

gru.acip: DE NYID KYI PHYIR SLOB DPON GYI ZHAL SNGA NAS KYANG, ,GAL TE MNGON SUM LA SOGS PA'I, ,DON GYIS 'GA' ZHIG DMIGS NA NI, ,SGRUB PAR MA BZLOG PAR BYA NA DE, ,MED PHYIR NGA LA KLAN KA MED, ,CES GSUNGS SO,,]
gru.wylie: de nyid kyi phyir slob dpon gyi zhal snga nas kyang, ,gal te mngon sum la sogs pa'i, ,don gyis 'ga' zhig dmigs na ni, ,sgrub par ma bzlog par bya na de, ,med phyir nga la klan ka med, ,ces gsungs so,,]
gru.english: And this is why the Master himself has said, I have no debate with you, Whether you seek to prove Or disprove that these things Could be seen, in & of themselves, By a perception that was direct, Or any other kind.

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR GZHI MA GRUB PA'I PHYOGS KYI SKYON DANG GZHI MA GRUB PA'I GTAN TSIGS KYI SKYON LDOG PA MED PAS 'DI LAN MA YIN PA NYID DO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA'I
gru.wylie: de'i phyir gzhi ma grub pa'i phyogs kyi skyon dang gzhi ma grub pa'i gtan tshigs kyi skyon ldog pa med pas 'di lan ma yin pa nyid do, ,zhes gsungs pa'i
gru.english: As such, your proposed solution is no solution at all-for you cannot escape the defect of your subject here where it simply cannot exist; and neither then can you escape the same defect with your syllogism itself.

gru.acip: MIG SOGS KYI RANG MTSAN SNANG BA LA LTOS TE MA 'KHRUL BA'I TSAD MAS NI MIG SOGS DON DAM PAR YOD PAR 'JAL DGOS KYI DON DAM PA'I KHYAD PAR DOR BA'I MIG SOGS TZAM PO 'JAL MI RUNG BA'I PHYIR, RTAGS SNGA MA LEGS LDAN RANG GI KHAS BLANGS KYIS GRUB STE,
gru.wylie: mig sogs kyi rang mtshan snang ba la ltos te ma 'khrul ba'i tshad mas ni mig sogs don dam par yod par 'jal dgos kyi don dam pa'i khyad par dor ba'i mig sogs tsam po 'jal mi rung ba'i phyir, rtags snga ma legs ldan rang gi khas blangs kyis grub ste
gru.english: Relative to the appearance of the actual expression of the eye or such, an accurate perception which was not mistaken would have to be considering an eye or such as something that existed in an ultimate sense; but it would be wrong to say that it was considering just the general form of the eye and the like, without regard to the distinction of it being ultimate. As such, the first part of the reason given here is validated by Master Bhavaviveka's own position.

gru.acip: GNYIS PA GRUB STE, DE NYID LAS, DE 'DRA BA'I TSAD MAS RNYED PA'I DON YIN NA SHES BYA PHYIN CI LOG YIN PAR 'GAL BAS RTAGS PHYI MA 'GRUB BO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: gnyis pa grub ste, de nyid las, de 'dra ba'i tshad mas rnyed pa'i don yin na shes bya phyin ci log yin par 'gal bas rtags phyi ma 'grub bo, ,zhes gsungs pa'i phyir
gru.english: The second part of the reason also holds true; for the same work states- The latter part of the reason also holds true, for it would be a contradiction to say that if something were the object that this type of accurate perception perceives, then it would at the same time be something perceived in a mistaken way.

gru.acip: DES NA RGOL BA GNYIS KAR MTHUN SNANG DU GRUB PA'I CHOS CAN MED PAS RANG RGYUD KYI SBYOR BA'I CHOS CAN MA GRUB BA'I SKYON LDOG TU MED DO,,
gru.wylie: des na rgol ba gnyis kar mthun snang du grub pa'i chos can med pas rang rgyud kyi sbyor ba'i chos can ma grub ba'i skyon ldog tu med do
gru.english: Given all this, we can say that-because there is no subject under consideration which appears in the same way to both debaters-there is an irrefutable problem with the idea of an independently effective logical statement, that the object under consideration cannot be valid. Should we add "ultimately"? Here is further commentary on the same subject by Kedrup Je Gelek Pel Sangpo (1385-1438), who is considered one of the two greatest disciples of Je Tsongkapa (the other being our author, Gyaltsab Je, himself). In his classic work Interlude on Emptiness, Kedrup Je offers another possibility of how the logical statement being discussed could have been put forth by Master Bhavaviveka, and then explains a refutation of it by Master Chandrakirti.

gru.acip: DE'I PHYIR YANG THAL RANG LA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB BA THA SNYAD DU'ANG 'DOD MI 'DOD KYI KHYAD PAR YOD PAR BLA {%BLO} MIG PHRAG DOG GI DUG CHUS MA BSLANG {%BSLAD} PA DAG GIS GSAL BAR RTOGS PAR 'GYUR RO,,
gru.wylie: de'i phyir yang thal rang la rang bzhin gyis grub ba tha snyad du'ang 'dod mi 'dod kyi khyad par yod par bla mig phrag dog gi dug chus ma bslang pa dag gis gsal bar rtogs par 'gyur ro
gru.english: As such, there is a vast difference between the Consequence and Independent groups, about whether-even in a nominal sense-things can exist through some nature of their own. This is something that thinkers with minds whose eyes have never been infected by the venom of jealousy can easily come to realize. A Mixed-Nut interlude As we've seen, the question of whether we need to add the phrase "in an ultimate sense" to Arya Nagarjuna's famous denial that things could grow from something else has been hotly debated for centuries. As we were translating this section, a member of our Mixed Nuts Translation Team at the Sedona College of International Management made an observation so insightful that we thought we would add it here; it may help our readers immensely in "cracking" this difficult concept. Translator Bets Greer observed: The reason that Master Bhavaviveka wants to add the qualification "in an ultimate sense" to Nagarjuna's sentence "Things don't grow from something else" is that he hopes the listener will realize that we're talking about things growing without the participation of karmic seeds opening up in our mind to make us see them grow. But what Master B doesn't realize is that a person who doesn't have the seeds to understand that already won't have the seeds to understand the clarification either! Kedrup Tenpa Dargye on primary & ancillary distinctions By the time that Kedrup Tenpa Dargye and his contemporaries are writing textbooks for the monasteries founded a century before them by Je Tsongkapa and Gyaltsab Je and their generation, the following list of "primary" and "ancillary" distinctions has developed.

gru.acip: GRUB MTHA' 'OG MA RNAMS DANG THUN MONG MA YIN PA'I KHYAD CHOS KYI GTZO BO LA DU MA YOD DE, RTZA BA'I DAM BCA' BRGYAD, 'PHROS PA YAN LAG LTA BU'I DAM BCA' DANG BCAS PA YOD PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: grub mtha' 'og ma rnams dang thun mong ma yin pa'i khyad chos kyi gtso bo la du ma yod de, rtsa ba'i dam bca' brgyad, 'phros pa yan lag lta bu'i dam bca' dang bcas pa yod pa'i phyir
gru.english: There are many principal distinctions that separate this school [the Consequence group of the Middle Way] from the lower systems. These can be presented in terms of eight primary positions, and then ancillary positions that branch off from them. The eight primary distinctions which set the Consequence Group apart

gru.acip: DANG PO LA BRGYAD YOD DE, RANG BZHIN GYIS MA GRUB PA GZHIR BYAS PA'I SGO NAS, GZHIR BYAS PA
gru.wylie: dang po la brgyad yod de, rang bzhin gyis ma grub pa gzhir byas pa'i sgo nas, gzhir byas pa
gru.english: Here is the first group, of eight; please keep in mind that-in the end-they all trace their roots to the idea that nothing exists through any nature of its own.

gru.acip: ZHIG PA DNGOS POR YOD PA DANG BCAS PA'I SGRUB PA'I DAM BCA' BZHI DANG,
gru.wylie: zhig pa dngos por yod pa dang bcas pa'i sgrub pa'i dam bca' bzhi dang
gru.english: (4) The process of an object ending is a functioning thing.

gru.acip: GZHI GRUB NA LKOG GYUR DANG, MNGON GYUR GNYIS KA YIN DGOS PA DANG,
gru.wylie: gzhi grub na lkog gyur dang, mngon gyur gnyis ka yin dgos pa dang
gru.english: (11) If something exists, it must exist both on the level of something which is beyond normal perception, and something which is obvious to normal perception.

gru.acip: RTZA BA'I DAM BCA' BRGYAD PO KHAS LEN PA DE, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS MA GRUB PA KHAS LEN PA LA THUG PA YIN TE,
gru.wylie: rtsa ba'i dam bca' brgyad po khas len pa de, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis ma grub pa khas len pa la thug pa yin te
gru.english: In conclusion, we can say that whether or not you accept the eight primary positions listed here all comes down to whether or not you accept the idea that nothing can exist in & of itself. Debunking independently effective reasons Crucial to grasping the unique differences between the Consequence and Independent groups within the Middle Way School is a clear understanding of the seventh primary position in the list of the differences between the two schools found above: the concept of an "independently effective" reason, from which in fact the latter school takes its name. We begin with a very helpful piece from Kedrup Tenpa Dargye that can help us get there; it's excerpted from another of his textbooks: A Dialectic Analysis of the Middle Way.

gru.acip: 'DOD NA, SLOB DPON GYIS RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS BZHED PAR THAL, RANG NGOS NAS GRUB PA'I RTAGS YANG DAG BZHED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: 'dod na, slob dpon gyis rang rgyud kyi gtan tshigs bzhed par thal, rang ngos nas grub pa'i rtags yang dag bzhed pa'i phyir
gru.english: Well then, I agree: These two masters do deny those two concepts, and accept the third. Suppose you do agree. So Master Haribhadra accepts the idea of a logical statement with components that have some inherent power to prove something, right? Why do you say that? Because he accepts the idea of a good reason which exists from its own side!

gru.acip: DER THAL, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA'I GTAN TSIGS YANG DAG BZHED PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: der thal, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa'i gtan tshigs yang dag bzhed pa'i phyir
gru.english: No he wouldn't accept the idea of a good reason which exists from its own side. But of course he would, because he would accept the idea of a good reason which existed in & of itself.

gru.acip: DER THAL, RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA BZHED PA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: der thal, rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa bzhed pa'i phyir te
gru.english: No he wouldn't accept the idea of a good reason which existed in & of itself! And yet he would, because he accepts the idea that there are things which exist in & of themselves!

gru.acip: DON DAM PAR RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA ZHES DGAG BYA LA DON DAM GYI KHYAD PAR 'GREL CHUNG NGU YANG YANG SMOS PA'I PHYIR DANG,
gru.wylie: don dam par rang gi mtshan nyid kyis grub pa zhes dgag bya la don dam gyi khyad par 'grel chung ngu yang yang smos pa'i phyir dang
gru.english: And that's true because, in his briefer commentary, he feels that he has to add the word "ultimately" to his description of what it is we deny: he repeatedly uses the phrase, "something that could exist ultimately from its own side."

gru.acip: YANG DAG KUN RDZOB BZHED PAS KYANG GRUB PA'I PHYIR,
gru.wylie: yang dag kun rdzob bzhed pas kyang grub pa'i phyir
gru.english: This point is also made because he accepts the idea that there could exist a "correct" form of the deceptive.

gru.acip: THAL 'GYUR BAS THAL 'GYUR TZAM GYI {%GYIS} DGAG BYA BDEN GRUB KHEGS PA DANG, BDAG MED DU SGRUB NUS PAR 'DOD,
gru.wylie: thal 'gyur bas thal 'gyur tsam gyi dgag bya bden grub khegs pa dang, bdag med du sgrub nus par 'dod
gru.english: Those who belong to the Consequence Group believe that a statement of absurdity-a statement that points out the absurd consequence of another person's position-is sufficient to disprove the idea that we deny: the idea of an object which could exist in truth. And they also believe that it is enough to prove the opposite idea: that nothing could have any nature of its own.

gru.acip: RANG RGYUD PAS DE LTAR MI NUS PAR RANG RGYUD KYI GTAN TSIGS YANG DAG GI DGAG SGRUB DE DAG BYED DGOS PAR 'DOD PA'I PHYIR TE,
gru.wylie: rang rgyud pas de ltar mi nus par rang rgyud kyi gtan tshigs yang dag gi dgag sgrub de dag byed dgos par 'dod pa'i phyir te
gru.english: Those who belong to the Independent Group, on the other hand, believe that a statement of absurdity is not sufficient for these purposes-and that, in order to deny the one idea and establish the other, we would have to use a good reason of the kind that has some independent or inherent power to prove its point.

gru.acip: SLOB DPON 'PHAGS PA KLU SGRUB KYIS MDZAD PA'I RTZA BSHES {%BA SHES} RAB LA 'GREL PA GRAGS CHE BA BRGYAD DU YOD CING, DE'I NANG NAS KYANG DGONGS PA PHYIN CI MA LOG PAR 'GREL PA {%BA} NI SLOB DPON SANGS RGYAS BSKYANGS DANG, SLOB DPON ZLA BA GRAGS PA GNYIS KYIS MDZAD PA 'DI GNYIS YIN LA,
gru.wylie: slob dpon 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis mdzad pa'i rtsa bshes rab la 'grel pa grags che ba brgyad du yod cing, de'i nang nas kyang dgongs pa phyin ci ma log par 'grel pa ni slob dpon sangs rgyas bskyangs dang, slob dpon zla ba grags pa gnyis kyis mdzad pa 'di gnyis yin la
gru.english: There are eight famous commentaries on the work of that realized being, Master Nagarjuna, entitled Wisdom: Foundational Verses. Two of these explain the master's true thought in an unerring way-these are the commentaries composed by Master Buddhapalita, and by Master Chandrakirti.

gru.acip: MTHA' GNYIS KYI SGRUB BYED DGAG
gru.wylie: mtha' gnyis kyi sgrub byed dgag
gru.english: 2. Refuting arguments in favor of the two extreme views

gru.acip: LUNG GI SGRUB BYED MI 'THAD PA,
gru.wylie: lung gi sgrub byed mi 'thad pa
gru.english: a. Demonstrating how it is incorrect to say that there are scriptural references which support these two views

gru.acip: 2) 'PHAGS PA LA BSTAN PA MA GRUB PA,
gru.wylie: 2) 'phags pa la bstan pa ma grub pa
gru.english: Showing that the arguments fail altogether when presented to a realized being

gru.acip: PHUNG SOGS GSUNGS PA DRANG DON DU BSGRUB PA,
gru.wylie: phung sogs gsungs pa drang don du bsgrub pa
gru.english: B. Establishing that statements about the parts of a person and so on were figurative

gru.acip: ,ZAB DON 'GREL PAR RGYAL BAS LUNG BSTAN PA, ,KLU SGRUB 'PHAGS PA LHA DANG ZLA BA GRAGS, ,BLO BZANG RGYAL BA GNYIS PA YAB SRAS SOGS, ,BSHES GNYEN RIM PAR BYON LA PHYAG 'TSAL LO, I make obeisance to the
gru.wylie: zab don 'grel par rgyal bas lung bstan pa, ,klu sgrub 'phags pa lha dang zla ba grags, ,blo bzang rgyal ba gnyis pa yab sras sogs, ,bshes gnyen rim par byon la phyag 'tshal lo, i Make obeiSaNce To The
gru.english: spiritual friends who one by one appeared To clarify the deepest teaching, as foretold by the Victors: Nagarjuna, and Aryadeva, and Chandrakirti too, Lobsang the Victor[10] come again—father and sons—and the rest.

gru.acip: BCOM LDAN 'DAS, BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA'I THEG PA LA YANG DAG PAR ZHUGS PAS JI LTAR GNAS PAR BGYI, JI LTAR BSGRUB PAR BGYI, JI LTAR SEMS RAB TU GZUNG BAR BGYI,
gru.wylie: bcom ldan 'das, byang chub sems dpa'i theg pa la yang dag par zhugs pas ji ltar gnas par bgyi, ji ltar bsgrub par bgyi, ji ltar sems rab tu gzung bar bgyi
gru.english: And now, o Conquering One, what of those who have entered well into the way of the bodhisattva? How shall they live? How shall they practice? How should they keep their thoughts?

gru.acip: ZHUS TSUL DNGOS NI BCOM LDAN 'DAS BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA'I THEG PA LA YANG DAG PAR ZHUGS PAS JI LTAR GNAS PAR BGYI, JI LTAR BSGRUB PAR BGYI, JI LTAR SEMS RAB TU GZUNG BAR BGYI ZHES DON TSAN GSUM ZHUS SO,
gru.wylie: zhus tshul dngos ni bcom ldan 'das byang chub sems dpa'i theg pa la yang dag par zhugs pas ji ltar gnas par bgyi, ji ltar bsgrub par bgyi, ji ltar sems rab tu gzung bar bgyi zhes don tshan gsum zhus so
gru.english: ,GNYIS PA LAN LA,This brings us to the actual way in which the sutra was requested. Subhuti asks the Conqueror, "What of those who have entered well into the way of the bodhisattva?" He phrases his question in three different sections: "How shall they live? How shall they practice? How should they keep their thoughts?" Here secondly we explain the Buddha's reply.

gru.acip: RAB 'BYOR, DE'I PHYIR NYON LA LEGS PAR RAB TU YID LA ZUNGS SHIG DANG, BYANG CHUB SEMS DPA'I THEG PA LA YANG DAG PAR ZHUGS PAS JI LTAR GNAS PAR BYA BA DANG, JI LTAR BSGRUB PAR BYA BA DANG, JI LTAR SEMS RAB DU GZUNG BAR BYA BA NGAS KHYOD LA BSHAD DO,,
gru.wylie: rab 'byor, de'i phyir nyon la legs par rab tu yid la zungs shig dang, byang chub sems dpa'i theg pa la yang dag par zhugs pas ji ltar gnas par bya ba dang, ji ltar bsgrub par bya ba dang, ji ltar sems rab du gzung bar bya ba ngas khyod la bshad do
gru.english: And since it is so, o Subhuti, listen now to what I speak, and be sure that it stays firmly in your heart, for I shall reveal to you how it is that those who have entered well into the way of the bodhisattva should live, and how they should practice, and how they should keep their thoughts.

gru.acip: DE BZHIN DU PHUNG PO 'DI LA BRTEN NAS NGA'O SNYAM DU 'BYUNG YANG, PHUNG PO'I TSOGS PA DANG RGYUN DANG CHA SHAS GANG YANG NGA'I MTSAN GZHIR 'JOG RGYU MED CING, PHUNG PO LAS NGO BO THA DAD PA GZHAN ZHIG KYANG NGA'I MTSAN GZHIR BZUNG MED PAS, NGA DE NI PHUNG PO LA BRTEN NAS BTAGS PA TZAM YIN GYI, RANG GI NGO BO NYID KYIS GRUB PA MED DO,,
gru.wylie: de bzhin du phung po 'di la brten nas nga'o snyam du 'byung yang, phung po'i tshogs pa dang rgyun dang cha shas gang yang nga'i mtshan gzhir 'jog rgyu med cing, phung po las ngo bo tha dad pa gzhan zhig kyang nga'i mtshan gzhir bzung med pas, nga de ni phung po la brten nas btags pa tsam yin gyi, rang gi ngo bo nyid kyis grub pa med do
